units.tr: To the magnificent and most generous prince of noble birth, Lord Christoph, Duke of Württemberg and Teck, Count of Mömpelgard, most revered patron of piety and learning: John Foxe, an Englishman, wishes perseverance and life immortal with the saints of God.

units.la: N EA NVNC tempora incidimus, ut mus in pi cem (Christopho re Germanici no minis non infimũ decus) ut mirificum quendã, prorsusq; supra humanam foelicitatẽ, se artificem praestet, oportet, qui monendo, aut scribendo, quicquam hodie opis adferre possit, rebus sic undiq; exulceratis. Vsque adeo uniuersæ Reipub. Christianæ partes, nescio quo pacto in ἀλυσιτελ quandam infoelicem, ac immedicabile inciderunt, sic per omnes uenas, ac abditissimã corpo
units.tr: In these times we have fallen upon such a state that anyone who hopes to bring any help today, by admonishing or by writing, must show himself a wonderfully skilled craftsman, almost beyond human good fortune, with affairs so ulcerated on every side. So far have all the parts of the Christian commonwealth fallen, somehow, into a certain unhappy and [ἀλυσιτελής] unprofitable state, and into an incurable one, with the contagion spreading through every vein and into the innermost marrow of the body.

units.la: { } Ioannes Foxus Anglus. ris medullam se spargente contagio, ut uicta iam humana medicina, solum in supremi medici misericordia sita esse res uideatur. Nam si nihil accederet præter bellicas has furias, quæ tanta humani generis pernicie, monarchas monarchis, regna regnis, cœlum denique terrę cōmiscent (ut nihil fere usquam tutum sit mortalibus) quantum uel hic calamitatis pelagus: Nūc eo ies redit, ut hic mi-nima humanæ infœlicitatis sit portio. Quippe externi bellorū tumultus, etsi pacem eripiunt, habent tamen leges suas qualescunqʒ, habent & inducias: certè hyems quamlibet hostiles pugnas dirimit, nec ultra corpora sęuiunt, quin nec uniuersos inuoluunt exitio, nonnunquam & hostis hostem compellat amicè, misfitiis etiam xeniolis ultro citroq; acceptis. Deinde utcunq; cadat Martis anceps alea, multis uel parcit misericordia, uel redimit pecunia. At hæc animorum dissidia, ac factionū pugnæ, quæ ubiqꝑ gentiũ magis ac magis efferuescũt, prꝑterquã quod pacẽ publicã uitiant, priuatam etiã libertatẽ tollunt è medio, ferías nul las concedunt diuturnitate ipsa cre- scunt, odio ac maleuolentia summos pariter ac infimos ad mutuam perni ciem exagitant. Quo enim nõ penetrarunt hodie inter Christianos par tium studia, quæ adeò neminem re- linquunt intactũ, ut simplicissimũ te rè acquiet issimũ quemqꝑ in discrimẽ potissimum pertrahant? Neqꝑ uero intra animorum mala duntaxat, sedi-tiosa hæc lues cõtinetur, quin & corporibus hominũ clades non cre-dendas inuehit, multoꝑ exitialius, quàm quæuis externa principũ bel la. Tritũ inter medicos est, plures oc cidit crapula, quàm ensis. Nunc ue rò nimis compertũ habetur, plures occidere Papismum, quàm illorum utrumqꝑ. Et tamen quasi parum ad huc factionũ sit in mundo, haud ces-sant noui factionum tituli, quotidie etiā inter nos ipsos enasci, dum Corinthiorum more, ipsi quoq; fere distracti, dicere consueimus, ego sum Apollo, ego sum Cephae. Quo fiet, ut factiunculas istas mox sequentur odia, porro deinceps calumniae, obtrectatio, proditiones. Atq; ne quod grauius tandem has scintillas excipiat incendium metuendum est, ni mature bonorū dexteritate prospiciatur. Mihi equidem, si dicendum sit, quod sentio, fontes caputq; malorum mecum perpendenti, uidetur profecto, haud facile futurum, ut turbulenti hi rerum Christianarum motus consilescat in serenitatem, ni unū quendam nimis iam diuturnū exulem, in communem uitam prius reuocemus, hoc est, si latine audire uelis, mutua fraternae charitatis coniunctionem, si Graece mauis, τῷ φιλαδελφίᾳ, aut si magis placet συνκατάθεσιν, quae tolleret, ignoscatq; mutuum. Nam quod multos hodie uidemus, editis uoluminibus, summo quidem
units.tr: John Foxe, an Englishman. So that the cure seems to lie solely in the mercy of the supreme physician, human medicine having already been defeated. For if nothing more were added besides these warlike frenzies, which with such ruin to the human race mix monarchs with monarchs, kingdoms with kingdoms, and indeed heaven with earth (so that almost nothing anywhere is safe for mortals), what a sea of calamity this alone would be. Now things have come to such a point that this is the smallest portion of human misfortune. Indeed, the tumults of foreign wars, although they take away peace, nevertheless have their own laws, of whatever kind, and they have truces. Winter, at least, puts an end to even the most hostile fighting, and they do not rage beyond the bodies, nor do they wholly engulf all in destruction; sometimes even an enemy addresses an enemy in a friendly way, gifts being exchanged on both sides in mourning and in small presents. Then, however the uncertain dice of Mars fall, mercy spares many, or money ransoms them. But these divisions of minds and battles of factions, which blaze up more and more among the nations everywhere, besides destroying public peace, also take away private liberty; they grant no holidays, they grow by their very long duration, and with hatred and ill will they drive the highest and lowest alike to mutual destruction. For where have the partisan passions among Christians not penetrated today? They leave no one untouched, so that they especially drag into danger the most simple and most peaceable man. Nor is this plague of seditions confined to the evils of minds alone; it also brings upon men's bodies slaughters not to be believed, and far more deadly than any foreign wars of princes. It is a commonplace among physicians that gluttony kills more than the sword. Now, however, it is too well known that the Papists kill more than both of these together. And yet, as if there were still too few factions in the world, new names of factions do not cease to spring up daily even among ourselves, while, after the manner of the Corinthians, we ourselves, almost divided, are accustomed to say: "I am of Apollos," "I am of Cephas." The result will be that hatreds soon follow these little factions, and then slanders, detraction, and betrayals. And unless good men foresee it in time with skill, we must fear that a greater fire will eventually catch these sparks. For my part, if I must say what I think, weighing with myself the sources and the head of the evils, it seems certain that these turbulent movements in Christian affairs will not easily settle into calm, unless we first recall to common life that one thing which has been long in exile, namely (if you wish to hear it in Latin) the mutual bond of brotherly love, or (if you prefer Greek) [φιλαδελφία] brotherly love, or if you prefer it, [συγκατάθεσις] mutual assent, which would remove wrongs and forgive one another. For that many today, publishing volumes with the greatest zeal, are busied in refuting errors, I do not deny is done by them with very great credit; but we must see that this alone is not enough.

units.la: Greek words in the line: τῷ φιλαδελφίᾳ, συνκατάθεσιν. quidem conatu, in confutandis erro ribus occupatos, præclarè quidè ab his fieri nõ nego, sed ne non id unū sit satis uidendum est. Odiosa fateor res est & detestanda, omnis opinio- num in doctrina discordia, ac peruer sitas, nec uulgaris profecto uirtus, uitiosa dogmata. & hæreses produ- ctas in lucē, docte grauiterqþ obrue- re. Alioqui quo pacto syncericas re- ligionis cōseruabitur? Verū quoniā satis non est quàm uehementer id id fiat nisi & fœliciter dextreqþ suc- cedat, (scita enim res est, & digna ar- tifice rei Ecclesiasticæ administra- tio) mihi profecto uidetur ad Chri- stianæ concordiæ unitatem nō pau lò referre magis, ut pariter cum odio uitiorum, coniungatur etiam homi- num amor. Quod etsi sapientes & moderati uiri semper faciunt : con- tra tamen à multis fieri uidemus: qui dum alteram partem nimis a- criter declinant, in diuersam fos- sam imprudentes incidunt. Vbi enim pietas non adhibetur, sed odio, prouocatione, inimicitia, contentione, res geritur, etiamsi errores hominum doctrina reuincantur, homines tamen ipsi non reuincuntur. Fit enim ubi odimus, lubenter opinione dissentimus, etsi conuicti, non uincitur tamen pertinacia.
units.tr: I admit that the discord and perversity of all opinions in doctrine is a hateful and detestable thing, and that it is surely no ordinary virtue to crush, learnedly and seriously, the vicious dogmas and heresies brought into the light. Otherwise, how will the agreement of religion be preserved? But since it is not enough how vehemently this is done, unless it also succeeds happily and skilfully (for the administration of the Church's affairs is a delicate matter and worthy of a skilled craftsman), it seems to me that for the unity of Christian concord it matters much more that the love of men be joined together with hatred of vices. Although wise and moderate men always do this, we see that many do the opposite: while they bend too sharply to one side, they unwittingly fall into the ditch on the other. For where piety is not applied, but affairs are conducted with hatred, provocation, enmity, and contention, then even if men's errors are refuted by teaching, the men themselves are not refuted. For where we hate, we gladly dissent in opinion, and even when convicted, obstinacy is not overcome.

units.la: Cötra amicitiæ, cum in ueris omnino, tum in falsis plerunq; etiam non persuasi cedimus. Neq; enim credibile est, quantus persuadendi artifex amor sit, & cum ciuili comitate coniuncta pietas. Quapropter dolendum est, has scintillas mutuæ dilectionis sic refrixisse in animis Christianorum, ubi pro φιλαδελφίᾳ adeo nunc φιλονεικίαι ac κακονθεῖαι invaluit per omnia, ut nihil fere nō luxatum, suis iam cōstet compagibus.
units.tr: On the contrary, friendship, both in true matters and, for the most part, even in false ones, brings us to yield even when we are not persuaded. For it is not easy to believe how great a persuader love is, and how piety joined with civil courtesy is. Therefore it is to be lamented that these sparks of mutual affection have so cooled in the minds of Christians, where, instead of brotherly love, contentiousness and ill will have now so prevailed in all things that almost nothing is held together in its joints any longer.

units.la: Non hic taxo omnes, quasi nusquam sint bonorum reliquiæ. Quanquam utinam non plerosque, utinam non & magnos theologos quosdam involueret querela mea, nimis fortasis sis iusta. Etsi maxime lapsus & erro res in aliena uita cospiciamus ac de- testamur,pectoris tamen erat Chri- stiani,hominem ipsum amplecti, ci- uilitatis saltem comiserari,uult etiā iuuare pietas,adesse,souere,hortari, fulcire,allicere, attrahere. Quid enim non impetret amor, & suauis quaedam consuetudo, qualem in Christo uidemus erga peccatores,in Paulo erga infirmos. Quis inquit il le,infirmatur, & non ego infirmor? Nunc uero,diuersa uoce, nescio quo- modo ἀλλὰ ἀσθενὴς ἃ Paulina hac ratione discrepamus. Quis infirma- tur,& nos non insultamus, sollicitu- do in supercilium, commiseratio in contemptum,charitas in odium uer titur,absente ubique carpimus, suspi- tione obruimus, nonnunquam & ignotos: In conuiuiis, in cōgressibus, in poculis, in colloquiis, uelut, ἀπ' ἀμαξῶν proscindimus, cynico morsu arripimus. At quotus quisque praesen tem adit,consilii s errantem instruit, beneficiis inuitat, consuetudine alle-ctat ad refipiscentiam. Quae modo si inter Christianos fierent, facilior foret, opinor, horum tumultuum ac dissidiorum exitus. Facile enim animorum coniunctionem sequeretur & opinionum consensus, aut non tam periculose erumperet. Quamobrem in tam perturbatis his Ecclesiae motibus, ut nullum praesentius est τὸ φιλαλήθης quàm mutua haec, quàm dixi, inter homines, φιλαδελφία: Ira rursus hic commonendi sumus, ut si hanc, nescio ubi tam diu exulante in Remp reducere cogitemus, Duos prius in Gracchos, perniciosissimos omnis seditionis authores, extermi-nio, quasī decemvirali proscriptio-ne e civitate eliminemus. Suspitionem uidelicet, & superbiam. Quarum altera nihil potest sentire de aliis recte, altera nihil de seipsa male. Nihil non carpit altera, quod alienum est: Nihil non admiratur altera, quod est suum. Altera dedignatur omnes, alte-
units.tr: I do not censure all here, as if there were no remnants of good men anywhere. Would that my complaint did not involve most, would that it did not involve even some great theologians, though perhaps it is too just. And although we see and condemn faults and errors most in the life of another, it belongs to a Christian heart to embrace the man himself, at least to pity him as a human being; piety also wishes to help, to be present, to cherish, to exhort, to support, to coax, to draw. For what will love not obtain, and that sweet kind of intercourse, such as we see in Christ toward sinners, and in Paul toward the weak? "Who is weak," he says, "and I am not weak?" But now, in a different voice, I know not how, we part from this Pauline principle, saying instead: "But he is weak." Who is weak, and we do not insult him? Care turns into arrogance, compassion into contempt, charity turns into hatred; in his absence we tear him apart everywhere, overwhelm him with suspicion, and sometimes even those we do not know. At banquets, in meetings, over cups, in conversations, we tear him to pieces, as from the carts, and seize him with a cynic's bite. But how few approach the one who is present, instruct the one who has gone astray in counsel, invite him with kindnesses, and attract him by friendship to repentance! If these things were done among Christians, I think the outcome of these tumults and dissensions would be easier. For agreement of minds and consensus of opinions would easily follow, or at least the breach would not be so dangerous. Therefore, in these so troubled movements of the Church, as nothing is more needed than that love of truth which is mutual brotherly love among men, as I have said, so again here we must be warned: if we think of bringing back into the commonwealth this brotherly love, which has been in exile so long, we must first banish, as by a decemviral proscription from the state, the two Gracchi, the most pernicious authors of all sedition: suspicion and pride. Of these, the one can judge nothing of others rightly, the other nothing ill of itself. The one carps at nothing that belongs to another; the other admires nothing that is not its own. The one disdains all; the other...

units.la: Suspitio & superbia, duo Graecchi Christianae societatis. altera indignatur fere omnibus &c. Atque de his quidem leuioribus factiunculis, uel haec hactenus dixisse sit satis, uel alia posthac quaeretur, plenius dicendi opportunitas. Verum inter omnia sectarum ac factionum γάγραγα (ut Comico vocabulo in re tragica utamur) nulla unquam ab omni charitate alienior, aut funestior saluti mortalium emersit, quàm unus papismus. Id quàm verum sit, utcunque opinor olim experta Germania uestra degustauit. Idem attestari poterit, & Galliae magna pars, & huic uicina Flandria, Bohemia, Scotia, nec ulla, tam procul remota Europae pars est, quae non abundè malis suis edocta idem fateatur. Sed nulla unquam illustrius id declarare poterit, quàm nostra Anglia. Quae quondam hospitium praebuit Ecclesiis, ac bonis uiris. Nunc postquam equus ille Troianus (siue Romanus potius) in urbe intromissus est, scan ditque fatalis machina muros, lacerata pene à fundamentis Respub. quan-tis damnis per τὰς Ἀρτολάτρας iltos mulctata sit, qui occulti gemitus bo-norum, quanta conscientiarum car-nificina, quæ strages Christiani san-guinis, quantum uulnus inflictum Reipub. quanta & maiora adhuc pericula, ceu ὁ τῶ πωτάλᾳ λίθῳ ἐπηρ-τήσθαι, imminere uideantur, non li-bet hic commemorare. Admoneret locus hic etiam de nobilissimi, fortis-fimiq; Ducis Suffolkcensis tristissi-mo funere, deq; illustrissima filia il-lius D. Iana in omni linguarum ac li-terarum notitia usq; ad stuporē ex-culta sœmina, aliquid dicere. Itidem de sanctissimis Episcopis ac Eccle-siastis nostris: Attamē quoniam pri-mata sunt hæc, ad publica accedamus potius. Principio, quæ bella iam diu intra Europæ fines, excitata sunt, quorum aut non origo aut aliqua sa-ne occasio, ab hac secta enata sit: Iam præter furores bellicos, Quis priua-tas cædes facile enumerare, ac lamenta bonobonorum qui passim à Martyromastigis istis exitio flammisq; expositi sunt. Quæ res si satis exponi posset oculis hominum, Non dubium quin horrendum spectaculum præberet piis quibusq; mentibus. Verum cum ea res nec facile sciri posset, nec quisquâ tere sit creditus, Non infrugiferum fore duxi, ut huius historiæ monumentum aliquod in Ecclesia Dei extaret. Syrus ille, in latina comœdia Terentianus, ubi meretricum mores, ingluviem & sordes, affabre depinxisset: Ethæc omnia, inquit, scire salus est adolescentibus. Equidem nec secus dixerim, salutiferum cum primis fore Christianis omnibus papisticæ uitæ factiosam crudelitatem, intolerabilem fastum, ac tyrannidè belluinam, ut in theatrum productam omnium hominum oculis innotescere. Quapropter cum alii non prodirent qui munus hoc capescerent melius, uti sum mihi est, clitellis his in humeros suscepti, susceptis, otii nonnihil, hoc in negotio collocare: idque duplici potissimū ratione. Primum, ut in his, qui affliɛti sunt diuinam constantiam cum summa patientia, parisq; innocentia coniunctam: In alteris rursus trucu-lentiam, ac ferociam plusquam infa-nam, cum omni impietatis genere, perspiciamus. Quorū alterū exem-plis, & consolatione nos instruere possit in tristissima temporū calamitate. Ex hac altero etiam admoneri possu-mus, quid de tota hac Papicolarum natura, ac factione sit sentiendum. Historiam uero ipsam in duas sec-tiones bipartitā, diuisimus. Quarū prior pars a Vuicleui temporibus quicquid in Religione gestū sit ad annum quingentésimum, complecti-tur. Altera a Martino Luthero exordium sumens (aspirante Christo Domino) posteriores has assiḋ Ecclesiæ persecutiones colliget, quantum sane inuestigando ac recor-dando consequi licebit. Nunc uero in
units.tr: Suspicion and pride, the two Gracchi of the Christian society; the one is indignant at almost everyone, etc. And indeed, let what has been said so far about these lesser little factions suffice, or another opportunity of speaking more fully will be sought hereafter. But among all the sects and factions, [γάγγραινα] a gangrene (to use a comic word in a tragic matter), none has ever arisen more alien to all charity, or more deadly to the salvation of mortals, than Papism alone. How true this is, your Germany, having perhaps long ago experienced it, has, I think, tasted in some measure. The same can be attested by a great part of France, and by Flanders nearby, Bohemia, Scotland, and no part of Europe so remote that it is not taught abundantly by its own evils and does not confess the same. But no country can declare this more brilliantly than our England. She once offered hospitality to the Churches and to good men. Now, since that Trojan horse (or rather Roman) has been admitted into the city, and the fatal engine has spread over the walls, and the commonwealth has been almost torn from its foundations, what losses it has suffered through those idolaters, who can say? I do not care to recount here the hidden groans of good men, the great butchery of consciences, the slaughter of Christian blood, the wound inflicted on the commonwealth, and the greater dangers still, which seem to hang over us like the stone of Tantalus. This place would also call on me to say something about the most sad death of the most noble and most brave Duke of Suffolk, and about his most illustrious daughter, Lady Jane, a woman trained in every knowledge of languages and letters to the point of astonishment, and likewise about our most holy bishops and churchmen. However, since these are first matters, let us rather proceed to public affairs. First, what wars have long been stirred up within the borders of Europe, of which neither the origin nor any plausible occasion arose from this sect? Besides the warlike furies, who could easily count the private slaughters, and the laments of good men who were everywhere exposed to ruin and flames by these scourgers of martyrs? If that matter could be set before men's eyes sufficiently, there is no doubt it would present a horrible spectacle to all pious minds. But since that matter could neither easily be known nor was hardly believed by anyone, I thought it would not be unfruitful if some monument of this history stood in the Church of God. That Syrus in the Latin comedy of Terence, when he had skilfully painted the manners of harlots, their gluttony and filth, said: "And it is good for young men to know all these things." Indeed, I would say no differently: it will be especially wholesome for all Christians that the factious cruelty, intolerable pride, and beastly tyranny of the papistical life be brought out into the theatre and made known to the eyes of all men. Therefore, since others did not come forward who might take up this office better, I, as I am, having taken up these panniers on my shoulders, have devoted to this task some of my leisure, and that for two main reasons. First, that in those who have suffered we may see divine constancy joined with the greatest patience and equal innocence; and in the others again, cruelty and a ferocity more than insane, together with every kind of impiety. Of these, the one may instruct and console us by examples in the most sad calamity of the times; from the other we may also be warned what must be thought of the whole nature and faction of these papal worshippers. Moreover, we have divided the history itself into two parts. The first part embraces whatever has been done in religion from the times of Wycliffe to the year five hundred. The second, taking its beginning from Martin Luther (with the Lord Christ breathing upon it), will gather up these later persecutions of the Church, as far as investigation and remembrance can carry it. Now indeed, in dedicating small works...

units.la: in nuncupandis opusculis, folenne esse scriptoribus solet, & ad suum quisque patronum, cui potissimum se deuinctū uidet, oculos mentemcp referat, quo pro officiis præstitis, ipsi uicissim nonnnullam grati clientis significatione remetiantur. Mihi uero cum Celsitudine tua (ter illu strissime Princeps) ut nulla hactenus officia, ita nec notitia intercessit aliqua. Verùm de singulari pietate tua, ac incomparabili Christianæ uecritatis studio, tam multa, huc aduenientes, ubicp predicari audio, tum insuper de propensa tua in Anglos nostros uoluntate, (qui procul a patria pulsi omni fere rerum subsidio desti tuimur) ita retulerunt quidam, ut si nihil aliud intercederat, uel amor ipse facile audacia subministraret, ad sublimitatem tuam, quamuis nec no tam, nec usam hactenus, accedendi.
units.tr: in dedicating small works it is customary for writers to turn their eyes and minds to whichever patron they see they are most bound to, so that in return for services rendered they may themselves repay him with some sign of a grateful client. For my part, with your Highness (most illustrious Prince), there has hitherto been no service and no acquaintance between us. But I have heard from those who come here, and wherever I go, so much spoken of your singular piety and incomparable zeal for the true Christian faith, and moreover of your favourable goodwill towards us Englishmen (who, driven far from our homeland, are left almost without any material help), that, even if nothing else had come between us, love itself would readily supply me with the boldness to approach your Excellency, although I have never before dared to approach you so closely or so familiarly.

units.la: Primùm ergo audaciæ ignoscat pietas tua, tum ut literarū hoc qualecun que studii erga te mei μνημόσυνον ne aspernetur, uehementer rogo. Quæ si à Celsitudine tua impetrari intellexero, efficies, ut in acerbo hoc exilio, non ipse modo mihi solatium aliquod, sed omnes etiam mecum nostri, maiorem de bonitate tua spem merito concipiamus. Dominus Iesus Ecclesiam suam, tecq; Ecclesię suę diu incolumem tueatur, ac fortunet in omnibus, in uitam æternam. Amen, Argentinæ 31 Augusti, Anno M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: First, then, I earnestly beg that your piety pardon my boldness, and that you not disdain this little work of mine, such as it is, as a memorial [μνημόσυνον] of my devotion to you. If I learn that your Highness grants this, you will make it so that, in this bitter exile, not only I myself but all of our countrymen with me may rightly conceive a greater hope in your kindness, and a certain consolation. May the Lord Jesus keep and bless his Church, and you, a long-lived member of his Church, in all things, unto eternal life. Amen. Strasbourg, 31 August, in the year 1554.

units.la: Celsitudini tuæ ad omne obsequium in Christo paratissimus.
units.tr: Most ready in Christ for every service to your Highness.

units.la: ETSI ANTE VVICLEVI tempora nonnullos extitisse constat qui in eadem, in qua Vuicleus noster, causa palaestraq; elaborarunt, quos continuis temporibus spiritus sanctus nunquam excitare destitit in Ecclesijs, ad traducendos quotidie inualescētes seculi errores, in qua farragine censentur in historiarum monumentis Berengarius sub Henrico 3. imperatore, an. 1051. & I. Scotus qui corporis & sanguinis ueritate auferebat Sacramento. Bruno Andegauensis, Okleus secū dus, Valdeses, Marsilius de Padua.
units.tr: Although it is established that before Wycliffe's time there were some who laboured in the same cause and contest as our Wycliffe, whom the Holy Spirit never ceased to raise up in the Churches at successive times, to refute the errors of the age as they daily grew stronger, the records of history count among this medley Berengarius under the emperor Henry III, in the year 1051, and John Scotus, who took the truth of the body and blood away from the Sacrament; Bruno of Angers; Ockleus the Second; the Waldenses; and Marsilius of Padua.

units.la: Ioannes de Gādino, Okchamus, cuiusdam eius scholae aliis: tamen cum hi uel non ita multi, uel sane ob scuri sint: nos à Vuicleuo historiae narrationem deducemus: à quo prima cœpisse exordia uidetur uniuersum hoc persecutionis incendium. Post hos igit, quos modo commemorauimus diuinis auspiciis in harena prosiliit magnus ueritatis antistes I. Vuicleuus insignis Theologus, nec minus in omni philosophiae genere exquisite uersatus. Quod nō solū ex doctissimis illius scriptis, ac diatribis, sed ex Vualdeni etiam acerrimi ipsius antagonistę cōfessione elucet, qui in epistola ad pontificē Martinū 5. se supra modū ait obstupuisse ad assertiones eius pregrandes, et ad autoritatū loca taxata cū uehementriis rationū, sic enim Vualdenus. Exijs qui rerum serie ac tempora obseruarunt, cōstat hunc effloruisse Vuiclef uū, circa annū 1371. principāte apud nos Edouardo 3. Sic etenim ex G. Caxtono in Chronicis legimus, An no, inquit, 1371. Rex Edouardus An glorum tertius in suo parlamento ad uerlabatur clero: Hæreticorū uoces libenter audiuit, cum quibusda e suo consilio: Et sinistras opiniones se- quebatur aduersus clerū: Propterea fortuna ex tunc aduersam sensit. Et mox, Anno Domini. 1372. ad Romanū inquit pontificem scripsit, ne ampliusintromittat aliquo mo- do in suo regno de beneficiorum referuationibus, et distributionibus, ut etiam episcopi sui gaudeant li- bertate pristina, & confirmentur à suis metropolitanis, ut olim retroa- ctis temporibus &c. Tantum ille. Cæterum de articulo annorum non est quod hæc curiositas magnopere nos habeat anxios. Illud modo est extra omnem ambiguitatem, in corruptissimo rerum hominumque statu, pariter ac deploratissimis religionis tenebris, in lucem hunc prodire, in quem recte id competere potest, quod de Simone quondam Oniæ filio proferebat Ecclesiasticus. Quasi stella matutina erat in medio nebulæ, et quasi luna plena in diebus suis & quasi sol refulgens effulsit in templo Dei. Hunc itaque in modum rebus desperatis perpetuo succurrit Deus, semper adiutor in opportunitate, iuxta psalmi uaticinium. Id nunquam dilucidius quam in uergente hac Ecclesiæ senecta, hoc est postremis huius mundi temporibus eminuit, in quibus tam depraua tus rerum humanarum tum maxime religionis status uidebatur, ut sicut apud medicos lethargus, nihilo secus apud theologos, res hæc omnem humanam medelam exierat. Solus Christi nomen remansit apud Christianos, at Christi uera ac efficax doctrina tam erat plerisque ignota, quam illius nomen receptum omnibus. De fide, de consolatione, de fine et usu legis, de Christi officio, de nostra impotentia, de spiritu, de peccati latitudine, de vera operum perfectione, de gratia ac gratuita Christiani hominis iustificatione & libertate, in quibus ceu cardine, summa nostrę professionis vertitur, nulla tradebatur mentio. Theologia ad paucos atqș in tra scholas redacta ad argutias delapsa est. Pro Paulo, pro Petro Aquinas ac Scotus successit in manus hominū. Mundus relicto spirituali evangelicæ philosophiæ vigore ad externas ceremonias ac humanas traditiū unculas totus obstupuit. In his omnes fere constituebantur Christianę perfectionis numeri, ex his omnis pendebat consequendæ salutis fiducia, his ita omnia tribuebantur, ut vix aliud in templis conspiciebatur, in coenobiis tractabatur, in vita agitabatur, præter umbraticas quasdam cerę monȷs cumulatas, nec unquam cumulandi finis. Nihil populus colere docebatur, nisi quod uidebat, nihil fere uidens quod non colebat. Eccle sia supra quam dici potest à Germana acapostolica degenerans institutione nomen quidem retinuit, at rem amisit, plusquam in phalaraismum collapsa, ubi Christi simplicitas ac paupertas in tyrannidem uersa est ac strepitum uitæ. Pro dotibus aposto licis ac continuis laboribus ignauia & ambitio arripuit sacerdotes. Acce debant ad hæc monachorum mille formæ ac factiones, plane omnis superstitionis seminaria. Interim in Sacramentis quanta depravatio, quam horrendi abusus irrepserunt, dum si mulachra rerum ac symbola pro rebus ipsis colere, quæque ad memoriam duntaxat sunt parata, eadem in adoratıonem conuertere cogebamur. Deniq; in religione Christiana nihil ųsquàm sincerum, nec sanum, quod non aliqua admisla uitiarat superfi tio. Tum quot laqueis, quot pedicis quotidie succrescentium ceremonia rum astringebantur ad libertatem re demptę conscientiæ, ut minimum uí deri poterat inter Christianismum & Iudaismum interesse, nisi quod Iu daeorum non paulo tolerabilior uisa est conditio. Ex fontibus nihil petebatur. Meris hominum decretis ac commentitijs ritibus, ceu naribus cir cumducebatur Christiana gens, quo uolebant pontifices, non quo uolebat Christus. Omnia erroribus ac te nebris conferta cofusaq; sunt. Nec mirum quum populus prophanus longe submotus a sacrarijs mysticæ scripturæ, tantum ea haurire satis habuit quæ a pastoribus tradebantur, nec quicquam fere tradebat ri, quod nō e Roma profectum est, cuiusque pars aliqua rendebat ad questum sui ordinis. Fides christiana nihil aliud putabatur, quam ut cuique persuadē retur, Christum aliquando passum, hoc est, ut omnes id scirent quod nec ignotu est daemonibus. Hypocrisis pro mira pietate habebatur. Adeo omnes affixi externis liturgiis ducebantur, ut vix aliud saperent vel ipsi etiam, qui absolutissimam sibi vendi cabant huius philosophiae professionem. Quod nec in plebeis solum doctoribus, sed & in summis Ecclesiae primoribus videre licuit, quorum omnis fere religio claudebatur in diebus, in cibis, in vestibus, aut rhetoricis quibusdam circumstantiis locorum, rerum, ac personarum. Hinc tot vestiendi formae, tot colorum ac cibo rum discrimina, tot locorum peregrinationes, quasi id agere Iacobus potuit Compostellę, quod no Christus posset Cantuariae, aut non idem esset Deus ubique efficax, aut nisi pedibus quaesitus inveniri haud poterat. Sic totius anni sanctimonia fere in quadragesima transferebatur. Nulla terra la terra sancta erat nisi Palestina, quā corporeis uestigijs calcauit Christus. Pro cruce Hierosolimitana, non secus ac pro unica maximaq; fidei nostræ arce pugnabatur ab omnibus. Hęc quantas turbas, quantas tragœdias ciebat apud omnes Christianæ Reip. ditiones, operæprecium fuerit relicta superiorum temporum monumeta perlegere. Perinde quasi parum constaret fides Euangelica lignea illa cruce destituta, nunc q; desti terunt præsules Romani scribendo, monendo, expostulando, principū animos euocare ad belli materiam.
units.tr: John of Gaunt, Ockham, and certain others of their school. But since these are either not so many or are indeed obscure, I shall begin the narrative of events with Wycliffe, from whom the whole fire of this persecution seems first to have taken its beginning. After those whom I have just mentioned, the great champion of truth, John Wycliffe, an outstanding theologian and no less thoroughly versed in every branch of philosophy, leapt into the arena under divine auspices. This shines forth not only from his most learned writings and disputations, but also from the confession of Walden, his most bitter opponent, who in a letter to Pope Martin V says that he was greatly astonished at Wycliffe's very weighty assertions and at his vehement arguments drawn from the passages of authority he cited. Thus Walden. Those who have observed the order and dates of events agree that Wycliffe flourished around the year 1371, when Edward III was ruling among us. For thus we read in the Chronicles of William Caxton: "In the year 1371," he says, "King Edward III of England, in his parliament, spoke to the clergy. He gladly heard the voices of heretics, together with certain men from his council, and followed wicked opinions against the clergy. For this reason fortune from then on found him adverse." And soon after: "In the year of the Lord 1372," he writes, "he wrote to the Roman pontiff that he should no longer meddle in any way in his kingdom with the reservations and distributions of benefices, so that his bishops too might rejoice in their former liberty, and be confirmed by their metropolitans, as in times past, and so on." Thus far Caxton. As for the exact year, there is no need for us to be greatly anxious over this curiosity. It is beyond all doubt only this: that in a state of things most corrupt, and among the most deplorable darkness of religion, he came forth into the light, and that which Ecclesiasticus said of Simon, son of Onias, applies to him rightly: "He was like the morning star in the midst of a cloud, and like the full moon in its days, and like the sun shining forth in the temple of God." Thus God always comes to the aid of desperate affairs, "always a helper in time of need," according to the prophecy of the psalm. This has never appeared more clearly than in this declining old age of the Church, that is, in the last times of this world, when the state of human affairs, and especially of religion, seemed so depraved that, as lethargy is among physicians, so in theology this condition had gone beyond every human remedy. The name of Christ alone remained among Christians, but the true and effective doctrine of Christ was as unknown to most as his name was received by all. Concerning faith, consolation, the end and use of the law, the office of Christ, our own powerlessness, the Spirit, the breadth of sin, the true perfection of works, and the grace and free justification and liberty of the Christian man, on which the sum of our profession turns as on a hinge, no mention was made. Theology was reduced to a few schools and sank into subtleties. In place of Paul and Peter, Aquinas and Scotus came into men's hands. The world, having abandoned the spiritual vigour of the evangelical philosophy, was wholly dazzled by external ceremonies and human traditions and trifles. In these almost everyone located the numbers of Christian perfection; on these depended all confidence of attaining salvation; to these everything was so attributed that scarcely anything else was seen in the temples, handled in the monasteries, or practised in life, except certain shadowy heaps of wax, with no end to their piling up. The people were taught to worship nothing but what they saw, and they saw hardly anything that they did not worship. The Church, degenerating beyond what can be said from its German and apostolic institution, kept the name but lost the reality, having collapsed into more than Phalaris's bull, where the simplicity and poverty of Christ were turned into tyranny and the clamour of life. Instead of the gifts of the apostles and their continual labours, idleness and ambition seized the priests. To these were added a thousand forms and factions of monks, clearly seedbeds of every superstition. Meanwhile, what great corruption crept into the sacraments, what horrible abuses, while we were compelled to worship the images of things and symbols in place of the things themselves, and to turn into objects of adoration what had been prepared only for memory. Finally, in the Christian religion nothing was anywhere sincere or sound that superstition had not corrupted by some admixture. How many snares, how many fetters of ever-growing ceremonies bound daily the conscience that had been freed by redemption, so that it could seem at least that there was little difference between Christianity and Judaism, except that the condition of the Jews appeared not a little more tolerable. Nothing was sought from the sources. By mere human decrees and invented rites the Christian people was led about by the nose, wherever the pontiffs wished, not wherever Christ wished. All things were crammed and confused with errors and darkness. Nor is it surprising, since the profane people, kept far away from the sanctuaries of mystical Scripture, thought it enough to drink only what the ministers handed down, and those ministers handed down scarcely anything that had not come from Rome, or some part of which did not redound to the profit of their own order. The Christian faith was thought to be nothing other than that each person should be persuaded that Christ had once suffered, that is, that all should know what is not unknown even to the demons. Hypocrisy was held to be remarkable piety. So completely were all bound to external liturgies that hardly anything else was savoured even by those who professed for themselves the most complete knowledge of this philosophy. This could be seen not only among the common teachers, but also among the leading men of the Church, whose whole religion was almost confined to days, foods, clothing, or certain rhetorical circumstances of places, things and persons. Hence came so many forms of vestments, so many distinctions of colours and foods, so many pilgrimages to places, as if James could do at Compostela what Christ could not do at Canterbury, or as if God were not equally effective everywhere, or could not be found unless sought on foot. Thus the holiness of the whole year was almost transferred to Lent. No land was holy except Palestine, which Christ had trod with his bodily feet. For the Jerusalem cross everyone fought as for the one greatest stronghold of our faith. How many disturbances and tragedies this stirred among all the realms of the Christian commonwealth, it would be worth while to read through the surviving records of earlier times. It is as if the Evangelical faith were so little established that it needed a wooden cross, and now the Roman prelates, by writing, admonishing and remonstrating, never cease to rouse the minds of princes to the matter of war.

units.la: Hinc Ricardi inuictissimi regis facta in Hierosolimam expeditio, qui mox eodem captus itinere, ac Cęsari deditus, uix triginta marcarum millibus redimi poterat. In eadem expeditione Fridericus Rom. Imperator augustissimæ uirtutis, in amne submersus interiit an. 1189. Quin & Philippus Gallorum rex uix sine luculentis damnis in patriam incolu-mis redijt. Tanti erat sanctæ urbis crucisq; recuperatio. Hæc una omni um oculos, omnium mentes ac devotionem tenuit. perinde ac si nihil aliud, aut nusquam esset crux Christi, nisi quæ esset Hierosolimis. Tanta huius erat tεporis superstitio, quæ nihil sapiebat, nisi quæ externa fuerant. quum longe aliis rationibus, aliis rationibus, aliis rationibus, aliis rationibus, altioribus mysteriis ingreditur religionis nostræ professio. Quid erat causæ cur Vrbanus se dolore conficeret quod Antiochia cum sancta cruce è manibus Christianorū amitteretur.
units.tr: Hence came the expedition of the most unconquered King Richard to Jerusalem. He was soon captured on the same journey and surrendered to the Emperor, and he could scarcely be ransomed for thirty thousand marks. In the same expedition Frederick, Roman Emperor of most august valour, was drowned in a river and died, in 1189. Indeed Philip, king of the French, scarcely returned home unharmed and without heavy losses. So great was the recovery of the holy city and cross. This alone held the eyes of all, the minds and devotion of all, just as if the cross of Christ existed nowhere else, or nothing else, except at Jerusalem. So great was the superstition of that time, which relished nothing except external things, whereas the profession of our religion proceeds by quite other ways, by higher mysteries. What was the reason why Urban consumed himself with grief because Antioch, with the holy cross, was lost from the hands of the Christians?

units.la: Sic enim reperimus in annalibus, quod ubi Hierosolima cū rege Guidone & cruce Domini in Sultani potestatem redigeretur, Vrbanus rei gravitate nimium ictus, curæ magnitudine occubuit, cui successit Albertus, qui Gregorius octavus dicitur, cuius instinctu receptum est à Cardinalibus, ut abiectis diuitijs et delitijs omnibus
units.tr: For thus we find in the annals that when Jerusalem, with King Guy and the cross of the Lord, was brought under the power of the Sultan, Urban, struck excessively by the gravity of the event, died of the greatness of his grief. He was succeeded by Albert, who is called Gregory VIII, at whose instigation the cardinals resolved that, with riches and all delights laid aside,

units.la: Vrbanus pontifex. Albertus papa. omnibus prædicarent crucem Christi & mendicando omnium primi ac ciperent crucem, aliosq; præcederet in terram Ierusalē. Sic enim habent historiæ uerba. Vnde haud obscure liquere potest non stupido lectori, in quantam crassitie id temporis degenerauit spiritualis doctrinæ Euangelicæ cultus. Iam in hoc ipso prima tu Rom. pontificis quanta cæcitas & caligo eadem hæc inuoluit tempora? Quasi uero ad rem ipsam magnopere faceret Petri ac Apostolorum successio. Quid refert in quo loco sedit aut non sedit Petrus? Magis id refert, ut quisq; studeat pro uirili petri imitari confessionem. Atq; hic demū mihi gnesius uidetur successor Petri, aduersus quem inferorum portæ non prævalebunt. Quod, si in euangelijs Petrus typū gerit ecclesiæ confitentis, quod omnium ferè suffragijs receptum est, quid tum dementius, priuata usurpatione ad unum id astringere, quod tanta latitudine ad tam multos pateat. At finge Petrum cathedram fixisse Romae, finge idem fecisse Antiochiae, quid hic Petri locus faceret ad remissionem peccatorum, ad interpretationem scripturæ, ad ligandi & soluendi claues? Quæ si non loci sed Spiritus Sancti sint opera ac fidei Christi anæ, nimis profecto ineptè ad Romanam sedem eadem quasi intra parietes à nobis restringuntur: nisi nusquam sit fides, nusquam spiritus energia præterquam Romæ. Quid illud retulerit, ubi Petrus inseruiebat suo Domino? Nobis id quærendum potius, qua in re Petrus suo domino approbatus sit, aut quamobrem, ut nos ad idem brabium pariter, eadem que uia, quatenus situm in nobis fuerit, enitamur. Quod si Petro singula re aliquod indultum à Christo priuilegium suspicamur, quod non idem cæteris item apostolis communicatum sit. tum fit, idcp ob priuatum aliquē hominis affectum, cuiusmodi multi in nobis dominātur affectiones, longē fallimur: Sin propter diuinam, sublimē, ac expeditam confessionē quam Petrus non solus, sed unus omnium nomine expresserat, iam non is qui in cathedram succedit Petri, illico ex primit fidem Petri, sed quisquis proxime exprimit Petri fidem, quacunque sedet cathedra, merito Petri successor habendus est, sicp successor est ut nihil tamen hinc humani splendoris ac glorie corroget: Functio est, non gradus, Ministerium non magisterium apostolatus. Quemadmodū necinter ipsos, opinor, apostolos ulla erat dignitatis, aut loci praeminentia, sed una omnes mente, eodem spiritu Domini non suum agebant negotium, sic ut qui minor inter ipsos foret, pluris haberetur apud Christum testem. Quocirca et horum successio laudem quidem apud Deum, apud mundum uero nullam dignitatem, emercebatur. Quo pacto enim ut praeclare apud Eusebium proconsuli respodet Polycarpus, cum mundanis, diuitiis, aut terreno fastigio cohaeret illorum professio, qui pro Christo omnia habet pro derelictis. At horum temporum pontifices nescio qua ambitione ecclesiasticam functionem prorsus in mundanam politiam immutarint, ut quemadmodum princeps principi, ita pontifex pontifici iure haereditario in cathedram succedat, qui terrenis opibus, & satellitio, mundano more muniatur, quique sic sibi uendicat principatum, ut ad eum unum omnis rerum potestas ac summa redeat. Caeterarum ecclesiarum nihil ualebant pastores, nisi quantum ab ipso permittebatur. Solus hic non ecclesijs, sed et regnis praesidebat omnibus. Solus terrori eratcunctis. Caeteris Christi ministris parum aut nihil tribuebatur ebatur. Ab uno pendebant ac pete-bantur omnia. Nusquam erat excommunicandi ius, nusquam relaxa di autoritas, nusquam interpretandi potestas, nisi in Romana basilica. In hac igitur tanta rerum perturbatione ac confusissimis ignorantiae tenebris, cum nulla propemodum scintilla relicta uideretur purioris doctrinae, exortus est diuinis auspiciis Vuicleus hic, in quo primum uoluit do minus mundum expergefacere plus nimio humanarum traditionum somnijs insepultum. Habetis igitur Vuicleui tempora. Nunc de confli- ctu ac concertationibus paucis acci- pite. Cum ergo Ioannes hic iam diu Oxoniae sustinuisset theologiae professionem, uidisset que ueram Christi theologiam tot pontificijs spurci- tijs, tot monachorum sectis, tot erro- rum tenebris adulteratam, diu apud se deliberans ac deplorans, occulto gemitu publicam orbis insciitiam postquam
units.tr: Urban pope. Albert pope. all should preach the cross of Christ and, going about as beggars, be the first to take up the cross and lead others into the land of Jerusalem. For so the words of the histories have it. Hence it can quite plainly be seen, by a reader who is not dull, into what coarseness the cultivation of evangelical spiritual doctrine had degenerated at that time. And indeed, in this very point, the primacy of the Roman pontiff, how great a blindness and darkness has enveloped these times! As if the succession of Peter and the Apostles mattered much to the thing itself! What does it matter in which place Peter sat or did not sit? It matters more that each man should strive, to the best of his strength, to imitate Peter's confession. And here, at last, the true successor of Peter seems to me to be the one against whom the gates of hell shall not prevail. Yet if in the Gospels Peter bears the figure of the Church confessing, which is received by almost everyone's agreement, what could be more senseless than to bind that to one man by private usurpation, when it is open with such breadth to so many? But suppose Peter had fixed his chair at Rome, suppose he had done the same at Antioch: what would that place of Peter achieve for the remission of sins, for the interpretation of Scripture, for the keys of binding and loosing? If these are works not of a place but of the Holy Spirit and of Christian faith, it is surely very foolish to restrict them, as if within walls, to the Roman see by us, unless faith and the energy of the Spirit exist nowhere except at Rome. What does it matter where Peter served his Lord? We ought rather to ask in what matter Peter was approved by his Lord, or why, so that we may strive for the same prize, in the same way, as far as it lies in us. But if we suspect that Peter had some privilege granted by Christ alone, which was not likewise shared with the other apostles, then we are greatly mistaken, and it is because of some private affection of a man, of which many affections rule in us. But if it is on account of the divine, lofty and clear confession which Peter expressed not alone but on behalf of all, then whoever most closely expresses the faith of Peter, wherever he sits, is rightly to be counted the successor of Peter, and he is the successor, without drawing from this any human splendour or worldly glory. It is a function, not a rank; a ministry, not a magisterium of the apostolate. Just as, I think, among the apostles themselves there was no difference of dignity or pre-eminence of place, but all, with one mind and by the same Spirit of the Lord, did not pursue their own business, so that whoever was least among them was held in higher regard by Christ the witness. Wherefore the succession of these men earned praise indeed before God, but before the world no dignity. For how, as Polycarp rightly answered the proconsul in Eusebius, can the profession of those who have all things as lost for Christ cohere with worldly riches, or with earthly grandeur? But the pontiffs of these times, by I know not what ambition, have utterly turned the ecclesiastical function into a worldly polity, so that, as prince succeeds prince, so by hereditary right pontiff succeeds pontiff into the chair, fortified with earthly wealth and a bodyguard, in the manner of the world, and who so claims the principate for himself that all power and the sum of affairs returns to him alone. The pastors of the other churches were worth nothing except so far as he permitted. He alone presided not only over the churches but over all kingdoms. He alone was a terror to all. Little or nothing was allowed to the other ministers of Christ. Everything hung upon one man and was sought from him. Nowhere was there a right of excommunication, nowhere authority of absolution, nowhere power of interpretation, except in the Roman basilica. In this so great upheaval of affairs and most thick darkness of ignorance, when hardly any spark of purer doctrine seemed to be left, there arose, under divine auspices, this Wycliffe, in whom the Lord first willed to rouse the world, buried under far too many dreams of human traditions. You have, therefore, the times of Wycliffe. Now hear briefly of the conflict and disputes. When John here had for a long time held the profession of theology at Oxford, and had seen the true theology of Christ adulterated by so many papistical filths, so many sects of monks, so many shadows of errors, deliberating and lamenting for a long time within himself, with secret groaning over the public ignorance of the world, after

units.la: Agones Vuicleui. postquam diutius ferre non potuit, tandē succurrendum putauit rebus sic periclitantibus. Ac quoniam sine magna perturbatione uidebat tam periculosam camerinam tētari haud potuisse; nec subito reuelli posse, quæ longa consuetudine iam inueterata omnium animis insederat, paulatim sibi hoc negotium tractandum existi mauit, sicut ille e cauda equina pilos euulsit. Itaque à minutioribus exor- sus, sic sibi aditum patefecit ad grandiora, ut primum in λογικοῖς ac metaphysicis tentarit aduersarios, disputans de idæis, de ampliatione temporis, ac esse intelligibili creaturę, aliisq́ue id genus haud ita magni momenti subtilitatibus, quæ tamen nonnihil præmunirent uiam de grauioribus disputaturo. In iis ergo determinauit I. Kenynghamus Carmelita aduersus Vuicleuum.
units.tr: Wycliffe's struggles. he could no longer bear it, at last he thought he must come to the aid of affairs so imperilled. And since he saw that so dangerous a canker could not be touched without great disturbance, nor suddenly plucked out what by long custom had grown inveterate and settled in the minds of all, he decided to handle this business little by little, as that man plucked the hairs from a horse's tail. Thus, beginning with smaller matters, he opened for himself the way to greater ones: first he tried his opponents in the logical [λογικοῖς] and metaphysical questions, disputing about ideas, about the extension of time, and about the intelligible being of creatures, and other subtleties of that kind, not of great moment, which nevertheless would somewhat fortify the way for one about to treat of weightier matters. In these, therefore, John Kenningham, a Carmelite, gave judgment against Wycliffe.

units.la: Ex his initijs factus est gradus ad altiora, tandem uentum ad Sacramentum tum eucharisticum, qua in re pluri- mum uir pius desudauit, publice in scholis adreftans, principale esse sua ut (loquebatur) intetione, ut in hac materia ecclesiam reuocaret ab ido lolatria. Atqui hoc ulcus tangi fine magno orbis dolore nequibat. Pri- mum uniuersa monachorum acme dicantium colluuies in rabiem esse- rebatur, qui ceu crabrones aculeatis morsibus, miserum undique adorti sunt, ἐγχεῖρ ἀσφτ, quod aiunt, pro suis dimicantes aris uel haris potius. Post hos tum sacerdotes, mox episco pi rem capescebant, postremo quum nec horum potentia satis ualere uide batur aduersus prorumpentem ueri tatem, ad fulmen pontificis tanqua ad triarios concursum est. Hæc enim extrema esse anchora solet in istiusmodi procellis, ubi monachorum clamores, ac pharisaica improbitas parum proficiunt. Aduersus hos i- gitur tam multos potentissimos aduersarios unus hic Vuicleuus causam sustinuit Sacramenti satis selicIter, tum ex diuinis literis, tum ex Doctorum autoritate, sed maxime uetustiorum. Nam recentiores, hoc est qui à mille Christi annis scripserunt hoc argumento reiecit, quod diceret post hosce annos solutum esse Satanam. Ex eo tempore magis obnoxiā esse erroribus humanam uitam: simplicissimā uigere in scripturis ueritatem: ad hanc amussim excutienda quaecunque humana sunt, tum potissimum quę recentioribus iss annis hominum commenta prodiderunt. Hæcce causa est cur neotericos istos decretistas respuerat, tantum innixus scripturis ac priscis scriptoribus: Ex iis fortissime astruens in Sacramento corporis quod pane celebratur nequaquam consistere accidentia sine subiecto id est, nō adesse Christum absque pane, quemadmodum vulgus id temporis sacrificulorum somniasomniabat. Quae autem illius fuerint argumenta, ne tam longa digressio a lectorem differamus, alio in libro tardius fortasse, at oportunius, Christo concedente, exequemur. Veritas hic primum (ut uere apud comicum est) opidoquam magnum odiū cōciliauit Vuicleuo apud plerosque, at potissimum monachos, ac lautioris fortunae praesules, Caterū praesidio regis Edouardi satis adhuc communitus aduersus horum morsus ac impetus uidebatur, quoad Rex uiueret. Quanquam et in huius postremo anno, comprehensus est Vuicleuus, per Archiepiscopū Cantuariensem, instigante pontifice, atque ad silentium adactus praesente duce Lancastriae & D. Henrico Perseo. Ast iterum nactus hic procerum quorundam patrocinia silentium hoc breui ruperat. Tandem ubi abreptus Rex, successit in habenas regni, Ricardus filius circa annum 1377.
units.tr: From these beginnings a step was made to higher things, until at last he came to the Eucharistic sacrament, a matter in which that pious man laboured greatly, publicly declaring in the schools that the principal aim of his effort (as he put it) was to call the Church back from idolatry in this matter. And yet this sore could not be touched without great grief to the whole world. First the whole swarm of monks, devoted to their own interests, was roused to fury, and like hornets they attacked the wretched man on every side with stinging bites, fighting, as they say, with every hand [ἐγχεῖρ ἀσφτ] for their altars or rather their hearths. After them the priests, and soon the bishops, took up the fight; finally, since the power of these men did not seem enough against truth breaking forth, they ran to the thunderbolt of the pontiff, as to the triarii. For this is commonly the last anchor in storms of this kind, when the clamours of monks and Pharisaical wickedness accomplish little. Against so many very powerful adversaries, therefore, Wycliffe alone sustained the cause of the sacrament, and did so with considerable success, both from the divine writings and from the authority of the teachers, but especially of the more ancient ones. For he rejected the more recent writers, that is, those who wrote from the thousandth year of Christ onward, on the argument that after those years Satan was loosed. From that time, he said, human life was more exposed to errors, while the simplest truth flourished in the Scriptures; and whatever is human, and especially whatever the inventions of men in more recent years have brought forth, must be tested by this rule. This is the reason why he despised those modern decretists, leaning only upon the Scriptures and the early writers. From these he most strongly maintained that in the sacrament of the body, which is celebrated under bread, accidents by no means subsist without a subject, that is, that Christ is not present without the bread, as the common sort of priests at that time were dreaming. But what his arguments were, lest we delay the reader with so long a digression, we shall set out in another book, perhaps later but more opportunely, Christ permitting. This truth, as the comic poet truly says, first brought Wycliffe no small hatred among many, and especially among the monks and the prelates of more comfortable fortunes. Meanwhile, protected by the favour of King Edward, he seemed sufficiently secure against their bites and attacks, as long as the King lived. Yet even in the last year of his life Wycliffe was seized by the Archbishop of Canterbury, at the instigation of the pontiff, and forced into silence in the presence of the Duke of Lancaster and Sir Henry Percy. But Wycliffe, having again gained the patronage of certain nobles, soon broke this silence. At last, when the King was carried off, Richard, his son, succeeded to the reins of the kingdom, about the year 1377.

units.la: Cuius animum natura alioqui gene rofiffimum, nunquam cessabat Gre gorius pontifex, per literas, per epi- fcopos, per bullas folicitare ad perse- quendū Vuicleuum, eiusque com- militones. Exemplar epistolæ etiam num extat ad Regem scriptæ.
units.tr: Gregory the pontiff never ceased, by letters, by bishops and by bulls, to stir up the mind of Richard, a king otherwise most generous by nature, to persecute Wycliffe and his companions. A copy of the letter written to the King still exists.

units.la: EXEMPLAR EPISTOLAE ARO. pontifice ad Richardum Angl. regem con scriptæ ad persequendum Vuicleuum.
units.tr: Copy of a letter from the pontiff to Richard, King of England, written to persecute Wycliffe.

units.la: CHARISSIMO IN CHRISTO filio Richardo regi Anglię illu stri Sal. &c. Regnum Anglię quod altissimus tuę supponit potestati, glo riosum nempe potentia & abundan tia facultatum, sed gloriosius pietate fidei & sacræ paginæ claritate cho- ruscum, consueuit uiros producere diuinarum scripturarum recta scien- tia præditos, maturitate graues, de- uotione feruentes, & catholicæ fidei defensores, qui non solum proprios præ
units.tr: TO MY MOST BELOVED SON IN CHRIST, Richard, illustrious King of England, greeting, etc. The kingdom of England, which the Most High has placed under your power, is glorious for its might and its abundance of resources, but more glorious still, shining with the piety of its faith and the clarity of the sacred page. It has been accustomed to produce men endowed with a right knowledge of the divine Scriptures, grave in maturity, fervent in devotion, and defenders of the Catholic faith, who not only

units.la: præceptis salutaribus instituebant, di rigebantqz in diuinorum scmitam mandatorum. Sed super cum ingen ti cordis amaritudine, plurimorum fide dignorum suggestione percepi-mus Ioannem Vuicleyff rectorem ecclesiæ de lutteruuorth lincol.dioc; sacræ paginæ profes-sorem utinam non magistrum errorum, in illam ne phandam & abominabilem proru-pisse demetiam, quod nonnullas pro-posuerit conclusiones plenas erroris bus&manifestam hæresim continen-tes, quæ statum totius ecclesiæ subuertere, & eneruare nituntur, quarum qz aliqz, licet quibusdam muta-tis terminis, sentire uidentur peruer-sas opiniones, & doctrinam indoctā damnatæ memoriæ Marsilij de Pa-dua & Ioannis de Gauduno, quorū liber per fœlicis recordationis Ioan-nem papā 22. prædecessorem nostrū reprobatus extitit & damnatus &c.
units.tr: instructed their own people with salutary precepts, and guided them in the way of the divine commandments. But with great bitterness of heart, on the reports of many trustworthy people, we have learned that John Wycliffe, rector of the church of Lutterworth in the diocese of Lincoln, professor of sacred writ (would that he were not a master of errors), has burst out into such a foolish and abominable madness that he has put forward a number of conclusions full of error and containing manifest heresy, which strive to subvert and weaken the whole state of the Church. Some of these, though with certain terms changed, seem to express perverse opinions and the unlearned doctrine of the men of damned memory, Marsilius of Padua and John of Jandun, whose book was reproved and condemned by our predecessor of happy memory, Pope John XXII, etc.

units.la: Audisti hactenus, cordate lesctor, incusatum Vuicleuuum a pon tifice. Nunc accipe rationes & argumenta, quibus illum apud regem refutat. Sequitur. Cum itaque venerabiles fratres nostri Archiepisc. Cantuar. & episc. Londinensis a nobis mandatum acceperunt præfatū Ioannem autoritate nostra capiendi & carceribus mancipandi,eiusque confessionem ad nos transmittendi,si in profecutione huius negotij noscantur fauore & auxilio tuo indigere maiestatem tuam, quemadmodum & tui progenitores inclyti,catholicæ fidei, cuius in hac parte res agitur, semper consueuerunt esse & prædicti Zelatores,requirimus,& deprecamur attente quatenus ob reuerentiam Dei, dictæ fidei & apostolicæ sedis & nostrum intuitum, digneris præfatis Archiepiscopo & episc.aliisque qui huiusmodi negotium prosequuntur, in ipsa profecutione tui fa-uoris & auxilij patrocinio exhibere. Proinde praeter humanae laudis praeconium, diuinę retributionis praemium, nostram & dictae sedis gratiam & beneuolentiam adepturus amplior. Dat. Romae apud S. Mariam maiorem. ii. K. Iunij. Anno pontificatus nostri 7. 1378.
units.tr: You have heard so far, discerning reader, that Wycliffe has been accused by the pontiff. Now take the reasons and arguments by which he refutes him before the king. It follows: Since, therefore, our venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London, have received from us a mandate to seize the said John by our authority and consign him to prison, and to send his confession to us, if in pursuing this business they are found to need the favour and aid of your majesty, as your illustrious ancestors, who have always been accustomed to be zealous champions of the Catholic faith, whose cause is here at stake, we request and beseech you earnestly that, for reverence to God, the said faith, the apostolic see and our regard, you deign to give the said archbishop and bishops, and the others who pursue this business, the patronage of your favour and aid in the very prosecution of it. Wherefore, besides the proclamation of human praise, you will obtain the greater reward of divine recompense and the grace and goodwill of ourselves and the said see. Given at Rome, at St Mary Major, on the 2nd day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate, 1378.

units.la: Haec firmamenta sunt & robora argumentorum, quibus christiana fides tuetur Apostolici pontifices, quibusq; orbi persuadent incendiū haereticorum. Mandamus, requirimus, & uolumus. Quid ratio quaeritur? stat pro ratione uoluntas. Quicquid papa pronunciat, hoc est, quicquid αὐτῷ ἰσχύει, tanti ideo est, ut nemo sit tam impudenter contumax, qui aufirfemel ἐπιτιμήσῃ. At qui succedunt in uicem apostolorum, apostolico spiritu ac mansuetudine, cum fratribus agere conueniebat, reputantes secum iuxta consilium euangelicum cuiusnam sint spiritus. Quicquid licet externo iudici, aut in prophana causa, Quicquid olim licuit tyrannis apud ethnicos, quicquid insuper ueteris testamenti pontificibus, non id statim competit in noui testamenti ministros, qui longe alium hauserunt spiritum, ipsius uid. qui ex se discere iubebat quod mitis esset & humilis corde. Meminisse igitur addecet istos quantumlibet apostolorum successione se iactitent, non solum ministros sese esse, sed cuius etiam ministri sint, Non habiturum se pro perito choraule dixit Themistocles, qui caneret praeter numeros. Nec secus istis uidendum est, ne in gerenda functione aliter se attemperent, quam ad eius regulae harmoniam qua profitentur. Etsi ter maximus erat haereticus Vuicle. ubi hoc didicit Ro. pontifex uinculis stringere, carceribus, ac ui opprimere, ac ignibus per sequi, quem adhuc nullo probabili argumento refutauit, cuiusq; non satis fortasse causam habebat cognitā.
units.tr: These are the props and strengths of the arguments by which the Christian faith is defended by the apostolic popes, and by which they persuade the world to the burning of heretics: "We command, we require, and we will." Why is a reason sought? Will stands in place of reason. Whatever the pope pronounces, that is, whatever [αὐτῷ ἰσχύει] prevails with him, is of such weight that no one is so shamelessly contumacious as to dare to rebuke it even once [ἐπιτιμήσῃ]. Yet those who succeed the apostles ought to deal with their brothers in the apostolic spirit and gentleness, considering among themselves, according to the counsel of the Gospel, of what spirit they are. Whatever may be permitted to an external judge, or in a profane cause; whatever was once permitted to tyrants among the heathen; whatever moreover was permitted to the pontiffs of the Old Testament, does not immediately belong to the ministers of the New Testament, who have drunk in a far different spirit, the spirit of him who bade them learn from himself that he was meek and humble in heart. It becomes these men, however much they boast of their succession from the apostles, to remember not only that they are ministers, but whose ministers they are. Themistocles said he would not regard as a skilled flute-player one who played out of tune. Nor should these men see to it otherwise, that in discharging their office they adapt themselves to anything other than the harmony of the rule which they profess. Even if Wycliffe were the greatest of heretics, where did the Roman pontiff learn to bind him with chains, cast him into prison, oppress him by force and pursue him with fire, when he has not yet refuted him by any probable argument, and perhaps did not have sufficient knowledge of his cause?

units.la: Tot libros latine scriptos ědiditin lucem I. Vuicleuus, qui si parū ortho doxi uiderentur, quanta fuerat apo-stolica ciuilitate dignius, rem prius cum homine communicare, aut inter doctos, (quoad licuerat) trāfigere, sal tem officij erat fortiter errores scri-pturis non ui reuincere. Certe apud Regem, tantumq; principem, tam te-mere accusare, cuius accusationis nulla tu causam aut nō poslis aut nō uelis afferre, insuetę ac barbaricę cu-iusdam immanitatis uidetur, ac leuitatis principum maiestate im-pudenter abutentis. Et tamen isti (ut nihil pudet) uideri postulant apo-stolorum successores a quorum mo-ribus exemplisq; non minus diffi-dent, quam æra lupinis, quod aiunt. Hæreticum hominem, inquit Pau-lus, post unam et alteram admoniti-onem deuita. At quotusquisq; apo-stolorum hæreticū hominem quan-tumuis hæreticum constrinxit unq; uinculis,carceribus mancipauit, redegit in cineres: Quasi uero parū per se potēs esse ueritas, aut Christus ueritatis assertor,ni uinculis,aut cruci-bus ad coher cēdos hæreticos iuuare tur. Paulus ecclesiasticum pastorem apostolicis præceptis imbuens, inter cętera habet ad Timotheū. Porro seruum domini non oportet pugnare, sed placidū esse erga omnes, propensum ad docendum,tolerantem malos, cum mansuetudine erudientem, non solum errore aut impe ritia seductos,sed eos inquit,qui ob stultunt,si quando det illis Deus pœnitentiam ad cognoscendum ueritatem. Et rursus ad Titum scribens,ut sit potens, ait, contradicentes reuincere. Quo pacto? Armis,ferro,actru culentia? Non arbitror. Sed armis ac potentia spiritus, sed uerbo Dei, sed [Greek]. Aliud est cum mundanis principibus belli gerari pro iure populi, Aliud de religionis gionis causa disputare in ecclesiis Dei. Fateor detestandum esse hæreti cum hominem iuxta Pauli vocem. Sed aliud est deuitare, aliud pro hæretico extinguere innocentem. Qui semel atque iterum admonitus in errore perstat, dignus est quem vitatum ab omnibus, carcer inaccessus excludat a bonorum contubernio. Sed qui ego sciam errorem esse, nisi tu meliora adduxeris? Iam unde hoc barbaricæ feritatis exemplum manauit in christianam hierarchiam, ut quem non solum argumentis nul lis deuiceris, sed ne semel quidem ad monueris, hunc illico ad capitis supplicium rapias, non ob aliud, nisi quod tibi hæreticus videatur. At qui tam confidenter de aliena pronunciat hæresi, huic peropus est constare prius, quæ sit vera fidei synceritas. Alioqui si satis id cuique esse debet, quod sibi cuiusque blanditur affectus, periculum esse potest, ne quod Iudæis
units.tr: Wycliffe has put out into the light so many books written in Latin. If these seemed little orthodox, it would have been more worthy of apostolic courtesy first to confer with the man himself, or, as far as was permitted, to discuss the matter among the learned. At the very least it was the duty to refute errors strongly by Scripture, not by force. Certainly to accuse so rashly before the king, and such a prince, a man for whose accusation you can give no cause, or will not, seems the savagery of some strange and barbarous cruelty, and the levity of men who shamelessly abuse the majesty of princes. And yet these men (since nothing shames them) want to be seen as successors of the apostles, from whose morals and examples they differ no less than brass from bean-pods, as they say. "Avoid a heretical man," says Paul, "after one or two admonitions" (Tit. 3.). But how few of the apostles ever bound a heretic, however heretical, with chains, consigned him to prison, or reduced him to ashes! As if truth were not powerful enough of itself, or Christ were not the champion of truth, unless he were aided by chains or crosses to restrain heretics! Paul, instructing an ecclesiastical pastor with apostolic precepts, says among other things to Timothy: "The servant of the Lord must not strive, but must be gentle to all, apt to teach, patient, instructing with meekness those who oppose, not only those led astray by error or ignorance, but those, he says, who resist, if perhaps God may give them repentance to know the truth" (2 Tim. 2.). And again, writing to Titus, that he may be able, he says, to convince the gainsayers (Tit. 1.). In what way? By arms, iron and cruelty? I think not. But by the arms and power of the Spirit, by the word of God, and by [Greek]. It is one thing to wage war with worldly princes for the right of the people; it is another to dispute about the cause of religion in the churches of God. I grant that a heretic is to be detested, according to Paul's word. But it is one thing to avoid him, and another to put an innocent man to death as a heretic. He who, admonished once and again, persists in error, is worthy to be shunned by all and shut out from the company of good people by an inaccessible prison. But how do I know that it is error, unless you bring forward something better? Now whence did this example of barbarous savagery flow into the Christian hierarchy, that you should not only fail to overcome by any arguments one whom you have not even admonished once, but at once hurry him to the punishment of death, for no other reason than that he seems heretical to you? But one who so confidently pronounces on another's heresy must first be certain what the true sincerity of faith is. Otherwise, if it were enough for each man that his own affection flatters him, there may be danger that what happened to the Jews

units.la: reuincunt hæreses. daeis olim acciderat, qui cum Christum ut seductorem crucifigere voluerint, pro seductore crucifixerunt filium Dei: idem & iis usu veniat ut in persequendis haereticis ipsi soli omnium maxime fiant haeretici. Iam multi sunt quos huc incitat naturae sequitia, vel stoliditas, aut inanis super stitio, qui cum haud fere plus uident in iis rebus, quam lusciosi in coloribus, mirum tamen quanto supercilio pronunciant de haereticis. Atque interim hi sunt, qui falli, errare, ac decipi non possunt, nec cuiquam fas est ad humani iudicii censuram horum exigere placita. O miseram fatis ecclesiae conditionem, postquam sic in unius nutu ac renutu pendet universus populi christiani status, ut quicquid hominconis unius indo cti putido cerebro placeat, aut secus: id cunctis mortalibus arripiendum, ad hoc omnis nostra accommodanda et formanda religio. At quid hoc aliud est, quàm ut religio Christi ad hominem, non homines ad religionem se componant? Caeterum relicto pontifice, redeo iam ad Vuicleuum, Qui etsi (ut diximus) per epi-scopos & pontifices silere coactus sit, sictame comprimi non potuit ue-ritatis uehementia, quin postea multo impotentius eruperit. Nactus igitur Vuicleuus fauentium aliquot procerum suffragia, iterum aggredi-tur in plebem sua aspergere dogmata. Iterum adsunt pharisaeorum pha-langes, miris tragoedijs tumultuantes, ut fit, aduersus emicantem euangelij lucem. Nec hic interim pontifex deest suis partibus, nunquam de sistens bullis ac literis horum euocare animos, suo alioqui ingenio satis insanientes. Extant huius epistolarum penes me exemplaria nonnulla, sed in quibus praeter uim meram, minas, ac bullas uerborum nihil continebatur. His ergo literis animati, par-tim tim insuper priuata fquitia stimulati Archiep. Cant. reliquique episco pi, mirum quanta confidentia ante concilium suum prouinciale publici tus profitebantur, se nec precibus cu iusquam, nec minis ullis, uel muneri bus abduci uelle, quo minus, ea in causa, strictam rigidamque iustitiam sequerentur, etiamsi uel capitis imminéret periculum. Magnifica profecto pollicitatio & recta, si iustitiam hanc rectis finibus definirent. Verum has molitiones, & fortitudine tantam episcoporum, minima occasi one eneruauit Dominus, aduersus quem nihil ualet humani consilij de creta. Appetente si quidem examí nationis die, cum ex aulicis proceri- bus Ludouicus quidam Clyfordus ingressus ad episcopos, uetare ne quid contra Ioannem hunc sententi- aliter diffinirent, tanto terrore cocuf sas illorum cristas referunt, ut in an- nalibus facti dicantur uelut homo non habens in ore suo redargutiones. Accedebat & illud, quod cum episcopi simul cum Vuicleuo in sacellum Archiepiscopi iam conuenirent lambeti, irrumpentes ilico ciues ac plebani Londinenses, uerba pro Vuicleuo facere, interturbato nonnihil concilio, non dubitabant. His rerum occasionibus adiutus Vuicleuus post habitam protestationem, non ita magno se labore expediuit e tendiculis episcoporum. an. 1377. Eius protestationis huiusmodi uerba fuerunt
units.tr: refute heresies. Once befell the Jews, who, when they wished to crucify Christ as a seducer, crucified the Son of God as a seducer. The same may happen to those who, in persecuting heretics, become themselves above all others the greatest heretics. Now there are many whom the wickedness of their nature, or stupidity, or empty superstition urges on, who, though they see scarcely more in these matters than the purblind see in colours, nonetheless pronounce about heretics with amazing arrogance. And meanwhile these are the men who, they claim, cannot be deceived, err, or be misled, and it is not right for anyone to bring their opinions under the censure of human judgment. O wretched condition of the Church, since the whole state of the Christian people hangs so much on the nod or refusal of one man, that whatever pleases the stinking brain of one unlearned man, or otherwise, must be seized upon by all mortals, and all our religion must be adapted and shaped to it! But what is this other than that the religion of Christ should adjust itself to a man, rather than men to religion? But, leaving the pontiff, I now return to Wycliffe, who, though (as we said) he was compelled to be silent by the bishops and pontiffs, nevertheless the vehemence of truth could not be suppressed, so that afterwards he burst out much more violently. Wycliffe, having won the support of some favouring nobles, again sets about scattering his doctrines among the common people. Again the phalanxes of the Pharisees are present, raging with their usual wondrous tragedies against the shining light of the gospel. Nor in the meantime is the pontiff lacking to his party, never ceasing to recall the minds of these men, otherwise sufficiently frenzied, by his bulls and letters. Some copies of his letters are in my possession, but they contain nothing beyond sheer violence, threats and empty bulls of words. Encouraged by these letters, and partly goaded also by private spite, the Archbishop of Canterbury and the other bishops, with remarkable confidence, publicly professed before their provincial council that they would not be turned aside from following strict and rigid justice in this cause, by the prayers of anyone, nor by any threats or bribes, even if the danger of capital punishment threatened. A splendid and upright promise indeed, if only they had defined this justice by right limits. But the Lord, against whom no human counsel avails, weakened these undertakings and the great courage of the bishops by the slightest occasion. For when the day of examination was drawing near, a certain Lewis Clifford, one of the courtier nobles, entered to the bishops and forbade them to pass any sentence against this John. They were so terrified, it is reported, that their crests were lowered, and in the annals it is said of them that they became like a man who has no rebukes in his mouth. Add to this that when the bishops were meeting with Wycliffe in the archbishop's chapel at Lambeth, the citizens and parish priests of London rushed in at once and did not hesitate to speak on Wycliffe's behalf, the council being somewhat disturbed. Aided by these occasions, Wycliffe, after the protestation he made, freed himself with no great difficulty from the snares of the bishops, in the year 1377. The words of this protestation were as follows.

units.la: PROTESTATIO I. VVICLEVI
units.tr: THE FIRST PROTESTATION OF WYCLIFFE

units.la: In principio protestor publice, sicut saepe feci quod propono & uolo ex toto corde meo, mediante Dei gratia, esse integre christianus, et qua diu manserit in me halitus profiteri atq; defendere quantum sufficio legem Christi. Et quod si exignorantia, tia, uel quacumq; alia causa in isto de fecero, rogo deum meum de uenia. Et nunc prout tunc reuoco atq; retracto submittes me humiliter correctioni sanctae matris ecclesiae. Et quia per pueros reportata est sententia fidei, quam in scholis & alibi, ac magis per pueros etiā usque ad Romanam curiam deportata. Ideo ne christiani scandalizentur in me, uolo in scriptis dare sententiam ex qua im petitus sum. Quam uolo usque ad mortem defendere. Sicut credo omnes christianos debere, sed speciali-ter Romae pontificem, & caeteros sacerdotes ecclesiae. Intelligo autem conclusiones ad sensum & modum loquendi scripturae & sanctorum doctorum, quem paratus sum expo-nere, & dato quod sunt fidei contrariae, uolo ipsos paratissime reuocare.
