Longum hic foret conclusiones huius libelli omnes percensere. Sed propter raram ac singularem in eis utilitatem, non putaui (Amice lector) mihi committendum, ut breui tatis quàm commodi tui uiderer stu diosior.
units.tr: At the outset I solemnly declare in public, as I have often done before, that I purpose and wish, with all my heart and by the grace of God, to be a whole Christian, and, for as long as breath remains in me, to profess and defend the law of Christ as far as I am able. If through ignorance or any other cause I have failed in this, I ask pardon of my God. And now, as then, I revoke and retract whatever is contrary to this, submitting myself humbly to the correction of holy mother Church. And because a statement of my faith has been carried about by boys, both in the schools and elsewhere, and even more by boys all the way to the Roman court, therefore, so that Christians may not be scandalised by me, I wish to set down in writing the opinion for which I have been impugned. I wish to defend it to the death, as I believe all Christians should, and especially the Roman pontiff and the other priests of the Church. I understand the conclusions in the sense and manner of speaking of Scripture and the holy teachers, which I am ready to explain; and even if they are contrary to the faith, I am most ready to recant them. It would be tedious here to go through all the conclusions of this little book. But because of their rare and singular usefulness, friendly reader, I did not think I should appear to care more for brevity than for your benefit.

units.la: CONCLVSIONES I. VVICLEVI in conuentu episcoporum aliquot Lam beti exhibitæ. 1377.
units.tr: The Conclusions of JOHN WYCLIFFE, presented in a meeting of several bishops at Lambeth, 1377.

units.la: TOTVM GENVS HVMA- num concurrentium citra Christum, non habet potestatem ordinandi simpliciter, ut Petrus & omne genus suum dominetur inperpetuum politice super mundum patet ex fide scripturæ. Quia oportet omnem ciuilitatem cessare ante finale iudicium 1.Cor. 15. Vbi apostolus loquens de die iudicij, ita scribit: Demum finis ubi tradiderit regnum Deo et patri, cum euacuauerit omnem principatum, et potestatem, & uirtutem. Qui ergo credit carnis resurrectione, credit et hunc articulum, quum amplius non erit exactio uel conuersatio secularis. Nemo igitur habet potestatem ordinandi contra decretum domini in hac parte.
units.tr: The whole human race gathered together apart from Christ does not have the power simply to ordain that Peter and all his kin should rule politically over the world forever. This is clear from the faith of Scripture, because all civil government must cease before the final judgment (1 Cor. 15). There the apostle, speaking of the day of judgment, writes thus: "Then comes the end, when he delivers up the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished all rule, authority and power." Whoever therefore believes in the resurrection of the flesh believes this article too, since there will then be no more exaction or secular administration. No one therefore has the power to ordain against the Lord's decree in this matter.

units.la: Deus nō potest dare homini pro se, & hęredibus suis in perpetuum ciuile dominium. Pro isto sumo, quod in perpetuū sumitur proprie, & famose, more ecclesiæ orantis, ut trinitati sit gloria nunc et in perpetuum. Sumo secundo, quod ciuile dominium intelligitur formaliter pro illo quod quis ciuiliter dominetur. Et tertio quod sit locutio de Dei potentia ordinata, uel reuelata in scripturis diuinis, & tunc conclusio ista sequitur ex priore, Loquendo autem de Dei potentia absoluta, uidetur multis probabile, quod dominus non potest continuare æternaliter uiatione sponsæ suæ, eo quod tunc fraudaret eam à præmio, aut corpori diaboli iniuste differre dare pœnam quam meruit.
units.tr: God cannot give to a man, for himself and his heirs, civil lordship forever. By "forever" I understand what is taken properly and commonly, in the manner of the praying Church: "to the Trinity be glory, now and forever." Secondly, I take civil lordship formally, as that by which someone rules civilly. Thirdly, I take the statement as concerning God's ordained or revealed power in the divine Scriptures, and then this conclusion follows from the former. But speaking of God's absolute power, it seems probable to many that the Lord cannot eternally prolong the wayfaring of his bride, since then he would defraud her of her reward, or unjustly defer giving the body of the devil the punishment it has deserved.

units.la: Chartæ humanitus inuentæ deliç reditate perpetua sunt impossibiles. Ista ergo fuit lateraliter dicta uni do ctori magnificanti chartas hominū, scriptura professionis christianæ postpositæ. Melius, inquam, foret de sensioni & expositioni scripturæ attendere, cum multæ huiusmodi chartæ sunt impossibiles. concedo conclusione, cum multæ chartæ affirmant de multis exheredatis & mortuis in testate, quod dantur eis pro se et heredibus suis in perpetuū charta diuina. Quodcū obuiet ordinationi diuinæ, non oportet canonizare chartas singulas scripturam fidei contemnendo.
units.tr: Charters devised by men for perpetual inheritance are impossible. This, then, was said in passing to a certain doctor who magnified men's charters while setting aside the Scripture of the Christian profession. Better, I say, would it be to attend to the sense and exposition of Scripture, since many such charters are impossible. I concede the conclusion, since many charters affirm, concerning many disinherited and dead men in their wills, that a divine charter is given to them and their heirs forever. Whatever opposes the divine ordinance, one need not canonize individual charters while scorning the Scripture of the faith.

units.la: Quilibet existens in gratia gratificante finaliter non solum habet ius ad rem, sed pro suo tempore ius in re super omnia bona Dei. Patet ex fide scripturæ satis famose. Math. 24. Amen dico uobis super omnia bona sua. &c. iuncto illo apostoli
units.tr: Anyone existing in gratifying grace who is finally saved has not only a right to the thing but, for his time, a right in the thing over all God's goods. This is clear enough from the faith of Scripture: Matt. 24, "Truly I say to you, he will set him over all his goods," etc., together with that of the apostle

units.la: Rom. 8. Deus proprio filio suo non pepercit sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, quomodo, inquit, non cum ipso omnia nobis donauit. Tres ergo primæ conclusiones impri munt mundialibus fidem Christi, ne submergantur in pelago seculi transeuntis cum concupiscentia eius, & quarta allicit ad amorem Dei, qui dilexit nos ad tot ueras diuitias.
units.tr: (Rom. 8): "God did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all; how will he not with him also give us all things?" Therefore the first three conclusions impress on worldly people the faith of Christ, lest they be submerged in the sea of this passing age with its lust, and the fourth entices them to the love of God, who loved us to such true riches.

units.la: Homo potest tantum ministratorie dare tam naturali filio, quàm filio imitationis temporale dominiû, uel donum in quibusdam & æternû implicitum. Patet per illud Luc. 6. Mensuram bonam & confertam, & coagitatam & superfluentem, dabût in sinum uestrum, Et quod solum ministratione, ex hoc patet, quod non licet puro uiatori dare aliquid nisi tâ quàm ministerio Dei, sub eius autoritate, iuxta illud apostoli. 15. Dico autem Iesum Christum ministrum fuisse, &c. Non ergo erubescat eius uicarius fungi ministerio eccle- fiæ,quũ fit uel debeat esse seruus ser- uorum Dei. Nam determinatio à modo loquendi sanctæ scripturæ,& fastus secularis dominij cum pruri- ento stilo seculari uidetur mihi di- sponere ad blasphemiam et extollen tiam antichristi, specialiter si uerita- tes sacræ scripturæ reputentur loliũ, fidei Christianæ contrarium, ab illis capitaneis,qui præsumunt quòd de- creto eorum in omni materia fidei oportet stare quantumcũnque igna- ri fuerint fidei scripturarum. Sic enim posset esse concursus ad curiã ad emendum damnationem scriptu- ræ sacræ, tanquàm hæreticę et dispo sitionem contra articulos fidei Chri- stianæ.
units.tr: A man can give only ministerially, both to a natural son and to a son by imitation, a temporal lordship or a gift in certain matters, and an implicit eternal one. This is shown by Luke 6: "Good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over, they will give into your bosom." And that it is only by ministry is clear from this: it is not lawful for a mere wayfarer to give anything except as a minister of God, under his authority, according to the apostle's words (Rom. 15): "I say that Jesus Christ became a minister..." Let therefore his vicar not be ashamed to discharge the ministry of the Church, since he is, or ought to be, the servant of God's servants. For the determination drawn from the manner of speaking of Holy Scripture, and the pride of secular lordship with its itching secular style, seems to me to dispose men towards the blasphemy and exaltation of Antichrist, especially if the truths of Holy Scripture are regarded as tares contrary to the Christian faith, by those captains who presume that in every matter of faith one must abide by their decree, however ignorant they are of the Scriptures of the faith. For in this way there could be a gathering at court to buy the condemnation of Holy Scripture as heretical, and a disposition against the articles of the Christian faith.

units.la: Si Deus est, Domini temporales possunt legitimè ac meritorie auferre bona fortunæ ab ecclesia delinquen te.Pro isto summo,quòd loquamur de posse,ut loquitur scriptura rectisfima & fumme autentica, Mat. 3. Potens eft dominus de lapidibus iftis fufcitare filios Abrahae. Concedo igitur confequentiam correlatiuam primo articulo fidei. Nam fi Deus eft, ipfe eft omnipotens, & fi lic, ipfe poteft dare dominis fecularibus huiufmodi poteftatem, & per confequens, ipfe poteft meritorie & legitime fic uti huiufmodi poteftate. Sed ne conclufio fit ex confequente impertinens, oftendi quod domini temporales poteftatem habent fubtrahendi fuas eleemofynas collatas ecclefiae, ipfa illis eleemofynis abutete; & quod talis ablatio in cafu foret fpirituale opus mifericordiae faluans animam a gehenna, & impetrans utranque beatitudinem. Collatio uero talis ecclefiae praedicta uel contra religionem, quam Chriftus inftituit releuat corpus a temporali miferia, tanquam eleemofyna corporalis. Et ut uidetur sicut dotatio potest esse occasio beatitudinis, sic uerisimilius ablatio. Dixi tamen quòd hoc non liceet facere nisi autoritate ecclesiæ in defectu spiritualis præpositi, & in casu in quo ecclesiasticus corripiendus fuerit à fide deuius, & inutilis.
units.tr: If God exists, temporal lords can lawfully and meritoriously take away the goods of fortune from a church that offends. I take this as the highest premise: that we speak of power, as Scripture speaks most rightly and most authentically: "God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham" (Matt. 3). I therefore grant the correlative consequence to the first article of faith. For if God is, he is omnipotent, and if he is omnipotent, he can give such power to secular lords, and consequently he can meritoriously and lawfully use such power. But lest the conclusion be drawn irrelevantly from the consequent, I have shown that temporal lords have the power to withdraw their alms conferred on the Church when it abuses those alms; and that such a taking away would in that case be a spiritual work of mercy, saving the soul from hell and obtaining both blessednesses. But the conferring of such endowments on a Church that acts against the religion Christ instituted relieves the body from temporal misery, as a bodily alm. And as it seems, just as endowment can be an occasion of blessedness, so taking away is more probably so. I said, nevertheless, that this may not be done except by the authority of the Church, when a spiritual prelate is lacking, and in the case where an ecclesiastic must be corrected for deviating from the faith and for being useless.

units.la: Scimus quod non est possibile, ut uicarius Christi pure ex bullis suis, uel ex illis cum uoluntate & consensu suo, aut sui collegij, quemquam habilitet uel inhabilitet. Patet ex fide scripturæ, qua credit ecclesia quòd oportet omnem habilitationem hominis primo à Deo procedere. Nullus autem Christi uicarius habet in isto potestatem, nisi uicarie, in nomine Domini notificare ecclesiæ, quem Deus habilitat. Ideo si quis quam facit non uicarie nomine Domini quem propter opus suum præcogitat autorem, est luciferina præsumptio,cū 1. Cor. 5. dicat Christus in suo apostolo: omnis nostra sufficientia ex Deo est.
units.tr: We know that it is not possible for Christ's vicar, purely by his bulls, or by those issued with his will and consent or that of his college, to qualify or disqualify anyone. This is clear from the faith of Scripture, by which the Church believes that every qualification of a man must first proceed from God. No vicar of Christ has power in this except to declare vicariously, in the name of the Lord, whom God has qualified. Therefore, if anyone does so not vicariously in the Lord's name, but on account of a work he has foreseen as its author, it is a luciferian presumption, since Christ says in his apostle (1 Cor. 5): "All our sufficiency is from God."

units.la: Non est possibile hominem excommunicari ad sui damnum, nisi excommunicetur primo & principaliter a semetipso. Patet quod omnis talis excommunicatio sapit excommunicati deteriorationem. Sed nemo potest secundum Chrysostomū, & scripturam sacram deteriorari, nisi laedatur per peccatum, quod oportet trahere originē a peccante. Nam meritoria suspensio hominis a Sacramentis & ingressu ecclesiae, non est excommunicatio, nisi æquivocē. Et quantum ad rationem meriti, est prius ab excommunicato, quam a Christi vicario excommunicante. Nemo enim ad sui damnum excommunicatur, si non per peccatum subtrahens divinum subsidium, ut patet, Esai. 59. Iniquitates vestrae diviserunt inter vos & Deum vestrum.
units.tr: It is not possible for a man to be excommunicated to his own harm unless he is first and principally excommunicated by himself. It is clear that every such excommunication tends to the deterioration of the one excommunicated. But no one, according to Chrysostom and holy Scripture, can be harmed unless he is injured by sin, which must originate in the sinner. For the meritorious suspension of a man from the sacraments and from entry into the Church is not excommunication, except equivocally. And as regards the reason of merit, it comes first from the excommunicated person, rather than from the vicar of Christ who excommunicates. For no one is excommunicated to his own harm, unless by sin he withdraws divine help, as is clear from Isa. 59: "Your iniquities have divided between you and your God."

units.la: Non
units.tr: Not

units.la: Nemo debet nisi in causa Dei excommunicare suspendere, interdicere, vel secundum quamcunque censuram ecclesiasticam vindicando procedere. Patet ex hoc, quod nemo debet vindictam expetere nisi in causa iustitiae, ergo concludo. Cum expec cato originatur omnis talis punitio, omne vero peccatum sit in Deum, iuxta illud psalmi 50, Tibi soli peccavi: patet quod nemo, nisi ad vindicandam Dei iniuriam debet ad punitionem talem procedere. Nam ex fide scripturae, nemo debet vindictam capere nisi secundum rationem, qua fit iniuria Deo suo, rationem personalis iniuriae remittendo, ut patet ex praecepto Christi: Mat. 18. Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, dimitte ei usque ad septuagies septies.
units.tr: No one ought, except in the cause of God, to excommunicate, suspend, interdict, or proceed by way of vengeance under any ecclesiastical censure. This is clear from the fact that no one ought to seek vengeance except in the cause of justice; therefore I conclude. Since every such punishment arises from sin, and every sin is against God, according to the psalm (50): "Against you only have I sinned," it is clear that no one, except to avenge the injury done to God, ought to proceed to such punishment. For by the faith of Scripture no one ought to take vengeance except according to the reason by which injury is done to his God, remitting the reason of personal injury, as is clear from Christ's precept: "If your brother sins against you, forgive him up to seventy times seven" (Matt. 18).

units.la: Ex istis patet decima conclusio, quod maledictio vel excommunicatio non ligat simpliciter, nisi de quanto fertur in adversarium legis Dei.
units.tr: From these things the tenth conclusion is clear: a curse or excommunication does not bind absolutely, but only insofar as it is directed against an adversary of God's law.

units.la: C patet sic, Talis maledictio non ligat quoad Deum, nisi de quanto ligatus offendit in legem suam, sed non ligat simpliciter, nisi de quanto ligaue rit quoad Deum, ergo concludo. Si enim Deus iustificat, quis est qui condenet? Deus autem non offenditur, nisi fuerit propter aduersantiam legis suae. Et isti articuli fidei iuuant, ut lex Christi fit charior, tamen ipsam oportet esse rationem dirigentem in quolibet processu legitimo, & ut fides scripturae ad Romanos. 12. melius imprimatur. Non uosmet ipsos defendentes chariff. sed date locum irae. Scriptum est enim: Mihi vindictam & ego retribuam.
units.tr: It is clear thus. Such a curse does not bind with respect to God, except insofar as the one bound offends against God's law; but it does not bind absolutely, except insofar as it binds with respect to God. Therefore I conclude: "If God justifies, who is it that condemns?" (Rom. 8). But God is not offended except on account of opposition to his law. These articles of faith help so that the law of Christ may be held more dear, yet the law itself must be the guiding principle in every lawful process, and so that the faith of Scripture is more deeply impressed (Rom. 12). "Beloved, do not avenge yourselves, but give place to wrath. For it is written: Vengeance is mine, I will repay."

units.la: Non est exemplata potestas a Christo suis discipulis excommunicandi subditum, praecipue propter negationem temporalium, sed e contra. Patet ex hoc quod Christus dicit honorem Dei & ecclesiae utilitatem ante personale commodum, vel negationem temporalium praeferendum. Et secunda pars patet per verbum Luc. 9. ubi prohibuit discipulos suos, volentes ignem de coelo descendere, ad excommunicandum infideles, iniuste detinetes à Christo & suis discipulis bona sua. Nescitis, inquit, cuius sitis spiritus: filius enim hominis venit salvare animas hominum, non perdere. Unde conclusio catholica est, quod non licet Christi vicario excommunicare proximum, nisi propter amorem, quo plus sibi afficitur, quam omnibus temporalibus huius mundi. Et patet negativa conclusio inductiva ac perdurcens ad impossibile, quod tunc fuisset in Christo, est, & non.
units.tr: It was not granted by Christ to his disciples to excommunicate a subject, especially on account of the refusal of temporal goods; rather the contrary. This is clear from the fact that Christ says the honour of God and the benefit of the Church are to be preferred to personal advantage or the loss of temporal goods. The second part is clear from the word of Luke 9, where he forbade his disciples, who wished fire to come down from heaven, to excommunicate unbelievers who unjustly withheld their goods from Christ and his disciples: "You do not know of what spirit you are. For the Son of man came to save men's souls, not to destroy them." Hence the Catholic conclusion is that it is not lawful for Christ's vicar to excommunicate a neighbour, unless on account of a love by which he is more affected toward him than toward all the temporal things of this world. And the negative conclusion is plain, since it leads to the impossible: that then there would have been in Christ both "it is" and "it is not."

units.la: Discipuli Christi non habent potestatem exigendi coactione civili, temporalia per censuras. Patet de apostolis, & aliis Christi discipulis, usque ad dotationem ecclesiae, qui in quantalibet magna egestate fideli um, non exercuerunt huiusmodi potestates, sed hortati sunt, secundum legem Dei, & deuotum ministerium ad tales benedictiones, quae debent esse eleemosynae uoluntariae. Sed postquam dotata est ecclesia, commixta est talis palliata censura & secularis exactio. Imo patet ex hoc quod benedictio ciuilis Luc. 22. fuit discipulis Christi prohibita.
units.tr: The disciples of Christ have no power to exact temporal goods by civil coercion through censures. This is clear from the apostles and the other disciples of Christ until the endowment of the Church. In however great a need of the faithful, they did not exercise such powers, but exhorted, according to the law of God and a devoted ministry, to such blessings as ought to be voluntary alms. But after the Church was endowed, such a cloaked censure and secular exaction was mingled in. Indeed it is clear from this that civil power was forbidden to Christ's disciples (Luke 22).

units.la: Non est possibile de Dei potestate absoluta, quod si papa uel aliquis christianus praetendit, quouis modo ligare uel soluere, eo ipso sic soluit uel ligat. Patet ex hoc quod omnis christianus posset in hoc errare defor miter ab ecclesia triumphate. Tunc animo non ligaret uel soluceret ut praetendit, ergo non potest esse, quod si praetedit se ligare uel soluere, ita facit. Vnde uidetur mihi quod usurpans hanc potestatem sibi foret ipse homo peccati, de quo 2. Thess. 2. scribitur bitur. Quod in templo Dei sedeat, & ostendat se tanquam sit Deus.
units.tr: It is not possible, by God's absolute power, that if the pope or any Christian claims to bind or loose in any way, he thereby binds or looses. This is clear from the fact that every Christian could in this grievously err, to the detriment of the triumphant Church. For then he would not bind or loose as he claims; therefore it cannot be that if he claims to bind or loose, he does so. Hence it seems to me that one who usurps this power would himself be the man of sin, of whom it is written in 2 Thess. 2 that he sits in the temple of God and shows himself as if he were God.

units.la: Credere debemus quod tunc solum ligat uel soluit simplex Christi uicarius, quando agit conformiter lege Christi. Patet ex hoc quod omnis potestas Christi uicarij solum tunc est in effectu legitima, quando beneplacito capitis ecclesiae regulatur.
units.tr: We must believe that the simple vicar of Christ binds or looses only when he acts in conformity with the law of Christ. This is clear from the fact that all the power of Christ's vicar is lawful in effect only when it is regulated by the good pleasure of the head of the Church.

units.la: Hoc credi debet catholice, quod quilibet sacerdos ordinatus rite, secundum legem gratiae, habet potestatem, secundum quam potest sacramenta quilibet ministrare, & per consequens, sibi confessum de quocunque peccato contritum absoluere. Patet ex hoc, quod potestates ordinis in quibuscunque sacerdotibus Christi sunt aequales: ut declarat Hugo 2. de Sacramentis. Aliquae tamen potestates inferiorum sacerdotum nunc sunt rationabiliter in substantia restrictae, et alias in ultimo necessitatis articulo sunt laxatae.
units.tr: This must be believed catholically: every priest rightly ordained according to the law of grace has the power by which he can administer any sacrament and, consequently, absolve a contrite penitent of whatever sin he has confessed. This is clear from the fact that the powers of orders are equal in all the priests of Christ, as Hugh declares in book 2 of On the Sacraments. Some powers of the lesser priests, however, are now rationally restricted in their substance, and elsewhere, in the final article of necessity, they are relaxed.

units.la: Licet regibus in casibus licitis iure, auferre temporalia a uiris eccle siasticis, ipsis habitualiter abutentibus. Patet de ratione posita in 5. con clusione. Nam ad opera maiora misericordiae, dominis temporalibus, magis facilia, sunt ipsi amplius obligati. Sed foret in casu maior eleemosyna, atque facilius dominium temporale, subtrahere eleemosynam suam ab aedificatione ad gehennam per eius abusum, quam dotare dictam eleemosynam ad subsidium corporale. Ergo concludo. Unde secundum legem triplicem specificatur ista sententia. Prima est lex ciuilis de collatione corrodii, collatione 10. Si clericus, inquit lex, veluti episcopus, vel abbas habens beneficium a rege data tum non solummodo personae sed ecclesiae, ipsum propter culpam suam perdat, eo viuente ad regem pertinet. Post mortem vero clerici ad successorem reuertatur. Secunda est lex lex canonica, 16. q. ubi sic dicitur, filijs ac nepotibus, & honestioribus propinquis eius, qui construxit, uel ditauit ecclesiam, licitum sit hanc habere solertiam, ut si sacerdotem aliquem ex collatis rebus defraudare praeuiderint, aut honesta conuentione compescant, aut episcopo uel iudici corrigenda denuncient. Quod si episcopus fuerit negligens, dicatur metropolitano, & tertio in eorum negligentia debet, ut dicit canon, regis auribus intimari. Nec credo id fingibile: At quid regi denuciens, nisi ut ipse correctione adhibeat? Nec dubium quin correctio regi pertinentior, atque salubrior in hac parte foret, bonorum, quorum ipse capitalis dominus, subtractio proportionaliter ad delictum. Tertia est lex Euan. 2. Thess. 3. ubi Apostolus sic scribit: Cum essemus apud uos, hoc denunciabamus uobis, quoniam si quis non uult operari non manducet. Ius ergo naturæ licentiat habentes regnorum gu- bernacula, rectificare abusus temporalium, qui præcipuè destruerent regna sua.
units.tr: In lawful cases, kings may by right take temporal goods away from ecclesiastical men who habitually abuse them. This is clear from the reasoning set out in the fifth conclusion. For temporal lords are more bound to the greater works of mercy, which are easier for them. And in such a case it would be a greater alms, and an easier temporal lordship, to withdraw one's alms from being built up toward Gehenna through their abuse, than to endow those alms for bodily relief. Therefore I conclude. Hence this opinion is specified according to a threefold law. The first is the civil law on the grant of a corrody (collatio 10): "If a cleric, such as a bishop or abbot, holding a benefice given by the king not only to the person but to the church, should lose it on account of his fault, then while he lives it pertains to the king; but after the death of the cleric it reverts to the successor." The second is canon law, 16 q.: "It is lawful for the sons and nephews and more honourable kinsmen of him who built or endowed the church to take this care, so that if they foresee some priest defrauding the goods conferred, they may either restrain him by honest agreement or denounce him to the bishop or judge for correction. If the bishop is negligent, let it be reported to the metropolitan; and thirdly, in their negligence, as the canon says, it must be intimated to the ear of the king." Nor do I think this can be feigned: but what is denounced to the king, except that he himself apply correction? Nor is there any doubt that correction, proportionate to the offence, by withdrawing the goods of which he is the chief lord, would be more fitting to the king and more wholesome in this respect. The third is the law of 2 Thess. 3, where the Apostle writes: "When we were with you, we declared this to you: if anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat." Therefore the law of nature licenses those who hold the reins of kingdoms to correct the abuses of temporal goods, which above all would destroy their kingdoms.

units.la: Siue Domini temporales, siue qui cunque alij dotauerint ecclesiam temporalibus, licet eis in casu auferre temporalia medicinaliter, ad cauendum peccata, non obstante excommunicatione, uel alia censura ecclesiastica, cum non nisi sub conditione implicita, sunt donata. Patet ex hoc, quòd per se conditio consequens ad donationem bonorum ecclesiæ est, ut honoretur Deus, & ecclesia ædificetur: Quæ conditio si defuerit, succedentefe, patet quòd perit titulus donationis, & per consequens Dominus dans eleemosinam rectificare debet errorem. Excommunicatio autem non debet obstare iustitiæ complemento. Quia sic posset clerus per excommunicationem præparatorie conquirere totum mundum.
units.tr: Whether temporal lords or any others have endowed the Church with temporal goods, it is lawful for them in such a case to take away those goods as a remedy, to guard against sins, notwithstanding excommunication or any other ecclesiastical censure, since they were given only under an implicit condition. This is clear from the fact that the condition inherent in the donation of church goods is that God be honoured and the Church built up. If this condition fails, it follows that the title of the donation perishes, and consequently the lord who gave the alms ought to correct the error. But excommunication ought not to stand in the way of the completion of justice, for thus the clergy could, by excommunication in advance, win over the whole world.

units.la: Ecclesiasticus etiā Rom. pontifex potest legitimè, à subiectis corripi & ad utilitatem ecclesiæ, tam à clericis, quàm à Laicis accusari. Prima pars patet, eò quòd omnis talis ecclesiasticus frater peccabilis, & per consequens ex lege correptionis fraternæ. Math. 18. Si peccauerit in quecunque, assistente de possibili opportunitate, debet eum corripere, & per idem, si adfuerit obstinata defensio prauitatis hæreticæ, uel alterius peccati urgentis ad spirituale damnum ecclesiæ, debet in casu penes superio res accusari ad finem, ut ex eius correptione periculum caueatur. Sic enim reprehensus est Petrus à Paulo Gal. 2. & multæ personę irregulares per imperatores depositi, ut narrat Castrensis in sua polychronica li. 5. Ecclesia enim est supra istum pontifice. ideo dicere, quòd iste non debet corripi, nisi à Deo, quomodocunque peccauerit, uidetur mihi impli…
units.tr: The ecclesiastical, and even the Roman pontiff, may lawfully be rebuked by his subjects and accused, for the benefit of the Church, both by clerics and by laymen. The first part is clear, since every such ecclesiastic is a sinning brother, and consequently falls under the law of fraternal correction (Matt. 18): "If your brother sins against you," the one who is present and has the opportunity ought to rebuke him. Likewise, if there is obstinate defence of heretical wickedness, or of another sin pressing to the spiritual harm of the Church, in that case he should be accused before his superiors, so that by his correction the danger may be averted. For thus Peter was rebuked by Paul (Gal. 2), and many irregular persons were deposed by emperors, as Castrensis relates in his Polychronicon, book 5. For the Church is above that pontiff; so to say that he should not be rebuked except by God, however he sins, seems to me to imply

units.la: D care, quod sit supra ecclesiam sponsam Christi. Christus enim licet immpeccabilis voluit esse subiectus principibus, etiam in ablatione suorum temporalium, ut patet, Mat. 17.
units.tr: that he is above the Church, the bride of Christ. For Christ, though impeccable, willed to be subject to princes, even in the surrender of his temporal goods, as is clear from Matt. 17.

units.la: Istas conclusiones dixerim ut granum fidei separatum a palea, quaignitur ingratum lolium, quod post florem ruboris uindictæ fœtentis, parat pabulum contra scripturam fidei antichristo. Cuius infallibile est signum, quod regnet in clero uenenum luciferinum, superbia consistens in libidine dominandi, cuius coniunx terrenorum cupiditas concreet filios diaboli, extinctis filijs euangelicæ paupertatis. Indicium uero huius propaginis patet ex hoc, quod multi etiam filij paupertatis degeneres fouent loquendo uel tacendo partem luciferi, non ualentes seu uolentes, aut non audentes propter femen hominis peccati iniecta in cordibus, aut timorem seruilem de amissione temporalium stare pro euangelica paupertate.
units.tr: These conclusions I would call the grain of faith separated from the chaff, the ungrateful darnel which, after the flower of a foul-smelling red of vengeance, prepares fodder for Antichrist against the Scripture of faith. An infallible sign of it is that a luciferian poison reigns in the clergy, pride consisting in the lust of domination, whose consort, the greed for earthly things, begets the children of the devil, the children of evangelical poverty having been extinguished. Evidence of this offspring is plain from the fact that many degenerate sons of poverty also foster, by speaking or by keeping silent, the part of Lucifer, either being unable or unwilling, or not daring, because the seed of sinful man has been sown in their hearts, or because a servile fear of losing temporal goods makes them stand for evangelical poverty.

units.la: Haec erant capita conclusionum episcopis hoc tempore a Vuicleuo exhibita. Quibus aut non lectis aut non intellectis, illi nescio quo pacto mitescentes liberam huic demissionem indulserant. Post haec statim obiit Gregorius pontifex. Cuius mors non parum foelix Vuicleuo fuerat. Mox huius pontificis obitum ilico excepit ingens et fatale dissidium inter Romanum & Gallicum papa, Quod schisma fere ad annos triginta perdurauit, non sine magnis utrinque tragoedijs, ac hominum strage. Quin & apud Anglos id temporis cruenta satis dissentio infra triennium oborta inter plebeios & patritios, remp. non dicendis motibus perturbant. In quo tumultu Archiepiscopus Cantuar. deprehensus a rusticis capite truncatus est Symon de Sudburia, in cuius deinde vicem subijt Guiliel. Courtneus, qui nihil o et ipse segnius obibat suas partes in debellandis hæreticis. Interea tamen occultis incrementis quotidie se prose-rebant, maioresque uires contraxerat partes Vuicleuianæ, donec Guil. qui dā Bertonus Oxoniæ, ut appellant, Cancellarius circa domini an. 1380. eius Academiæ prefecturam tenuit. Qui conuocatis ad seoco doctoribus monasticis, alijsque quatuor cum reliquorum suorum consensu literis appositio sigillo publico, euulgabat edictum, singulis eius scholæ denuncians, grauissimaque interminans, ne quis deinceps Vuicleuianis assertio ribus sese adiugeret. Vuicleuoipsi post triduanam admonitionem canonicam, ut uocabat, & peremptoriam ni resipiscerent, pariter cum cæteris eius fautoribus uniuersis incarcerationē ac excommunicationem maiorem comminabatur.
units.tr: These were the headings of the conclusions which Wycliffe presented to the bishops at this time. The bishops, whether they did not read them or did not understand them, grew somehow milder and granted him a free dismissal. Soon after this Pope Gregory died, and his death was not a little fortunate for Wycliffe. Immediately upon the death of this pontiff there followed a huge and fatal dissension between the Roman and the French pope, which schism lasted almost thirty years, not without great tragedies on both sides and the slaughter of men. Indeed, in England at that time a bloody enough dissension arose within three years between the common people and the nobles, and disturbed the commonwealth with uprisings not to be described. In this tumult the Archbishop of Canterbury, Simon of Sudbury, was seized by the peasants and beheaded, and in his place succeeded William Courtenay, who was no less zealous himself in combating heretics. Meanwhile, however, the Wycliffite party grew daily by hidden increases and had gathered greater strength, until about the year of the Lord 1380 one William Berton, as they call him, Chancellor of Oxford, held the governorship of that university. Having summoned to his council the monastic doctors and four others, with the consent of the rest, he issued under the public seal a decree, warning each member of that school and threatening the gravest penalties, that no one should henceforth attach himself to Wycliffe's assertions. Wycliffe himself was threatened with imprisonment and major excommunication, together with all his supporters, unless after a canonical admonition of three days, as he called it, and a peremptory one, they repented.

units.la: Quod ubi Vuicleuus intellexerat, licet in hoc cancellarij mandato nihil uideret quod sententiam suam ut aie bat, infringeret, maluit tamen ad regis maiestatem relictis papae ac eccle siasticorum coetibus appellare. Sed interueniens Lancastriae Dux prohi bebat, ne quid rerū huiusmodi post- hac inceptaret, quin potius iudicio ac censurae ordinarij se dederet. Vn- de Vuicleuus inter angustias utrin- que ceu inter συμπλκηγαδλας constitu tus, denuo sui dogmatis exhibere co sessionem adactus est: in qua, rerum ipsam asperitatem, uerborum inuo- lucris, ac molliori lenocinio, quoad dabatur, temperauit, quo sic aduersa rios uel mitigaret, uel eluderet. Se- quente deinde anno, (qui erat 1382.) iterum indicto cocilio Londini per Guil. Cantuar. iubetur adesse Vui- cleuus. Hicque minime praetereun- dum uidetur diuinae comonitionis ostentum. Congregatis siquidem cum Archiepiscopo suffraganeis, alijsque theologiæ doctoribus, aciu-ris utriusq; confultis, simul cum glo-merata fraterculorum, ac cucullionũ manu, qui de Vuicleui libris, ac tota illa secta essent deliberaturi: ubi iam apud predicatores Londini sese ad auspicandum negocium, sed malis auspiciis collegerant, in ipso Dunsta-ni die, à prandio eademq; hora qua rem aggressuri essent secunda, infor-tunatus ac terribilis terræ motus uniuersam peruasit Angliam. Vnde ex suf-fraganeis nonnulli tanquam sinistri ominis interpretatione deterriti ab incœpto negotio desistedum censu-erunt. At Archiep. militiæ, imo magis litiq; potius dux audacior, quam pru-dentior, longe in diuersum interpre-tans quod acciderat, delapsos suorum animos in suscepto instituto confir-mat perfortiter. Qui demum ex-cussis non ad sacros scripturæ canones, sed ad priuatos affectus, autad humana commenta Vuicleui con-clusionibus, clusionibus, quasdam simpliciter hæreticas, alias semierroneas, nonnullas irreligiosas ac scandalosas, parũq; Romanas enunciauit.
units.tr: When Wycliffe learned of this, although he saw nothing in this decree of the chancellor that would overturn his opinion, as he used to say, he preferred to appeal to the majesty of the king, leaving aside the pope and the assemblies of churchmen. But the Duke of Lancaster intervened and forbade him to undertake anything of this kind afterwards, urging him rather to submit himself to the judgment and censure of the ordinary. Wherefore Wycliffe, placed between the two pressures as between συμπλοκαδες [two wrestlers locked together], was compelled to present again a session of his doctrine, in which he softened, as far as was allowed, the harshness of the matter by a veil of words and a smoother flattery, so that he might either mollify or evade his opponents. Then in the following year, which was 1382, a council being again convened at London by William of Canterbury, Wycliffe was ordered to attend. Here it seems not to be passed over that there was a sign of divine warning. For when the archbishop with his suffragans and other doctors of theology, and the lawyers of both laws, had gathered together, along with a crowd of friars and hooded men who were to deliberate on Wycliffe's books and his whole sect, and had already assembled at the Dominicans' house in London to begin the business, but under bad auspices, on the very day of St Dunstan, after dinner and at the same hour in which they were about to take the matter in hand, an unlucky and terrible earthquake invaded all England. Whereupon some of the suffragans, alarmed as by an interpretation of an ill omen, judged that they should desist from the begun business. But the archbishop, a man more of the sword and strife than of prudence, interpreting what had happened quite the other way, firmly strengthened the fallen spirits of his men in the undertaking they had begun. At length, having sifted out the conclusions of Wycliffe, not by the sacred canons of Scripture but by private affections or the human inventions, he pronounced some as plainly heretical, others as half-erroneous, some as irreligious and scandalous, and some as rather Roman.

units.la: CONCLVSIONES PRO HAERETICIS damnatæ.
units.tr: CONCLUSIONS CONDEMNED AS HERETICAL

units.la: SVBSTANTIA PANIS MATERIALIS & uini manet post consecrationem in sacramento altaris.
units.tr: The substance of material bread and wine remains after consecration in the sacrament of the altar.

units.la: Accidentia non manent sine subiecto in eodem sacramento post consecrationem.
units.tr: Accidents do not remain without a subject in the same sacrament after consecration.

units.la: Quod Christus non sit in sacramento altaris identicè, uerè, & realiter in propria persona corporali.
units.tr: That Christ is not in the sacrament of the altar identically, truly, and really in his own corporal person.

units.la: Quod si episcopus uel sacerdos sit in peccato mortali non ordinat, conficit, nec baptisat.
units.tr: That if a bishop or priest is in mortal sin, he does not ordain, consecrate, nor baptise.

units.la: Quod si homo fuerit debitè contritus, omnis confessio exterior est sibi superflua & inutilis.
units.tr: That if a man has been duly contrite, every outward confession is superfluous and useless to him.

units.la: Quod non est fundatum in Euangelio, quod Christus missam ordinauit.
units.tr: That it is not founded in the Gospel that Christ ordained the mass.

units.la: Si Papa fit praescitus ac malus homo, ac per consequens membrum diaboli, non habet potestatem super fideles Christi ab aliquo sibi datam, nisi forte à Caesare.
units.tr: If the Pope is foreknown and a wicked man, and consequently a member of the devil, he has no power over the faithful of Christ given to him by anyone, unless perhaps by Caesar.

units.la: Quod post Vrbanum 6. non est aliquis recipiendus in Papam, sed uiuendum est more Graecorum, sub legibus proprijs.
units.tr: That after Urban VI no one is to be received as Pope, but one must live after the manner of the Greeks, under their own laws.

units.la: Quod est contra scripturam, quod uiri ecclesiastici habeant possessiones temporales.
units.tr: That it is contrary to Scripture for churchmen to have temporal possessions.

units.la: Pro erroneis habebantur istae.
units.tr: These were held to be erroneous.

units.la: Quod nullus praelatus debet aliquem excommunicare, nisi prius sciat ipsum esse excommunicatum à Deo.
units.tr: That no prelate ought to excommunicate anyone unless he first knows that the person has been excommunicated by God.

units.la: Quod sic excommunicas ex hoc sit haereticus, vel excommunicatus.
units.tr: That whoever excommunicates in this way is thereby a heretic or excommunicated himself.

units.la: Quod praelatus excommunicans clericum, qui appellauit ad regem, et consilium regni, eo ipso traditor est regis & regni.
units.tr: That a prelate who excommunicates a clergyman because he has appealed to the king and the council of the realm is by that very act a traitor to the king and the realm.

units.la: Quod illi qui dimittunt prædicare, seu audire uerbum Dei, uel euangelium prædicare propter excōmunicationem, sunt excommunicati, & in die iudicij traditores Dei habebuntur.
units.tr: That those who cease to preach or to hear the word of God, or to preach the gospel, on account of excommunication, are themselves excommunicated, and will be counted traitors to God on the day of judgement.

units.la: Quod liceat alicui, etiam diacono, uel presbytero prædicare uerbum Dei, absque authoritate sedis apostolicæ, uel episcopi catholici.
units.tr: That anyone, even a deacon or a presbyter, may preach the word of God without the authority of the apostolic see or of a catholic bishop.

units.la: Quod nullus est episcopus, nullus est prælatus in ecclesia Dei, dum est in peccato mortali.
units.tr: That no one is a bishop, and no one is a prelate in the Church of God, while he is in mortal sin.

units.la: Item quod Domini temporales possunt ad arbitrium eorum, auferre bona temporalia ab ecclesiasticis, habitualiter delinquentibus.
units.tr: Likewise, that temporal lords may, at their discretion, take temporal goods away from churchmen who habitually offend.

units.la: Quod decimæ sunt puræ eleemo-syne, & quod parochiani possunt propter peccata suorum curatorum eas detinere, & ad libitum aliis conferre.
units.tr: That tithes are pure alms, and that parishioners may withhold them on account of the sins of their parish priests, and confer them on others as they please.

units.la: Item, quod speciales orationes applicatæ uni persónæ per prælatos, uel religiosos, non plus prosunt eidem personæ, quàm orationes generales, cæteris paribus eidem.
units.tr: Likewise, that special prayers offered for one person by prelates or religious do no more good to that person than general prayers, other things being equal.

units.la: Quòd eo ipso, quòd aliquis ingreditur religionem priuatam quamcunque, redditur ineptior, & inhabilior ad obseruantiam mandatorum Dei.
units.tr: That by the very fact that someone enters any private religious order whatever, he is made less fit and less able to observe the commands of God.

units.la: Quod sancti instituentes religiones priuatas quascunque tam possessionatorum, quàm mendicantium, in sic instituendo peccauerunt.
units.tr: That the saints who founded private religious orders of any kind, whether of landed or of mendicant orders, sinned in so founding them.

units.la: Quòd religiosi viuentes in religionibus priuatis, non sunt de religione christiana.
units.tr: That religious living in private orders are not of the Christian religion.

units.la: Quòd fratres teneantur, per laborem manuum, & non per mendicationem, victum suum acquirere.
units.tr: That brothers ought to earn their living by the labour of their hands, and not by begging.

units.la: Quòd conferës eleemosynâ fratribus, uel fratri prædicanti, est excommunicatus, & recipiens.
units.tr: That whoever gives alms to friars, or to a friar who preaches, is excommunicated, and so is the one who receives them.

units.la: Damnatis his ergo conclusionibus bus in concilio terræmotus (utap-pellitat Vuicleuus) datum est in mā datis Rob. Ryggæo, ut eius minifte rio publice per Academiam diuul-getur conclusionū damnatio. At cā-cellarius propensior, ut uidebatur, in partes Vuicleuianas, fauit, quod po tuit, ueritatis incolumitati, multa dis-simulans, atqz indulgens, promouēs qúe simul pro oportunitate laboran tem euangelij causam. Sicubi incide ret ut habendæ essent conciones mul titudini, rem potius committebat iss, quos in Vuicleuū rescierat addictio res. Inter quos, cuidā Repyngtono delegata est ea tepestate prædicandi prouincia, in ipso corporis festo, ubi inter multa hæc prodidisse fertur.
units.tr: These conclusions, then, having been condemned in the council called the earthquake (as Wycliffe calls it), were entrusted to Robert Rygge, so that the condemnation of the conclusions might be published publicly through the University by his ministry. The chancellor, however, seemed rather inclined toward the Wycliffite side, and did what he could for the safety of the truth, dissembling and indulging in many things, and at the same time promoting, as opportunity allowed, the cause of the gospel. Wherever it happened that sermons were to be given to the crowd, he preferred to entrust the business to those whom he had found devoted to Wycliffe. Among these, the province of preaching was then assigned to a certain Repyngton, on the feast of Corpus Christi, when he is said to have put forward many such things.

units.la: Quicunqz recommendat papam, uel episcopos, ante Dominos tempo rales, facit contra scripturam sacram.
units.tr: Whoever recommends the pope or the bishops before temporal lords acts against holy Scripture.

units.la: Item quod Mag. Vuicleuus est doctor maxime catholicus.
units.tr: Likewise, that Master Wycliffe is a most catholic teacher.

units.la: Quod nunc Vuicleuus aliter de territerminauit,uel docuit, in materia de sacramento altaris,quàm tota ecclesia Dei tenet.
units.tr: That Wycliffe now determined or taught otherwise, on the matter of the sacrament of the altar, than the whole Church of God holds.

units.la: Quòd opinio ipsius de sacramento altaris esset uerissima.
units.tr: That his opinion concerning the sacrament of the altar was most true.

units.la: In peroratione denique in hanc sententiam dimisit populum.
units.tr: Finally, in his closing address, he dismissed the people with this sentiment.

units.la: In doctrina autem speculatiua, cuiusmodi est materia de sacramento altaris,ponam,inquit,custodiam ori meo,donec Deus aliter illustrauerit uel instruxerit corda cleri.
units.tr: But in speculative doctrine, such as the matter of the sacrament of the altar is, he said: "I will set a guard over my mouth until God shall enlighten or instruct the hearts of the clergy otherwise."

units.la: Quibus rebus exasperatus Archipontifex, iterum collecto magistrorum coetu, accersi iussit Ryggaeum Cancellarium,simulque procuratores I. Huntemanum, & Gualt. Dafchus una cum altero M.Brytuuello,in quos septem suspiciones, seu euidentias, ut appellare maluit,intentabat,conuicturus eos Vuicleuianę factionis. Illi primum tergiuersando,excusando,ac ambiguis uerborum sensibus, elabi
units.tr: Exasperated by these things, the archbishop, having again gathered an assembly of masters, ordered that the chancellor Rygge be summoned, together with the proctors John Huntington and Walter Daustin, along with another Master Brytwell, against whom he intended to bring seven suspicions, or evidences, as he preferred to call them, in order to convict them of the Wycliffite faction. At first they slipped away by evasion, excuse, and the ambiguous senses of words.

units.la: Huntemanus & Dafchus procurat. academ. elabi enitentes,cum id non succede-ret,sententiam tandē simpliciter profiteri cogebantur, facta prius protestatione,in qua, inuiti concedebant cunctas illas conclusiones intelligendo eas,ut uerba sonant,uel hæreticas uel erroneas. Cancellarius aduolutis genibus ueniam apprecans, inter cessione episcopi Vuinto, impetrat immunitatem,sub hac tamen dimissus lege, ut domū reuersus inita per Academiam inquisitione cōpescerēt, quoscunq; Vuicleui Herfordi, Repyngtoni,aftoni,aut Bednami re periret fautores, simulq; damnatas Vuicleui conclusiones in summo templo publicaret, cæteris ad purgationem, aut abiurationem impulsis, si quos huic nactus esset factioni affines. Cui quum Cancellarius uicisim,id se mortis metu minime audere respondere et. Quid, inquit Archipontifex, Adeon Oxonia ergo hæreseon fautrix est, ubi veritas catholica
units.tr: Huntington and Daustin, the university proctors, struggling to slip away, when this did not succeed, were at last compelled to profess the sentence plainly, after first making a protestation in which, unwillingly, they conceded all those conclusions, understood as their words sound, to be either heretical or erroneous. The chancellor, kneeling and begging pardon, obtained immunity through the intercession of Bishop Wine, but was dismissed on this condition: that on returning home he should, after an inquiry conducted through the University, suppress whatever supporters of Wycliffe, Hereford, Repyngton, Aston, or Bedeman he might find, and should publish the condemned conclusions of Wycliffe in the principal church, while others were driven to purgation or abjuration, if he had found any of them connected with this faction. When the chancellor in turn replied that he dared not answer this for fear of death, the archbishop said: "What, then, is Oxford so much a favourer of heresy that Catholic truth cannot be published there?"

units.la: Oxonia hæreseos notæ infamia lica publicari nequeat?
units.tr: Oxford, with the infamy of the mark of heresy?

units.la: Postridie re ad consilium dellata per Archipræsulem, demum à regio senatu accepit in mandatis cancellarius, ut Archiepiscopi mandatu quam obnixissime exequeretur. Cum his mandatis domum redit cancellarius. Ibi impotentius odia inter partes gliscere coeperunt. Atqui religio sis potissimum infensi infestique omnes reddebantur, quibus hic quicquid excitatum est tragœdiarum, ceu autoribus, unice imputabatur. Inter hos quidam erat Henr.Crompeius monachus Cistertiensis theologiæ candidatus, qui postea hæreseos postulatus est ab episcopis. Is quia id temporis hereticos est ausus Iollardos appellare, ab actibus suis, (ut cum scho lis loquar) publice suspenditur per cancellarium. Profectus is ilico Londinum querelam Archiepiscopo suo exponit, ercofilio regis. Unde iterum accersitus cancellarius cum pro cura
units.tr: The next day the matter was referred by the archbishop to the council, and at last the chancellor received from the royal senate instructions that he should carry out the archbishop's orders as earnestly as possible. With these instructions the chancellor returned home. There the hatred between the parties began to blaze more violently. And indeed all the religious orders were made especially hostile and unfriendly, since on them alone was blamed, as the authors, whatever tragedies had been stirred up here. Among these was a certain Henry Crompe, a Cistercian monk and candidate in theology, who was later charged with heresy by the bishops. Because at that time he dared to call the heretics Lollards, he was publicly suspended from his acts by the chancellor (to speak with the schools). Setting out at once for London, he laid his complaint before his archbishop and the king's council. Whereupon the chancellor was summoned again.

units.la: Ryggæus cancellarius, iterum accersitus ante praesules. turatoribus, regis et consilij nomine sed pōtificis instinctu, noua accepit mandata, ad inuestigandos, persequendosq; hæreticos. Ibi Philipp. Repyngtonus & Nic. Herfordus clam admoniti per cancellarium, statim ad D. Ioannem Lancastriæ Ducem se receperunt. Sed ab illo repulsi ad cesuram Archiepiscopi, ab equis, quod aiunt, ad asinos sunt relegati. Verum de ijs aliàs. Interim quid de Vuicleuo sit factum nihil certi constat, nisi ex Vualdeno colligere liceat, abactū fuisse in exilium. Unde denuo reuersus in parochia sua, Luterworthæ, cum ius ipse agebat pastorem, obdormi- uit in Domino, an. 1387. die Silue-stri. Qui demum post quadragesimum primum obitus sui annum, exhumatus iussu pontificis, igni tradi-tus, inde & in aquā proiectus est, in tria resolutus elementa, in terrā, igne, et aquam, metuentibus opinor episc. quod
units.tr: Rygge the chancellor, summoned again before the prelates and the commissioners, in the name of the king and council but at the urging of the pontiff, received new instructions to search out and prosecute the heretics. There Philip Repyngton and Nicholas Hereford, privately warned by the chancellor, at once withdrew to John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster. But repulsed by him, they were sent back, under the archbishop's censure, from horses, as they say, to asses. But of these men elsewhere. Meanwhile, nothing certain is known of what became of Wycliffe, except that it may be gathered from Walden that he was driven into exile. Returning from there again to his parish at Lutterworth, where he himself performed the duties of pastor, he fell asleep in the Lord in the year 1387, on the feast of Silvester. Afterwards, forty-one years after his death, by order of the pontiff he was exhumed, burned, and then thrown into water, dissolved into the three elements, earth, fire and water, the bishops, I suppose, fearing what the Pharisees once feared when burying Christ, that something might happen that would bring him back to life.

units.la: Lancastriæ Dux quod olim maiores sui metuerant pharisaei in sepeliendo Christo, ne qua foret ut reuiuisceret. Sed Christus in suis no moritur, quantum uis isti non in uiuos solum, sed & in mortuos desaeuiant phalarides.
units.tr: The Duke of Lancaster ... What the Pharisees once feared in burying Christ, lest there be some means by which he might revive. But Christ does not die in his own people; however much these Phalarides rage, they rage not only against the living but also against the dead.

units.la: Scripserat Vicleuus hic opuscula complura, quae Oxoniae ann. 1410. in ignem iniecta conflagrarunt, pre sidente cancellario Abbate Salopie. Vtinam hanc nobis felicitatem fata non inuidissent. Quanquam hoc nomine haud uulgari laude dignus est I. Balaeus, cuius exquisitissima cura, ac inuestigatione effectum est, ut non modo tituli ac argumenta librorum, sed & monumenta, ut audio, nonnulla uindicentur e tenebris: uir nec hac solum parte de studiis melioribus benemeritus. Inter caetera non praeteriemus silentio epistolam huius quandam ad Vrbanum 6. missam. Ann. 1584. in qua se purgat, quod iussus Romam appellere
units.tr: This Wycliffe had written many little works, which were burned in a fire thrown into them at Oxford in the year 1410, the chancellor Abbot of Shrewsbury presiding. Would that the fates had not grudged us this good fortune. Nevertheless, John Bale deserves no common praise for this, whose most exquisite care and investigation have brought it about that not only the titles and subjects of the books, but also, as I hear, some monuments are being rescued from darkness; a man who has deserved well of better studies in this respect too. Among other things, we shall not pass over in silence a letter of his, sent to Urban VI in the year 1384, in which he excuses himself for not coming to Rome when ordered to appear, and at the same time sets out a brief confession of his faith. The copy of the letter reads as follows.

units.la: {*} Balaeus. lere non uenerít. exposita simul bre ui fidei suæ confessione. Exemplar epistolæ sic habet.
units.tr: {*} Balaeus. ... did not come. The text of the letter reads as follows.

units.la: EPISTOLA I. VVICLEVI AD Vrbanum 6. pp. missa an. 1384.
units.tr: Letter I. Of Wyclif to Urban VI, sent in the year 1384.

units.la: GAVDEO PLANE DETEGEre cuicunqʒ fidem meam quàm teneo, & specialiter Rom. pontifici. Quia suppono, quòd sit orthodoxa, ipse fidem meam humiliter confirmabit, & si sit erronea emendabit. Suppono autem, quòd euangelium Christi sit corpus legis Dei. Christũ autem, qui euangelium illud immediate dederat, credo esse uerum Deum, & uerum hominem, & in hoc, legem euangelij omnes partes scripturæ aliàs excedentem. Suppono iterum, quod Rom. pontifex cum sum mus Christi uicarius in terris sit, ad illam legem euangelij inter uiantes maximè obligatus. Maioritas enim
units.tr: I am glad to make plain to anyone my faith, which I hold, and especially to the Roman pontiff. Since I suppose it to be orthodox, he will humbly confirm my faith, and if it is erroneous he will correct it. I suppose, moreover, that the gospel of Christ is the body of God's law. I believe that Christ, who gave that gospel directly, is true God and true man, and in this the law of the gospel surpasses all other parts of Scripture. I suppose again that the Roman pontiff, since he is the vicar of Christ on earth, is most bound to that law of the gospel while he is a wayfarer. For greatness among Christ's disciples is measured not by worldly magnitude but by imitation of Christ in conduct.

units.la: E inter Christi discipulos non penes magnitudinem mundanam, sed penes Christi imitationem in moribus mensuratur. Iterum ex isto cordelegis domini, patet er elicio, quod Christus fuit pro tempore huius uiatio-nis, homo pauperrimus, omnem dominationem mundanam abijciens, patet per fidem euangelij, Mat. 8. & 2. Cor. 8. Ex istis communiter elicio, quod nec ipsum papam, nec aliquem sanctorum debet fidelis aliquis imitari, nisi de quanto ipse imitatus fuerit Dominum Iesum Christum. Nam Petrus & filij zebedei cupiendo dignitatem mundanam contra istam imitationem deliquerant: Ideo non sunt in istis erroribus imitandi. Ex istis elicio tanquam concilium, quod papa dimittat seculari brachio dominium temporale, & ad hoc clerum suume efficaciter exhortetur. Sic enim Christus fecit, signanter per suos apostolos. Si autem in istis errauero, uolo humiliter etiam per morte, si oporteat, emendari. Et si in persona propria ad uotum potero laborare, uellem praesentiam Rom. pontifi cis humiliter uisitare. Sed Dominus me necessitauit ad contrarium, et communiter me docuit, plus Deo quàm hominibus obedire. Cum autem Dominus dederit papę nostro instinctus iustos euangelicos, rogare debemus, quòd instinctus illi non per subdolum concilium extinguantur, nec quòd papa aut cardinales aliquid agere contra legem Domini moueantur. Igitur rogamus Deum nostrum cuiuslibet creaturę quòd sic excitet papam nostrum Vrbanum, 6. ut incoeperat, ut imitetur cum clero suo etiam in moribus Dominum Iesum Christū, ut ipsi efficaciter doceant populum in hoc fideliter ipsos imitari. Et rogemus specialiter papam nostram a maligno consilio preseruari: quòd iterum cognoscimus, quod inimici homines domesticiėus. Et Dominus non permittet nos tentari supra id quod possumus, multo plus a nulla creatura requirit, ut faciat quod non potest. Cum illa sit patens conditio antichristi.
units.tr: Again, from this heart of the Lord's law it is plain, and I deduce, that Christ, for the time of this pilgrimage, was a most poor man, casting off all worldly lordship. This is plain through the faith of the gospel, Matt. 8 and 2 Cor. 8. From these things I commonly deduce that no faithful man ought to imitate the pope himself or any of the saints, except insofar as he has imitated the Lord Jesus Christ. For Peter and the sons of Zebedee sinned against this imitation by desiring worldly dignity; therefore they are not to be imitated in those errors. From these things I deduce, as advice, that the pope should relinquish temporal dominion to the secular arm, and should effectively exhort his clergy to do the same. For so Christ did, notably through his apostles. If I err in these things, I wish to be humbly corrected, even by death if need be. And if I am able, in person, to labour as I wish, I would gladly visit the presence of the Roman pontiff in humility. But the Lord has compelled me to the contrary, and has generally taught me to obey God rather than men. Since the Lord has given our pope just evangelical impulses, we ought to ask that those impulses not be extinguished by crafty counsel, nor that the pope or the cardinals be moved to do anything against the law of the Lord. Therefore we ask our God, the Creator of every creature, that he so stir up our pope Urban VI, as he had begun, to imitate the Lord Jesus Christ in conduct along with his clergy, so that they may effectively teach the people to imitate them faithfully in this. And let us especially ask that our pope be preserved from evil counsel, since we know again that a man's enemies are those of his own household (Matt. 10). And the Lord will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (1 Cor. 10); much less does he require of any creature that it do what it cannot. Since that is the plain condition of Antichrist.

units.la: Nec illud fortasse cognitione indignū, quod Ricardo 2. Angliæ Regi in primo regni sui anno ab illo scitanti respondisse dicitur Vuicleuus.
units.tr: Nor perhaps is it unworthy of being known what Wyclif is said to have replied to King Richard II of England in the first year of his reign, when the king asked him.

units.la: RESPONSVM VVICLEVI AD RICARD. 2. de iure Regis & papæ.
units.tr: Wyclif's answer to King Richard II on the right of the king and the pope.

units.la: QVAESITVM AVTEM EST utrum Regnum Angliæ possit legitime, imminente necessitate suæ defensionis thesaurum regni detinere, ne deferatur ad exteros, etiam Domino papa sub poena censurarū, & virtute obedientiæ hoc petente. Vuicleuus. Relicto uiris peritis quid dici debet in ista materia, secundum ius canonicum, secundum ius Angliæ,uel ciuile: solum restat persuadere partem affirmatiuam dubij, secundum principia legis Christi. Principio sic, Omne corpus naturale habet à Deo potentiam resistendi suo contrario, et conseruandi se in esse de bito, ut nouerunt philosophi, in tantum, quod corpora inanimata ornantur tali potentia, ut patet de lapide, cui datur duritiēs ad resistendū frangentibus, & frigiditas ad resistendū calido dissoluenti. Cum ergo regnū Angliæ ad modum loquendi scripturæ debet esse unum corpus: atque clerici, et communitas eius membra, videtur quod ipsum regnum habet à Deo potentiam talem datam, & eo signatius, quo corpus illud est Deo preciosius uirtute & scientia praeornatum. Cum ergo non datur à Deo alicui creaturæ potestas ad aliquid, nisi qua potestate possit ad illud uti legitime, sequitur quod regnum nostrum potest legitime detinere thesaurum suum, pro sua defensione in quocunque casu, in quo necessitas hoc requirit.
units.tr: The question is whether the kingdom of England may lawfully keep back the treasure of the realm when necessity threatens its defence, so that it is not carried off to foreigners, even if the lord pope demands it under penalty of censures and in virtue of obedience. Wyclif: Setting aside what learned men should say on this matter according to canon law, the law of England, or civil law, it remains only to persuade the affirmative side of the doubt by the principles of Christ's law. First, thus: every natural body has from God the power to resist its contrary and to preserve itself in its due being, as the philosophers know, so much so that even inanimate bodies are endowed with such power. This is plain of stone, which is given hardness to resist things that break it, and coldness to resist the hot agent that dissolves it. Since, then, the kingdom of England, in the manner of speaking of Scripture, ought to be one body, and the clergy and the commonalty are its members, it seems that the kingdom itself has been given such power by God, and all the more so because that body is more precious to God and adorned with virtue and knowledge. Since God gives no power to any creature for anything except such power as it can lawfully use for that thing, it follows that our kingdom can lawfully keep back its treasure for its defence in whatever case necessity requires it.

units.la: Secundo probatur idem ex parte legis Euangelicæ. Nam dominus papa non potest uendicare thesaurum huius sine titulo eleemosynæ, & per consequens sub forma operum misericordiæ, secundum regulas charitatis. Sed cessare debet omnino in casu posito titulus eleemosynæ, ergo & ius thesaurum regni nostri necessita resupposita uendicandi. Cum enim omnis charitas incipitâ seipsa non est opus charitatis, sed fatuitatis mandare eleemosynas regni ad exteros, ipso regno prætextu illius eleemosynæ succumbente. Quod autem oportet eleemosynam fundare titulum Christi uicarijs in redemptione temporalium, ex hoc patet, quòd Christus caput Ecclesiæ, quem omnes sacerdotes Christiani debent imitari
units.tr: Secondly, the same point is proved from the side of the gospel law. For the lord pope cannot claim the treasure of this kingdom under the title of alms, and so under the form of works of mercy, according to the rules of charity. But in the case supposed the title of alms must cease altogether; therefore the right to claim the treasure of our kingdom, necessity being presupposed, also ceases. For since all charity begins from oneself, it is not a work of charity but of folly to send the alms of the kingdom abroad while the kingdom itself is overwhelmed under the pretext of that alms. That alms must found the title of Christ's vicars in the redemption of temporal things is clear from this: Christ, the head of the Church, whom all Christian priests ought to imitate,

units.la: uixit eleemosynis deuotarum mulie rum,ut patet Lucę 7. 8. Esuriuit e- nim & sitiuit,hospes fuit,& alias ege states sustinuit, nedum in membris, sed in propria persona, sicut restatur Apostolus Cor.8. ita dicens. Pro uo bis egenus factus est,ut illius inopia uos diuites effetis. Vnde in prima dotatione Ecclesiæ,quicunque cleri ci temporalia habebant, secundum formam perpetuæ eleemosinæ, sicut tam chartæ, quàm chronicæ conte- stantur. Vnde beatus Bernardus declarans secundo libro ad Eugeni- um,quòd non potest ex iure successi onis uicarie sancti Petri uendicare se culare dominium,ita scribit. Quod si Ioannes alloqueretur ipsum pa- pam, sicut Bernardus Eugenium, nunquid creditur patienter accep- taret. Esto ut alia tibi uedices, sed nō apostolico iure. Quomodo autē po tuit ille tibi dare quod non habuit:
units.tr: lived on the alms of devout women, as is plain from Luke 7 and 8. For he hungered and thirsted, was a guest, and endured other needs, not only in his members but in his own person, as the Apostle witnesses, 2 Cor. 8, saying: "For your sakes he became poor, that through his poverty you might become rich." Hence in the first endowment of the Church, whoever clerics had temporal goods held them according to the form of perpetual alms, as both charters and chronicles attest. Hence blessed Bernard, declaring in his second book to Eugenius that by right of succession to the vicariate of St Peter he cannot claim secular dominion, writes thus: "But if John were to address the pope himself, as Bernard addressed Eugenius, would he be believed to accept it patiently? Grant that you may claim other things for yourself, but not by apostolic right. How could he give you what he did not have?"

units.la: quòd habuit hoc dedit,sollicitudinẽ super ecclesias. Nunquid dominatisonem? Audi ipsum. Neque dominantes inquit, in clero, sed forma factigregis. Et ne dictum sola humilitate putes,nõ etiam veritate,uox Domini est in euangelio. Reges gentiũ dominantur eorum: uos autem non sic. Plane autem apostolus interdicitur dominatus, ergo & tu usurpare audes? Aut Dominus apostolatum, aut Apostolicus Dominatum plane ab alterutro prohiberis, si utrunque habere uelis perdes utrunque. Alioqui non te exceptũ putes de isto numero, de quibus Deus sic queritur. Ipsi regnauerunt,sed non ex me, princes extiterunt, & ego non cognoui. Iam si sine dominio regnare iuuat,habes gloriam,sed nõ apud Deum. At si interdictum tenemus, audiamus edictum. Qui maior est uefstrum,ait,fiat sicut minor, & qui præcessor est, sicut qui ministrat. Forma aposto-
units.tr: "What he had, he gave: care over the churches. Does he give lordship? Hear him: 'Neither as lording it over the clergy,' he says, 'but being made a pattern for the flock.' And lest you think this said by humility alone and not also by truth, it is the voice of the Lord in the gospel: 'The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them; but you are not so.' Plainly the apostle forbids lordship; do you dare to usurp it too? Either the Lord forbids the apostolate or the apostolic office forbids lordship; you are plainly prohibited from one or the other, and if you wish to have both you will lose both. Otherwise do not think yourself excepted from that number, of whom God complains: 'They reigned, but not by me; they became princes, and I did not know it.' If it pleases you to reign without lordship, you have glory, but not before God. But if we keep to the prohibition, let us hear the edict: 'Let him who is greater among you be as the least, and he who is chief as he who serves.' The apostolic form..."

units.la: Fastus papæ arguitur.
units.tr: The pride of the pope is accused.

units.la: Papa dominans autnõ apostolus, aut apostolus nondominans. apostolica est hæc: Dominatio inter dicitur, indicitur ministratio. Ex ijs uerbis huius beatiss. sanEti,quem co‑lit ecclesia, patet quod Dominus pa‑pa non habet potestatem occupandi bona ecclesiæ, ut Dominus, sed tan‑quam ministrator,& pauperum pro‑curator. Et utinam illud fastuosum crementum dominationis, quam ue‑dicat ista sedes,non sit pręambulum uiam pręparans antichristo. Constat quidem ex euangelio quod Chri‑stus sua paupertate,humilitate,et pas‑sione iniuriæ conquisiuit filios regni sui. Et hûc credo beatû Bernardum, lib.5. ad Eugenium sic alloqui. Nul‑lum tibi uenenum tantum formido, sicut libidinem dominandi. Hæc Vuicleuus,pręter multa id genus fi‑milia, quæ hic breuitatis necessitate præcidimus.
units.tr: The Pope either dominates or is an apostle who does not dominate. The apostolic rule is this: "domination" is forbidden, and "ministry" is enjoined. From these words of this most blessed saint, whom the Church honours, it is clear that the Lord Pope has no power to seize the goods of the Church as a lord would, but only as a steward and a caretaker of the poor. I wish that this proud increase of domination, which this see claims for itself, were not a forerunner preparing the way for Antichrist. It is certainly plain from the Gospel that Christ won the sons of his kingdom by his poverty, humility and the suffering of injuries. And I believe that blessed Bernard, in book 5 to Eugenius, speaks to him thus: "I fear no poison so much as the lust for domination." These are Wiclif's words, along with many other passages of this kind, which for brevity's sake we cut out here.

units.la: Vuicleuus hic etsi in uita complu‑res grauissimoscþ perpessus sit aduer‑sarios, at nullos uirulentiores quàm ex coetu ecclesiastico. Habebat idem tamen & bonos angelos nonnullos, viros non solum ex infimorum forte, sed & aulica dignitate pollentes aliquot. Inter quos ex equestri hireferuntur, Io. Clauuoius, Ludouicus Clyffordus, Ric. Sturius, Tho. Latimerus, Guilielmus Neuilus, I. Montacutus, qui cunctas in ecclesia sua imagines demolitus est. Accedebat & his Comes Salburiensis, in quo sa tis atrociter notatu est, quod in mortem confessionem ac sacramentum altaris papistici indignius repuerunt. Deinde Io. de Northamptonia, Praetor Londinensis, quem ferunt instinctu Vuicleui in fornicarios ac adulteros eius ciuitatis, summo decore, ac exquisitissimis probris onustos, tam acriter animaduertisse, ut non iis modo qui peccarunt pudorem, sed & caeteris peccandi metum fere uniuersis incuteret. Praeda rum profecto exemplum praetoriae fe ueritatis. Quod si pari, cum officio, ad
units.tr: Although Wiclif, in his lifetime, suffered many very grievous adversaries, none was more virulent than those from the ecclesiastical assembly. Nevertheless he also had some good angels, men of influence not only from the lower ranks but several of high court dignity. Among these, from the knightly class, are listed John Clanvow, Lewis Clifford, Richard Sturry, Thomas Latimer, William Neville, and J. Montacute, who tore down all the images in his church. To these was added the Earl of Salisbury, of whom it is fairly shocking to note that at his death they treated the confession and the papistical sacrament of the altar with great indignity. Then there was John of Northampton, Mayor of London, who, they say, at Wiclif's instigation punished the fornicators and adulterers of that city, laden with the greatest disgrace and the most exquisite insults, so severely that he struck fear of sinning into almost everyone, not only shame into those who had sinned. Truly this was a notable example of praetorian firmness. But if our ancestors had imitated, or were now imitating, this example of punishing adulterers with equal duty and vigilance, things would surely, I think, be conducted more blamelessly according to Christian morals, and we would either not have fallen into, or would still be warding off, this fatal storm of evils by which the English realm is today so wretchedly shaken.

units.la: De plectendis adulteri exemplum iuncta uigilantia imitati essent, aut nunc imitarentur maiores nostri, inculpatius equidē, ut opinor, cū Christianorū moribus ageretur, simul & fatale hanc malorū tempestatem, quibus tā misere hodie cōcutitur anglię imp. aut nō incidissemus, aut adhuc propelleremus. Nūc uero dū augurijs attendunt Principes, Episcopi ἱερεῖς, ambitione insaniunt theologi, occidūtur prophetę. Magnates lasciuiūt, cōniuent magistratus, uulgus in oēm ruit licentiā, stupra, repudia, adulteria, auaritia, fraus, temulentia, cōtentio, crapula, usura, periuria, cū omni deniq; uitiorū segete, uelut effractis claustris, qua data porta ruit: quid mirū, si luxatis undiq; reip. cōpagibus, ruinā demū ac περιπατεῖν spectare omnia uideantur. Atq; hactenus satis opinor malis miserīsque edocti edidicimus, quid sit in manus Domini incidere, quid sit abuti Euangelio ipsius. Tempus nūc postulat, ut pertæsi corruptelas nostras, iram Dei uertamus tandem in misericordiam. Id fiet si uita in me lius correcta, uitia in uirtutes ipsi pri us commutabimus. Verum hac de re alius erit (Christo permittente) dis seredi locus. Nunc ad fautores Vuiclei redeamus: quibus praeterea accensetur D. Cobhamus, qui aperte profiteri auditus est, quemadmodum ex Vualdeno autore constat, peccatum se nunquam ex animo odisse, priusquam Vuicleui doctrina hac imbueretur. Atque hi primarij quidem omnes. Nec deerant etiam apud ignobiles, qui dogmata illius obnixius propugnarent, sed potissimum Oxonienses, e quibus nullus tamen fine aliquo stigmate immunis euasit, quin ad palinodiam aut sit adactus turpiter, aut ad ignem crudeliter adiudicatus.
units.tr: Now, however, while princes attend to augury, bishops [ἱερεῖς] ... theologians rave with ambition, and prophets are killed. The magnates grow wanton, magistrates connive, and the common people rush into every licence: debauchery, repudiation, adultery, avarice, fraud, drunkenness, strife, gluttony, usury, perjury, and finally every harvest of vices, as if the barriers were broken and they rush through any gate that is open. Is it any wonder, if on all sides the joints of the commonwealth are dislocated, that all things seem to be heading towards ruin, and, as it were, walking [περιπατεῖν] towards it? And so far, I think, we have been taught by evils and miseries well enough, and have learned what it is to fall into the hands of the Lord, and what it is to abuse his Gospel. The time now demands that, weary of our corruptions, we at last turn the anger of God into mercy. This will happen if, having corrected our life for the better, we first change our vices into virtues. But there will be another place to discuss this matter (Christ permitting). Now let us return to Wiclif's supporters: to them is also reckoned Lord Cobham, who was heard to declare openly, as is clear from the author Walden, that he had never truly hated sin in his heart until he was imbued with Wiclif's doctrine. These were all the chief men. Nor were there lacking among the lowborn those who defended his doctrines more stubbornly, but especially the men of Oxford, of whom none, however, escaped without some stigma, since he was either shamefully forced to recant or cruelly condemned to the fire.

units.la: DE ROB. RYGGAEO CANCELLARIO. Herfordo. & Ph. Repyngtono.
units.tr: On Robert Rygge, the chancellor; Herford; and Philip Repyngton.

units.la: AC DE HERFORDO ET REPYNpyngtono supra insparsimus quæ-dam. Nunc hic locus admonet, ut hi-storiam altius pleniusq; repetitā per sequamur. Quanquam ne hic qui-dem satis licebit indulgere prolixi-ti. Non enim locos tractamus com-munes, sed catalogū scribimus, ubi de omnibus potius quam omnia di-cendum sit. Herfordus ergo hic quū diu fauebat fouebatq; Vuicleui par-tes, primum in suspicionem uenit a-pud aduersarios, mox ubi liberius profiteri coeperat quædam, quæ ad defensionem Vuicleui tendebant. Hinc infestiores iam illi, Carmelitæ ac religiosorum ordines reddit i,non paucas impegerunt hęreses ex ipsius excerptas sermonibus, acin certam formam per notarios redactas, ope-ra cuiusdam Petri Stokisei carmeli-tæ: ut hoc hominum genus semper ad lites ac clamores accinctū est, quasi uni huic officio natū, alioqui pror-sus inutile. Huiusmodi quiddam de arane-
