units.tr: We have touched above on some matters concerning Herford and Repyngton. This place now reminds us to go back over the history more fully and at greater length. Yet even here we shall not be allowed to indulge in long digressions. For we are not treating common topics but writing a catalogue, in which one must speak about all things rather than about everything. Herford, then, who for a long time favoured and supported Wycliffe's cause, first fell under suspicion with his adversaries, and then, once he had begun to profess more openly certain things that tended to defend Wycliffe, they grew more hostile to him. The Carmelites and the orders of religious men then brought against him no small number of heresies, drawn from his sermons and reduced to a fixed form by notaries, through the work of a certain Peter Stokesey, a Carmelite. So this kind of men is always girded for quarrels and clamour, as if born for this one office, and otherwise quite useless.

units.la: aranearum natura tradunt physiolo-gi, quod hæ quicquid sit in herbis læ-tiferum, exugunt, ac in uenenū con-uertunt. Ar cuculliones isti hoc no-mine omnes araneas antecedunt, qui non solum, quod in homine est pessimum uenantur, ac rodunt, sed ex opinionibus ὀρθολοξάτως, schismata conficiunt, ac hęreses. Tanta est ar-tis procliuitas, natura ubi adiuuat.
units.tr: Natural philosophers tell of a certain quality of spiders: whatever is deadly in herbs, they suck out and turn into poison. But these hooded fellows surpass all spiders in this respect. They hunt out and gnaw at not only what is worst in a man, but also, from opinions [ὀρθολοξάτως], they manufacture schisms and heresies. So great is the readiness of the craft where nature lends its help.

units.la: Demum anno 1382. euenit ut Ni-colao publice in Cœmiterio Fridef-uuidæ sermocinandum esset ad ple-bem, festum erat assensionis. Hic ite-rum Herfordo noua intentatur schis-mata, quod publicitus Vuicleuum tueri ausus sit: uirum fidum, bonum ac innocentem. Iam quoque appetebat se-stum Corporis, quo die, ut diximus, expectabatur Repyngtoni concio. Erat hic canonicus Licestrensis, iam quæ primum gradum fecerat ad Do-ctoratum, quo tempore concionem ad Braclenses quandam habuit, ob quam
units.tr: At last, in the year 1382, it happened that Nicholas was to preach publicly to the people in the cemetery of Friday Street, on the feast of the Ascension. Here again new schisms were charged against Herford, because he had dared to defend Wycliffe in public: a faithful, good and innocent man. The feast of Corpus Christi was also drawing near, the day on which, as we said, a sermon by Repyngton was expected. He was a canon of Leicester who had already taken the first step toward the doctorate. At that time he gave a sermon to the Brackley men, on account of which he was made hateful and suspect to the Pharisees.

units.la: Repingto-nus. quam pharisæis inuisus, suspectusq; reddebatur. Cæterum obingenij nigueum quendam, quem omnibus ubi que præ se tulit, cum pari comitatum modestia, candorem, uel superauit, uel temperauit certe hanc Nemesin: moxq; in Doctoratum publica theatri approbatione adoptatus est. Qui simul atq; iam sumpta Doctoris persona, in scenam tandem, fabulam saltaturus, prodiit: coepit protinus bene caelatum ac dissimulatum ingenium prodere, publice attestatus, Vuide-uum se in omni materia morali defensurum. De re uero sacramentaria Pythagorisare uelle, donec Dominus afflasset cleri animos. Hunc ergo Babylonij, quum breui concionaturum intellexerant, subuertentes ne ulcera religionis non satis ciuiliter perfricaret, cum Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi egerunt, ut hoc ipso die, sub concione Philippi, in publico totius collectæ uniuersitatis consessu, conclusiones Vuicleui, priuatim condemnatę, publice diffamarentur. Satis astutum commentum, siquid tamen humana astutia polleret aduersus consilii Domini. Breuiter. Data resest Petro Stokyseo. Hic triarius erat pseudo-sacerdotum miles, acunicus gallinæ filius albæ. Simulqz datæ literæ ad cancellarium uti is patrocinio suo asset Petro in publicandis conclusionibus. Cancellarius erat hoc tempore, (ut prædiximus) Rob. Rygge us, qui occulte, sed sedulo, quicquid potuit, adnitebatur in promouenda euangelij causa. Is acceptis Archiepiscopi literis, simul intellecta Carmelitæ impia molitione, maiorem in modum exacerbatus est in fratercu-lum, expostulans cum eo, suiquesi-milibus, nec immerito, de perturbato uniuersitatis statu, quodqz per eos priuilegia ac immunitates huius scholæ eneruari diceret: affirmans nec
units.tr: Yet by a certain brilliant cleverness, which he displayed to everyone everywhere, together with a corresponding modesty and candour, he either surpassed or at least tempered this Nemesis. Soon he was admitted to the doctorate by the public approval of the hall. As soon as he had assumed the role of doctor and came out on the stage, as if about to dance in a play, he at once began to reveal the talent he had so well concealed and disguised, publicly declaring that he would defend Wycliffe in every moral matter, but that on the sacramentarian question he wished to play the Pythagorean until the Lord breathed on the minds of the clergy. The Babylonians, learning that he would soon preach, feared that he would rub the sores of religion too roughly. So they dealt with the Archbishop of Canterbury that on this very day, under Philip's sermon, in the public assembly of the whole gathered university, the conclusions of Wycliffe, condemned in private, should be publicly denounced. It was a rather clever contrivance, if human cleverness could prevail against the counsel of the Lord. In short, letters were given to Peter Stokesey. He was a soldier of the pseudo-priests, and a cockerel, the son of a white hen. At the same time, letters were sent to the chancellor so that he would support Peter in publishing the conclusions. The chancellor at this time was (as we said before) Robert Rygge, who, quietly but diligently, did whatever he could to advance the cause of the gospel. When he received the Archbishop's letters, and at the same time understood the Carmelite's impious scheme, he was roused to greater anger against the little friar. He reproached him, and others like him, not without reason, for the disturbed state of the university, and said that through such men the privileges and immunities of this school were being weakened. He affirmed that neither the bishop nor the archbishop would have authority over that university, not even in a heresy case.

units.la: P. Stokyseus antefi gnanus pa pistarum.
units.tr: Peter Stokesey, forerunner of the Papists.

units.la: Ryggæus Oxoniæ cancellarius. nec Episcopo nec Archiepiscopo su per uniuersitatem illam imperium, ne in haeresis quidem actione, futu-rum. Demum habita deliberatione, Cancellarius cum procuratoribus, aliisque regentibus, et non regentibus, aperte nec dissimulanter dictitabat, nullo se pacto Carmelitę in hoc nego-cio affuturum. Quid multis? Con-scendit ad concionę Philippus. Vbi inter caetera haec praecipue sutorio atramento notata sunt. Quod affere-ret Dominos temporales debere pri-us recommendari in sermonibus quam papa, vel episcopos. Deinde quod dux Lancastriae multum hac in cau-sa afficeretur, uelletque istiusmodi quoscunque in clientelam complecti: praeter alia quae in Vuicleui laudem ac defensionem attingebantur.
units.tr: Rygge, chancellor of Oxford. At length, after deliberation, the chancellor, together with the proctors and the other regents and non-regents, openly and without disguise declared that the Carmelite would in no way take part in this business. In short, Philip mounted the pulpit. Among the other things, these points were especially marked as crude: that he asserted temporal lords ought to be commended in sermons before the pope or the bishops; and that the Duke of Lancaster was greatly moved by this cause and wished to take such men into his following; besides other things that touched on the praise and defence of Wycliffe.

units.la: Exacta demum concione Philip-pus se in ecclesiam Fridesuuidae rece-pit, stipatus amicis quibusdam (utque inimici insimulabant) tecte sub uestI bus ab armatis. Carmelita metu im-mar tyrij, non ausus prorepere, sese intra templi asylum continuit. Cancellarius & Philippus in aedis prostibulo sese excipientes suauiter, dimissa concione, recesserunt ad sua. Nec parua inde lætitia per totam academiam exorta concione consequuta est. Nec interim conquiescit irrequietus Carmelita, sed primum per commentaria totam rei gestae seriem Archiepiscopo exponit, sua pericula exaggerat, implorato ipsius subsidio, nihil praeter mittens, quod Archiepisc. animum satis sua natura efferuescente, ceu oleo caminū posset excitare. Ad haec post triduū ipse minas, ac herefes spirans, gladiatorio spiritu, uiam in scholas affectat, probaturus (si mulis placet) papam & episcopos oportere antè dominos temporales recommendari. Haec dum magno conatu sed maiori risu agit in scholis frater de carmelo, ascitus per literas ad Archiepiscopum episcopum Londinum proficiscitur. Nec mora. Sequitur Cancellarius cum Brytuuello, purgaturus se, & suos, contra Petri criminationes. Examinati deinde de conclusionibus damnatis, consentiunt tandem, digne damnatas esse. Cancellarius vero de contemptu literarum accusatus, quum refellendo non erat, suppliciter flexis genibus veniam petiit. Quam demum opera (ut diximus) Vuintoniensis, licet aegre, quum exorasset, ac demum dimitterentur cum mandatis quibusdam, ac suspensione haereticorum, statim Philippo & Herfordo excommunicationis mandatum exponit. Illi mox ad Ducem Lancastriae confugiunt praesidii causa. Adsunt illi copontifices, veluti serpentes semper Christi insidiantes calcaneo. Quibus tamen dux, primo satis sed difficile, acerbum praebuit. at postea, nescio quo pacto victus a pontificis, clientes miseros destituit. Illi ab hoc asylo repulsi, atque ad Archiepiscopum religati, ubi iam multis molestiis ac carceribus affecti essent, tandem ad palinodiam duplicem adacti sunt. Quoniam priorem ambiguam propo-suerunt, circa Domini annum 1382. Quorum alter nariis postea sacerdotis donatus est. Repingtonus vero episcopus Lincolniensis, demum ex episcopo persecutor est factus.
units.tr: When the sermon was finished, Philip withdrew into the church of Friday Street, surrounded by some friends (as his enemies alleged, armed men had secretly accompanied him under their clothes). The Carmelite, out of fear of martyrdom, did not dare to creep out, and kept himself within the sanctuary of the church. The chancellor and Philip were received courteously in the hall, and after the sermon they withdrew to their own homes. A considerable joy arose from this throughout the whole university, following the sermon. Meanwhile the restless Carmelite does not rest. First, by written reports, he sets out the whole course of the affair to the Archbishop, magnifies his own dangers, and, having implored his help, sends nothing except what might stir the Archbishop's mind, which of its own nature boils over, as oil might set a furnace ablaze. Then, three days later, breathing threats and heresies, with a gladiatorial spirit, he himself makes his way into the schools, intending to prove (if it pleases the Muses) that the pope and the bishops ought to be commended before temporal lords. While the brother from Carmel does this with great effort but still greater laughter in the schools, he is summoned by letter to the Archbishop and sets out for London, to the Bishop of London. Without delay the chancellor follows, with Brytuuell, to clear himself and his men of Peter's accusations. Afterwards, when examined about the condemned conclusions, they at last agree that they were rightly condemned. The chancellor, accused of contempt of letters, since he could not refute the charge, humbly begged pardon on bended knees. At last, after the Bishop of Winchester had with difficulty persuaded them (as we said), they were released with certain instructions and the suspension of the heretics. At once the mandate of excommunication against Philip and Herford was published. They fled straightaway to the Duke of Lancaster for protection. The pope's men came up, like serpents always lying in wait for Christ's heel. The duke at first showed them a harsh face, though with difficulty; but afterwards, somehow overcome by the pope's men, he abandoned his wretched clients. Driven from this refuge and bound over to the Archbishop, where they were already worn down by many troubles and imprisonments, they were at last forced into a double recantation, since they first proposed an ambiguous one, around the year of the Lord 1382. One of them was afterwards given a parish priesthood. Repyngton, however, was at last made bishop of Lincoln and became a persecutor.

units.la: Erat autem eodem in numero & causa id temporis I. Aston-us artium candidatus, & eleganter doctus. Is etsi in priore confessione non renuebat, panem virtute verborum sacramentalium vere idem corpus esse Christi numero, quod de virgine susceptum est, attamen quia de subiecto & accidente rogatus non respondet simpliciter & categorice, secundum traditionem Romanam de transmutata panis substantia, custodiae seculari traditus, inde in carceres abductus, unde haud unquam emersisse. fisse dicitur, extinctus est. Sed de isto postea.
units.tr: There was also at that time, in the same company and the same cause, I. Aston, a bachelor of arts and an elegant scholar. Although in his earlier confession he did not deny that, by the power of the sacramental words, the bread is truly the same body of Christ in number that was taken from the Virgin, nevertheless, because when asked about the subject and the accident he did not answer simply and categorically, according to the Roman tradition of the transmutation of the bread's substance, he was handed over to secular custody and led thence into prisons, from which he is said never to have emerged, and there he died. But more of him later.

units.la: De Gulielmo Suinderbeo.
units.tr: On William Swinderby.

units.la: Eodem anno Gulielmus Suinderbeus Lincolniensis ὁ προσβύτερος apud episcopum Lincolnienfem haereseos incusatus per Rogerum Sribium Franciscanum, I. Hunclaum Augustinensem, et Th. Blacstonum Dominicanum, cum facta prouocatione ad Regem, parum hic opis affulserat, reductus ad episcopum, petito ad deliberandum spacio, tandem compulsus in celeberrimis Lincolniae ac Lo ceftriae ecclesiis reuocatas abiurat opiniones.
units.tr: In the same year William Swinderby, a Lincolnshire priest [ὁ προσβύτερος], was accused of heresy before the bishop of Lincoln by Roger Sribius the Franciscan, John Hunclaum the Augustinian, and Thomas Blacston the Dominican. He appealed to the King, but received little help there. He was sent back to the bishop, and after asking for time to consider, was finally compelled to abjure his opinions in the most famous churches of Lincoln and Leicester.

units.la: I. Purueus.
units.tr: John Purvey.

units.la: Sub idem tempus I. Purueus Oxoniensis accusationem subiit haereseos. De hoc sic habetur apud Vualdenum Tomo 2. Librarius lollardorum, & Vuicleui glossator, erat Io. Purueus. Dicebat Abrahae adoratio nem salutationem fuisse. Et in tomo 5. Iste I. Purueus cū Herfordo doctoretheologo in carcere de Saltu uod maximis poenis astrictus, tandem palinodiam cecinit Londini ad crucem Diui Pauli sub Th. Arundello Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo. Postea denuo incarceratus fuit sub Henrico Cheycleo Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi anno 1421. Hęc Vualdenus. Huius assertiunculas omnes per Ricardum Lanyngamum eius aduersarium excerptas, dignissimas equidem censerem commemoratione, de Sacramento Eucharistiae, de Sacramento poenitentiae, de Sacro Ordinis, de Potestate clauium, de Praedicatione Euangelij, de Coniugio, de Votis, de Possessionibus, de Correctione cleri, de Legibus & decretis Ecclesiae, de Conditione acta tu papae & cleri. De iis enim uniuersis & acute & grauiter scripta reliquit monumenta. Caeterum quoniam
units.tr: At about the same time John Purvey of Oxford was accused of heresy. Concerning him, this is what Walden reports in volume 2 of his Doctrinale: "The Lollards' librarian and the glossator of Wycliffe was John Purvey. He said that the adoration of Abraham was only a greeting." And in volume 5: "This John Purvey, together with Herford the doctor of theology, was held in prison at Saltwood, and was subjected to very severe punishments. At last he recanted, at London at St Paul's Cross, under Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury. Afterwards he was imprisoned again under Henry Chichele, Archbishop of Canterbury, in the year 1421." So far Walden. I think all of Purvey's little assertions, which Richard Lyngam, his opponent, extracted, are most worthy of mention: on the Sacrament of the Eucharist, on the Sacrament of penance, on sacred orders, on the power of the keys, on the preaching of the Gospel, on marriage, on vows, on possessions, on the correction of the clergy, on the laws and decrees of the Church, and on the condition of the pope and the clergy. For he left writings on all these matters, written both sharply and weightily. But since these matters require a fuller treatment, we will set them aside for now and, Christ willing, give another opportunity later.

units.la: Purueiope ra. niam prolixiorem postulant tractationem, hisce in praesentia intermissis aliam posthac (Christo annuente) daturi sumus oportunitatem.
units.tr: Purvey's ... [see above]

units.la: Hos deinde consecuti Henricus Crompeus, monachus Cisterciensis, qui prius persecutor Vuicleui fuerat, Ricardus Vuythus, Regin. Pecokus episcopus primum Assensis, deinde & Cisterciensis: verum de hoc paulo post explicatius.
units.tr: After these came Henry Crumpe, a Cistercian monk who had earlier been a persecutor of Wycliffe; Richard Wyche; and Reginald Pecock, bishop first of St Asaph and then of Chichester. But of this I shall speak more fully a little later.

units.la: Posthunc deinceps, Anno 1496, complures alij, episcoporum oppressi condemnatione, ad crucem Pauli similiter subierunt poenitentias. Rursus post triennium alij praeterea duodecim. Quin & sequenti anno Prior Diuae Osithae, cum alijs quinque, ad eandem crucem statuuntur reuocaturi opiniones.
units.tr: After him, in the year 1496, several others, oppressed by the condemnation of the bishops, likewise underwent penances at St Paul's Cross. Again, three years later, twelve more did so. Indeed, in the following year the Prior of St Osyth, with five others, was made to stand at the same cross to recant their opinions.

units.la: Habuit praeter hos, Vuicleuus co plures adsectatores, qui etsi a persecutoribus interfecti non sint, uariis tamen modis afflicti uexabantur.
units.tr: Besides these, Wycliffe had many more followers, who, although they were not killed by their persecutors, were nevertheless harassed and troubled in various ways.

units.la: In hoc albo ac scriptoribus recen-sentur Laurentius Redmannus, artium professor, Dauid Sotræus theologus, I. Afchuuarbeus vicarius (ut appellant) Diuæ Mariæ apud Oxonienses, Guil. Iamis, iuuenis eloquenter doctus, Th. Brituuellus, Guiliel. Haulamus leguleus, Rodolp. Grenherstus, I. Scuttus, Petrus Payneus, qui Oxonia Bohemiâ profugiens, strenuè pro utroq; sacramentorum spe cie cum sophistis dimicabat. Philip. Noris, qui à papa Eugenio 4. excommunicatus, anno 1446. ad concilium ὀικουμενικον appellauit.
units.tr: In this roll of martyrs and writers are listed: Lawrence Redman, professor of arts; David Sawtrey, theologian; John Ashwarby, vicar (as they call him) of St Mary's at Oxford; William James, a young man learned in eloquence; Thomas Bristowe; William Hawlam, a lawyer; Rudolph Grenherst; John Scut; Peter Payne, who fled from Oxford to Bohemia and there vigorously fought with the sophists for both kinds in the sacrament; and Philip Nore, who was excommunicated by Pope Eugenius IV and in 1446 appealed to an ecumenical council [ὀικουμενικον].

units.la: De his modo retulimus quibus duntaxat grauis ac periculosa erat euangelicæ veritatis professio, quos tamen non existimaui, suo defraudā dos elogio. Nunc ad istos flectemus orationem, qui ad extrema perdurantes ad uitæ usq; iacturam, agnū secuti sunt, quocunq; iret. Atque hic inprimis liberet, si causæ breuitas pa-teretur,
units.tr: We have so far mentioned only those for whom the profession of evangelical truth was grave and dangerous. Yet I have not thought they should be defrauded of their proper praise. Now I will turn my address to those who, persevering to the end, endured even the loss of life, and followed the Lamb wherever he went. And here, if the brevity of my subject allows, I should like to speak briefly against human cruelty.

units.la: Note: marginal names in left margin: Redmannus. Sotræus. Afchuuarbeus. Guil. Iamis. Brituuellus. Haulamus. Grenherstus. I. Scuttus. P. Payneus. Euangelium ab Angliâ ad Boemos delatum. Ph. Noris. teretur, paucis cum humana crudeli tate expostulare, Postquàm sic mortalium genus, excusso omni humani tatis sensu, usq; adeo ad ferream æta tem, uel ferinam potius immanita tem degenerauit, ut nunquam æ- queopinor à rerum primordijs, lo- cus Plautino prouerbio fuerit. Homo homini lupus. Atque inter hos lupos omnium immanissimi sunt, qui agni se titulo maxime uestiunt, quosque potissimum pacis commen dat professio. Olim apud Israelitas Christi ac apostolorum temporibus cultus ac religio Dei in pharifaismi commutari cœpit. nunc pharifais- mus in phalarismum (nescio quo pa sto) abiit inter Christianos. Quan- quam huius uero incommodi mini- ma profecto portio in eos recidit, qui Christi studio uim ac iniuriam perse runt. Nam cum cæteri omnes mortui sunt, soli hi demum uere uiuunt, qui in Christo moriuntur. Rara itaque nec nisi paucorum dignitas est, atque adeo, si rem integri reputemus, hoc solum habet aerumnosissima alioqui vita haec nostra felix, si cui quid contingat pro Christo pati. Iterum hoc idem repeto. Nihil est in mundo hoc vere magnum, nisi Christi nomine, proque nomine ipsius ὁ ϑάνατος ... Unde non absurde a Paulo, gloriae tributum est, non solum quod per illum fiduciam, sed & afflictionem sustineamus. Utcunque hominum iudicia rem metiuntur, nulla verior est vita, quam quae Christo ceu depositum committitur, nulla absolutior gloria, quam pro filio dei violari. Sed gloria haec humanis sensibus mundi huius coeno obuolutis, minus adhuc apparet. Apparebit aliquando, ac citius forsan, quam expediet quibusdam, nisi matura poenitentia, ad meliorem frugem resipiscant. Quod quo facilius fieri possit, pace tua liceat (amice lector) paulisper cum his τοῖς μαρτυροφορταῖς agere, quo vel admoniti resipiscant. piscantur, uel si minus uelint, ipsi salte nephariam crudelitate suam, ac stra- ges hominum, uelut e theatro produ- ctas, magno pudore suo, uel inuiti co- tuentur. Praeclara profecto mimi uox illa, prophani alioqui hominis: Principi, inquit, turpia sunt no minus multa supplicia, quam medico multa funera. Et quid tu dicemus reuerendis istis ecclesiae praesidibus? Si principes sint, unde tot in Christi caulas inuecta supplicia? Si medici, unde tot ouium funera? Verum priusquam lite hanc adoriar, iterum iterumque te moneo (pie lector) quod et subinde mihi in hoc argumento repetendum est. Primum ne quid hic ita interpreteris, quasi dogmatibus usque impiis batis fomentum praebeat. Vt heretici sque ueri sunt non faueo, ita falsis sane epistulis multo minus. Rursus, ut neutris horum, neque his ad tyrannidem, nec illis ad errorem licentia laxo, sic neque potestate etiam gladii ciuilis hic uelli co, quod haud frustra gestat a magistratibus.
units.tr: Since the human race, having cast off all human feeling, has so degenerated into an iron age, or rather a savage brutality, that, as I believe, the saying of Plautus, "Man is a wolf to man," has never been truer since the beginnings of things, and among these wolves the most savage are those who most clothe themselves in the title of lambs, and who most commend themselves by the profession of peace. Long ago among the Israelites, in the times of Christ and the apostles, the worship and religion of God began to be changed into Pharisaism; now Pharisaism has passed among Christians into a [...] I know not what kind of pastry. Yet the smallest portion of this evil certainly falls on those who, for the sake of Christ, suffer violence and injury. For when all others are dead, these alone truly live, who die in Christ. Rare, then, and granted to few, is this dignity; and indeed, if we consider the matter rightly, this alone makes our otherwise most miserable life happy: that one suffers something for Christ. I repeat this again. Nothing in this world is truly great except in the name of Christ, and for his name, [ὁ θάνατος] ... Hence it is not absurd that Paul ascribed to us glory, not only because through him we have confidence, but also because we endure affliction. However human judgements measure these things, no life is truer than that which is committed to Christ as a deposit, and no glory is more complete than to be wronged for the Son of God. But this glory, wrapped in the mire of this world and obscured to human senses, appears even less. It will appear at some time, and perhaps sooner than it will be convenient for some, unless by timely repentance they come to a better mind. So that this may be done more easily, let me, with your leave, dear reader, speak a little with these those martyr-bearers [τοῖς μαρτυροφορταῖς], so that, admonished, they may come to their senses; or, if they will not, that at least they may see their own wicked cruelty and the slaughter of men, displayed as if in a theatre, with great shame to themselves, even against their will. Truly that saying of a mime, a man otherwise profane, is notable: "For a prince," he says, "many punishments are no less shameful than many funerals are for a doctor." And what shall we say to those reverend leaders of the Church? If they are princes, whence so many punishments inflicted on Christ's flock? If they are physicians, whence so many deaths of sheep? But before I take up this quarrel, I warn you again and again, dear reader, as I must repeatedly do on this subject: first, do not interpret anything here as if it gave encouragement to impious dogmas. As I do not favour heretics, so much less do I favour false teachings. Again, as I grant licence to neither of these, neither to tyranny for the one nor to error for the other, so here I do not wish to touch even the power of the civil sword, which magistrates rightly bear.

units.la: Habent ij suas leges, suos iudices, adeoque necessaria in rep. suppli cia: sine quibus nulla vitae societas nec disciplina constat mortalibus. Tantum mea querimonia eos attingit, qui, quum supra reliquam vulgi sortem spiritualem vitae perfectionem profitentur, deberentque omnis pie tatis ac clementiae magistri esse, vix ullos fere ijs ipsis, ira, odio, malitia, vindicta, omniq tyrannidis genere virulentiores conspicias. Quis primus in orbem Christianum has inuexit palinodias, fasciculos, ignes, ac rogos exurendis uiuis hominum corporibus opinione aberrantium, nisi religiosorum coetus, ac viri ecclesiastici, quorum potissimum erat mede ri, non extinguere errantes: exemplo summi praeceptoris qui venerat non perdendis, sed seruandis omnibus. Nunquam tam bene actum est cum humanis opinionibus, quin ali qui interdum lapsus & errores se in-termitermisceant, modo primam illam ecclesiae puritatem excipiamus. Nec tamen quilibet error statim haereticus facit, ni obstinata accedat & pervicax contentio. Neque hic etiam scio, an extrema tentanda, sed herefeos qualitas uidenda est, uidendum quid suadeat regula euangelica, quid cuiusque deceat professionem. Olim non recipiebatur inter haereses, nisi quae blasphemiam, aut fidei periculum grauius inueheret, ubiue Christi maiestas laederetur. Cuiusmodi erant Donatistae, Manichaei, Apollinaristae, & Arriani: Et tamen eatum episcoporum erat moderatio, ut ne sic quidem caesaris praesidia implorarent, nisi haereticorum caede, ac schismate, omnia miscentium ceu necessitate quadam huc pertraheret improbitas. Quemadmodum cum ex aliis tum ex Augustino perspicue liquet, cui adeo potestatis prophanae non placuit imploratio, in negotiis istiusmodi modi, ut apud Dulcitium tribunum se etiam aduocatum interponeret, ne quem letaliter istorum feriret. Idem-que apud praeside agit, opinor, Macedonium, existimans haud aliis armis, hoc in genere agendum, quam uerbo Dei, precibus, doctrina, aut si malū foret infanabilius, exclusione ecclesiastica. Quod autem sententia postea reduxerat, rei magis successu quam iudicio suo ductus, Parum id nostrorum temporum seuitiam sub leuat. Principio quo successu suam hanc in membra Christi tyrannidē exerceant, pyracmones hi Babilonij, res ipsa docet. Porro hos ipsos in quos tum sequitum est Manichæos ac Donatianos quales fuerint, infpicia mus, quos nomine haereticos, reipsa furiosos sicarios, ac praedones fuisse ignorat nemo. ut res non iā ecclesiae officium, sed tribunalitiā magis pote state, etiamsi tacere ecclesia, spectare uideretur. Quo factum est, ut tempo-rum periculosa malignitate, eo tandem adigerentur episcopi, ut necessa rio leges Caesariae essent in auxilium aduocandae. Tumc nec aliud leges illę minabatur, quā ducibus tantum modo capitis poena, quemadmodū in Cod. lib de Manichaeis, & Samaritanis uidere est. Discipulis multa pecuniaria dicebatur. His uero q neglectis principū legibus conteptius perfisterent, profligatio statuebatur. Quid ꝗd nec ullę id temporis scholę Academicae (quas appellamus) erigebatur, quę obuias se hiscemalis op ponerēt. Cōtra nulla nunc fere regio est, quę nō suis cōmunita academijs existat, unde paratiss. esse p̄sidium possit, si tātopere ab heresiticis metua mus. Et qd tandē hominū nunc quo rundā moribus accidit, qui relictis academijs, relictis argumentis, quibus ut facilius, ita rectius reuinci possent, obliti deniq; omnis mansuetudinis, quā tātopere nobis litere cōmendan tur Christi et Apostolorū, nulla utiq; rōne, nisi crucib. fasciculis, et ignibus agendum cum hæreticis arbitran-tur. Et quis demum usus fructus-que academiarum fuerit, si haud aliter, quam vinculis, & fustibus, tuendam veritatem ducimus. Atque hæc hactenus de hæreticis adduximus, qua si hoc ipsum uere sint, quod nunc falso insimulantur. Iam uideamus illa cuiusmodi sint, de quibus tantis tragœdiis, totque incendiis tumultuan-tur papicolæ uentres. Inter tot qui recentiore hac ætate ambusti sunt, quis tandem tres mihi proferat, qui palam de Deo aut senserint aut dixerint impie, qui Christi diuinæ naturæ uel unicam detraxerint, qui ullam in spiritum sanctum blas-phemiam docuerint. Denique qui in ullo fidei articulo minus orthodoxe dissenserint? Tantum de circum-stantiis quibusdam locorum, temporum, ac personarum, atque de humanis traditionibus omnis hæc pertur-bata est camerina.
units.tr: They have their own laws, their own judges, and indeed punishments that are necessary in the commonwealth; without these no society of life nor discipline among mortals can stand. My complaint touches only those who, although they profess a spiritual perfection of life above the common lot, and ought to be teachers of all piety and mercy, you can scarcely find anyone more virulent in anger, hatred, malice, vengefulness and every kind of tyranny. Who first introduced into the Christian world these recantations, bundles of faggots, fires, and pyres for burning the living bodies of men who hold opinions that err, if not the assemblies of religious men and churchmen, whose chief duty was to heal, not to destroy those who err, following the example of the supreme teacher, who came not to destroy but to save all? Never has anything been so well done with human opinions that some lapses and errors have not sometimes crept in, unless we except that first purity of the Church. Nor does every error immediately make a man a heretic, unless obstinacy and stubborn contention be added. Nor do I know whether here extreme measures should be tried; rather, the nature of the heresy must be considered, what the rule of the Gospel suggests, and what befits each profession. Formerly nothing was counted among heresies except what brought blasphemy or a more grievous danger to the faith, where the majesty of Christ was injured. Such were the Donatists, the Manichaeans, the Apollinarians and the Arians. And yet it was the moderation of those bishops that they did not even then implore the protection of Caesar, unless the wickedness of heretics, stirring up everything with slaughter and schism, drew them, as if by some necessity, to it. This is clearly shown both from other writers and from Augustine, who did not approve of seeking help from secular power in matters of this kind, so much so that before the tribune Dulcitius he even interposed himself as an advocate, lest he should cause any of them to be killed. And, I think, he did the same before the governor Macedonius, judging that in this kind of dispute nothing should be done with other weapons than the Word of God, prayers, teaching, or, if the evil were past cure, exclusion from the Church. As for his later change of view, he was led more by the outcome of the matter than by his own judgement. This hardly eases the cruelty of our own times. For the outcome itself shows with what success these Babylonian firebrands exercise their tyranny over the members of Christ. Moreover, let us look at what the Manichaeans and Donatists were, whom they then pursued; no one is ignorant that, though called heretics, in fact they were furious assassins and robbers. Yet it was thought that the office of the Church was not to do this, but rather the power of the tribunal, even though the Church seemed to be silent and to look on. As a result, through the dangerous malice of the times, bishops were at last driven to the point where they had to call in the laws of Caesar to help. Those laws threatened nothing else than capital punishment for the leaders alone, as can be seen in the Code, book on the Manichaeans and Samaritans. Fines were imposed on the disciples. But those who, disregarding the laws of the princes, persisted in contempt, were sentenced to exile. Indeed, at that time there were not even those academic schools (as we call them) set up to oppose the evil. On the contrary, there is now almost no region that does not have its own academies, from which a defence could be ready if we fear heretics so greatly. And what, finally, has happened to the morals of some men today, who, having abandoned the academies, and abandoned the arguments by which they could be more easily and more rightly refuted, and at last forgetting all the gentleness which the letters of Christ and the apostles so strongly commend to us, think that they must deal with heretics by no means except crosses, faggots and fires? And what use or fruit would the academies have, if we think that the truth must be defended in no other way than with chains and clubs? Thus far we have said these things about heretics, which would be true only if they were what they are now falsely accused of being. Now let us see what kind of things these are, over which the Papist bellies make such a tumult with so many tragedies and so many fires. Among the many who in this more recent age have been burned, who will at last produce for me three who openly either thought or said anything impious about God, who took away even the single nature of Christ's divinity, or who taught any blasphemy against the Holy Spirit? Finally, who dissented in any article of faith less orthodoxly? All this uproar has been stirred up only over certain circumstances of places, times and persons, and over human traditions.

units.la: Quid hoc adeo retulerit, si quis pie adoret Christum in coelo, etiamsi non adoret in sacramento. Quid magni hoc momenti sit, si cum Christo ac Paulo panem uocemus corpus Christi, etiamsi non concipiamus cum scholis, accidens ibidem suo cassum subiecto consistere? Quid si sacerdoti non retegamus peccatorum confessionem, si apud Christum uere coram ipsi couertimur ad resipiscentiam? Quid si relicta operum fiducia, quid si spretis pontificum indulgentiis iustitiam in Christo unice pontifice ac indulgentiam reponimus, num minus propterea fides nostra suis constabit articulis ab Apostolis tradita? Quid si antiquatis diuorum imaginibus, Christum unicum in spiritu, ac veritate colamus, an minus eo Christiani erimus, aut Christus non unus satis pro omnibus? Euangelium duo tantum sacramenta nouit, ea si quis sola amplectatur, aut pie tra-
units.tr: What would it matter if someone devoutly worships Christ in heaven, even though he does not worship him in the sacrament? What great weight would it carry if, with Christ and Paul, we call the bread the body of Christ, without holding with the schoolmen that an accident remains there, empty of its subject? What if we do not disclose our confession of sins to a priest, but truly turn to repentance before Christ, in his presence? What if, abandoning trust in works and setting aside the indulgences of the pontiffs, we place our righteousness and indulgence in Christ, the only high priest? Will our faith for that reason stand any less firmly on its articles handed down by the Apostles? What if, with the images of the saints set aside, we worship the one Christ in spirit and in truth? Shall we be any less Christians for that, or is Christ not one sufficient for all?

units.la: G ƒtet, exclusis interim ijs, quae exx hu-mana institutione subnata sunt, quid inde, res Christiana perferet incom-modi? Sic scriptura Dei concubinam non permittit, uxorem permittit quibuslibet, modo unam, modo umi, utrū modo astrictius obligare, Dei-ne voluntatem, an uotum hominis con-ueniet? Siue, interrupto illegitimo uo-to sacerdos uxorem appellare quam concubinam malit, qua cum assueue-rit, quid hic tandem gyaris et carcere dignum?
units.tr: The Gospel knows only two sacraments. If someone embraces these alone, or handles them devoutly, while setting aside those things that have arisen from human institution, what harm will the Christian cause suffer as a result? So Scripture does not permit a concubine, but permits a wife to anyone, provided she is one woman and he is bound to one man. Does it agree with God's will, or with a man's vow, to bind more tightly? Or again, if the illegitimate vow is broken off and a priest prefers to call the woman he has lived with his wife rather than his concubine, what here is really deserving of the island of Gyaros and of prison?

units.la: Porro nec ideo, opinor, statim col-labitur Ecclesiae regimen, aut Ecclesi-arum ordo, si unus Italiae episco-pus, excusso primatu, quae nulla scrip-tura uendicat, in reliquorum ordi-nem ac numerum episcoporum redi-gatur. Atqꝫ illa haec tam grandia sunt blasphemiae piacula, ob quae tantis furoribus exagitantur Christiani in Christianos. Hic iterum refricanda, toties illa repetita admonitio, nihil à nobis in leges politicas, dictum aut cogitatum: at in hos duntaxat, quos quum omnium mitissimos esse, professione coueniebat, natura omnium sunt saeuissimi. Constitutiones id de clarant ipsorum, in Decretalibus lib. 5. quibus iubetur haereticus in errore conuictus, sed quo pacto couictus? autoritate magis, quam scripturis, seculari tradi potestati. Nec id hactenus satis, quod gladium secularem sanguine imbuant, ni & ipsum per se acutum satis, sua etiam malitia exacuant. Adiciunt itaque glossomatographi ad comburendum. Atque hi sunt demum, qui si superis placeat, Christum ipsum nobis repraesentare in terris uolunt, clamitantes interim quod omnis Christi actio, nostra sit instructio. Atqui si ad Christi actiones, institutio sit nostra dirigenda: quid minus suadent exempla illius, quam sequitiam hanc, tum uero in mi nistris maxime quibus tanto studio mansuetudinem commendat ac dile-ctionem mutuam, ceu unicum Euan-gelij sui Symbolū: diserte interdicēs, ne in euellendis zizaneis sint præci-pites, metuens id fortassis euentu-rum, quod nunc euenit: ne simul cum zizaneis triticū eruatur. Tum quid hic dicendum, ubi non solum cum zizaneis, sed pro zizaneis, ip-sissimum euellitur triticum, ex areis domini. Id quàm bene respondeat actioni Christi, uideant ipsi: Ego ni-mis profecto uereor, ne non ita ma-gnam ineant gratiam, apud messis dominum, quo die redditurus est cuiq; iuxta facta sua. Non hic acuo-catū ago hæreticorū, si qui uere sint hæretici. Neq; equidem hic excutio, quoufq; se porrigit ius ciuilis gladij, quidue per ciuiles liceat constitutio-nes. Certe quicquid ciuilis agit pote statis necessaria seueritas, erit tamen sacerdotum, ac ecclesiæ procerum, semper mansuetudinis meminisse, ac ad exemplum illius, qui nunquam cogere ad religionem suam quenq; uoluit. Quid enim ille? Qui aures, in quit, habet audiendi audiat. Non sta tim non audienti mortem intentat. Non uenit ille ciuilem occupaturus autoritatem, atq; ut non occupauit ipse, ita nec quenquam ciuili potesta ti tradidit. Quanquam nec diffiten-dum est, quin ita usuuenire interdū possit, ut indigeat hierarchia Christi ana, accersita magistratus ope. Quē-admodum (contra Donatistas necef-saria erant legum præsidia) præsertim si hæresis exeat ad tumultū, ad schis-ma, ad seditionem, ad latrocinium, aut uitæ communis perniciem. Ibi demum magistratui arbitror exter-no prospiciendum, ne quid respub-lica capiat detrimenti. Alioqui si hu-iusmodi sit hæresis, quæ intra priua-tum duntaxat errorem se continens, ulterius non peruagetur, ad episco-pos, ad Academias unice spectare ut detur: Neque quid ciuilis hic potestas agat admodum uideo. Ita enim faciLius felicius reprimuntur haereses, magis ratione conuictae, quam auto ritate oppressae. Iam aliquammultis annis in haereticos saeuitum est, tantis odiis, exquisitisque tormentis. Quid hac ratione profectum sit, nemo non uidet. Quanto id uero mihi consultius digniusque nomine uidetur Christiano, si priscorum ingressi uestigiis ac exemplis, nostri in Christo patres, id studio habuerint potius, litteris, linguis, pietate, spiritus uerbique potentia, quam mundana potentia praemiis nere? Iam multos uidemus, quibus nulla uidetur alia, ecclesiam contra haereticos propugnandi ratio, quam sola uis, ac maiestas episcoporum.
units.tr: Moreover, I think, the government of the Church does not therefore collapse at once, nor does the order of the churches, if one bishop of Italy, shaken off his primacy, which no Scripture claims for him, is reduced to the rank and number of the other bishops. And yet these are such grave offences of blasphemy that Christians are harried with such fury by Christians. Here again I must press that warning, so often repeated: nothing has been said or thought by us against civil laws. Our words are aimed only at those who, though they ought by profession to be the gentlest of all, are by nature the most savage of all. Their own constitutions declare this, in book 5 of the Decretals, where a heretic convicted of error is ordered to be handed over to the secular power. But convicted how? By authority rather than by Scripture. Nor is it enough for them that they steep the secular sword in blood, unless they also sharpen it by their own malice, though it is sharp enough in itself. So the glossators add the words "to be burnt." And these are the very men who, if it please the gods above, want to represent Christ himself to us on earth, while crying out meanwhile that every action of Christ is our instruction. But if our instruction is to be directed by Christ's actions, how much less do his examples urge this cruelty! Especially upon ministers, to whom he commends gentleness and mutual love with such eagerness, as the one creed of his Gospel. He expressly forbids them to be hasty in uprooting the tares, fearing perhaps that what now happens would come about: that the wheat would be uprooted along with the tares. What is to be said here, where the very wheat is uprooted from the Lord's threshing floors, not only along with the tares but in place of the tares? Let them see for themselves how well this accords with Christ's action. For my part I greatly fear that they will not find such great favour with the Lord of the harvest, on the day when he is to render to each according to his deeds. I am not here pleading as an advocate for heretics, if any truly are heretics. Nor do I here examine how far the right of the civil sword extends, or what is permitted by civil constitutions. Certainly, whatever necessary severity the civil power exercises, it remains for priests and leaders of the Church always to remember gentleness, and to follow the example of him who never wished to compel anyone to his religion. For what did he do? "Let him who has ears to hear, hear," he said. He did not at once threaten death to one who would not listen. He did not come to seize civil authority, and just as he did not seize it himself, so he did not hand anyone over to the civil power. Yet it must not be denied that it can sometimes happen that the Christian hierarchy, when summoned, stands in need of the help of the magistrate. So it was that against the Donatists the protection of laws was necessary, especially if heresy breaks out into tumult, schism, sedition, robbery, or the ruin of common life. There, at last, I think, the magistrate must look to outward matters, lest the commonwealth suffer harm. Otherwise, if a heresy is of such a kind that it keeps itself within private error and does not spread further, it should be referred solely to bishops and universities, and I do not see what the civil power has to do here at all. For thus heresies are more easily and happily suppressed when they are convicted by reason than when they are crushed by authority. For some years now there has been savage treatment of heretics, with such hatreds and exquisite tortures. What has been gained by this method, no one fails to see. How much more prudent, and how much more worthy of the Christian name, it seems to me, if our fathers in Christ had followed in the footsteps and examples of the ancients, and had made it their aim to contend with letters, languages, piety, and the power of the Spirit and the Word, rather than with worldly power and its rewards. Already we see many for whom there seems to be no other way of defending the Church against heretics than the bare force and majesty of bishops.

units.la: Quo factum est, ut ministratio ecclesiastica, a Christo ac Apostolis alienissimis quidem illis a mundo, olim incoepta, nunc ad secularis cuiusdam imperii imaginem, ad regales pene opes, imò phalarismum desciuerit. Verum ad dissipandas hæreses, si ea res nobis tantopere cordi sit, haud a liud mihi expeditius uidetur compe dium, quàm si ecclesiæ partes studio se caueant, ne tanta articulorum tur- ba Christi obruantur ecclesiæ. Ita fi- et, non solum ut facilius hæreseon ex tinguantur plantaria, ubi enafci coe- perint, sed ne quando omnino emer gant, quas extinguamus. Nam si ue rum fatendum sit, unde secula hæc tam fœcunda dissentionū, nisi quod omnia adeo conferta atque confcisa sunt, tot articulis, tot censuris, elen- chis, cautionibus ac placitis scholasti corum. Necullus est articulus, qui nō adiunctam suam trahit hæresim, ut umbram corpus. Adeoq; res mo- do progressa est, ut nihil tā circum- spectè fere efferri possit, quin alicubi impingat in aliquam hæreseos tendi culam, aut certè suspicionem. Tot sunt laquei constitutionum, decretorum, tot tituli reprehensionis, ac captionis, praesertim ubi huc insuper pro charitate nescio in qua pathmon procul nunc relegata, succeßit, rerum deprauatrix Erinnys, omnia sua calumnia commiscens, quam minima etiam, aut nulla interdum occasione. Quae quum ita habeant, nihil erat, mea opinione, prius, quam ut mutua animorum coniunctione redintegrati, materiam (quoad licet,) fraternae offensionis omnem subtrahamus, unde potissimum malum hoc suppu-lat. Si hęresim facimus quicquid hu-manis decretis & articulis reluctatur, praestiterat minus esse articulorum in mundo iam sua sponte concident haereses. Hinc enim mali profluxit scaturigo, indidem exordienda me-delae methodus. Iam quid si ponti-ficia decretalia suam non exeant Ita-liam. Quid si in neceßariam fidem, quę paucissimis contenta est, nihil recipiatur, nisi articuli Apostolici sym-boli boli ut à concilijs probatioribus proponuntur, quid tandem Christi ipsius ecclesiae decederet? Et tamen ob haec τὰ πτερύγια passim uidemus exurì senes, iuuenes, ac fœminas. Nec se xui, nec aetati parcitur, nec generi, ut minoris penè periculi sit, maximorum principum laedi maiestatem, quam uel leuissimi episcopi sanxiones uiolari. Quae quidem persecutionis tempestas sic nostris his temporibus incruduit, ut nulla fere Europę sit pars, quae non effuso martyrum sanguine cruentata sit. Et si uero quam maximè decreta haec scripturis consentirent (donemus hoc illis) attamen theologorum erat docere, cogere tyrannorum est. Iam quale est, propter articulos quosdam controuersos, & ambiguos, parum etiam sanos nonnullos, & scripturis forsan dissentaneos, ad ignem pertrahi, non solum haereticos, sed pro haereticis innoxios & innocentes? Et, mira interim hoc minum stupiditas, hanc dum Jamie-nam quotidie exercent lycaones in caulis Christi, litando humano san-guine, perinde ac si non uulgare pie-tatis officium Deo exhibeant, sibi quasi re benegesta magnifice triumphabundi adgratulantur. Non se cus ac in externis principum bellis, summæ habetur strenuitatis, si quis quamplurimos occiderit perduellio-nes, itidem apud ecclesiæ magnates, hæc unica laus & contentio, ut quis-que quamplurimū haurire poterit hæretici sanguinis. Quemadmodū de Petro quodā Stoksleo episcopo Londinensi iactatū audiuimus, qui iam moriturus suprema uoce Deo agebat gratias, quod unus supra tri-ginta hæreticos litarat orco. Beluæ sane uox, non hominis.
units.tr: As a result, the ecclesiastical ministry, begun long ago by Christ and the Apostles, who were entirely alien to the world, has now degenerated into the image of some secular empire, into almost royal wealth, nay, into the pomp of a Phalaris. But for scattering heresies, if this matter is so close to our hearts, no shorter method seems to me available than for the leaders of the Church to take care, with zeal, that the Church of Christ is not overwhelmed by such a crowd of articles. In this way the seedlings of heresies will be more easily extinguished where they have begun to sprout, and they will never emerge at all to be extinguished. For if the truth must be confessed, whence comes this age so fruitful of dissensions, except that everything is so crammed and confused with so many articles, censures, refutations, cautions and the opinions of the schoolmen? There is no article that does not drag along with it its attached heresy, as a body casts its shadow. So far has the matter advanced that scarcely anything can be put forward so cautiously that it does not somewhere run into some snare of heresy, or at least of suspicion. There are so many snares of constitutions and decrees, so many titles of reproach and entrapment. This is especially so since, in place of charity (I know not what passion, now long banished far away), there has succeeded the Fury who corrupts affairs, mixing everything with her calumny, on the smallest occasion or sometimes on none at all. Since matters stand thus, in my opinion nothing should come first, before we, renewed by a mutual union of minds, remove as far as we may all material of brotherly offence, from which this evil chiefly springs. If we make heresy of whatever resists human decrees and articles, it would have been better for there to be fewer articles in the world; then heresies would fall of their own accord. For from here flowed the spring of evil, and from the same place the method of cure must begin. What if the papal decretals did not go beyond Italy? What if nothing were received as necessary faith, which is content with very few things, except the articles of the Apostles' Creed as they are set forth by the more approved councils? What, after all, would be lost to the Church of Christ itself? And yet, on account of these trifles [τὰ πτερύγια], we see old men, young men and women burned everywhere. No account is taken of sex, age or rank, so that it is almost less dangerous to injure the majesty of the greatest princes than to violate the decree of even the most trivial bishop. This storm of persecution has raged so fiercely in our own times that there is scarcely any part of Europe that has not been stained with the spilt blood of martyrs. And even if these decrees agreed most fully with Scripture (let us grant them that), still it is the business of theologians to teach, and of tyrants to compel. Now what kind of thing is it, on account of certain controverted and ambiguous articles, some of them scarcely sound and perhaps at odds with Scripture, to drag to the fire not only heretics but those who are harmless and innocent in place of heretics? And, what a marvellous dullness of mind, while the wolves in the fold of Christ carry on this practice every day, sacrificing human blood, as if they were performing no ordinary act of piety towards God, they congratulate themselves and exult magnificently, as if they had achieved some great deed. Just as in the foreign wars of princes it is accounted the height of valour if someone has killed very many enemies, so likewise among the great men of the Church this is the only praise and rivalry: that each may drain as much heretical blood as he can. As we have heard it reported of a certain Peter Stokesley, bishop of London, who, about to die, gave thanks to God with his last breath that he alone had sacrificed more than thirty heretics to Orcus. Surely that was the voice of a beast, not of a man.

units.la: At uideant isti ne dum inductio-ne magis animi, quā iudicio ducti, tantopere studeant hæreticos litare Plutoni, ipsis idem eueniat, quod Iu-daeis daeis olim, qui quum in Christū ceu seditiosum uirum essent grassaturi, impegerunt in filium Dei. Id ut ne fiat, praestabit, primum in episcopis eruditio, articulorum imminutio, iudicium, animus euangelicus, mansuetudo, zelus pariter cum scientia coniunctus, cura seruandi, magis quam perdendi homines, mens quae nihil tribuens affectibus, totam se scriptu ris ac aequitati regendam permittit.
units.tr: But let them see that they, moved more by inclination than by judgement, do not so eagerly offer heretics to Pluto, lest the same thing happen to them that once happened to the Jews. When the Jews were about to rage against Christ as a seditious man, they ran headlong into the Son of God. To prevent this, bishops will need first of all learning, a reduction of articles, sound judgement, an evangelical spirit, gentleness, zeal joined with knowledge, care to save men rather than destroy them, and a mind that yields nothing to the passions but lets itself be governed wholly by the Scriptures and by equity.

units.la: At omnino supprimenda est haeresis. Certe nec apud me patrocinium inueniet pestis haeretica. Tantū in symmistis orthodoxis requiro, si non apostolicam, saltem ciuilem modestiam, ut moderatis potius rem rationibus transfigere, quam clamoribus, et seditiosa temeritate malint, requiro [illegible, ~1 word], quae saltem legitime conuincat quos uelit opprimere, requiro doctrinam, quę haereses magis ipsas quam haereticos iugulet. In sa- niant, quantum liber, contra haereticorum corum nomen isti. Mihi sane uidetur: Si tempora hęc tam parum Christiana, sex haberent Hieronymios, totidemq; Augustinos, etiam si niihil accederet praelidri amplius, haud ima gnopere haberet opinor ecclesia, quòd sibi ad profligandos haereticorum cuneos, admodum desiderarèt. Sed quoniam in feruescente hac nnū di crudelitate, ubi omnis adeo tefri-xit charitas, haud me latet, quam pa- rum haec fidem apud nonnullos in- uentura sint, quemadmodum & ca- terorū ante me, ab his spreta sint mo- derationis consilia, consultius fuerit hoc hominū genus suis ingenijs re-linquere, quā surdis canendo, simul & tepus et laborem frustra prĕterire. Nunc ergo ad martyres redeamus. Verum priusquam hanc tam lugu-brem historiam ingrediamur, operae precium forsan facturi sumus, si quę dam a nobis hominum Sibyllinorum uaticinia praelibentur, quibus tot tatæ seculi perturbationes præsignabantur.
units.tr: But heresy must be utterly suppressed. Certainly the plague of heresy will find no patronage with me. I require only of the orthodox men among the symmists, if not apostolic, at least civil moderation: that they prefer to settle the matter by measured arguments rather than by clamour and seditious rashness. I require [illegible, about one word] that at least legitimately convicts those they wish to crush. I require a doctrine that slays the heresies themselves rather than the heretics. Let them rage as much as they like against the name of these heretics. It seems to me that if these times, so un-Christian, had six Jeromes and as many Augustines, then even with nothing further added to the clergy, I think the Church would scarcely need anything more for crushing the bands of heretics. But since in this seething cruelty of our age, where all charity has grown cold, I am well aware how little these words will find faith with some, just as the counsels of moderation offered by others before me have been spurned by them, it would be wiser to leave this kind of men to their own wits than to sing to the deaf and waste time and labour in vain. Now then, let us return to the martyrs. But before we enter upon this so mournful history, perhaps it will be worth our while to taste beforehand certain prophecies of these Sibylline men, by which so many great disturbances of the age were foreshadowed.

units.la: Vt ergo primum à Ioachimo Ab bate exordiamur, quid de hoc in ues tusto Houedi monumento repertū sit referemus. Sic enim ille. Ricardus, inquit, Angliæ Rex, in expedi-tione Ierosolimitana accepta fama Ioachimi Calabriensis abbatis de Curacon, qui spiritu prophetico uentura prędicebat, quo tempore Ciciliæ ageret, eum ad se accersit, auditurus, quid de antichristo inter cætera denunciare posset. Hic ergo explicans mysterium 7. regum, in Apocalypsi, quorum quinque ceciderint &c. Reges 7, inquit, septem sunt persecutores. Herodes, Nero, Constantius, Mahumet, Melsemutus, Saladinus, Antichristus. De antichristo sic aiebat, quod iam is in urbe Roma prognatus esset, & in sede apostolica sublimabitur, de quo apost. Extollitur, et aduersatur super omne quod dicitur Deus. Hęc Houedenus. Annus uero huius abbatis erat 1290.
units.tr: So that we may begin first with Abbot Joachim, let us report what has been found about him in the ancient record of Hoveden. For he speaks thus: Richard, King of England, on the expedition to Jerusalem, having heard the fame of Joachim, abbot of Curazzo in Calabria, who foretold future events by prophetic spirit, while he was in Sicily summoned him to himself, wishing to hear what he could announce about Antichrist, among other things. He, therefore, explaining the mystery of the seven kings in the Apocalypse, of whom five have fallen, etc., said: The seven kings are seven persecutors: Herod, Nero, Constantius, Mahomet, Melsemutus, Saladin, Antichrist. About Antichrist he said that he was already born in the city of Rome and would be raised up in the apostolic see, of whom the apostle says: he is lifted up and opposes everything that is called God. So Hoveden. Now the year of this abbot was 1290.

units.la: Est & Hildegardis cuiusdam prophetia apud Vincetium li. 29. Amno inquit post incarnationem Christi 1200. Apostolorum doctrina & ardes iustitia, quā in spiritualibus & Christianis constituerat Deus, tardare & in hesitationem uerti coepit. Sed hoc muliebre tempus non tam diu durabit q huc usq; perstitit. Hęcille. Nec dubitauit Fluentius antistes publicus depredicare antichristū suis q de temporibus esse natum apud Sabell.
units.tr: There is also a prophecy of a certain Hildegard in Vincent of Beauvais, book 29. In the year 1200 after the incarnation of Christ, he says, the teaching of the apostles and the burning justice that God had established among spiritual and Christian people began to slacken and turn into hesitation. But this womanish time will not last as long as it has endured until now. So he. Nor did Fluentius, the public bishop, hesitate to proclaim that Antichrist had been born in his own times, as Sabellicus reports.

units.la: Quin & ante hæc tepora an. 1239. in lib. de conseruatione seruorum Dei Gerardus Laodicen. episc. ex rare scente prophetiæ, atq; curationū docno appropinquare antichri. coniicit.
units.tr: Even before these times, in the year 1239, in his book on the preservation of God's servants, Gerard, bishop of Laodicea, conjectures from the decay of prophecy and the teaching of cures that Antichrist is at hand.

units.la: Extat et Hiero. Sauonarolę (si fide res digna sit) prophetica quędam prænunciatio ante annos uno minus 70. in qua huncin modum affirmat, Italiam flagellis Dei expiandā, propter pter peccata multiplicia in principi-bus, tā ecclesiasticis, quā secularibus. Florentia, urbeq; Ro. euersis renoua-tione ecclesiae futura, quodq; hęc ci-to deberet fieri, Turcas & Mauros nostris temporibus ad Christianū cul-tū cōuerti debere: Praedixit etiā quen-dā alpes transituru in Italiā Cyro si-mile qui subuertere deberet Italiam. Tantum in Gasparo Hedione, inli, cui inscribit titulus Paralipomena.
units.tr: There also exists a prophetic announcement of Hieronymus Savonarola (if it deserves belief), made less than seventy years ago, in which he affirms in this way: Italy is to be purged by God's scourges on account of the manifold sins of princes, both ecclesiastical and secular; after Florence and the city of Rome have been overthrown, there will be a renewal of the Church; and this ought to happen quickly, and the Turks and Moors ought to be converted to Christian worship in our times. He also predicted that a certain man like Cyrus would cross the Alps into Italy, who was to overthrow it. So he says in Gaspar Hedio, whose work is entitled Paralipomena.

units.la: Nec carere arbitror suo uaticinio, quòd an. 1501. passim per Ger. in ue-stibus hominum cruces uisae sunt, co-ronae spineae, clavorum similitudo, guttaeq; sanguinis de caelo cecide-runt, interdū etiā intra domos dela-psa haec mulierculae saepe multos di-es in ricis suis circumferebant, si mo-do uera sint quae narrat Casparus.
units.tr: Nor do I think that its prophecy is lacking: in the year 1501, crosses were seen everywhere on people's garments, crowns of thorns, the likeness of nails, and drops of blood fell from heaven, and sometimes these even fell inside houses. Women often carried them about in their kerchiefs for many days, if indeed what Caspar relates is true.

units.la: Adjiciedum & ijs quod de I. quo dā Rochetaylada Francisçano, apud Frossardū nostrū legimus: nō quod certū hic quicq; habeamus, tantū qd hic habetur profero. Is itaque in Anemone dicitur an. 1346. praediixisse ecclesiasticum ordinem multa passurum propter ambitionem, avaritiam atque superbiam, quamobrem ipse a pontifice Innocentio 6. in vincula coniectus est.
units.tr: One should add also what we read about a certain J. Rochetaillade, a Franciscan, in our Froissart. I do not claim anything certain here; I offer only what is found there. He is said in the Anemone to have predicted in 1346 that the ecclesiastical order would suffer much on account of ambition, avarice and pride, and for this he was cast into chains by Pope Innocent VI.

units.la: Necreticendū forsan, quòd Manfredus Vercellensis Dominicanus praedixisse dicitur: Antichristum suo tempore emersurū, quemadmodum apud Antoninum elt.
units.tr: Nor perhaps should I pass over that Manfred of Vercelli, a Dominican, is said to have predicted that Antichrist would emerge in his time, as in Antoninus.

units.la: Arnoldus de villa nova Cathalanus Mathematicus, simul & medicus, ex Daniele, & Sybilla Erithrea edisserebat, Antichristum plene post annum Dom. 1300. in pios saeviturum, et futuram in ecclesia persecutionem. Dicebat claustrales falsifica re doctrinam Christi, Sacrificium altaris nec uiuis prodesse nec mortuis, nec consultationibus papalibus scientiam inesse, nisi humanorum operarum. Missus tandem a Friderico Siciliae tilis Regead Rom. pontificem inter nauigandum periit, Genuae sepul tus.
units.tr: Arnold of Villanova, a Catalan mathematician and also physician, expounded from Daniel and the Erythraean Sibyl that Antichrist would rage fully against the pious after the year of Our Lord 1300, and that a persecution would come upon the Church. He said that the monks falsify the doctrine of Christ, that the sacrifice of the altar profits neither the living nor the dead, and that papal consultations contain no knowledge except of human works. Finally sent by Frederick, son of the King of Sicily, to the Roman pontiff, he perished while sailing and was buried at Genoa.

units.la: Poteram & Io. Aquitani Franciscani in Vasconia huc accersere testimonium, qui post alia diuinabat, quod in nouissimis temporibus lex apparet libertatis. Qui deinceps a furore, per Clementem 4. haereticus declaratur, exusto mortui cadauere, si Guidoni credimus, Perpinianensi.
units.tr: I could also bring in here the testimony of John of Aquitaine, a Franciscan in Gascony, who among other things prophesied that in the last times the law of liberty would appear. Thereafter, under the fury of Clement IV, he was declared a heretic, and his dead body was burned, if we believe Guido of Perpignan.

units.la: Tum quae de Luthero exorituro, tot ante annos, a multis frequenter praenunciata, atque a Melanchthone collecta sint, ex huius libris constabit rectius. His itaque prelibatis, simul ac commemoratis his, quos usque ad palinodiam, ac mortis terrorem duntaxat, afflixit calamitosa haec, ac fatalis persecutionis tempestas. Nunc ad eos accedat Historia, quibus maiorem pectoris constantiam, simul ac fidei robur, ad morte usque praestiterat Deus. Quan-
units.tr: Then what has been foretold by many, over so many years, about Luther's coming, and collected by Melanchthon, will be established more correctly from his books. Having thus touched on these matters, and mentioned those whom this calamitous and deadly storm of persecution afflicted only to the point of recantation and terror of death, let history now turn to those to whom God gave greater constancy of heart and strength of faith, even unto death.

units.la: quam nec horum quidem omnium catalogum polliceri queam, quum tot per omnes mundi plagas extite- runt Christi martyres, quorum mul ti fraude, ac dolo circumuenti, quí- dam ueneno sublati, ceteri publicis tormentis excruciati, nonnulli priua ta, ac ignota cæde oppressi, alij carce ribus, fame alij, alijsque modis publi- cè priuatimq; exhausti, ut uixexi- guam eorum noticiam licuerit con- sequi. Aut si nomina scire contige- rit, modum tamen supplicij, caufasq; omnium, qui in tot, tamque longin- quis partibus occubuerunt, nulla ra tione uenari posset, quin nec unius esse hominis arbitror indagare. Quā quam hoc unum in omnibus his cer tum fere, & perpetuum esse possit, ut quicquid uni horum cuipiam euene rit, ex hoc gnomone quid cun- ctis acciderit perspicuum habeas. Quandoquidem una semper fuit fere omnium pontificum in istos crudecrudelitas, eadem iudiciorum forma, eadem condemnandi ratio, idemque mortis genus, Neque multum adeo diuersa omnium causa extitit, cum propemodum ex una hac Sacramenti superstitione, paucisque ceremoniis, atque ambitione ecclesiasticorum, profluxit uniuersum huius turbinis caput, ac seminarium.
units.tr: Although I cannot promise a catalogue of all of them, since Christ's martyrs have arisen in so many regions of the world, many of whom were overcome by fraud and deceit, some carried off by poison, others tortured by public torments, some destroyed by private and secret slaughter, others by prison, others by hunger, and others by various means, both publicly and privately, so that we can gather only a very slight knowledge of them. Or even if it were possible to learn their names, still no reasoning could track down the manner of punishment and the causes of all those who perished in so many and such distant parts; I do not think this is the work of one man. Yet in all these cases there may be almost one certain and constant rule: whatever happened to any one of them, from this measure you may see clearly what happened to all. For there was almost always one cruelty of the popes against these people, the same form of judgements, the same method of condemning, and the same kind of death. Nor was the cause of all very different, since nearly all of this whirlwind's source and seedbed flowed from this one superstition of the Sacrament, a few ceremonies, and the ambition of churchmen.

units.la: Diximus initio, si singuli mihi in hanc farraginem coniiciendi sint, quotquot his quingentis annis post Satanam e vinculis liberum, exitio sunt ab ecclesiae primoribus traditi, altius hanc esse repetendam historiam. Cum in Narbonensi provincia (ut apud Massaeum est) centum & quadraginta referuntur, qui incendij quantumlibet graues poenas subire maluerunt, quam preter ius scripturae, fidem decretis quibusdam astruere, quae a Ro. ecclesia obtrudebantur. anno Do. 1210. Parisijs similiter. 24. -rursusque apud eundem anno 1211. quadringentos hæreticos flammis traditos reperimus, octoginta decol latos, principem Armericum suspen sum, Dominam castri lapidibus ob rutam.
units.tr: We said at the outset that if I were to cast into this medley each of those who, in the five hundred years since Satan was loosed from his chains, have been given over to destruction by the leaders of the Church, this history would have to be traced back further. In the province of Narbonne (as is found in Massaeus), one hundred and forty are reported who preferred to undergo the gravest punishment by fire rather than, against the law of Scripture, affirm by their faith certain decrees that the Roman Church imposed. In the year 1210, likewise in Paris. 24. And again in the same author, in the year 1211, we find four hundred heretics given to the flames, eighty beheaded, the prince Armericus hanged, and the lady of the castle buried under stones.

units.la: Erphurdiæ Beghardus hæreseos titulo igni traditus. anno 1218. Oxo-nię Diaconus. 1222. autore Treueto nostro. Quin et Cantipratensis autor est in Camerarensi patria combustos à Dominicanis hæreticos.
units.tr: At Erfurt a Beghard was burned for heresy in 1218. At Oxford a deacon was burned in 1222, according to our Treveto. Indeed Thomas of Cantimpré also records that heretics were burned by the Dominicans in the Cambrai region.

units.la: Nec scio cur à Papa, rex quídam cōmendatur apud Boethium, quod pro uno quadringentos occiderit, ceteris castratis, nili pro hæreticis fuerint obtruncati. Præterea interim annum Millesimum, centesimum, octogesimum secundum. in quo apud Francos multi comburebantur hæretici, teste Houedeno, quorum quídā publicani, alij Cathari, aliqui Paterini, alij alijs uocabulis appella-bantur. Nec multum Vuicleui tem-pora pora prǫcessit Eckhardus Dominicanus qui Heidelbergæ dānatur hæ reseos, autore Tritemio, anno. 1330. Taceo hic Albigenses qui tempore Ioannis Anglorum Regis flammis expositi sunt.
units.tr: I do not know why a certain king is praised by Boethius for having killed four hundred men for one, with the rest castrated, unless they were slaughtered as heretics. Moreover, in the year 1182, when many heretics were burned among the Franks, according to Hoveden, some were called Publicans, others Cathars, others Paterines, and others by other names. Not long before Wycliffe's time came Eckhard the Dominican, who was condemned for heresy at Heidelberg in 1330, according to Trithemius. I pass over here the Albigenses, who were given to the flames in the time of John, king of the English.

units.la: Præterea & Eremitam illum, cuius facit mentionem Io. Bacon, & sententˀ dist. 2, quæsti. 1. qui in Ecclesia Paulina disserebat, non esse sacramenta, quorum tunc usus erat in ecclesia, à Christo instituta. an. 1306. Fortassis Ranulphus is erat, cuius fit mentio in floribus historiarum, qui postea interijt incarceratus, nec multum discrepat annorum numerus.
units.tr: Likewise, that hermit whom John Baconthorpe mentions, in his commentary on the Sentences, distinction 2, question 1, who argued in St Paul's Church that the sacraments which were then in use in the Church were not instituted by Christ, was condemned in 1306. Perhaps this was Ranulph, mentioned in the Flores historiarum, who afterwards died in prison; the number of years does not differ much.

units.la: Duo Franciscani.
units.tr: Two Franciscans.

units.la: Poterant & his accenseri duo Franciscani, de quibus ita extat apud Polid. Virgilium lib. 19. nostræ historiæ. Londini illos igne cæsos, quòd de religione parum integrè sentirët. Sed transcursis his iam ad Vuicleui accedamus tempora, quae ut nostrae memoriae uiciniora, ita causam plurimus habent testibus cognitam: Quae quidem ipsa haud alia fere uideba- tur, quam de traditiunculis ac possef sionibus ecclesiae, de scolatria, atque Eucharistiae subiecto, caeterisque Sacramentis differentiens a quorundam pseudologia, opinio. Post Vuicle- uum ergo meminit cuiusdam in An glia parlamenti Vualdenus ad Mar tinum papa 5. & in libro contra Vui cleuiftas 2. arti. 3. cap. 50. Item de sacramentalibus. 55. post cuius, in- quit, actum, plures mortem sustinu- erunt acerbissimam, pluresque regnū deseruere. Sed hi quinam fuerunt aut quod supplicij genus, nullam re liquit memoriam. Nos quorum no mina licuit expiscari, non sinemus si lentio obliterari. Ac dolet profecto nihil aliud quam nomina duntaxat hominum ad uos peruenisse. Vtinam et totam uitæ seriem, iudicij actionisque formam, quid in aduersa rɭs obseruandum, quid in ipsis laudandum fuerit, ac constans, nobis superiorum conseruasset diligentia. Quanquam nec ea res nobis magno pere desiderio fuerit, quum neque ea potuerint omnia paucis voluminibus contineri, tu ex ijs paucis promptum fuerit æstimari, quid de papistica huius ecclesiæ crudelitate sit sentiendum.
units.tr: Two Franciscans could also be counted among these, of whom the following is recorded in Polydore Vergil, book 19 of our history: that in London they were burned at the stake because they held rather unsound opinions about religion. But, having passed over these, let us now come to the times of Wycliffe, which, as they are closer to our own memory, also have most of their causes known to many witnesses. That controversy was almost nothing other than about the traditions and possessions of the Church, about the worship of images, about the subject of the Eucharist, and about the other sacraments, differing from the opinion of certain false teachers. After Wycliffe, then, Walden, in his book against the Wycliffites, mentions someone in England, in the parliament of Martin V, in book 2, article 3, chapter 50, and also concerning the sacramentals, chapter 55: after whose action, he says, many suffered a most bitter death, and many deserted the realm. But who these were, or what kind of punishment they suffered, has left no record. Those whose names we have been able to draw out we will not allow to be buried in silence. And it is truly a pity that nothing has come down to us but the mere names of these men. Would that the diligence of our predecessors had preserved for us the whole course of their lives, the form of their trial and proceedings, what was to be observed in adversity, and what was to be praised in them, and a constant record. Yet this has not been greatly missed by us, since all these things could not have been contained in a few volumes, and from these few it will be easy enough to judge what must be thought of the Papists' cruelty toward this Church.

units.la: I. Astonus.
units.tr: I. Aston.

units.la: Primum ergo à Ioanne Astono huius telæ exordium ducerem, qui cum esset συνχρονος Vuicleui, ac Oxoniæ donatus artium professione per Arundellum Archiep. Cantuariensem accitus, condemnationis tulit sententiam. Verum quum incertum sit, in carcere ne, an incendio periit: nos ad annum Domini Millesimum quadringentesimum transilie-mus, quoniam ex hoc fere anno, initium, ac materiam sumpsit, quicquid iam diu durauit in ecclesia persecutionis.
units.tr: I shall therefore begin this web with John Aston, who, being a contemporary of Wycliffe, and having been granted the profession of arts at Oxford, was summoned by Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury, and received a sentence of condemnation. But since it is uncertain whether he died in prison or by fire, we shall leap ahead to the year of the Lord 1400, since from about this year the beginning and material of the persecution that has long endured in the Church arose.

units.la: Sacerdos quidam Suuinderbeus.
units.tr: A certain priest, Swinderby.

units.la: Exacto itaq; anno Domini supra millesimum, quadringentesimo primo, post Vuicleui vero obitum 13. principante apud Anglos Henrico 4. Cum iam Ricardus e fastigio regiae sublimitatis, in turrim abreptus occubuisset, factum est Londini par lamentum in quo edictum est, ut manibus iniectis prehenderentur, quicunq; Vuicleui se assertores ostenderent, qui tum Lolardi appellabantur, qui si pertinacius insisterent susceptae doctrinae, Diocaesano episcopo traditi, inde seculáris magistratus gladio plectendi committerentur.
units.tr: Therefore, when the year of the Lord 1401 had passed, and after Wycliffe's death, with Henry IV reigning among the English, while Richard had already fallen from the summit of royal majesty and died after being dragged off to the Tower, a proclamation was issued in London that whoever showed themselves to be supporters of Wycliffe, who were then called Lollards, should be seized by hand. If they persisted more stubbornly in the doctrine they had embraced, they were to be handed over to the diocesan bishop, and from there committed to be punished by the sword of the secular magistrate.

units.la: Haec lex in supplicium adduxit, eodem anno Sacerdotem quendam, qui in circo illo Smithfildensi multis aspectantibus exustus est. Hęcex psegmate uetustae historiae. Atque ut certissimum est, hunc pro veritissimae fidei affirmatione succubuisse incendii supplicijs, ita quod nomen fuerit Sacerdotis, non satis ex historia liquet: mihi tamen ex coniecturis quibusdam diuinanti apparet, Suuinderbeum fuisse hunc, quem modo ad palinodiam adactum ab episcopo Lincolniensi retulimus. Verum an ad priorem cantionem denuo redijt, cæteri quod uidetur, ego quid mihi probabile sit, aperui.
units.tr: This law led a certain priest to his punishment in the same year, who was burned in that Smithfield arena before many spectators. This is an example from the record of ancient history. And just as it is most certain that he succumbed to the punishment of burning for affirming the truest faith, so what the priest's name was is not sufficiently clear from history. Yet to me, conjecturing somewhat, it appears that this was Swinderby, whom we have just reported as driven to a recantation by the Bishop of Lincoln. Whether he afterwards returned to his former song, others may say what seems to them; I have set out what seems to me probable.

units.la: Faber Laicus.
units.tr: A lay craftsman, a smith.

units.la: Sacerdotem hunc deinceps secutus Laici ordinis faber, an. Domini 1410. Is hanc tuebatur assertionem, quod non sit Christi corpus realiter illud, quod sacramentaliter tractatur in ecclesia, qui cum nullo pacto secum abduci permitteret, ab opinionis constantia, cui omnino immorari secum constituisset, traditus est iudicio seculari.
