Cumque iam condemnationis sententia, in forum suburbanum traheretur infractus Christi martyr, dolio includendus, (quando quidem nondum taurus cherilli in usum uenerat apud episcopos:) a de rat.ut fit, princeps Henrici Regis primogenitus. Hic ceu bonus Samaritanus, quem Leuitæ, ac Pharisęi superciliosi dedunt morti, ad uitam revocare annititur, monet, consulit, ut sibi consulens mature reduceret pedem, ab illis opinionum labyrinthis, nihil non adhibens arietum, quod cuiusquam posset pectus labefacere. Sed neglexit illustris Christi pugil, principis blanditias, omnibus humanis machinis superior, citius laturus supplicij quantamlibet gravitatem, quam tantæ idolatriæ impietatem. Itaque dolio inclusus, affligitur à decorante flamma, mugit miserabiliter inter incendia innocens anima. Clamore tam horribile permotus princeps, iterum adit hominem, revocaturus ad uitam. Quam communis naturę
units.tr: After this priest, a craftsman of the lay order, in the year of the Lord 1410. He maintained the assertion that the body of Christ is not really that which is sacramentally handled in the Church. When he would by no means be led away from it, he was handed over to the secular judgment because of his steadfast adherence to an opinion he had firmly resolved to keep. And when, the sentence of condemnation now pronounced, the unbroken martyr of Christ was being dragged to the suburban court, to be shut up in a barrel (since the bull of Perillus had not yet come into use among the bishops), as is usual, the prince, eldest son of King Henry, intervened. Like the good Samaritan, whom the Levites and the haughty Pharisees gave over to death, he sought to call him back to life. He warned him and advised him, while he was still able, to withdraw his foot in good time from those labyrinths of opinion, and left no battering-ram untried that could shake anyone's heart.

units.la: Dolio in clusus Christianus martyr. naturæ sensus insequit, hanc tam inusitatæ mortis acerba novitas, et nova acerbitas adaugere poterat. Iussit ignis materiam subtrahi, ardorem longius amoveri, consolatur afflictum, promittes adhuc incolumitatis spe, si accederet suis monitis, addens praeterea, quotidie tres sibi denarios a fisco regio irrogatum iri. Iterum ille respuit humanæ pollicitationis ob lationem, non dubium quin uehementius divino flagrans spiritu quā terrenis flammis. Quem, cum adhuc perstiteret sententia immobilis, iussit princeps iterū includi dolio, gratiam nullam posthac consecuturum. Verum ut nullis delinitus præmijs, ita nec terroribus fractus, usque se in uictum præstitit, inconcussus Christi athleta, non sine magno quidem certamine, sed maiori victoriæ trium pho, semper Christi spiritu in suis vincente, quicquid mundus hic habet furoris ac potentiæ.
units.tr: A Christian martyr shut in a barrel. But the illustrious champion of Christ neglected the prince's flatteries, superior to all human devices, and was ready sooner to bear any weight of punishment than the impiety of so great an idolatry. So, shut in the barrel, the innocent soul was afflicted by the scorching flame and groaned miserably amid the fire. Moved by such a horrible outcry, the prince approached the man again, intending to call him back to life. The natural feeling of the common man follows, and the bitter novelty of so unusual a death could increase that bitterness. The prince ordered the fuel of the fire to be removed and the heat to be moved further away; he comforted the afflicted man, holding out still the hope of safety if he would accede to the prince's admonitions, and adding that three pence a day would be paid to him from the royal treasury. Again he rejected the offer of human promises, no doubt burning more fiercely with the divine Spirit than with the earthly flames. When he still persisted, immovable in his sentence, the prince ordered him shut up in the barrel again, and said he would obtain no favour from then on. But, as he was not softened by any rewards, so he was not broken by any terrors; he showed himself unconquered to the end, an unshaken athlete of Christ, not without a great struggle, but with the greater triumph of victory, the spirit of Christ always prevailing in his followers over whatever fury and power this world has.

units.la: Gulielmus
units.tr: William

units.la: Anno 1414. insecutum est publi cum concilium Constantiæ, per pon tificem Ioannem coactum, hærese os repurgandæ causa, quod pluribus bonis uiris funestum fuit. Hoc an no Gulielmus Cleydonus Vuicleui anæ disciplinæ affectator, deprehen sus, ac conuictus, seu oppressus poti us, à Pontificijs Londini combustio ne perimitur, regnante rege Henri co 5. ac expeditione in Galliam faci ente.
units.tr: In the year 1414 the public council of Constance followed, gathered by Pope John for the purpose of purging heresy, which proved deadly to many good men. In this year William Clyderow, an admirer of Wycliffe's discipline, was caught and convicted, or rather overwhelmed, and was put to death by burning in London by the Papists, while King Henry V reigned and was making his expedition into France.

units.la: Quo etiam tempore de Minorita no quodam Anglo, apud Hardin gum nostrum est proditum. Qui cû Benedicti 13. legatus in Scotiam su iffet, ni fuga tempestiua sibi confulu iffet, fasciculos ignitos effugere ob hæresim, quæ illi impingebat, haud quaquam potuisset.
units.tr: At this same time something is also reported of a certain English Minorite, in our Hardyng. When the legate of Benedict XIII had gone into Scotland, he would by no means have escaped the burning faggots for the heresy charged against him, had he not provided for his safety by a timely flight.

units.la: Io. Huffus Bohemus.
units.tr: John Huss the Bohemian.

Verum cum id aperta ratione non posse fe intelli- gerent, propter Bohemorum poten tiam, ac uires, quibus tum ille com- munitus erat, obliquis consilijs rem aggrediuntur, uel hinc facile fe pro- dentes cuius spiritu agebantur, omni no ad fe accersendum Huffum statu erunt, quoq; facilius eum euocaret, fuco seu esca quadam illito hamo, occultare pernitiosa consilia uisum est, addunt immunitatis spem, polli- centes indemnem fore, ac sine pericu lo, si Bohemi ciues, suae fidei homine permitterent. Hi nihil subesse doli rati, in tam sancta pollicitatione, prę fertim quae à tam sanctis patribus proficisceretur, Huffum suum epi- scopis, hoc est, agnum lupo commi- serunt: Qui ubi primum in nassam illorum illectus incidisset, statim ex sacrosancto concilij consensu denun ciatum est, Non fore illegitimum, quicquid effet haeretico homini pro missum, id postea irrita pactione, rescindere. units.tr: Meanwhile, in this same council, in the year 1415, there was debate about John Huss, whom the ecclesiastical nobles laboured by every means to snatch from life. But since they realised they could not do this by open means, on account of the power and strength of the Bohemians, by which he was then protected, they approached the matter by oblique counsels. Since they would easily betray by this very act the spirit by which they were driven, it seemed good to conceal their pernicious designs, as if a bait were smeared upon a hook, so that they might more easily summon Huss to them. They added the hope of immunity, promising that he would be unharmed and without danger if the Bohemian citizens would entrust their man of faith to them. Those citizens, thinking there was no deceit under so holy a promise, especially one coming from such holy fathers, committed their Huss to the bishops, that is, the lamb to the wolf. As soon as he had been lured into their net, it was at once announced, by the consent of the most sacred council, that it would not be unlawful to break whatever had been promised to a heretic, and afterwards to annul the pact. O holy fishers of men! O faith worthy of apostolic councils! What more? By this decree of the senate the way back to Huss was closed, and at the same time their faith in deceiving was kept intact. Indeed such is the power and majesty of the apostolic see that there is nothing so contrary to law or to nature that its authority, finding it, cannot easily subject to its own laws. How cruelly he was oppressed, how many snares surrounded him, how he was convicted by no Scriptures, how many adversaries he overwhelmed with Scripture passages that were quite manifest, how great his prudence in answering, his acuteness in refuting, his knowledge of the Scriptures, his purity of life, his patience in persecution and in prisons, his constancy in death, and what the whole form of the judgments was: since these matters are already, through the handling of many, made known to the world and are nearly on everyone's lips as history, I think there is no great need to go through each thing again one by one, as the orators do. This alone will suffice for our purpose: to touch on the chief heads of these matters, as in passing.

units.la: iam multorum tractatione orbi per uulgata, omniumque pene in ore historia est, non opus admodum arbitror ut singulatim denuo quaeque ut gesta sint Oratorum ritu refricare. Tantum quod instituto nostro satis erit, potiora cum taxat rerum capita, uelut in transcursu annotata, ac petita ab ijs, qui ipsum audiebant, delibabimus.
units.tr: Since the story has now been spread across the world by the discussion of many and is almost on everyone's lips, I think it is not at all necessary to go over again, one by one, how each thing was done, in the manner of orators. It will be enough for our purpose to touch on the principal heads of the matters, noted as if in passing, and taken from those who heard him speak.

units.la: Euocatus itaque ad concilium Constantiense constantissimus Christi martyr I. Huffus, per conducti-as Sigismundi Imp. literas, protinus in carcerem apud monachos ordinis praedicatorij abducitur, inde & in alium monasterium lignipedorum adseruandus ablegatur. Aduersarios & testes habebat Stephanum Paletium (qui multis abeo beneficijs affectus fuerat) Michaelem parochum olim Sinradium, aliosque Boemos aliquot. Inter iudices causae praesidebat episcopus Florentinus, Crimina, quae intenintentabantur, partim per testes subornatos conuicta, partim ex libris ipsius truncatim, ut quaecunque arrodere poterat mendax calumnia, arcesceba ntur in articulos 39. digesta. Subinde impetitus animus innocens crebris accusationibus pertentabatur. Sic tamen, ut nec testes scire nec refutare licuit. Tandem exijt per fidi concilij sceleratum decretum quo episcoporum simul ac Imp. vocce, clareilli denunciatum est, harum utram vellet optionem intelligeret, aut se noxae dederet erroribus retractatis, aut mòrti se pararet. Locus interim erroris manifesti nullus, nec si errarer, scriptura qua doceretur nusquam proferebatur. Ille contra, docere paratum se, impietatem vero, cuius nunquam esset conscius, agnoscere nec velle, nec sine mendacio potuisse, quidquid se prius passurum dicitabat.
units.tr: Summoned therefore to the Council of Constance, the most steadfast martyr of Christ, John Hus, under a safe-conduct from the emperor Sigismund, was at once led off to prison in the monastery of the Dominican order, and from there was sent away to another monastery of the barefoot friars to be kept. His opponents and witnesses were Stephen Páleč, who had been loaded with many benefits by him, Michael, once parish priest of Sinradium, and some other Bohemians. The bishop of Florence presided among the judges of the case. The charges brought against him, partly proved by suborned witnesses and partly drawn from his books torn out of context, so that whatever lying calumny could gnaw at was gathered into thirty-nine articles. Then the innocent mind, once attacked, was tested by frequent accusations, yet in such a way that the witnesses could not be known, nor was he permitted to refute them. At last there went out, by the wicked decree of the council, a proclamation made clear by the voice of the bishops and the emperor: he was to understand which of the two options he wished, either to submit himself to punishment by retracting his errors, or to prepare himself for death. Meanwhile there was no place of manifest error, and if he was in error, no Scripture by which he might be taught was brought forward anywhere. He, on the contrary, said that he was ready to be taught, but that he neither wished nor could, without lying, acknowledge an impiety of which he had never been conscious; whatever he had said before, he would suffer.

units.la: Non ita multo post, Iunij. 5. a Sigismundo Imp. legati ad Husitas ueniunt Barones quídam D. Ioan-nes Chlumensis, D. Vuenceslaus, cum episcopis quatuor, eo missi, ut ipsum, quibus possent machinis, de sententia deiycerent, ac in castra sua traducerent. Is ubi e carcere eductus coram legatis constitit, mox D. Io. Chlumensis hunc ita affari incipit. Pie Magister, nos qui imperiti homines atque ignari sumus, bene tibi uelle quimus, consulere nequimus, proin ipse quid tibi consultissimum sit, uideas. Si harum te accusationum reum sentias, ne pigeat, mutata sententia, errores profiteri. Sin minus, cave, contra conscientiam committas quicquam, neu potior sit apud te uitae quàm ueritatis diuinae iactura. Tum ille profusus lachrymis, quàm modestissime his respondit: Suspiciende uir, Deum attestor meum, si quid haʃtenus in libris, aut concionibus à me usquam erratum sit, adeo non grauabor cedere, ut uehemen-
units.tr: Not long after, on 5 June, certain barons sent by the emperor Sigismund came to the Hussites: Lord John of Chlum and Lord Wenceslaus, together with four bishops, sent there so that they might by whatever machinations they could bring him down from his sentence and take him to their own camp. When he was led out of the prison and stood before the envoys, Lord John of Chlum at once began to address him thus: "Pious master, we are unlearned and ignorant men. We can wish you well, but we cannot advise you; so see for yourself what is most advisable for you. If you feel you are guilty of these accusations, do not be ashamed to change your opinion and profess your errors. But if not, take care not to commit anything against your conscience, and do not let the loss of divine truth weigh more with you than your life." Then he, pouring out tears, answered them as modestly as he could: "Reverend sir, I call God to witness that if anything has hitherto been taught in error by me, in my books or sermons anywhere, I will be so far from being reluctant to yield that I will eagerly

units.la: {*} Hic deest aliquid. ter expetam,ac gratias insuper habi-turus sim, si quisquam prodeat, qui refutatis meis, probabili aliqua scriptura, saniora ac firmiora me doceat. Ad hanc vocem exclamans unus episcoporum, Hui, inquit, tun' ergo plus universo concilio sapere postulas? Hulfus, Nequaquam, o bone, Sed neq; rursus universum concilium plus sapere debet, quàm scriptura Dei. Tantum vero a me abest, quod obijcis: ut nihil equidem detrectem, uel ab infimo totius concilij tyrunculo instituti, qui iustis rationibus mecum agens, meliora afferat. Ibi reliqui episcopi sublata voce, Heu, inquiunt, quàm pertinax ille est in sua haeresi. Nam haeresim appellant hi, quicquid libidini suae non placet, aut cum dignitate pugnat. Atque haec fere huius diei acta sunt. Postero die qui erat lunij sextus, dus ab Archiepiscopo Rigentino, ad summum Constantiae templum, uenit inuictus Christi pugil. Verum, quia nodum sacra in templo perficerentur, tantisper dum tempus missae perageret, iussus est aliquandiu expectare foras. Quid nisi? Quippe, opinor, ne integerrimi ac sanctissimi martyris contubernio, ter adorandae papisticae stultitiae naeniae, polluerentur. Ridiculum: Nil intra est olea, nihil extra est in nuce duri. Sed quid multis. Peractis demum muniis papisticis, episcopi, pharisaei, ac principes sacerdotum, in sua quisque sedilia conscenderant. Ea, theatrica pompa, praealtis tabernaculis erigebantur. Spectari diceres floralia. Caeteris sublimior sub corona aurea eminet Imperator. In medio theatri, mensa quaedam, ac in mensa truncus apponebatur, rursus in trunco uestes, quibus sacrificaturi uti consueuerunt, consternebantur. His ita praeparatis, introducitur tandem inter lupos rapaces, misera pro Christo mactanda. da ouicula I. Huffus iussus ante men sam consistere. Is in terram procum bens, diufcule precibus immoratur. Interea monachus quidam episco pus, in suggestum, ingenti impetu prouolat, Landinus quibusdam, mi hi quisquis erat, Ate rectiore cognomento dicetur: cuiusmodi non paucas hodie furias mundus hic gignit, haud in aliud, quam in seditionem ac discordiam natas: Concionem hic in tres partes distributam habere dicitur. Quarum prima quam acerrime in pestem haereticam inuehebat: in secunda, principes ac magistratus uelut classico euocabat ad curam reip. ecclesiasticae, tum potissimum in profligandis haereticis. Postremo loco, commoda percensuit, quae ex ea re, publice priuatimque consequentur. Attamen uerentes pontifici ne satis magnas flammas in animis auditorum reliquissent, frigidus hic concionator alterum adhuc Henricum cum quendam, concilij oratorem, in eundem locum subagitarunt, qui de Husi condemnatione maiore acumine, ac ἀληθῶς quanta posset, pero-raret. Quibus confectis, Episcopus quidam, iubente concilio, in pulpitum prosiliens, formulam causae Hussia-næ, quæ habita est cum Archiepiscopo Pragensi, reliquaque crimina recitat, quæ illi tum intendebantur. Hæc ipse postea omnia in carcere perscripta fratribus legenda miserat, quo iudicum calumnias, ac mendacia, veritas patefacta redargueret. Si singula accusationum capita perceserem, haud exigui res negotij foret. Perstringam, quæ a fidelissimis accepta, satis ad huius iudicij iniquitatem exprimendam, fuerint. Interalia hoc illi obiectum est: Quod alicubi diceret unicā esse ecclesiam catholicam, quæ coetus esset omnium credentium, ad vitam praedestinatorum. Hoc, inquit ille, concilium sacrosanctum pro hæresi damnat. Huius. Imò equidem nil addubito, quin una sit ecclesia sancta, catholica, quæ est credentium congregatio, tum in hoc mundo, tum defunctorum ac in cœlis agentium, porro & eorum qui occultum corpus Christi Iesu sunt, qui est caput. Hæc itaque alia quum diceret, simulque ad alios articulos pararet respondere, Cardinalis Cameracensis, veluti lupus homini uocem adempturus. Tace, inquit, modo, postrespondebis simul ad omnia. Huffus. At quam iniquè hoc à vobis comparatum est: nunc quum sin gulis respondere liceat, prohibetis, post ubi congestam criminum turbam meminisse nequeam, tum permittetis: simulque ad alia respondere properabat. At insurgens illico Cardinalis Florentinus unus iudicum. Tace, inquit, obtundis nimiū, præconibus, quiq; astiterant accusatoribus mandans, ut coherceretur.
units.tr: {*} Here something is missing. seek it, and I will even give thanks, if anyone comes forward who, by refuting what I have written, teaches me something sounder and firmer from some credible Scripture." At this speech one of the bishops cried out: "Hui! Do you therefore demand to be wiser than the whole council?" Hus: "By no means, good sir. But neither ought the whole council to be wiser than the Scripture of God. Yet I am so far from refusing anything, as you charge me, that I would not refuse even the lowest novice of the whole council, if he argued with me by just reasons and brought something better." Then the other bishops, raising their voices, said: "Alas, how obstinate he is in his heresy!" For these men call heresy whatever does not please their lust or clashes with their dignity. These things were about all that was done that day. On the next day, which was the sixth of June, the unconquered athlete of Christ was brought by the archbishop of Riga to the great church of Constance. But because sacred rites were being performed in the church, he was ordered to wait outside for a while until the time of the mass was over. Why? Surely, I suppose, lest the papistical trifles, to be adored thrice over, be polluted by the company of that most upright and most holy martyr. Ridiculous! "Nothing within the olive, nothing hard outside the nut." But why say more? When the papistical rites were at last finished, the bishops, Pharisees and chief priests had each mounted to his seat. These were raised on very high platforms, with theatrical pomp. You would have said that the Floralia were being watched. The emperor stood out above the rest, under a golden crown. In the middle of the theatre a table was set, and on the table a block, and again upon the block were spread out the vestments that sacrificing priests were accustomed to wear. With these things so prepared, the poor sheep, to be slaughtered for Christ, John Hus, was at last led in among the ravening wolves and ordered to stand before the table. He, prostrating himself on the ground, lingered a while in prayer. Meanwhile a certain monk, a bishop, rushed with great vehemence onto the platform. Whoever he was, he would more rightly be called by another name, "Landinus," since this world today breeds not a few such furies, born for nothing but sedition and discord. He is said to have divided his sermon here into three parts. In the first he attacked the heretical pest most bitterly; in the second he summoned princes and magistrates, as if by a trumpet call, to the care of the ecclesiastical commonwealth, especially in stamping out heretics; last, he went through the advantages that follow from that business, both public and private. Yet, fearing that they had not left the flames in the hearers' minds large enough for the pontiff, they urged on this cold preacher, and another, a certain Henry, an orator of the council, into the same place, to hold forth on Hus's condemnation with greater acuteness and, truly [ἀληθῶς], as much as he could. When these were finished, a certain bishop, at the council's command, leaped onto the pulpit and recited the formula of Hus's case, which had been held with the archbishop of Prague, and the other charges then brought against him. Hus himself had afterwards sent all these things, written out in prison, for the brothers to read, so that the truth, laid open, might refute the calumnies and lies of the judges. If I were to go through each head of accusation, it would be no small task. I will touch only on those which, received from the most faithful sources, were enough to express the iniquity of this judgment. Among other things this was objected to him: that somewhere he said there is one holy catholic church, which is the assembly of all believers destined for life. "This holy council," he said, "condemns as heresy." Hus: "Indeed I have no doubt at all that there is one holy catholic church, which is the congregation of believers, both in this world, and of the dead and those dwelling in heaven, and further of those who are the hidden body of Jesus Christ, who is its head." While he was saying these and other things, and at the same time preparing to answer the other articles, the cardinal of Cambrai, like a wolf about to take a man's voice away, said: "Be quiet now; afterwards you will answer everything at once." Hus: "But how unjustly this has been arranged by you! Now, when I am allowed to answer each point, you forbid it; afterwards, when I cannot remember the heap of charges piled up, you will permit it." And at the same time he hurried on to answer other points. But at once the cardinal of Florence, one of the judges, rose up: "Be silent! You are too importunate!" And he commanded the criers and the accusers who stood by to restrain him.

units.la: Tum Huflus uoce ac manibus ad coelum reflexis: At enim Dei omnipotentis nomine uos appello, ob eos saltē qui hic circumstant auditores, q̄ me liberem apud ipsos omni suspicione, ut me benignis animis audiatis, q̄d ubi feceritis postea utimini in me arbitratu uestro. Verū quū nec lo quendo, nec orando quicq̄ ,pficeret, tandē humi prostratus genibus, Deo ęquissimo iudici, se causam q̄ cōmen dauit, idemq̄ crebrius, inter accusan dū, factitabat. Post hos articulos exlī bris ipsius corrasos, insequūtur mox illa crimina per testes ac accusatores maleficos introducta. Cuius generis hęc aliaq̄ fuerant. Quōd à cōsecrati one eucharistiae, diceret in altari remanere panē materialē, et substantia lē. Deinde q̄d sacerdos mortali pec cato pollutus, nec consecrare, nec baptif. possit, praeter alia quę his similia proponebant. Ad ea respōdere fata genti, iterū à C. Florent. indicū est silentium. Ille uero nihilo secus precibus instabat, ut se benigne audiant, uel ob istos, inquit, qui adsunt, ne falso hos in me errores suspicentur. Nam quod obiicitis, ex meo auditum, post consecratum sacramentum, panem manere materialem, id constanter pernego. Deinde adsero, quod baptismus, consecratio, rerumq; sacrarum tractatio facta per sacerdotem mortalis peccati reum, exosa est coram Deo, neque enim talis idoneus est rerum diuinarum minister. Itaq; & ad alias criminum responsiones obiectiones, uel aptè refellendo nonnullas, uel pie adferendo.
units.tr: Then Hus, raising his voice and hands to heaven: "In the name of almighty God I appeal to you, at least for the sake of those who stand here as listeners, so that I may be cleared of all suspicion before them and you may hear me with kindly minds; and when you have done so, you may deal with me afterwards as you please." But when he achieved nothing by speaking or by praying, at last he lay prostrate on his knees on the ground and commended his cause to God, the most just judge, and he did this more often while he was being accused. After these articles, scraped from his books, there immediately followed those charges introduced through witnesses and malicious accusers. Of this kind were these and others: that from the consecration of the Eucharist he said material and substantial bread remains on the altar; then that a priest polluted by mortal sin can neither consecrate nor baptize; besides other things of this sort that they put forward. When he was about to answer these, silence was again commanded by the cardinal of Florence, one of the judges. He, nonetheless, kept insisting with prayers that they hear him kindly, "at least," he said, "for the sake of those present, so that they do not falsely suspect these errors of me." "For as to what you object, that it was heard from me that after the sacrament is consecrated material bread remains, I flatly deny it. Next I assert that baptism, consecration, and the handling of sacred things done by a priest guilty of mortal sin is hateful before God, for such a man is not a fit minister of divine things." And so he answered the other charges and objections, either refuting some of them aptly or setting forth the truth piously.

units.la: Haec dum aguntur, nouum quoddam commenti genus in eum conquent, idq; Doctoris cuiusdam testimonio confirmatum, uidelicet quod sanct. Triadi, quartam nescio quam personam adiiceret. Tum Huffus. proferte, quaeso, doctoris huiusce nomen. At episcopi hoc perpetuum habehabebant. Quoties testimoniis urgebatur Hussus, scisscitanti testis nomen, sic respondebatur. Huius, inquiunt, criminis testes sunt duo canonici Pragenses, & totidem parochi, altarij tres, et unus doctor. At nomina hominum celabantur. Mox Hussus: Deus, inquit, tantum auertat nephas, ut miser ego in Triade sacra, quartam personam adnecterem, quod nunquam mihi (ita me amet Christus) ne per somnium quidem in mentem venit, imo equidem certo confiteor, quod tres personae, pater, filius & spiritus sanctus, unus Deus, & una essentia in diuinitate sunt. Repulsi itaque ab hoc lemmate episcopi, ad id confugiunt, simulque verba recitant, ubi paulo superius Deum ipsum, ut ad summum prouocando iudicem, appellauit; quam quidem ipsam appellationem, velut pro immo errore (o blasphemam episcoporum impietatem) damnauerunt.
units.tr: While these things were going on, they brought forward a new kind of charge against him, confirmed by the testimony of a certain doctor: that he added some fourth person, I know not whom, to the holy Trinity. Then Hus said: "Please, name this doctor." But the bishops always kept to one practice: whenever Hus was pressed with testimonies and asked for the name of a witness, they answered: "The witnesses to this crime are two canons of Prague, as many parish priests, three altarists, and one doctor." But the names of the men were concealed. Soon Hus said: "God forbid such a wickedness, that I, wretched as I am, should join a fourth person to the holy Trinity. That never (so help me Christ) came into my mind, not even in a dream. Indeed I certainly confess that the three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, are one God and one essence in the Godhead." Repulsed from this charge, the bishops took refuge in the words he had used a little earlier, when he called God himself to witness as the highest judge. That very appeal they condemned as an error (O the blasphemous impiety of the bishops).

units.la: Notanda episcoporum blasphemia.
units.tr: Note the blasphemy of the bishops.

units.la: Quòd quum audisset ille, uoce subalta exclamauit, En optime Iesu, quid hoc concilium molitur, tu aliquando ab inimicis tuis oppressus, Deo patri iustissimo iudici, causam commendasti tuam, nobis relicto exemplo, ut in afflictis rebus nos similiter ad te auxilij gratia discamus accurrere. Atqui hoc isti erroris ac malefacti loco impingunt. Additçp. Ego uero, ego inçp, audacter affirmo, nullã certioré appellatione esse, çp ad Do. Iesum, qui nec muneribus flectitur, nec testimoniis fallit, nec uersutia imponit, quemadmodum nec ipse fallitur, at suum cuiqç preciū reddit. Post hæc, struitur & altera calumnia, quòd excommunicationem Pont. sioccifecerit, nihiloç minus à missæ officio non abstinens. Ad hoc Hussus. Equidem excommunicationem hanc contemptui non habebam, sed publice in concionibus appelappellabam ad iudicem, pergens utique in sacris. Quin neque hoc co-ram tentus, ad summum pontificem inte-rea miseram, qui pro me satisface-rent. Qui tamen ut audirentur (nam mihi de causis uobis significatis, as-desse non licuit) impetrari nequitū est. quibusdam carceribus multa-tis, aliis per contumeliam exclusis, atque excruciatis miserè. Cuius rei testes sunt hae tabulae: itaque in con-cilium hoc ueni liber, innocentiam meam testaturus fide publica acce-pta ab Imperatore, qui praesto adest, me ab omni ui tutum fore. Haec cū loquerétur, oculos in Imperatorem defixos habuit. Ille statim uehemen-ter erubuit, eiusq; uerecundus tin-xerat ora rubor.
units.tr: When he heard this, he cried out in a loud voice: "Behold, excellent Jesus, what this council is contriving! You, once oppressed by your enemies, committed your cause to God the Father, the most just judge, leaving us an example that in afflicted circumstances we too should learn by the grace of your help to run to you. Yet these men charge this against me as a crime and a wrong." He added: "Indeed I, I, boldly affirm that there is no surer appeal than the one made to the Lord Jesus, who is neither bent by bribes, nor deceived by testimonies, nor imposed upon by cunning, just as he himself is not deceived, but renders to each his due reward." After this another calumny was built up: that he had despised the excommunication of the Pontiff, and nevertheless had not abstained from the office of the Mass. To this Hus replied: "Indeed I did not hold this excommunication in contempt. Publicly, in my sermons, I appealed to the judge, and I continued, of course, in the sacred duties. Moreover, not even being held to this, in the meantime I sent men to the supreme pontiff who would make satisfaction for me. Yet they could not obtain a hearing (it was not permitted me to be present, for reasons already made known to you). Some were thrown into prisons, others were excluded with insult, and were wretchedly tortured. These documents are witnesses to this matter. Therefore I came to this council of my own free will, intending to testify to my innocence, having accepted a public safe-conduct from the Emperor, who is present here, that I shall be safe from all violence." As he said these things, he kept his eyes fixed on the Emperor. At once the Emperor blushed deeply, and a modest blush colored his face.

units.la: Finitis tandem criminum capití-bus, lecta est ilico, à iudice Ponti-ficio, condemnationis sententia. In qua, quum ad illud uentū est quod multos annos pertinaciter inhaerit erroribus. Prorsus, inquit Huffus, id ego pernego. Siquidem me talem semper praestiti, atque nunc praesto, ut cupidissimum me discendi sentiat, quisquis ex scriptura me edocere, atque erroris commonefacere poterit. Rursus quum sententia illa proferebatur, qua libri illius omnes Latine & Boemice scripti, abolerentur. Sic ille. Qui inquit, potestis scripta mea damnare iuste, quum libenter ad scripturarum normam me corrigi cupiam, Dein quum nec quisquam hactenus prodierit, qui firmo scriptura argumento, erroris convicerit. Postremo, qui Boemice prorsus ignari estis, quo pacto ea lingua scriptos libros vel intelligere, vel damnare poteritis? Porro pergit alter in recitata condemnatione. Hic vero, quum loqui non permitteretur, coelum aspectans, ac genibus flexis ac sculptans articulis, orabat. Finita demum condemnatione, Huffus pro inimicis suis, uoce clara ita deprecatus est. Domine Deus per misericordiam tuam precor, hostibus meis digneris ignoscere. Scis enim me ab his iniuste accusatum, falsis testibus circumuentum, confictis criminibus oppressum, denique iniquè condemnatum, propter mise ricordiam igitur tuam, culpam eis remitte. His auditis sacerdotum seniores plærique, ac præsertim episcopi toruo uultu inspicientes eum irride bant.
units.tr: When at last the articles of the charges were finished, the sentence of condemnation was read out at once by the Pontifical judge. When it came to the clause stating that for many years he had obstinately clung to errors, Hus said: "I utterly deny that. Indeed I have always shown myself so eager to learn, and I am still ready, that whoever can teach me from Scripture and warn me of error will find me so." Again, while the sentence was being pronounced, by which all his books, written in Latin and in Bohemian, were to be burned, he said: "How can you justly condemn my writings, since I am willing to be corrected by the rule of Scripture? Moreover, since no one has yet come forward who has convicted me of error by a firm argument from Scripture. Lastly, you who are utterly ignorant of Bohemian, how will you be able to understand, or to condemn, books written in that language?" Meanwhile the other man went on reading the condemnation. But Hus, since he was not permitted to speak, gazed up at heaven, knelt, clasped his fingers, and prayed. When the condemnation was at last finished, Hus, praying for his enemies, said in a clear voice: "Lord God, I beseech you through your mercy to deign to pardon my enemies. For you know that I have been accused unjustly by these men, surrounded by false witnesses, oppressed by invented crimes, and at last wickedly condemned. Therefore, for the sake of your mercy, remit their guilt." When these words were heard, many of the senior priests, and especially the bishops, looked at him with grim faces and mocked him.

units.la: Demum septem ab episcopis desi gnabantur, qui sacerdotium illi adepturi, amiculo sacrificorum, ac si missa ei celebranda foret, induerunt. Ac principio albam uestem induens, dixit: Dominus meus Iesus Christus cum ab Herode mitteretur ad Pilatū, in ueste candida illusus est. Postea hoc ita apparatu indutus sanctus martyr, ab episcopis commonetur, ut errores illos, dum liceret, retracta ret, iuramento etiam adiecto. Tum ille, à mensa ad turbam paululum cō uersus, sic eam adloquitur. En hic episcopi me hortantur ad errores retractandum. Verum id ego ut faciam triplici nomine absterreor: Primum, ne mendacij olim in conspectu Dei arguar, si errorum me reum esse faterer, quorum nunquā essem conscius. Tum ne conscientiam simul meam, & veritatem diuinā hoc pacto offenderem, quippe qui articulos illos non modo nunquam asse ruerim, (falso enim per testimonia mihi obtruduntur.) sed contrariā sæpe etiam & scripsi, & docui. Dein de ne animi tantæ multitudinis, cui hactenus concionatus sum, hoc pacto offensi, à veritate resiliant, acalio rum quoque, qui uerbi diuini fideles sunt ministri. Id audientes episcopi cum tota factione in hęc uerba acclamant. Iam tandē perspeximus quàm quam peruicax sit in malitia, atque tenax in sua haeresi. Ac continuo Hus so mandarunt ut de mensa descenderet. Ibi sacerdotium ei admentes, principio auferunt ab eo calicem, dicentes: O Iuda maledicte qui deserens consilium pacis, iniisti consilium cum Iudaeis. En auferimus a te calicem hunc, in quo sanguis Iesu Christi offertur in redemptionem mundi. Tum illi alta voce exclamauit uicissim. Ego uero spem ac fiduciam in seruatore meo fixissimam habeo, confidens constanter fore, ut is calicem salutaris a me nunquam transferat, quodque adiutus praesidio ipsius, hodie in regno eius hunc bibi turus sim. Illi uero reliquo apparatu hominem exuere pergunt: sic, ut singulis uestibus singulas execrationes adderent, Huss interea respondente. Illusiones has se, aequissimo animo pro nomine & veritate Domini nostri Iesu Christi iferre.
units.tr: At last the bishops designated seven men who were to confer the priesthood on him. They dressed him in the priestly vestments, as if he were to celebrate Mass. Putting on the white garment first, he said: "My Lord Jesus Christ, when he was sent by Herod to Pilate, was mocked in a white robe." Afterwards the holy martyr, thus equipped, was urged by the bishops to retract those errors while it was still allowed, and an oath was added too. Then he turned a little from the table toward the crowd and addressed it thus: "Behold, these bishops exhort me to retract the errors. But I am deterred from doing this for three reasons. First, lest I be convicted of lying before God, if I confessed myself guilty of errors of which I was never conscious. Next, lest in this way I offend both my conscience and divine truth, since I have not only never asserted those articles (for they are falsely thrust upon me by testimonies), but have often both written and taught the contrary. Last, lest the minds of so great a multitude, to whom I have hitherto preached, be offended in this way and turn away from the truth, and likewise those others who are faithful ministers of the divine word." Hearing this, the bishops with their whole faction shouted out these words: "Now at last we have perceived how stubborn he is in malice, and how tenacious in his heresy." At once they ordered Hus to come down from the table. Then, as they stripped him of his priestly things, they first took the chalice from him, saying: "O cursed Judas, who, forsaking the counsel of peace, entered into a plot with the Jews! Behold, we take from you this chalice, in which the blood of Jesus Christ is offered for the redemption of the world." He then cried out in a loud voice in turn: "But I have the firmest hope and confidence in my Saviour, trusting steadfastly that he will never take from me the cup of salvation, and that, aided by his protection, I shall drink it today in his kingdom." They, however, went on stripping the man of the rest of his vestments, adding a curse to each garment, while Hus meanwhile answered that he bore these mockeries with the utmost calm for the name and truth of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Detracto itaque uniuersocultu,tandem ad uerticis rasuram accessum est. Hic perplexa satis dissentiuncula,inter tartareos hos mastygas oboritur,quo potissimum instrumenti genere, nouaculane, an forsice haec nota abradeda sit. Inter haec conuersus ad Imperatorem Huffus,Eya,inquit, nondum inter istos conuenit, quo ludibrij genere me irrideant satis. Variantibus diu studijs,obtinet tandem sententia illa,ut forsice, crudele mysterium expediatur. Itaque capillis in quatuor partibus crucis in formam, detonsis,uerticem illum orbicularem dispungunt, adiecto hoc epiphonemate. Iam sacrum hoc concilium Constanti. Ioannem Hussum ordine sacrificali, quo exornatus fuit,amouet,ea re declaras,quod hominem hunc, ecclesia Dei abscefe abdicauerit,ac destitutum suo praesidio potestati seculari tradiderit. Moxque coronam papyraceam inludibrium dibrium imposituri, illud accinunt: Animam tuam devouemus diabolis inferni. Contra ille manibus compli catis caelum suspiciens, ait. At ego eam commendo benignissimo Domino meo Iesu Christo. Corona ue rò huiusmodi erat ex papyro facta, et ad speciem pyramidis acuminata, cubitali fermè longitudine, in qua tres horrendi cacodaemones depingebantur, cum inscriptione criminis: Iste est haeresiarcha. Eam ubi vi derat ille, dixit. Dominus meus Iesus Christus pro me misero, longè asperiorem ac spineam coronam innocens ad infame mortis genus gestare dignatus est, quapropter ego miser peccator hanc multò leuiorem coronam, nominis ipsius ac veritatis causa, lubens feram. Tum imperator Ludovico Clementis filio Ducì mandarat, ut acceptum Hussum Lictoribus traderet.
units.tr: With all the ornaments removed, they at last came to the shaving of the crown. Here a rather perplexing little dispute arose among these Tartarean scourges: with what kind of instrument this mark should be scraped off, with a razor or with shears. Meanwhile Hus turned to the Emperor and said: "Look, they have not yet agreed among themselves on what kind of mockery will sufficiently ridicule me." After long debate, the opinion prevailed that the cruel rite should be carried out with shears. So, with the hair cut away in the four parts of a cross, they shaved the round crown, adding this exclamation: "Now this holy council of Constance strips John Hus of the priestly order with which he was adorned, declaring by this act that it has cast this man out of the Church of God, and, having left him without its protection, hands him over to the secular power." Then, about to place a paper crown on his head as a mockery, they sang: "We devote your soul to the devils of hell." Against this he, with hands folded and gazing up to heaven, said: "But I commend it to my most gracious Lord Jesus Christ." The crown was made of paper and tapered to a point like a pyramid, about a cubit in length; on it three horrible demons were depicted, with the inscription of the crime: "This is the arch-heretic." When he saw it, he said: "My Lord Jesus Christ, for me a wretched man, deigned, though innocent, to bear a far harsher, thorny crown to an infamous kind of death. Therefore I, a wretched sinner, will gladly bear this much lighter crown for the sake of his name and truth." Then the Emperor had ordered Louis, son of Duke Clement, to take Hus, once received, and hand him over to the lictors.

units.la: Is igitur hanc gestans coronam, è templo ad supplicium ducitur, turba undique armata comitatus, incensis primum sub eius conspectum libris. Hoc ubi uidit, subrisit Huffus, ac ad rogum profectus, turbam commonet, ut ne crederent se propter errores exustum iri, falsis enim nominibus ac testibus insimulatum se, ac ut oppressum. Deinde nec quemquam omnium esse, qui rectius ex sacra scriptura sese edoceret hactenus, id quod ego, inquit, unice semper cupiebam.
units.tr: He was therefore led from the church to execution, wearing this crown and surrounded on all sides by a crowd of armed men, and his books were first burned before his eyes. When Huss saw this, he smiled, and as he went to the pyre he warned the crowd not to believe that he was being burned for errors. He said he had been falsely accused by false names and false witnesses, and that he was being crushed. Then he said that there was no one among them all who could teach him more correctly from Holy Scripture, and that this was what he had always most eagerly desired.

units.la: Postquam ad locum supplicii peruenerum est, qui situs erat inter hortos suburbij Constantiensis, haud procul ab arce, Pius ac innocens Christi martyr, flexo poplite, manibus, ac oculis in coelum resupinis, psalmos aliquot recitat, praesertim quinquagesimum et tricesimum. subinde uersu illo: In manus tuas Domine commendo spiritum meum, uoce clara, ac uultu hilari repetito, ita ut facile a circumstantibus audiretur. Quod cum
units.tr: When they had come to the place of execution, which lay between the gardens of the suburb of Constance, not far from the castle, the pious and innocent martyr of Christ knelt down, and with his hands and eyes raised toward heaven he recited several psalms, especially the fiftieth and the thirtieth. Repeatedly he said in a clear voice and with a cheerful countenance the verse, "Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit," so that he could easily be heard by those standing near.

units.la: {y} cum quidam ex plebe illiterati animaduerterent, dicitant. Quid hic prius docuerit, dixeritue, nescimus, certe nunc uidemus, & audimus ex eo sacra eloquia, ac pias preces. Alij item optabant illi adhiberi confessorem. Ad hoc Sacerdos quidam magna pompa obequitans respondit. Quid illi confessorem, Haereticus est? Quanquam ex epistola eius quadam in carcere scripta, liquet, septimo ante passionem die, a monacho quodam Doctore, sibi a concilio concessō, confessum esse, & absolutum. Euenit interim inter orandū, ut probrosa illa corona de capite deciderit, quam conspicatus uir bonus, subrisit. Clamitantibus interea satellibus quibusdam, restituatur rursus capiti, ut cum diabolis dominis suis, quos coluit, exuratur. Huiusmodi tum a carnifice erectus, clara uoce, ut ab omnibus facile perciperetur, sic orabat. Domine Iesu Christe, crudelissimā hoc, ac horrendum supplicium, propter sanctum euangelium, ac praedicationem uerbi tui, libens ac humiliter subeo, tu autem omnibus inimicis meis ignosce precor. Tum a lictoribus circumductus, iterum hortari coepit omnes, ne quis ullos in se errores haerere crederet, tantummodo fictitios, falsisque testibus firmatos titulos, quos nunquam docueri tadscribi sibi. Tandem ab eis petijt, ut carceris custodes conuenire liceret. Quibus ad se accedentibus, Gratias egit pro summis in se collocatis beneficijs. Fratres enim, inquit, mei nedum custodes fuistis: Ac scitote, quod constanter credo seruatori meo, cuius nomine haec tam acerba fero, & lubenter fero, nihil addubitans, quin cum eo una hodie regnaturus sum. His aliisque sermonibus finitis, mox uestitu usque ad indusium exutus, ad crassum quendam ac perforatum asserem, manibus reuinctis, sex aut septem funibus alligatur. Primo proxime talos, deinde sub genibus, mox supra genua, praeterea iuxta inguina, sextus medium corpus ambit, postremus sub brachiis. Itaque palus ille terrae intrusus firmabatur. Sed nonnullos aegre habebat hoc, quod constitutus esset facie ad orientem versa: iubetes ut occasum versus obuertereтur, esse enim haereticum, Id quod statim factum est. Porro ne quid ad ultimam ignominiam deesset, cathena quadam aspe ctu horrenda, rubigine, & fuligine aterrima, in qua miserlus quidam homuncio prius ahenum appende bat, ceruix sanctiss. uiri astringitur. Qua conspecta Huffus sublaetus arrisit, dicens. Dominus meus Iesus Christus, redemptor meus aserua tor meus charissimus, longe crudeli ore catena propter me vinctus erat, cur ego miser erubescam propter ipsius nomen sacrosanctum fuliginosa hac constringi? Praeterea pedi-bus, quam uastissimo compede cin-ctis, duo lignorum fasces substruun-tur. Additur sarmentorum ac fasci-culorum strues, comiftis simul stra-minibus, ceruicetenus. Verum pri-usquam materia incenderetur, accef-serunt ad eum ciuitatum imperiali-um, marschalcus (quem uocant,) cum Ludouico Duce, agentes cum Huf-so, ut uitae seruandae mature consu-lat, spem veniae fore, si dogmata & errores abneget. Huffus. Errores, inquit, Quos? quorum ego consci-us non sum, nec unquam fui? An ut illa in me agnoscam, quae nunc admisi, ac ultro innocentiam meam prodam, num id postulatis, aut æquu arbitramini? Testes ac arbitros, qua-les uultis subornatis, impudentissi-me in me mentientes, quibus quoni-am lubentius acquiescitis, quam mi-hi, quid ego in hoc foro contendam amplius. Ego qui probe mihi con-sciu
units.tr: When some of the unlettered common people noticed this, they said: "What he taught or said here before we do not know; certainly now we see and hear from him holy words and pious prayers." Others likewise wished that a confessor be provided for him. To this a certain priest, riding up with great pomp, replied: "Why a confessor for him? He is a heretic!" Yet from a letter of his, written in prison, it is clear that on the seventh day before his passion he confessed to a certain monk who was a doctor, granted to him by the council, and was absolved. Meanwhile, during his prayers, it happened that the shameful crown fell from his head. When the good man saw this, he smiled. Some of the guards kept shouting that it should be put back on his head, so that it might be burned together with the devils, his masters, whom he had worshipped. Then, raised up by the executioner, he prayed in a clear voice, so that everyone could easily hear: "Lord Jesus Christ, I gladly and humbly undergo this most cruel and horrible death for the sake of your holy gospel and the preaching of your Word. But I pray that you forgive all my enemies." Then, led round by the officers, he began again to exhort everyone not to believe that any errors clung to him, only fictitious charges, confirmed by false witnesses, which he had never taught and which were being written against him. At last he asked them to allow him to speak with the keepers of the prison. When they came to him, he thanked them for the great kindnesses shown to him. "My brothers," he said, "you have been not only my keepers. Know this too: I firmly believe in my Saviour, in whose name I bear these so bitter things, and I bear them gladly, not doubting at all that today I shall reign together with him." When these and other words were finished, he was stripped of his clothing down to his undershirt and was tied to a thick stake with a hole in it, his hands bound behind him, with six or seven ropes: first around the ankles, then below the knees, then above the knees, next about the groin; a sixth went around the middle of the body, and the last under the arms. So the stake was fixed firmly in the ground. But it troubled some of them that he had been set up facing east; they ordered him turned toward the west, since facing east was heretical, and this was done at once. Moreover, so that nothing of ultimate disgrace should be lacking, an iron chain, terrible to see and covered with rust and the blackest soot, in which some wretched little fellow had previously hanged a kettle, was fastened around the holy man's neck. When Huss saw this, he smiled broadly and said: "My Lord Jesus Christ, my Redeemer and my most dear Saviour, was bound with a far crueller chain for my sake. Why should I, wretch that I am, be ashamed to be bound with this sooty one for the sake of his most holy name?" Besides, two bundles of wood were piled up around his feet, which were bound with a huge fetter. Then a heap of brushwood and bundles of kindling was added, mixed with straw, up to his neck. But before the fire was lit, there came to him the marshal (as he is called) of the imperial cities, together with Duke Louis, urging Huss to look soon to saving his life, promising hope of pardon if he would renounce his doctrines and errors. Huss replied: "Errors? Which? Of which I am not conscious, and never have been? Or do you ask me to acknowledge those things which I am now charged with, and to betray my innocence of my own accord? Is that what you demand, or do you think it fair? You have suborned witnesses and judges of whatever kind you wish, shamelessly lying against me; since you yield to them more willingly than to me, why should I contend any further in this court?"

units.la: Purgatio Io. Huffi sub morte. scius sum, id satis noui, atque apud Deum testor omnium rerum iudicem, ac καταλαγγώσιν, nunc me uel docuisse, uel scripsisse hactenus, quod non ex scripturae fontibus uerissimum sit, quodque mortales e peccati tyrannide posset eripere. Quod si quis sit, qui merito iuxta doctrinam scripturae euangelicae, me possit coarguere, semper me paratissimum ad omnem disputationem praebui. Nec enim officium in me, sed in illis rationes defuerunt. Quae si ab illis afferentur, non sum tam praefracte contumax, qui non perlibenter cedere rem. Nunc quum non afferuntur, quid a me exigant amplius, ut veritatis causam sciens deseram, quod etsi illi a me postularent, conscientia non permittit? At quanto id aequius, ut hi veritati accederent potius. quae uincet tandem uel inuitis omnibus? Quapropter quum eo res redijt, ut aut Deus ipse in me sit prouocans dus, aut humana malitia, potius quā illum inimicum habeam, agat mortalium uis, quòd possit. Ego sane ueritatem, quam hactenus docui lætus hoc mortis pignore hodie obsignare non dubitabo. Dominus misertus succurrat mihi ac ignoscat illis.
units.tr: Purgation of John Huss at death. I know well, being conscious of it, and I call God to witness, the judge of all things and the searcher of hearts [καταλαγγώσιν], that I have taught or written nothing up to now which is not most true according to the sources of Scripture, and which could not rescue mortals from the tyranny of sin. If there is anyone who can rightly refute me by the doctrine of the evangelical Scripture, I have always offered myself most ready for every disputation. For the fault lies not with me but with them, who have lacked arguments. If these were brought forward by them, I am not so stubbornly obstinate that I would not gladly yield the point. Now that they are not brought forward, what more do they demand of me, that knowing the cause of truth I should abandon it? Even if they asked this of me, my conscience does not permit it. How much more just it is that they should rather come over to the truth, which will in the end prevail even against the will of all! Therefore, since the matter has come to this, that either God himself is calling me to account, or human malice, rather than that I should regard him as my enemy, the power of mortals may do what it can. For my part I shall not hesitate, glad, to seal with this pledge of death today the truth which I have taught until now. May the merciful Lord come to my aid and forgive them."

units.la: Quo audito Ludouicus cum collega suo manibus complosis ab eo discedunt. Carnifices statim admoto igne, pyram accendunt. Ibi Hufsus præalta uoce semel atq; iterum exclamauit: Christe fili Dei uiui miserere mei. Tertio canentem, obor-to uento, flamma eum præfocauit, atq; ita conticuit. Ac interea tam diu nutabat capite, ac ora mouebat dum quispiam dominicam oratio-nem bis aut ter absolueret. Deinde ita tacitus intra se orans, emisit spiritum. Porro fascibus lignorum am bustis, dum corpus adhuc ad assere ligatum hæreret, tortores id cum as-fere in ignem intruserunt fustibus, moxque accurrentes ligna aggere-bant, cadauer urentes. Ibi uideas ex quisitam carnificum in singula membra crudelitatem. Nam (proh dolor) ossa fustibus comminuentes tu-debant, quo citius igne absumeren tur. Deinde caput inuentum palo disseecuerunt. Porro cor in intestinis repertum obelo ligneo infixum inter comburendum fustibus caedebant. Interea carnifex quidam uestem Husfi tenebat. Ludouicus autem simul atque cognouit esse tuni cam Husfi, iussit eam ac cingulum, denique quicquid ipsius esset, iniicere in ignem, dicens: Boëmi enim id uice Sacramenti haberent ac colerent. Deinde carnifici pollicitus est iacturam hanc compensaturum se. Postremo omnia igne in cinerem cò cremata, cum puluere, ac terra altius effossa in bigas impositere, dein in Rhenum praeterlabētem disiecerūt, quo ipsius nomen prorsus apud fideles extinguerent.
units.tr: When Louis heard this, he and his colleague clapped their hands and left him. The executioners at once applied the fire and lit the pyre. There Huss cried out in a very loud voice, once and again: "Christ, Son of the living God, have mercy on me." When he sang it a third time, a wind arose, and the flame choked him, and so he fell silent. Meanwhile he kept nodding his head and moving his lips for as long as it took someone to say the Lord's Prayer twice or three times. Then, praying silently within himself, he gave up his spirit. Moreover, while the body was still hanging bound to the stake, the torturers, with clubs, drove the bundles of wood into the fire, and at once others came running and heaped on more wood, burning the corpse. Here you might see the peculiar cruelty of the executioners toward each limb. For (alas!) they beat the bones with clubs to break them up, so that they would be consumed by the fire more quickly. Then they split open the head, which they had found, with a stake. Moreover, the heart, which they found among the entrails, they struck with clubs while it was being burned, having fixed it on a wooden spit. Meanwhile one executioner held Huss's garment. When Louis learned that it was Huss's tunic, he ordered it, together with the belt and whatever else belonged to him, to be thrown into the fire, saying: "For the Bohemians hold and worship it in place of a sacrament." Then he promised the executioner that he would make good this loss to him. Finally, when everything had been burned to ash, they gathered the ashes together with the dust and earth dug up deeper, put them on carts, and scattered them in the Rhine, which flows past, so that his name might be utterly wiped out among the faithful.

units.la: Multa in hoc homine dignissima calamo, cogor breuitatis studio transilire, quae in alienis tradita monumentis, ex ipsis peti malim quam non digno penicillo materiam tam bonam corrumpi. Illud e multis carptim ceu primarium flosculum lectori excerpendum duximus, quod etsi quibusdam somnium hominum uideri possit: inter haec tamen somnia numerandum quae ex exitu certissimam habent prophetiae fidem, ut non inscite hic locum habeat Nestoris illud T' ὄναρ ἐκ Διὸς ἐστι.
units.tr: Many things in this man are most worthy of the pen, but I am compelled, out of regard for brevity, to pass over them. I would rather that they be sought from the records of others, where they are handed down, than that such good material be spoiled by an unworthy brush. Of the many things, we have thought fit to pick out for the reader one flower as the chief: although it may seem to some to be the dreams of men, yet among such dreams must be counted those which, from their outcome, have the most certain credit of prophecy. So here the saying of Nestor fits well: the dream is from Zeus [τ' ὄναρ ἐκ Διὸς ἐστι].

units.la: Hic aliquando apud Bohemos ecclesiae Bethlemiticae praepositus est, in qua sibi per somnium visus est Christi sanctorumque imagines nonnullas picturā expressisse, at mox accedente pontifice cum suis impeditu illum, ac imagines erasas esse. Quod ubi sit factum, post paululum adesse uidet pictores alios, multoque plures, qui denuo restitutis ijs quae per pontificios obliterarentur, alias deinceps picturas non parum plures artec celebriores adiecerunt, adeoque numero, potentiaque prevaluisse pictores istos, ut iam omnes cardinalitiae centuriae cum pontifice ipso, ijs rursus delendis impares extitissent. Hoc enigmate usum est Deo, quid esset secuturum servo suo, pateface-re nec ipse fefellit exitus, quamquam nos sonnij prophetici sententiam aliorum coniecturis aestimandum relinquimus.
units.tr: Here, at one time among the Bohemians, he was made head of the Bethlehem church, in which he seemed in a dream to have painted some images of Christ and the saints; but soon, when the pope came with his men, he was prevented and the images were erased. When this had happened, after a little while he sees other painters, and many more of them, who, restoring the things that had been wiped out by the Papists, afterwards added other pictures, not a few more and more celebrated, so that these painters prevailed by their number and power, and all the cardinalitian centuries together with the pope himself were unable to delete them again. God used this enigma to show what was going to follow for his servant, and the outcome itself, which did not deceive, makes it plain; although we leave the meaning of the prophetic dream to be weighed by the conjectures of others.

units.la: HISTORIA HIERONYMI PRAGENSIS ex Poggio, aliisque deprompta.
units.tr: The History of Jerome of Prague, drawn from Poggio and others.

units.la: PROXIMO, AB HVIVS MARTYRIO, anno uidelicet post Christum 1416. praeceptorem Hussum insequutus est Hieronymus Pragensis, florida & aetate & eloquentia iuuenis. Qui ut eandem causam, quam Huffus, habuerat, ita eosdem fere hostes ac accusatores sortitus est. Tum ut in omni vita illi coniun ctissimus erat, ita nec morte a veteri sodali ac pietatis socio admodum di strahebatur. Vt ergo praetermissis iis quae ad vitā ipsius, ad mores, ad indolem, ac studia spectant, causam ipsam illico adgrediamur. Hieronymus hic simul atque Io. Huffum ad concilium accitum, ac iamiam iturū intelligeret, sedulo officio adest ami co suo, consolatur, rogat, ac adanimat, ut memor virtutis ac constantiae suae, rem graviter gerat pro Christo, ac veritatis incolumitate. Iam tempus adesse, quo maxime se declaret talem, quem hactenus tot concio nibus se ostendit omnibus, ipsequē semper habuerit. Quòd si ita eueni at, ut res ipsa opem operamq; suam efflagitet, intellecturū se, quòd nec pietati, nec officio suo, nec amico sit defuturus. Verum quemadmodū in Petro olim, ita in hoc pio adolescente comperimus haud uanam esse prouerbij illius fidem: Spondæno xa præsto est. Quippe non ita multo post, quum in turrim quandam coniectus, duricie carceris supra modum affligeretur, impulsus partim minis, partim elabendi spe, ut Hussi anæ condemnationi subscriberet, haud recusauit. Quæ sane res postea, maioris constantiæ illi materiæ subministrauit. Sed digressi ab ordine historiæ iam redeamus. Hieronymus, intellecta iam Hussi condemnatione, partim dolore percitus, ac metu periculi sui, partim æstu quodam diuinæ pietatis accensus, gestiebat & ipse concilium adire, succensuriaturus, si opus esset, atque etiam purgandi sui causa, sed ita, ut condu-ctitijs literis, ceu uadimonio obstrictos haberet aduersarios. Eas ubi exorare nequit, Boemiam redire parat. In itinere, hostium proditione, à seruis
units.tr: Next after Hus's martyrdom, in the year 1416 after Christ, Jerome of Prague followed his teacher. He was a young man, flourishing in both age and eloquence. He had the same cause as Hus and almost the same enemies and accusers. Just as he had been closely bound to Hus throughout his life, so he was not greatly parted from his old comrade and partner in piety even by death. Passing over what concerns his life, character, disposition and studies, let us go straight to the cause itself. As soon as Jerome learned that John Hus had been summoned to the council and was about to go, he dutifully stood by his friend, consoled him, asked him, and encouraged him. He urged him to remember his own courage and steadfastness, and to act bravely for Christ and for the safety of the truth. The time had come, he said, for Hus to show himself the man he had always shown himself to be in so many sermons. If it came about that the matter itself demanded his help and effort, Hus would find that Jerome would not be wanting either to piety, to duty, or to friendship. But, as we have found in Peter long ago, so in this devout young man the proverb holds true, that the promise is ready at hand. Indeed, not long afterwards, when he had been thrown into a tower and was greatly afflicted by the harshness of the prison, he was moved partly by threats and partly by hope of escape, and did not refuse to subscribe to the condemnation of Hus. That act afterwards supplied him with matter for greater constancy. But let us leave the order of the history and return. Jerome, having now learned of Hus's condemnation, was stirred partly by grief and fear for his own danger, and partly by a certain heat of divine piety. He longed to go to the council himself, to defend Hus if need be, and also to clear himself. But he wished to do so only under a safe-conduct, so that he would hold his opponents bound as if by a bond. When he could not obtain these letters, he prepared to return to Bohemia. On the journey, through the betrayal of enemies, he was seized by the servants of Duke John, son of Clement, and taken to him.

units.la: . seruis ducis Ioannis filij clementis, captus, atqz ad ipsum deductus est. Interea Clemetis inclementissimus filius, literas nactus ab imperatore ac concilio, Hieronymum manibus reuinctis misit Constantiam. Quem Ludouicus alter filius Clemetis hospitio excipit, ac per totam Vrbem circumducit (triumphantis in morem, nam ipse praeibat) quanta cum ignominia ac contumelia, hic non refero. Donec ad monasterium lignipedorum, ubi sacerdotū ac pharisaeorum factio confluxerat, peruentum est. Ibi postea causa demum Hieronymi coepta est. Cum multa in hunc Hieronymum congesta essent quibus arguebatur haeresis, atqz ea testibus firmata: tandem pla-cuit, ut publice singulis, quae sibi obiciebantur, responderet. Ita in concionem deductus, cum iuberetur ad illa respondere, diutius recusauit, asserens se debere prius causam suam agere, quam respondere maledictis aduersariorum, Ita fe prius pro sedi centem audiendum esse asseuera-bat, tum ad æmulorum suorum pro-bra in eum congesta deueniendum. Sed cum hæc conditio sibi denega-retur, tu stans in medio concionis: Quænam est hæc iniquitas, inquit, ut cum 540. diebus, quibus in durif-simis carceribus fui, in sordibus, in squalore, in stercore, in compedi-bus, in rerum omnium inopia, ad-uersarios atque obtrectatores meos semper audieritis, me unam horam audire nolitis? Hinc est, ut dum illis singulorum aures patuerint, atq; in tam longo tempore uobis persuase-rint me hæreticum, hostem fidei, ec-clesiasticorum persecutorem, mihi autem me defendendi nulla detur fa-cultas, uos me prius improbum ho-minem iudicaueritis in mentibus ue-stris, quàm, qui forem, potueritis co-gnoscere. Atqui, inquit, homines non dij estis,non perpetui, sed mor- tales,labi, errare, falli ,decipi, seduci potestis. Hic mundi lumina hic orbis terrarum sapientiores esse dicuntur, maxime uos decet elaborare,ne quid temere,ne quid inconsulte,neue quid praeter iustitiam faciatis. Equidem ego homuncio sum,cuius de capite agitur, nec pro me haec loquor,qui mortalis existo, Verum in dignum mihi uidetur sapientia, aliquid tot uiros aduersum me statuere praeter aequitatem, non tam re,qua exemplo nociturum. Haec & multa praeterea ornate differebat, strepitu & murmure plurimorum sermone eius interpellante. Tandem decretum est,ut primum ad errores qui in eum conferebantur, responderet, deinde loquendi quę uellet,daretur facultas. Legebantur igitur ex pulpito singula capitula accusationis, deinde testimoniis confirmabatur, tum rogabatur an quid uellet objicere. Incredibile dictu, quam callide respondéret, quibus se tueretur argumentis. Nihil unquam protulit indignum bono viro, ut si id in fide sentiebat, quod verbis profitebatur, nulla in eum nedum mortis causa inveniri iusta posset, sed ne quidem leuissimae offensionis. Omnia esse falsa dicebat, omnia crimina conficta ab aemulis suis. Inter caetera cum recitaretur illum sedis apostolicae detractorem, oppugnatorem Romani Pontificis, Cardinalium hostem, persecutorem praelatorum et Cleri, Christianae religionis inimicum, tum surgens querebunda voce, & manibus porrectis: quo nunc me vertam, inquit, patres conscripti? quorum auxilium implorem? quos deprecer? quos obtester? Vos nec. At isti persecutores mei vestras mentes a mea salute abalienaverunt, cum universorum hostem me esse dixerunt, eorum qui me sunt iudicaturi. Nempe
units.tr: ...by the servants of Duke John, son of Clement, was taken captive and brought to him. Meanwhile Clement's most merciless son, having obtained letters from the emperor and the council, sent Jerome to Constance with his hands bound. Ludovicus, the other son of Clement, received him into custody and led him through the whole city, in the manner of a triumph, for he himself went ahead. With what disgrace and insult, I do not relate here. At last they came to the monastery of the wooden-shoed friars, where a faction of priests and Pharisees had gathered. There Jerome's case at last began. Although many charges of heresy had been heaped upon Jerome and were confirmed by witnesses, it was finally agreed that he should answer publicly to each of the charges brought against him. So he was led into the assembly, and when he was ordered to answer those charges, he long refused, declaring that he must first plead his own cause before answering his adversaries' slanders. He insisted that he must first be heard as one speaking for himself, and only then come to the insults heaped on him by his rivals. But when this condition was refused him, he stood in the middle of the assembly and said: "What injustice is this? For 540 days I was in the harshest prisons, in filth, squalor, dung and chains, and in want of everything, and you have always listened to my adversaries and detractors. Will you not grant me one hour? The result is that, while their ears have been open to each of them, and over so long a time they have persuaded you that I am a heretic, an enemy of the faith and a persecutor of churchmen, while I am given no opportunity to defend myself, you have already judged me a wicked man in your minds before you could know what I am. And yet, he said, you are men, not gods; not eternal but mortal; you can slip, err, be deceived, misled and seduced. You who are said to be the lights of the world and the wisest men on earth should above all take care not to do anything rashly, inconsiderately, or contrary to justice. Indeed, I am a poor man whose life is at stake, and I do not say this for my own sake, since I am mortal. But it seems unworthy of wisdom that so many men should decide something against me contrary to fairness, a thing that would harm not so much in its own substance as by the example it sets." He went on at length with these and many other eloquent points, while the noise and murmuring of many people interrupted his speech. At last it was decided that he should first answer the errors charged against him, and then be given the opportunity to say whatever he wished. So the articles of accusation were read out one by one from the pulpit, each was confirmed by testimony, and then he was asked whether he wished to object to anything. It is incredible to say how cleverly he answered and with what arguments he defended himself. He never said anything unworthy of a good man, so that if he truly held in faith what he professed in words, no just ground could be found against him, much less one for death, nor even for the slightest offence. He said that everything was false and that all the charges had been fabricated by his rivals. Among other things, when it was read out that he was a detractor of the Apostolic See, an assailant of the Roman Pontiff, an enemy of the cardinals, a persecutor of prelates and clergy, and an enemy of the Christian religion, he rose with a plaintive voice and outstretched hands and said: "Where now shall I turn, Fathers? Whose help shall I implore? Whom shall I beseech and entreat? You? No. My persecutors have turned your minds away from my salvation, when they called me an enemy of all the men who are to judge me. Surely they reckoned,

units.la: L arbitrati sunt, si etiam quæ in me sin xerunt, leuia uiderentur: tamen uos uestris sententijs oppressuros commune omnium hostem atque oppugnatorem, qualem me isti falsissi me mentiti sunt. Ita si eorum uerbis fidem dabitis nihil est, quod de mea salute sperandum sit. Multos salibus perstrinxit, multos lœdoriis, multos persæpe in re mœsta ridere coegit, iocando in illorum obiurgationes.
units.tr: that even if the things they invented against me seemed trivial, you would still overwhelm with your judgments a common enemy and assailant of all, such as they have falsely lied me to be. So if you give credence to their words, there is nothing to hope for concerning my salvation." He pricked many with witticisms, lashed many with jibes, and often made many laugh even in a sad matter, joking at their rebukes.

units.la: Cum rogaretur quid sentiret de sacramento, inquit: Antea panem, postea uerum Christi corpus, et reliqua secundum fidem. Tum quidam aiunt te dixisse, post consecrationem remanere panem. Tum ille: apud pi storem inquit, panis remanet. Alij cuidam ex ordine prædicatorum acrius inuehenti, Tace, inquit, hypocrita. Alteri per conscientiam suam contra seiuranti, hæc, inquit, tutissi-ma est ad fallendum uia. Quendam præcipuum aduersarium, nunc q ni-si canem si canem aut asinū appellauit. Cum uero propter criminum multitudi-nem ac pondus, res eo die transigi nequiret, in diem tertium est dilata. Qua die cum singulorū criminum argumenta recitata essent, ac subin-de plurimis testibus adsirmarentur, tum surgens ille: Quoniam, inquit, aduersarios meos tam diligenter au-distis, conueniens est, ut me quoque dicetem æquis animis audiatis. Da-ta tandem est, licet multis perstre-pentibus, facultas ei dicendi. Hic primum à Deo exorsus, deprecatus est eam sibi mentem dari, eam dicen-di facultatem, quę in commodum ac salutem animæ suæ uerteretur. Dein descio, inquit, R. D. plures fuisse ex-cellentissimos uiros, indigna suis uir-tutibus perpessos, falsis oppressos te-stibus, iniquissimis iudicijs condem-natos. Incipiens autem à Socrate, quem iniuste à suis condemnatum setulit, nec cum posset, euadere uoluisse, ut duorum, quæ asperrima hominibus uiderentur, metum demeret, carceris scilicet & mortis. Tū Platonis captiuitatem, Anaxagoræ fugam, ac Zenonis tormenta. Multorum præterea gentilium iniquas damnationes, Rupilij exilium, Boëtij simul & aliorum, quos ipse Boëtius refert, indignam mortem commemorauit. Deinde ad Hebræorū exempla transiit: Et primum Moysen illum liberatorem populi, & legumlatorem sæpissime à suis calūniatum esse dixit, tanqꝫ seductor esset, aut contemptor populi. Ioseph insu per à fratribus uenditum ob inuidiam, post ob stupri suspitionem in uincula coniectum recensuit. Præter hos Esaiam, Danielem & ferme prophetas omnes tanquam contemptores Dei, tanquam seditiosos, iniquis circumuentos sententiis. Hinc etiam Susannæ iudicium subiecit, multorum præterea, qui cum uiri sanctissimi
units.tr: When he was asked what he thought of the sacrament, he said: "Before consecration, bread; afterwards the true body of Christ; and the rest according to faith." Then some said that you had asserted that after consecration bread remains. He replied: "With the baker, bread remains." To another of the Dominican order who was inveighing sharply against him, he said, "Be quiet, hypocrite." To another who swore against him by his own conscience, he said, "This is the surest way to deceive." He called one particular leading adversary nothing but a dog or an ass. But since, because of the number and weight of the charges, the matter could not be finished that day, it was put off to the third day. On that day, when the arguments for each charge had been read out and at once confirmed by many witnesses, he rose and said: "Since you have listened so diligently to my opponents, it is fitting that you should hear me with equal fairness." At last he was granted the chance to speak, though many kept shouting. Beginning with God, he first prayed that he might be given a mind and a power of speech that would turn to the advantage and salvation of his soul. Then he said: "I know, Reverend Lords, that there have been many most excellent men who suffered what was unworthy of their virtues, were overwhelmed by false witnesses and condemned by most unjust judgments. Beginning with Socrates, who was unjustly condemned by his own people, and though he could have escaped, did not wish to, so as to remove the fear of two things that seem most harsh to men, namely prison and death. Then he recalled the captivity of Plato, the flight of Anaxagoras and the torments of Zeno. Besides these, he mentioned the unjust condemnations of many Gentiles, the exile of Rupilius, and the unworthy death of Boethius and of others whom Boethius himself records. Then he passed to examples from the Hebrews. First, he said that Moses, that deliverer and lawgiver of the people, was very often slandered by his own people, as though he were a seducer or a despiser of the people. Moreover, he recounted how Joseph was sold by his brothers out of envy, and afterwards thrown into chains on suspicion of unchastity. Besides these, Isaiah, Daniel and almost all the prophets, as despisers of God and as seditious men, were ensnared by unjust sentences. Hence he also brought in the judgment of Susanna, and of many others who, though they were most holy men, nevertheless perished through unjust sentences.

units.la: stissimi îî [illegible, ~3 letters]tiffimi extitissent, iniustis tamen sententijs perierunt. Postea ad Ioan nem Baptistam, deinde ad Saluato- rem nostrum descendens, falsis testibus condemnatos, inquit, omnibus constare. Deinde Stephanum a sacerdotum collegio interfectum, apo ftolos autem omnes morti damnatos, non tanquam bonos, sed ut fedi tiofos populorum concitatores, contemptores Deorum, & malorum operum effectores. Iniquum esse condemnari iniuste sacerdotem a sacerdote, & id factum fuisse docuit iniquissime a sacerdotum Concilio, id etiam accidisse monstrauit. Haec diserte, & magna cum omnium expectatione disseruit. Atq; cum omne pondus causae in testibus situ effet, multis rationibus docuit, nullam his testibus fidem adhibendam, prae fertim cum non ex ueritate, sed ex odio ac maleuolentia & inuidia omnia dixissent. Tum odij causas, ita explicuit, ut haud procul abfuerit a persuadendo, Ita erant uerisimiles, ut (excepta fidei causa) parua illis testimonijs fides adhibita esset. Commotæ erant omnium mentes, & ad misericordiam flectebantur. Addiderat enim se sponte ad Concilium uenisse, ad se purgandum, uitam suam, & studia exposuerat officiorum plena ac uirtutum. Dixerat hunc modo rem priscis doctissimis uiris ac sanctissimis fuisse, ut in rebus fidei sententijs discreparent, non ad pessundandam fidem, sed ad ueritatem reperiendam. Ita Augustinum & Hieronymum dissensisse, nec solum diuersa sensisse, sed etiā contraria, nulla hęresis suspitione. Expectabant autem omnes, ut semel se purgaret, retractando obiecta, uel erratorum uniam postularet. At ille nec se errasse asseuerās, nec se retractare alio rum falsa crimina uelle, ostendens.
units.tr: Though they had been most holy men, they nevertheless perished through unjust sentences. Then, passing on to John the Baptist and afterwards to our Saviour, he said that all of them had been condemned by false witnesses. Next, he said that Stephen was killed by the college of priests, and that all the apostles were condemned to death, not as good men, but as seditious stirrers-up of the people, contemners of the gods, and workers of evil deeds. He taught that it is wrong for a priest to be condemned unjustly by a priest, and he showed that this had happened most unjustly through the council of priests. He argued these points eloquently and to the great expectation of everyone. Since the whole weight of the case rested on the witnesses, he showed by many arguments that no faith should be given to these witnesses, especially since they had said everything out of hatred, malice and envy, not out of truth. Then he explained the causes of that hatred so well that he came close to persuading his hearers; the accusations were so plausible that, apart from the matter of faith, little credit was given to those testimonies. The minds of all were moved and inclined to pity.
