For he had added that he had come to the council of his own accord, to clear himself, and he set out his life and studies, full of duties and virtues. He had said that it had happened to the most learned and holy men of old that they disagreed in opinions on matters of faith, not to overthrow the faith but to discover the truth. Thus Augustine and Jerome had disagreed, and not only thought differently but held contrary views, without any suspicion of heresy. Everyone expected that he would clear himself once and for all by retracting the objections, or at least acknowledge some of his errors. But he, neither asserting that he had erred nor showing that he wished to retract the false charges of others, [remained silent on both points].

units.la: Tandē descendens in laudationem Ioannis Huffi ad ignem damnati, utrum istum bonum, iustū & sanctum appellans, & illa morte indignum, Se quoq; paratum quoduis suppli‐cium adire forti animo & constanti, seqs inimicis suis cedere, & testibus impudenter mentientibus. Qui ta‐men aliquando coram Deo, quem fallere nō potuerint, essent rationem eorum quæ dixissent reddituri. Magnus erat circumstantium animi dolor. Cupiebant enim virum tam egregium saluari, si bona mens adfuisset. Ille autem in sententia sua persseuerans, ultro mortem appetere uidebatur. Laudansqs Ioannem Hussium, ait: Nihil illum aduersus eccle‐siæ Dei statum sensisse, sed aduersus abusus clericorum, aduersus superbiam, fastum, ac pompam prælatorum. Nam cum ecclesiarum patrimonia primo deberentur pauperibus, tum hospitibus, deinde ecclesiarum fabricis, indignum illi bono uiro uideri, dispendi illa meretricibus, conuiuijs, equorum ac canum saginae, cultui uestimentorum, & aliis rebus indignis religione Christi. Hic autem maximi ingenij fuit. Cum interrũperetur saepius oratio sua uarijs rumoribus, lacesfereturq; a nonnullis sententias eius carpentibus, neminem eorum intactum reliquit, pariterq; omnes ulciscens, uel erubescere coegit, uel tacere. Surgete murmure silebat, turbam quandoque increpans, postea orationem prosequebatur, orans atq; obteftas, ut fe loqui paterentur, quem non eff sent amplius audituti. Nunquam ad hos rumores expauit, mente firma atq; intrepida. Illud uero admirabilis memorię argumentũ: CCCXL. diebus fuerat in fundo turris foetidae atq; obscurae, cuius asperitatem ipsemet questus est, asserens se ut fortem & bonum uirum decet, non propterea ingemiscere quod indigna perpefperpessus esset, sed mirari aduersus se inhumanitatem. Quo in loco, nedum legendi, sed ne uidendi quidem habuit facultatem. Mitto anxietatem mentis, qua oportuit illum quotidie agitari, quae omnem memoriam excutere debuisset. Tamen cum tot doctissimos & sapientissimos uiros, in testes suarum opinionum allegaret, tot doctores ecclesiasticos in medium protulit in sententiam suam, ut satis superque satis fuisset, si toto hoc tempore, summo in oratio, summa in quiete, sapientiae studiis operam dedisset. Vox eius suauis, aperta, resonans erat, quadam cum dignitate gestus oratorius, uel ad indignationem exprimendam, uel ad commouendam commiserationem quam tum nec postulabat, nec consequi cupiebat. Stabat impauidus, intrepidus, mortem non contemnens solum, sed appetens, ut alterum Catonem dixisses. O uirum dignum
units.tr: Finally, coming down to praise John Hus, who had been condemned to the fire, he called him good, just and holy, and one unworthy of such a death. He said that he himself was also ready to undergo any punishment with a brave and steady mind, and that he yielded to his enemies and to witnesses who lied shamelessly; yet they would one day have to give account before God, whom they could not deceive, for what they had said. The grief of the bystanders was great, for they desired that so outstanding a man be saved, if only a good disposition had been present. But he, persisting in his opinion, seemed to be seeking death of his own accord. Praising John Hus, he said that Hus had held nothing against the state of God's Church, but only against the abuses of the clergy, against the pride, arrogance and pomp of the prelates. For when the church's patrimony ought first to have gone to the poor, then to guests, and then to the upkeep of church buildings, it seemed unworthy to that good man that it should be spent on prostitutes, banquets, the feeding of horses and dogs, the adornment of vestments, and other things unworthy of the religion of Christ. Hus was a man of the greatest talent. Although his speech was often interrupted by various noises, and some people attacked him by criticising his opinions, he left none of them unanswered; he punished them all equally, forcing them either to blush or to be silent. At times he kept silent amid the uproar, rebuking the crowd, and afterwards he went on with his speech, praying and begging them to let him speak, since otherwise they would hear him no more. He never trembled at these outcries, his mind firm and fearless. There is also a remarkable proof of his memory: for three hundred and forty days he had been in the bottom of a foul and dark tower, the roughness of which he himself complained of, declaring that, as befits a brave and good man, he did not lament the indignities he had suffered, but marvelled at the inhumanity shown towards him. In that place he had the opportunity not only of reading but even of seeing nothing. I say nothing of the anxiety of mind with which he must have been troubled daily, which ought to have driven all memory out of him. Yet when he cited so many most learned and wise men as witnesses for his opinions, he brought forward so many ecclesiastical teachers in support of his view that it would have been more than enough, had he spent all this time, at his best in speech and at his best in quiet, on the studies of wisdom. His voice was sweet, clear and resonant, his oratorical gestures had a certain dignity, either to express indignation or to stir up pity, which at that time he neither sought nor desired to obtain. He stood undaunted and fearless, not only despising death but seeking it, so that you would have called him another Cato. O man worthy of everlasting memory among men.

units.la: memoria hominū sempiterna. Non inuenio quid aduersus instituta ecclesiæ sentiebat, doctrinam admiror, plurimarum rerum scientiam, eloquentiā, dicendi suauitatem, argutiam respondendi. Nec dubiū quin magno ecclesiæ bono hæc sibi à natura fuerint concessa. Datum deinde spacium pœnitendi biduo. Multi ad illum accesserunt uiri eruditissimi, ut ipsum à sua sententia dimouerent, inter quos Cardinalis Florentinus eum adiit, ut flecteret ad uiam rectam. Sed cum pertinacius in erroribus perseueraret, per Concilium hæresis damnatus, & igni combustus est. Iucunda fronte & alacri uultu ad exitum suum accessit: non ignem expauit, non tormenti genus, non mortis. Nullus unquam stoicorum fuit tam constanti animo, tamque forti, mortem perpessus, quam ille appetiisse uidetur. Cum uenisset ad locum mortis, seipsum exuit uestimentis. tis. Tum procumbens flexis genu- bus ueneratus est palum, ad quem post ligatus fuit: primum funibus madentibus, tum cathena, nudus ad palum constrictus fuit, ligna deinde circumposita, pectoretenus non minuscula, sed grossa, paleis interiectis. Cum flamma adhibita, canere coepit hymnum quendam, quem su mus & ignis uix interrupit. Hoc maximum constantis animi signum, cū lictor ignem post tergum (ne id uideret) iniicere uellet, Huc, inquit, accede, et in cōspectu accende igne. Si enim illum timuissem, nunquam ad hunc locum, quem fugiendi facultas erat, accessissem. Hoc modo uir (praeter fidem) egregius consumptus est. Horum ita fere recensentur dogmata, apud Bernardum Luzenburgum.
units.tr: I do not find what he thought against the institutions of the Church; I admire his learning, his wide knowledge, his eloquence, the sweetness of his speech and the sharpness of his replies. There is no doubt that these gifts were granted him by nature for the great good of the Church. Then a space of two days was given him for repentance. Many very learned men approached him to turn him from his opinion, among whom the Cardinal of Florence came to him to bring him back to the right way. But since he persisted more stubbornly in his errors, he was condemned as a heretic by the Council and burned at the stake. He came to his end with a cheerful face and an eager look: he did not dread the fire, nor any kind of torture, nor death. No Stoic was ever so constant and so brave in suffering death as he seems to have been in seeking it. When he came to the place of death, he stripped himself of his garments. Then, kneeling down, he reverently kissed the stake to which he was afterwards bound: first with wet ropes, then with a chain, he was tied naked to the stake; then wood was piled around him, up to his breast, not little but thick logs, with straw placed between them. When the flame was applied, he began to sing a certain hymn, which the smoke and fire scarcely interrupted. This was the greatest sign of his constant mind: when the executioner wished to light the fire behind his back, so that he would not see it, he said, "Come here, and kindle the fire in my sight. For if I had feared it, I would never have come to this place, where I had the chance to flee." In this way that man, outstanding (apart from the faith), was consumed. These are the doctrines, as they are briefly listed, according to Bernard of Luxemburg:

units.la: Romanum praesulem reliquis episcopis parem esse.
units.tr: The Roman bishop is equal to the other bishops.

units.la: In Sacerdotibus nullum discrimen men Presbiterum non dignitatem, sed uitæ meritum efficere.
units.tr: There is no distinction among priests; it is merit of life, not dignity, that makes a presbyter.

units.la: Purgatorium ignem nullum inueniri.
units.tr: No purgatorial fire is to be found.

units.la: Mendicantium ordines malos dæmones inuenisse.
units.tr: The orders of mendicants have invented evil demons.

units.la: Item quòd Paulus nunquam fuit membrum diaboli, licet fecerit quosdam actus ecclesiæ malignantis simi les.
units.tr: Likewise, that Paul was never a member of the devil, although he performed some acts similar to those of the malignant Church.

units.la: Item duæ naturæ, diuinitas, & humanitas sunt unus Christus.
units.tr: Likewise, that the two natures, the divinity and the humanity, are the one Christ.

units.la: Quòd condemnatio 45. articulorum Io. Vicleui per doctores facta, est irrationabilis & iniqua.
units.tr: That the condemnation of the forty-five articles of John Wycliffe by the doctors was unreasonable and unjust.

units.la: Confirmationem, quæ crismate constat, & externam unctionem, inter sacramenta non contineri.
units.tr: That confirmation, which consists of chrism, and the external anointing are not contained among the sacraments.

units.la: Auricularem confessionem nugacem esse.
units.tr: Auricular confession is trifling.

units.la: Sufficere sua quemcunque Deo confiteri peccata.
units.tr: It is enough for anyone to confess his sins to God alone.

units.la: Baptisma fluuialis unde nulla in teriecta sacri olei mixtura recipiedū Cœmiteriorum inanè esse superstitionem.
units.tr: Baptism in a river, or any baptism where no mixture of consecrated oil is received, and the consecration of cemeteries are empty superstitions.

units.la: Corpora ubicunque sepeliantur, parum referre.
units.tr: It matters little where bodies are buried.

units.la: Templum Dei latè patetis ipsum mundum esse: eius maiestatem coarctare eum, qui ecclesias, monasteria, oratoriaque construunt.
units.tr: The temple of God, widely open, is the world itself; those who build churches, monasteries and oratories confine his majesty.

units.la: Sacerdotales, vestes, altarium ornamenta, pallas, corporalia, calices, patenas, vasaque huiusmodi nil habere momenti.
units.tr: Priestly vestments, altar ornaments, palls, corporals, chalices, patens and vessels of this kind have no importance.

units.la: Sacerdotem, quocunque loco, aut tempore, sacrum Christi corpus conficere posse, poenitentibusque ministrare.
units.tr: A priest, in any place or at any time, can consecrate the sacred body of Christ and minister it to penitents.

units.la: Suffragia sanctorum in coelis frustra impetrari, quae iuvari nil poterint.
units.tr: The intercessions of the saints in heaven are sought in vain, since they can help nothing.

units.la: In canonicis horis cantandis, dicendisque, frustra tempus teri.
units.tr: Time is wasted in vain in singing and saying the canonical hours.

units.la: Nulla die ab opere cessandum, nisi quae dominica appellatur.
units.tr: No work should be ceased from on any day except what is called the Lord's day.

units.la: Celebritates, divinorum reiciedas.
units.tr: Festivals of the divine kind are to be rejected.

units.la: Ieiunijs Ienunrjs ab ecclesia indictis nihil inesse momenti.
units.tr: Fasts appointed by the Church have no weight at all.

units.la: Hi Articuli, etsi ad Euangelicam amussim cp rectissime omnes consentiant, tamen non tam ab istis proditos esse, quam ab aliis suspiciosa quadam coniectura collectos arbitror. Quod facile exuita ac defensio neillorum æstimandi copia est, quæ si recte a nobis perpendatur, haud aliud fere in his coperiemus, quod episcoporum tantum furorem acodium excitarit, præter unicum hoc duntaxat, quod intollerabilem eorum fastum, ac uitæ plusquam Alexandrinas delicias ferre non potuerint.
units.tr: These articles, although they all agree most exactly with the rule of the Gospel, I think were not so much put forward by those men as gathered by others through a certain suspicious guesswork. This can easily be seen from their life and defence, and if we weigh it rightly we shall find little else in them that stirred up such fury and hatred against the bishops, apart from this one thing: that the bishops could not bear the men's criticism of their intolerable pride and their luxury, which outdid even that of Alexandria.

units.la: Guliel. Taylerus Anglus.
units.tr: William Taylor, English.

units.la: Sed nulla unquam regio fœcundior fuit, magisq; ferax martyriorū cp una Anglia, siue id, ex singulari diuinæ gratiæ priuilegio, huic Insulæ indultum, siue ex barbara, atq; indocta quorundam, qui tum ecclesiam tenebant, saeuitia, euenit, incertum. Oxonia, ceu perpetua nunc scaturigo, Christianę cognitionis uisa, unde uelut ex equo Troiano, tot prosilierunt inuictissimi Christi, ac ueritatis testes, qui cum singulari eruditione, conuincto etiam sanguine, non solum de suo tempore, sed de omni hominum posteritate quàm optimè meriti sunt. Inter quos non infimum decus emicuit Gulielmus Taylerus artium professor ac Vuicleuo fauens. Hic quia de non inuocandis sanctis aliaque quaedam scripserat, post recantatos articulos nouem, relapsus denuo in uiam, Londini in foro ferrario ignibus dedit poenas, non sine magna constantia. Anno 1422. 2. Martij.
units.tr: No region was ever more fruitful or more productive of martyrs than England alone, whether this happened through a singular privilege of divine grace granted to this island, or through the savage and ignorant cruelty of those who then held the Church; it is uncertain which. Oxford, like a perpetual spring, was seen as a source of Christian knowledge, and from it, as from the Trojan horse, so many most invincible witnesses of Christ and of the truth leapt forth. They, with singular learning and even with their blood, have deserved very well not only of their own time but of all posterity. Among them William Taylor, professor of the arts and a supporter of Wycliffe, shone with no small distinction. Because he had written about not invoking the saints and certain other matters, after recanting nine articles he relapsed into his error, and in London, at Smithfield, he paid the penalty by fire, not without great constancy. In the year 1422, on 2 March.

units.la: Gulielmus Vuhyghtus Anglus.
units.tr: William White, English.

units.la: Proximus in hoc album succedit Gulielmus Vuhyghtus, sacrificus, sed longe à uulgari hoc sacrifico-rum genere dissidens, uere in eorum numero collocandus de quibus à sapiente dicitur. labia sacerdotis custodiunt sapientiam. Hic quum ex fœliciter haustis Vuicleui sermonibus ad maiorem uitæ pietatem profecerat, sacerdotio, quod illi satis tu opimum erat, relicto, quo sanctius uitam suam, secundum Dei præcepta, attemperaret, Io. uirgunculam quandam in uxorem duxit, tamen nihilominus inseruiês Christi spon si sui gloriæ, nec cessans interim ab officio semel suscepto, ubi quid uel legendo, uel docendo, lucri afferre potuit sacerdotalis functio: relictis insuper ingenij sui monumetis non-nullis, quæ ad communem plebeculæ utilitatem conscripserat. Noruuici tandem captus pro 30. articulis per Guilhelmū Noruuicēsem ignitus est Noruuici Anno 1428. mense septembri, Cuius & uxor Ioanna, eadem retinens & spargens dogma ta,digna tali marito coniunx,eodem anno multa per eudem episcopum perpessa dicitur.
units.tr: Next in this roll follows William White, a priest, but very far removed from the common sort of priests, and rightly to be counted among those of whom the wise man says: "the lips of the priest keep knowledge." After he had profited toward a greater piety from the sermons of Wycliffe, which he had happily drunk in, he left the priesthood, which was quite rich for him, so that he could order his life more holily according to God's precepts. He took as his wife a young woman named Joan. Nevertheless, still serving Christ his spouse for his glory, and not ceasing in the meantime from the office he had once undertaken, he used his priestly function wherever it could bring some gain, whether in reading or in teaching. Moreover he left behind some monuments of his genius, which he had written for the common benefit of the humble folk. At last he was taken at Norwich, condemned for thirty articles by William, bishop of Norwich, and burned there in September of the year 1428. His wife Joan, who held and spread the same doctrines, a wife worthy of such a husband, is said to have suffered much in the same year at the hands of the same bishop.

units.la: Ricardus Houendenus.
units.tr: Richard Hovenden.

units.la: Anno 1430. post solennem regis Henrici 6.coronationem,coronatus est martyrio quidam Ricardus Houendenus Lanarum consarcinator, ciuis Londinensis. Qui cum nullis persuasionibus à Vuicleui assertionibus propelli potuit, per Præsules condemnatur hereseos,ac prope arcem Londinensem secundum Fabianum combustus.
units.tr: In the year 1430, after the solemn coronation of King Henry VI, a certain Richard Hovenden, a patcher of woollen cloth and a citizen of London, was crowned with martyrdom. Since he could not be moved from the assertions of Wycliffe by any persuasion, he was condemned for heresy by the prelates, and according to Fabyan he was burned near the castle of London.

units.la: Tho. Bagleus.
units.tr: Thomas Bagley.

units.la: Quo autore accepimus etiam sequenti anno Thomam Bagleum sacerdotem, pastorem, vicarium de Mauenden in comitatu Essexiensi prope Vualdenu, ac Vuicleui strenuum assertorem Londini per epi-M scopos condemnari haereseos, circa medium quadragesimae degradari atque exuri in circo ferrario an. 1431.
units.tr: On whose authority we have learned that in the following year, 1431, Thomas Bagley, a priest, pastor, and vicar of Mavesden in Essex near Waldon, and a vigorous champion of Wycliffe, was condemned for heresy in London by the bishops. Around the middle of Lent he was degraded and burned at Smithfield.

units.la: Paulus Craus Bohemus.
units.tr: Paul Craw, Bohemian.

units.la: Eodem anno Paulus Crauus natione Bohemus, apud sanctum Andream deprehensus ab Henrico episcopo, Seculari potestati ad comburendum traditur, propter dogmata de Eucharistia, de veneratione diuorum, de sacerdotali confessione, ceterisque Vuicleui assertionibus. 1431.
units.tr: In the same year Paul Craw, a Bohemian by nation, was arrested at St Andrew's by Bishop Henry and handed over to the secular power to be burned, on account of his doctrines concerning the Eucharist, the veneration of the saints, sacramental confession, and the other assertions of Wycliffe. 1431.

units.la: HISTORIA THOMAE RHEDONENSIS Galli, ac Carmelitae in Italia, Christi nomine exusti.
units.tr: The History of Thomas of Rhedon, a Frenchman and a Carmelite, burned in Italy in the name of Christ.

units.la: DIXIMVS SVPERIVS PERsecutionis hanc fatalem turbinem, quae primum apud Anglos exorta, diu hic, multumque in sanctissimorum hominum capita exarsit, ex hac demum Insula, facta irruptione, in Bohemos demigrasse, moxque interiecto teriecto deinde tempore, & Scotos grassante paulatim incendio, corripuisse. Inde nunc facto ad ulteriores nationes gradu in Italiam quoq; transfuolat procax rabies, nec ullam fore orbis partem immune finit ab innocentissimorum laniatu. Accesserat forte fortuna in Italiam, anno sequente cum Venetis oratoribus Thomas quidem Gallus, ex ordine eorum, qui ex monte Carmelo, religionis titulum circumferunt. Iam enim & montes habent suos sectarum ordines. Quid miramur si Franciscus sui nominis, ac sanctimoniae relinquat admiratores, quum & mons Carmelus suos inuenit carmelitas. Et quid possit tam ineptum esse, cuius non alicubi, in tanta sectarum foecunditate, suos applausores templumq; reperias. Sed hic quamuis huius erat gregis, qui pro Christianis, Carmelitae appellabantur, longe tamen diuersa ratione institutus, Christi uerbum sapiebat, qui non in monte hoc, neque Hierosolimis duntaxat, sed in spiritu, & veritate Deum sibi colendum exi-stimauit. Hic ergo uerus Carmelita, toto pectore, Christi nouum illud mustum spirans, dum Christianae integritati uestigia, magno studio, uotoque se-ctatur, in Italiam primum proficisci parat, illic, aut nusquam se repertu-rum sperans, quorum conuictu melior fieri potuit. Vbi enim magis uir tutum omnium segetem suppullare conueniebat, quam illic ubi totius regionis arx quaedam, ac fons habe-batur. Nam qui fieri potuit, ubi tanta omnis sanctimoniae professio iactabatur, ubi omnium hominum oculi ceu in theatrum quoddam conij-ciebatur, ubi sanctissimi Petri sedes, ac totius ecclesiae regimen credebatur, qui omnia illic digna tanta expectatione uigerent. Haec dum in oculis, atque in animo, sibi proponeret sanret sanctissimus uir, magna spe relicta ciuitate sua, Romam petit, certissimam spem concipiens, futurū, ut tot illustrissimorum hominum adiutus exemplis, magnum sibi, & pietatis, & doctrinae lucrum acquiret. Caeterum hanc spem longe destituit successus. Quippe omnia dissimilia, fucum ac meram hypocrisim esse quaecunque uiderat, denique pro auro nihil quàm carbones, imo ut uerius fatear, nihil aliud quàm aurum, ac argentum reperit. Pro donis coelestibus, regnabat cultus, ac prouidentia huius seculi, pro pietate luxus, pro literis ac studio, ignauia ac superstitio, pro simplicitate Apostolica, tyrannis, ac supercilium omnia occupans, ut non solum discendi quod ignoraret, sed nec tradendi, quod quisquam recte sciret, locus iam amplius relinqueretur. Postremo nihil nō inuersum, nihil nō praeter suam existimationē, quaqua uer sum se flecteret, illi offerebatur. Sed nihil magis sanctissimum pectus offendit, quam intolerabilis ambitio, ac plus quam regalis strepitus, in iis, quos potissimum humilitatis exempla orbi commendare debeant. Etsi hic nihil fere cerneret, quod ad Apostolicae imitationis normam quadraret, illa tamen usque adeo omnem modum, ac patientiam exuperabat, ut nullo pacto linguam sibi temperandam, in tanta ecclesiae cruptela, exististimaret. Quum in aedificii ejus, quum in vestitu, quum in palatis, in victu, in famulorum comitatu, in admiratorum turba, in vitae apparatu, in equis, in armis etiam ambitiosum factum cerneret. Quo quo magis a Euangelica praescriptione recedebant, hoc minus cohiberi vox potuit sanctissimi hominis, etsi aliqui haud ita multum loquendo consecuturum se intelligeret. Nam si quid proficeret admonitio, non deerant Vuirant Vuicleui,cæterorumcplibri,nõ deerant & nuper Hufli,ac Hieronymi clarissima testimonia, ac sanguis effusus etiam, quorum tamen effica cissimis hortatibus adeo nihilo ηj correctiores sunt facti,ut duplo esse raciores uiderentur. Quancp neque ea res perterruit admodū Thomam nostrum,quintam salubri ac necessa rio officio uitam quoque,si opus sit, impenderet. Sic qui cæteris uenerat discipulus futurus,ηsdem nunc doctor esse cogitur, quorumcp mores imitari constituerat, ηs nunc uersa uice suam uitam spectandam immitandamque proposuit. Sic enim uixerat apud hos, utomnibus posset esse regulæ. Sic docuerat ut quibusque esse posset pædagogus. Sed quod Paulus prædixerat ηs, qui in Christo pie uiuere student,ut persecutionem habeant comitem, simile & huic euenit præmium à suis. Ille dedit pietatis fructus quos immiten tur. Isti rursus martyrij huic diade‑ma reposuerunt. Ille ad salutem o‑ftendit uiam,isti pro uitæ beneficio, mortem retaliant. cuiusque summis laboribus nulla satis digna fuerunt præmia,eum summa cum ignomi‑nia ad supremum rogū persequun‑tur,Nam dum diutina prædicatione satis graue sibi odium conflarat a‑pud purpuratos quamplurimos, tā dem agitari cœptum est, quibus ma‑chinis uita huius circūueniri potuit. Hic ad consuetum remedium con‑fugitum est. Est enim hæciam olim, apud ecclesiasticos dominos peculi‑aris ac perpetua consuetudo,ut si qs cui displiceat, cuius molesta uidea‑tur oratio, aut lucro ipsorū paululū offectura, statim hæreseos alicuius fabricant articulos quos in caput il‑lius cotorqueant. Quemadmodum cæterorum animantium sua sunt cu‑iusque tela peculiaria quibus se ab iniuria uindicent. Aprum dente ar‑mauit mauit natura, histrix suos habet acu-leos: Est leo unguibus formidabi-lis, Suus est morsus canibus. Cor-nu taurus pugnat, nec asino sua de-est calx. Ita & unica hæc episcopo-rum armatura est, ut hæresi aliqua inuolutum strangulent, si quis uo-luntati eorum uel ambitioni obstre-pere audeat. Id quod cum in aliis pene innumeris, tum in hoc sanctissi-mo uiro facile uidere est. Qui ubi iam, ut dictū est grauior esse cœpit, nec ferri potuit, quid tū illi? Ad ar-tes ueteranas fugiunt, quodque mo-do in Hussio ac Hieronymo desi-gnarūt, idem & in hunc iam moliun-tur. Sufpitione obruunt, quæstioni-bus inuoluunt, iudicio examinant, articulos struunt, hæresim impin-gunt, hæreticum condemnant, da-mnatum abripiunt, tolluntque è medio. Atque hæc est illa pietas, ac pacificus ordo nostrorum sacerdo-tū quibus interim religio est ensem, ac scutum circumferre, cum tamen liuorem, malitiam, uindictam, uenenum, insidias in mente gerunt, quouis gladio acutiores. Ne quis eorum in plateis ferro depugnet, quibus legibus, quanta solicitudine cauetur, cum in iudiciis, in accusationibus, ubi liceat fratrem opprimere, nullus est sicarius, qui aut paratiorem ultionem, aut uiliorem fratris sui animam habeat. Non ipsi hauriunt sanguinem, non feriunt, non occidunt, sed alijs occidendos tradunt. quid quaesto interest, nisi quod illi autores, hi tantum ministri sunt facinoris. Nulli caedem inferunt, ut sicarij, quid tum, si non eodem modo, at aliter idem efficiant. Porro articuli, quos in hunc confinxerunt, huiusmodi tradütur à quibusdam.
units.tr: We have said above that this fatal whirlwind of persecution first arose among the English and for a long time blazed here against the heads of the most holy men. From this island it broke out and migrated into the Bohemians. After some time had passed, the fire gradually spread and seized the Scots as well. Now, having advanced to further nations, this headstrong rage flies on into Italy too, and it lets no part of the world be free from the butchering of the most innocent. By chance, in the following year, Thomas the Frenchman came into Italy with the Venetian envoys. He belonged to the order of those who bear the title of religion from Mount Carmel, for mountains too have their orders of sects. Why are we surprised if Francis leaves admirers of his name and holiness, when Mount Carmel too has found its Carmelites? And what can be so foolish that you would not find, somewhere in such a fertile field of sects, its applauders and its temple? Yet although he belonged to that flock which Christians called Carmelites, he had been instituted on a very different plan. He savoured of the word of Christ, who held that God is to be worshipped not on this mountain, nor at Jerusalem only, but in spirit and truth. This true Carmelite, breathing with his whole heart that new must of Christ, pursued with great zeal and desire the traces of Christian integrity. He prepared first to set out for Italy, hoping to find there, or nowhere, people in whose company he might become better. For where was it more fitting for a man to gather the safe harvest of all than where the citadel and fountain of the whole region was held? How could it happen otherwise, where such a profession of all holiness was boasted, where the eyes of all men were cast as on a kind of theatre, where the seat of the most holy Peter and the government of the whole Church were believed to be, and where everything would flourish worthy of such great expectation? With these things before his eyes and mind, the most holy man left his city with great hope and made for Rome, conceiving a firm expectation that, aided by the examples of so many most illustrious men, he would win for himself a great gain both of piety and of learning. But success fell far short of this hope. He found that everything was unlike what he had seen: pretence and mere hypocrisy; for gold, nothing but coals, or rather, to confess the truth, nothing but gold and silver. In place of heavenly gifts, worldly pomp and worldly prudence reigned; for piety, luxury; for letters and study, idleness and superstition; for apostolic simplicity, tyranny and arrogance occupied everything. So there was left no room not only to learn what one did not know, but even to teach what anyone rightly knew. Finally, nothing was not turned upside down, and wherever he turned, nothing was offered to him except what suited their own estimation. But nothing offended that most holy breast more than the intolerable ambition and more than royal display in those whom they ought chiefly to commend to the world as examples of humility. Although he saw almost nothing there that squared with the norm of apostolic imitation, the ambition exceeded all measure and patience, so that he judged that in such ruin of the Church he could in no way hold his tongue. He saw ambition in their buildings, their clothing, their palaces, their food, the retinue of their servants, the crowd of their admirers, the whole equipage of their life, their horses, even their arms. The further they receded from the evangelical rule, the less the voice of the most holy man could be restrained, although he understood he would achieve little by speaking much. For if admonition did any good, there were not lacking the clearest testimonies of Wyclif and the other books, nor lately those of Hus and Jerome, and blood shed too. Yet by these most energetic exhortations they became no more correct at all, so much so that they seemed twice as mad. Nor did this terrify our Thomas much; he would give even his life, if need be, in a healthy and necessary duty. So he who had come as a disciple of others was now compelled to be a teacher of the same men whose morals he had resolved to imitate. Now, in turn, he proposed his own life to be looked upon and imitated. For he had lived among them in such a way that he could be a rule for all, and he had taught in such a way that he could be a tutor to each. But what Paul had foretold, that those who wish to live piously in Christ have persecution as their companion, befell him too, with a similar reward from his own people. The one gave the fruits of piety, which they hurl back; these in turn have set the crown of martyrdom upon this man. The one showed the way to salvation; these, for the benefit of his life, repay him with death. For whose greatest labours no reward was worthy enough, they pursue with the greatest ignominy to the final pyre. For while long preaching had gathered a fairly grave hatred against him among very many purple-clad men, at last it began to be plotted by what machinations his life might be entrapped. Here recourse was had to the customary remedy. For among the ecclesiastical lords it has long been a peculiar and unfailing custom that if anyone's speech displeases someone, or seems troublesome, or likely to harm their profit, they immediately fabricate the articles of some heresy and twist them onto his head. As each of the other animals has its own peculiar weapons with which to defend itself from injury, the boar is armed with its tusk, the porcupine has its quills, the lion is formidable with its claws, dogs have their bite, the bull fights with its horns, and the ass does not lack its kick, so this is the sole armour of the bishops: they strangle with some heresy anyone wrapped up in it, if anyone dares to resist their will or their ambition. This can easily be seen in almost countless others, but also in this most holy man. When he became, as has been said, more troublesome and could no longer be borne, what then? They flee to their old arts. What they had devised against Hus and Jerome, they now set in motion against this man too. They overwhelm him with suspicion, entangle him in questions, examine him in judgment, construct articles, fasten heresy upon him, condemn him as a heretic, snatch the condemned man away, and take him out of the way. This is that piety and peaceful order of our priests, who meanwhile have religion on their lips and carry sword and shield, yet bear in their minds envy, malice, vengeance, poison and snares, sharper than any sword. Lest any of them fight with iron in the streets, by what laws and with what great care it is guarded! Yet in judgments and accusations, where it is permitted to oppress a brother, there is no assassin who has either a readier revenge or a cheaper regard for his brother's life. They do not draw the blood themselves, do not strike, do not kill, but hand their victims over to others to be killed. What difference does it make, except that they are the authors of the crime and these men only its ministers? They inflict no slaughter like assassins; what then, if they accomplish the same thing, though not in the same way but otherwise? Moreover, the articles which they devised against this man are handed down by certain persons in the following form.

units.la: Quod ecclesia eget reformatione, quòd flagellabitur ac reformabitur.
units.tr: That the Church needs reformation, that it will be scourged and reformed.

units.la: Quod infideles Iudaei, Turcae, & Mauri conuertentur ad Christum tempotemporibus ijs ultimis.
units.tr: That the unbelieving Jews, Turks and Moors will be converted to Christ in those last times.

units.la: Quod abominationes fiunt Romae
units.tr: That abominations are done at Rome.

units.la: Quod iniusta Papae excommunicatio timenda non sit, quodque eam non obseruantes non peccant. Sed his nunc articulis deest adhuc minister, quanquam neque hic Romae diu desiderari potuit, ubi omnia uenalia, etiam animae hominum. Ad hoc uero ministerium nemo accommodatior est uisus, quam Gulielmus Rothomagensis diui Martini in montibus Cardinalis, Romanae curiae Vicecancellarius. Praesidebat, id temporis, princeps sacerdotum Eugenius nomine, sed nomine tantum. Apud hunc captus, accersitur Thomas noster. Accersitus carceri deditur. Iterum post carcerem, post tormenta, post cruciatus, ad iudices producitur. Iudicio praeest Lupus, accusatur agnus. Quamobrem quia turbarit fontem. Quid multis: Thomas quia resistere non ualuit malitię potentiorum, fatis pec casse creditur, facileque conuinci- tur incendio adiunctus, sed sic, ut prius tamen, gradibus, per quos a- scenderat ad sacerdotium, verum denudandus fit. Nephas enim ha- betur ut sacerdos prophanis succû- bat supplicijs, cum id interim sum- me fas sit, Sacerdotes, quemuis Lai cum, quantumuis insontem dedere neci. Ne lædatur maiestas sacerdotalis officij, quam hic religiose procu- rant isti: at ne lædatur conscientia falsis iudicijs, ac premendis infon- tibus, quàm nihil habent pensi. Itaq; priusquam ad supplicium, uentum sit, degraduandus est sanctus Tho- mas. Sunt enim gradus isti (ut obi- ter ne ingnores) nō inter differētias, quibus distinguimur à cæteris, neq; inter propria, quæ semper conueni- unt, sed inter accidentia illa com- munia, quæ adesse, & abesse poterint pro arbitrio episcoporum. Ita à physiologis docemur ab habitu ad priuationem procliuem esse motum, at retrorsum, à priuatione ad habitum impossibilem esse regressionem. Non est igitur, quod mireris, pie lector, quo pacto is nunc laicus perire potuit, qui modo sacerdos uixerat. Magis id tibi mirum sit, quae haec tanta fatuitas istorum occupare animos potuit, qui talibus factis, uniuerso orbi se deridendos propinant, nec tam hominibus ridiculi, quae Deo abominabiles.
units.tr: That an unjust excommunication by the Pope is not to be feared, and that those who do not observe it do not sin. But these articles still lacked a minister, although here at Rome too one could not long be lacking, where everything is for sale, even men's souls. For this ministry no one seemed more suitable than William of Rouen, Cardinal of St Martin in the Mountains and vice-chancellor of the Roman curia. At that time the prince of priests presided, Eugenius by name but only by name. Our Thomas is taken by him and summoned. Summoned, he is handed over to prison. Again after prison, after torments and tortures, he is brought before judges. The wolf presides over the judgment, and the lamb is accused, because he had troubled the spring. To cut it short: because Thomas could not resist the malice of the more powerful, he is believed to have fallen by fate. He is easily convicted and joined to the fire; but first, he must be stripped of the grades by which he had ascended to the priesthood. For it is held a sin for a priest to submit to profane punishments, whereas it is entirely lawful for priests to hand any layman over to death, however innocent he may be. Lest the dignity of the priestly office be harmed, which these men guard so religiously, but lest their conscience be harmed by false judgments and by oppressing the innocent, they have no care at all. So, before he came to the punishment, St Thomas had to be degraded. For these grades (lest you be ignorant, by the way) are not among the differences by which we are distinguished from others, nor among the proper features which always belong to us, but among those accidental common features which can be present or absent at the bishops' pleasure. Thus the physicians teach us that movement from a state to its privation is easy, but backward, from privation to the state, return is impossible. It is therefore no wonder, kind reader, by what means he who had only just been a priest could now perish as a layman. Rather, you should wonder how such great folly could occupy the minds of those who, by such deeds, offer themselves to be mocked by the whole world, and are not so ridiculous to men as they are abominable to God.

units.la: Postquam ergo ita episcopis placuit, sacerdotem hunc, iis gradibus, quibus olim initiarant, exauctorare, neque id illis satis est uisum, postea & uita simul cum sacerdotio spoliant, ac flammis iniiciunt comburendum, post quadriennium, quo ad urbem uenerat. An. dom. 1436. Sicque crudelissimorum praesulum immanitate periit Martyr hic tam inno*
units.tr: Therefore, after the bishops decided to strip this priest of the orders in which they had once ordained him, and that seemed not enough to them, they afterwards deprived him of life along with his priesthood and cast him into the flames to be burned, four years after he had come to the city. In the year of the Lord 1436. And so this martyr, so inno-, perished by the savagery of the most cruel prelates.

units.la: {f}innoxius quanquam haud quidem perisse credendus est. Corporis qui demiacturam fecit, sed illi, in maiorem salutis cessit cumulum apud Deum iudicem. Neque enim dubium est, quin is iam summo uiuit olympo, unà cum iis, quorum sanguinem dominus ulturus est nimis fortassis cito, istorum quibusdam, quos terra hæc nimis diu inultos sustinet.
units.tr: Yet he is not to be believed to have perished at all, though he was innocent. He suffered the loss of his body, but that loss turned to a greater increase of salvation before God the judge. For there is no doubt that he now lives on the highest Olympus, together with those whose blood the Lord will avenge, perhaps too quickly, and with some of those whom this land endures too long unavenged.

units.la: CARMINA QVAEDAM IN EIUS laudem reperta, apud Nicolaum Harlamensem.
units.tr: Certain verses composed in his praise, found with Nicolaus Harlamensis.

units.la: Claustra Thomas Gallus primus qui laspa refor mat Carmeli gregis heu cadit immerito, Compulit hunc feruor domini conspargere semen Exilium uitijs uita modesta dabat Dogmata præconis miracula concomitantur Illum quæ docceant pectus habere pium
units.tr: Thomas the Frenchman, the first to reform the fallen cloisters of the flock of Carmel, alas, falls undeserved. The zeal of the Lord drove him to scatter the seed. A modest life gave exile to vices. Miracles accompany his preaching; the doctrines taught him to have a pious heart.

units.la: Quantum sic populum zabuli de dentibus egit
units.tr: How much of the people he snatched from the devil's teeth.

units.la: Et uita & uerbo credere nemo potest.
units.tr: And no one could believe it, by life or by word.

units.la: Lippis lux oculis nocuit, non sustinuere
units.tr: The light harmed bleary eyes; they could not bear it.

units.la: Viuere tam sanctum foeda Romana cohors.
units.tr: The foul Roman cohort could not endure a life so holy.

units.la: Sistitur haereseos fictus, quod sitque sacerdos
units.tr: He is brought forward on a fabricated charge of heresy, though he is a priest.

units.la: Eugenio Papae, & friuola quaeque, patent:
units.tr: Before Pope Eugenius, and all the trifling charges are laid open.

units.la: Institiut sacris antistes hunc Rhedonensis
units.tr: The bishop of Rennes instituted proceedings against him.

units.la: Testis apud Gallos publica fama uolat.
units.tr: Public rumour flies abroad as witness among the French.

units.la: Sordida Roma Thomam Papa sordete petebat:
units.tr: Filthy Rome, with the Pope's filthiness, sought Thomas.

units.la: Flamma sorbendum, quamq; tyrannus alit.
units.tr: He is to be swallowed up by the flame, which the tyrant feeds.

units.la: Vrget ad hoc primas Gulielmus Rhotomagesis.
units.tr: William, archbishop of Rouen, presses on to this end.

units.la: Cardinei coetus. Sic perit innocuus.
units.tr: The college of cardinals. Thus the innocent man perishes.

units.la: Perstitit igne Thomas constanti pectore firmus.
units.tr: Thomas stood firm in the fire with a steadfast breast.

units.la: Quod Christi exemplo uiuere chorus habet.
units.tr: This is what the choir has, to live by Christ's example.

units.la: Eugenius memorans tandem quod insidiosa
units.tr: Eugenius, recalling at last how treacherous

units.la: Morte uiri fuerit credulus ipse malis
units.tr: by the man's death, he himself was credulous of the evils.

units.la: Ingemuit crebro uir quod tam sanctus obisset
units.tr: The man often groaned that so holy a man had died.

units.la: Hoc quoque prae cunctis conqueritur abiens
units.tr: This above all else he laments as he departs.

units.la: Non nocuit flamma ista Thomae sed martyrium dat
units.tr: That flame did not harm Thomas but gave him martyrdom.

units.la: Immortalis ei parta corona manet
units.tr: An immortal crown won for him remains.

units.la: Post tormenta pius (sibi dant quae carcer & ignis)
units.tr: After the torments, which prison and fire give him, the pious man

units.la: Martyr ad aethereas convolat ille domos.
units.tr: flies as a martyr to the heavenly mansions.

units.la: HISTORIA DO. I. COBHAMI Illustriss. ac fortiss. martyris pro Christo exusti.
units.tr: HISTORY OF LORD JOHN COBHAM, most illustrious and most valiant martyr, burned for Christ.

units.la: VERVM INTER CAETEROS, quos hactenus commemorauimus, aut sumus posthac commemoraturi, ut nullus est, qui in externa dignitate, cum nobilissimo, omnique laude praestantissimo heroë Domino Cobhamo conferri queat, ita nec qui in Christo cordatior, aut qui plura, denique acerbiora tormenta emensus sit, etiam cum omnes simul conseris, haud fere quenquam reperies. Quod eo maiori huic laudi uertendum censeo, quo rariora nobis exempla occurrunt eorum, qui in tanta fortunae amplitudine, Christum per angustam illam ianuam in sequi dignantur. In caeteris enim, si paupertas plerunque expeditiores reddit homines ad regnum Dei, laudandum quidem & hoc, at minus tamen admirandum est. Id demum perquam rarae ac summae cuiusdam felicitatis existit, si quis in tam excel-so situs loco, tot obsitus mundi far-cinis, poterit sui quam Christi oblivi sci prius. Quo nomine imprimis hic unus, si quisquam alius laudandus est, vel Dei potius in illo laudanda singularis benignitas, qui sic in utro que laudis genere excelluit caeteris, ut, cum, omnibus esse exemplo, potuit, qui tamen exemplum hoc sint imitati haud multos nostra haec hactenus aetas vidit. Primus hic aulam Christo inseruire docuit, quae hactenus solebat longe aliis affigi obsequijs, aliis auferri cupiditatibus. Si quis principis sui fauorem, multorum annorum officijs tandem utcumque ad se attrahere potuit, in hac re unica, quasi summo potitus voto acquiescebat, hac summam felicitatis suae, hac supremam quandam nobilitatem metiri consueuit, huc omnia omniu fere studia referebant, hic omnium solatia, ac spes requie- fcebant. At hic postquam eximijs uirtutibus suis, maximisque rerum gestarum triumphis, quum felicissime ad principis fui fauorem emersisset, unde facile sibi reliqua il- la confequutus effet, quę apud istos maxima esse iudicantur, indeq; iam gradus sibi ad conspicuam nobilitatem fecisset, parum tamen hanc du- xit esse nobilitatem, nisi in Christo etiam effet nobilis. Cætera omnia fluxa, ac fortuita, in hoc solam uidebat consistere & ueram celsitudinem, quo quisque foret in Christo sublimior. Contra, friuolam esse felicitatem in ijs rebus sitam, cuius tibi nullam æternitatem, ac ne diuturnitatem quidem polliceri queas. Hæc dum partim apud fe reputando, partim ex Vuicleuicis institutionibus perceperat, quotidie in Christo auctior, excelfiorq; redditur. uttandē haud ueritus fit in autoritatis suæ pa trocitrocínium, ceu intra murum recipe- re quoscunque in ecclesia periclitan tes uiderat. Nec id diu latebat epi- scopos. Quid enim non uident isti Argi, per suos corycæos, sic per om- nes terras, ac maria uolitantes. Hi ergo ubi hoc duce, conatus suos fra ginonnihil comperiunt, in hunc om- ni conuerso impetu, consilia, ma- chinas, insidiasque deriuant, quip- pe in alios parum se effecturos rati, qui comites essent socisque eius instituti, nisi sublato prius eo unde cæteris agendi fiducia subministra- retur. Quid multis? Adit principem Ricardum Thomas Archiepisco- pus Cantuariæ, traducitur inclytus Christi miles, exponitur querela, intentantur crimina, confinguntur etiam quædam, Exaggerantur peri- cula perturbatæ ecclesiæ. Denique nihil omittitur. Ibi rex prudentissi- mus, accepta episcopi criminosa ora- tione, quæ alioqui quamuis modeftiffimum principem posset inflam-mare, nihil tamen temere ftatuen-dum existimans in tam fidum ma-uortiumque militem, quem tot no-minibus deuinctum coniunctiffi-mo fauore complecteretur, ita ar-chiepiscopum dimisit, ut inducias aliquot cum suis episcopis, expecta-re iuberet, in quibus ipsum, de rebus ipsdem, conueniret prius, tentaturus quàm maxime, incolumi illius ho-nore, litem inter se, & ecclesiasticos, quoad liceret, componere. Verum cum ne sic quidem Christianissimi pectoris expugnari constantia po-tuit, semel in summo principe con-stabilita, iterum queritante archiepi-scopo, res tandem ad episcopos de-uoluitur, à quibus quid actum sit, quid illi intentatum, quo pacto ab il-lo depulsum, qua calliditate cir-cumuentus, quanta crudelitate op-pressus, quibus tormentis affectus reliquit uitam, ex literis Archiepi-scopi scopi Cantuariensi ad Lodinensem, eadem de re scriptis, uidebimus omnia. Quas propterea hic subnecte re uisum est, quo certiorem Historiae fide conciliet orationis antiquitas.
units.tr: Among all the others whom we have so far recalled, or shall recall hereafter, there is hardly anyone to be found who can be compared with that most noble hero, Lord Cobham, who excelled in every kind of praise. Nor will you find many who were more steadfast in Christ, or who endured more numerous and more bitter torments, even if you set all the others together. I think this should be counted to his greater credit, since we meet with few examples of those who, in such great prosperity, deign to follow Christ through that narrow gate. For among others, poverty generally makes men more ready for the kingdom of God. That too deserves praise, but it is less remarkable. It is truly a very rare thing, and a kind of supreme happiness, for a man placed in so high a position, surrounded by so much worldly rubbish, to be able to forget himself and Christ too. For this reason especially he is to be praised above any other, or rather, the singular goodness of God toward him is to be praised, since he excelled in both kinds of praise above the rest, so that, though he could be an example to all, our age has seen few who have imitated this example. He was the first to teach that the court should serve Christ, a court that had hitherto been bound to quite different services and drawn away by other desires. If anyone had somehow managed, by many years of service, to win the favour of his prince, he would rest content as if he had attained the highest goal of his wishes, and by this alone he used to measure his highest happiness and a kind of supreme nobility. To this almost all men's efforts and hopes were directed, and here all their comforts and expectations found rest. But he, after by his outstanding virtues and his greatest triumphs in war he had risen most happily into his prince's favour, from which it was easy for him to obtain the other things that men judge to be greatest, and had thus made for himself a step to conspicuous nobility, nevertheless thought this to be of little worth as nobility, unless he were also noble in Christ. He saw that all other things were fleeting and accidental, and that true height consisted in this alone: that a man be the more exalted in Christ. On the contrary, he saw that happiness placed in such things is frivolous, since they can promise you no eternity, not even any lasting duration. While he was gaining these insights partly by reflecting on them himself and partly from the teaching of Wycliffe, he grew daily greater and more exalted in Christ. And so he did not hesitate to take up the protection of his authority for those whom he saw in danger in the Church, as if receiving them within a wall. Nor was this kept hidden from the bishops for long. For what do those Argus-eyed men not see, flitting over all lands and seas through their agents? When therefore they found their attempts, under this leader, to be of little avail, they turned all their force against him, and directed their plans, schemes and snares against him alone, thinking that they would achieve little against the others, who were his companions and associates in this teaching, unless the one from whom the others drew their confidence in acting were first removed. What more? Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, approaches the king, Richard, the famous soldier of Christ is accused, a complaint is set forth, charges are brought, some things are even invented, and the dangers to the disturbed Church are exaggerated. In short, nothing is left out. Then the most prudent king, having heard the archbishop's accusatory speech, which might otherwise have inflamed even a most moderate prince, yet judging that nothing should be rashly decided against so loyal and brave a soldier, whom he embraced with the closest favour, bound to him by so many ties, dismissed the archbishop with the order that he should wait some days for a truce with his bishops, in which he himself would first meet with them about the same matters, intending as far as possible, with the archbishop's honour unharmed, to settle the quarrel between himself and the churchmen as far as might be. But since not even so could the constancy of that most Christian heart be overcome, once it had been firmly fixed in the supreme prince, and since the archbishop complained again, the matter was at last referred to the bishops. What was done by them, what was attempted against him, how he was driven off by him, by what cunning he was circumvented, by what cruelty he was oppressed, and with what torments he was afflicted until he left this life, we shall see in full from the letters of the Archbishop of Canterbury to the Bishop of London, written on the same matter. These letters have therefore been thought fit to be added here, so that the antiquity of the account may lend greater trust to the history.

units.la: EXEMPLAR EPISTOLAE ARCHIEPISCOPI CANT. ad Londinensem scriptae, in qua tota illa actio, defensio, ac condemnatio clariss. D. Cobbami continetur.
units.tr: A copy of the letter of the Archbishop of Canterbury, written to the Bishop of London, in which the whole proceeding, defence and condemnation of the most distinguished Sir John Cobham is contained.

units.la: REVERENDO IN CHRISTO patri ac domino, domino Roberto, Dei gratia Herfordensi episcopo, Ricardus permissione diuina Londinensis episcopus, salutem, & sincerę dilectionis continuum incrementum. Literas reuerendissimi in Christo patris & D. Domini Thomae Dei gratia Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi totius Anglię primatis, & Apostolicae sedis legati, nuper recepimus in haec uerba. Thomas permissione diuína Cātu. Archiep, totius Angliæ ,primas & Apostolicæ sedis legatus,uenerabili fratrino stro domino Ricardo Dei gratia Londinensi epíscopo, salutem, & fraternam in domino charitatem. Nuper coram nobis,in conuocatione Prælatorum, & cleri,nostræ Cantuariensis prouinciæ, in ecclesia nostra sancti Pauli, ultimo celebrata, cum ijsdem prælatis,& clero, super unione, & reformatione ecclesiæ Anglicanæ,tractantibus, inter cæte ra,per nos, & eosdem prælatos, & clerum,conclusum extitit, quasi pro impossibili,scissuram tunicæ domini inconsutilis,reformare,nisi prius certi magnates regni, autores, fauto res,protectores , defensores & receptores horum hæreticorum,qui dicuntur lollardi,essent rigide repræhensi,ac si opus fuerit, per censuras ecclesiæ, unà cum inuocatione brachij seculáris, à suis deuijs reuocati. Et facta subsequenter, in eadem con uocatione, inter Procuratores cleri & alios, qui de singulis diocoesibus eiusdem nostrae provinciae, ibidem in magno numero interfuerunt, inquisitione diligenti repertum fuit, inter eosdem, ac nobis detectum, & delatum, quod Dom. Ioannes Oldcastellus miles, fuerat, & est principalis receptator, fautor, protector & defensor eorundem, ac quod praesertim in diocoesi Londinensi, Roffensi & Herfordensi, ipsos lollardos, ab ordinariis siue diocoesanis locorum, minime licentiatos, contra constitutionem provincialem inde factam, ad praedicandum trasmisit, ac eorum praedicationibus nepharijs interfuit, & contradictores, si quos repererat, minis & terroribus, ac gladij saecularis potentia compescuit, asserens & affirmans inter caetera, quod nos, & confratres nostri suffraganei, nostrae provinciae non habuismus, nec habemus potestatem aliquam huiusmodi constitutionem faciendi: Aliterque sentist, & sentit, ac dogmatizat, et docet de sacramentis altaris, & pœnitentiæ, peregrinationibus, & adorationibus imaginum, & clauibus, quàm Romana, & uniuersalis ecclesia docet, & affirmat. Quare ex parte eorundem prælatorum, & cleri, tunc fuimus requisiti, ut de & supra præmissis, contra eundem dominum Olcastellū procedere, dignaremur. Nos tamen ob reuerentiam domini nostri regis, cuius, ad tunc, idem dominus Ioannes familiaris exiterat, ac ob honorem, nihilo minus ordinis militaris, unà cum omnibus confratribus, & suffraganeis nostris, dictæ nostræ prouinciæ, tunc præsentibus, & magna parte cleri, eiusdem nostræ prouinciæ, ad præsentiam dicti domini nostri regis, tunc in manerio suo, de Kenyngton existentis, personaliter
units.tr: To the reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord Robert, by the grace of God Bishop of Hereford, Richard, by divine permission Bishop of London, greeting and a continual increase of sincere affection. We have lately received the letter of the most reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord Thomas, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England and legate of the Apostolic See, in these words: "Thomas, by divine permission Archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England and legate of the Apostolic See, to our venerable brother Richard, by the grace of God Bishop of London, greeting and fraternal charity in the Lord. Recently, before us, in the convocation of prelates and clergy of our province of Canterbury, celebrated last in our church of St Paul, while the same prelates and clergy were treating of the union and reform of the English Church, it was concluded by us and those prelates and clergy, among other things, that it is as though impossible to repair the rent in the Lord's seamless coat, unless first certain great men of the realm, authors, favourers, protectors, defenders and receivers of these heretics who are called Lollards, be sharply rebuked and, if need be, by the censures of the Church, together with the invocation of the secular arm, be recalled from their errors. And afterwards, in the same convocation, a careful inquiry was made among the proctors of the clergy and others who were present there in great number from each diocese of our province; and it was found and disclosed and reported to us that Sir John Oldcastle, knight, has been and is the principal receiver, favourer, protector and defender of these men. In particular, in the dioceses of London, Rochester and Hereford, he has sent those Lollards, who had not been licensed by the ordinaries or diocesans of the places, to preach contrary to the provincial constitution made on this matter; he has been present at their pernicious preaching, and he has restrained any opponents he found with threats and terrors and the power of the sword. He has asserted and affirmed, among other things, that we and our suffragan brethren of our province have had no power, and have none, to make any such constitution. He also thinks, teaches and holds otherwise than the Roman and universal Church teaches and affirms concerning the sacraments of the altar and of penance, pilgrimages, the adoration of images and the keys. Therefore, on behalf of the same prelates and clergy, we were then asked to deign to proceed against the said Sir John Oldcastle regarding the matters set out above. Nevertheless, out of reverence for our lord the king, whose familiar servant the same Sir John then was, and out of respect for the knightly order no less, we, together with all our brethren and suffragans of the said province then present, and a large part of the clergy of the same province, went in person to the presence of our said lord the king, who was then at his manor of Kennington, and there, deposing a complaint against the same Sir John, we recited in part the defects of the same Sir John.

units.la: I. Oldcastellus miles Aurautus Regi suo charus.
units.tr: I. Sir John Oldcastle, knight, golden-spurred, dear to his king.

units.la: liter, accedentes, contractu eundem dominum Ioannem querelam deponentes, defectus eiusdem domini Ioannis partim recitauimus. Sed ad rogatu ipsius domini nostri regis, ipsum dominum Iohannem, sine dedecore, ad unitatem ecclesiae reducere cupientes, omnem executionem praemissorum ad tempus magnum distulimus. Sed demum, quia praefatus dominus noster rex, circa reductionem eiusdem, post magnos labores non profecit, prout idem dominus noster rex nobis tam uerbo, quam in scriptis referre dignabatur: Nos subsequenter eundem dominum Ioannem, de & super praemissis, personaliter responsuru coram nobis, ad certum terminum effluxum, decreuimus euocandum, ac nuncium nostrum, cum his nostris citatoriis, ad dictum dominum Ioannem transmisimus, tunc in castro suo de Couulyng degentem: cui nuncio nostro dedimus in mandatis,ut castrum dicti domini Ioannis, nullo modo ingrederetur,nisi licentiatus. Sed per medium cuiusdam Ioannis Botteleri Hostiarij camerae dicti domini nostri regis,ipsum dominum Ioannem requireret, quatenus aut daret dicto nuncio nostro licentiam ingrediendi,ut citaret eundem,ceu saltem extra castrum suum prædictum, faceret sui copiam, ut sic citatione posset apprehendi.Qui tamē dominus Ioannes, dicto Ioanni Bottelero exparte domini nostri regis, sibi præmissa exponenti publi cèrefpodit, quod nullo modo citari voluit,nec citationem ipsius aliqua-liter tolerare. Noscę praeterea, de præmissis nobis facta fide,ulterius legitimè procedentes,facta nobis primitus fideli relatione, quod idem D. units.tr: But at the request of our lord the king himself, wishing to bring the same Sir John back to the unity of the Church without disgrace, we put off all execution of the above for a long time. But at last, since the said lord our king, after great labours concerning his restoration, made no progress, as our same lord the king deigned to report to us both by word and in writing, we afterwards decided to summon the same Sir John to answer in person before us, concerning and upon the above, at a certain appointed term, and we sent our messenger, with these our citations, to the said Sir John, who was then staying in his castle of Cowling. To this messenger of ours we gave instructions that he should not enter the castle of the said Sir John unless he had been licensed. But he was to ask the said Sir John, through a certain John Butler, usher of the chamber of our said lord the king, who would set out these matters to him on our lord the king's behalf, either to give our said messenger licence to enter, so that he might cite him, or at least to come outside his castle, so that he could be seized by the citation. But the said Sir John openly answered John Butler, on behalf of our lord the king, who set these things before him, that he by no means wished to be cited, and would in no way tolerate a citation of himself. Moreover, it is known that, the matters having been reported to us on trustworthy evidence, and our proceedings being lawful, after first receiving a faithful report that the same Lord John could not be seized by personal citation, we decided that he should be cited by edict, to be publicly posted on the doors of the church

units.la: {a} Scilicet quam astu teincedunt serpentes. clesiæ cathedralis Roffen. sibi uici‐næ, & nisi modicum ultra tria milia‐ria Anglicana, à dicto Castro de Couuling distantis, publice affigen‐dum, pro ut eum sic citari fecimus, & huiusmodi edictum nostrum in ual‐uis dictæ ecclesiæ publice, & paten‐ter affigi, ad comparendum coram nobis ii die Septembris iam præteri‐ti, de & super præmissis, atqp nihilo‐minus, certis alijs, hæreticam prauitatem concernentibus, personaliter respônsurum. Quo die aduenien‐te, nobis in capella maiori, infra ca‐strum de Iedys, nostræ diocef. quod tunc inhabitabamus, & ubi tunc re‐sidebamus, cum Curia nostra, pro‐tribunali sedentibus, facta fide quæ requiritur in præmissis, ac audita per nos & recepta relatione, iuxta assertionē, et prout cōmuniter prædi‐catur in partibus, ubi dictus domi‐nus Ioannes se incastellat, & fortifi‐cat in Castro suo prædicto, ac opi‐niones
units.tr: {a} Namely, how cunningly the serpents creep. The cathedral church of Rochester, neighbouring to us, and not much more than three English miles distant from the said Castle of Cowling, was to be posted publicly, as we caused him to be cited in this way; and this our edict was to be publicly and plainly posted on the doors of the said church, requiring him to appear before us on the second day of September now past, concerning the aforesaid matters and, besides, certain other matters touching heretical depravity, and to answer in person. On that day, when we had arrived in the greater chapel within the castle of Ightham in our diocese, where we were then living and where we then resided with our court, sitting on the tribunal, the proof required in the aforesaid matters having been made, and the report having been heard and received, according to the assertion and as is commonly preached in the parts where the said Lord John entrenches and fortifies himself in his aforesaid castle, and defends his opinions

units.la: ὀυ‐ς τὴ λεόντ‐ς niones suas defendit, claues ecclesiæ, ac potestate archiepiscopalem multi pliciter contemnendo. Nos eundem D. Io. sicut præmittitur citatum publice, & alta uoce præconizari fecimus, ac sic præconizatum, diutius expectatum, & nullo modo comparentem, reputauimus, pro ut erat, merito contumacem, & in pœnam contumaciæ suæ huiusmodi, ipsum in scriptis excomunicamus tunc ibidem. Et quia ex serie præmissorum, & aliis perspicuis iudicijs, & factorum evidentiis, concepimus, quod idem Do. Io. in defensionem huiusmodi erroris sui, contra claues ecclesiæ, se fortificat, & incastellat, ut præmittitur: quorum prætextu uehemens suspicio hæresis, atque schismatis, insurgit contra eundem: Decreuimus ipsum Do. Ioannem, iterato personaliter, si apprehendi poterit, alios qui per edictum, ut prius citandum, ut compareat coram nobis, die sabbati
units.tr: (defends his opinions), contemning the keys of the church and the archiepiscopal power in many ways. We caused the said Lord John, cited publicly and by a loud voice as set out above, to be proclaimed, and when he had been proclaimed and long awaited, and in no way appeared, we judged him, as was the case, rightly contumacious; and for the penalty of his contumacy we excommunicated him in writing there and then. And because from the sequence of the aforesaid matters, and from other clear judgments and evident facts, we have concluded that the same Lord John fortifies and entrenches himself against the keys of the church in defence of this his error, as set out above, and by pretext of which a vehement suspicion of heresy and schism arises against him, we have decreed that the same Lord John be cited again personally, if he can be apprehended, and the others by edict as before, to appear before us on the Saturday

units.la: Satis pro imperio sed licet.
units.tr: Enough for the command, but it is permitted.

units.la: Excommunicatus D. Cobham mus. bati proximo post festum S. Mathei apostoli & euangelistæ proximo futuro: causam rationabilem si quam habeat, quare contra eundem ad graviora procedi non debeat, tanquam publicum hæreticum, schismaticum, ac hostem universalis ecclesiæ quare etiam pro tali pronunciari no debeat, ac auxilium brachij secularis contra eundem solenniter invocari, personaliter propositurum, ulteriusque responsurum, facturum, & recepturum circa omnia & singula præmissa, quod iustitia suadebit. Quo termino, videlicet die Sabbati proximo post festum S. Mathei prædicto 25. die eiusdem Septembris, adveniente, coram nobis in domo capitulari ecclesiæ S. Pauli Londinensis pro tribunali sedentibus, assi dentibusque nobis venerabilibus confratribus nostris, Dominis, Ricardo Londinensi, & Henrico Vuynton, Dei gratia episcopis, comparuit personaliter fonaliter D. Ro. de Morley miles, custos turris Londoniēsis, secumqꝫ præfatum D. Ioannem oldcastellū, militem adduxit, et coram nobis collocauit (Nam parum ante per regi os ministros comprænsus est & in turrim clausus.) Cui quidem D. Ioanni Oldcasteilo sic personaliter præsenti, nos totam seriem facti, pro ut in actis diei præcedentis continetur, bonis, & modestis terminis, ac modo multum suaui, recitauimus, uidelicet quo modo, idem Do. Io. de & super articulis superius recitatis, in conuocatione prælatorum, & cleri, dictæ nostræ prouinciæ, ut præmittitur, detectus, & delatus extiterat. Quomodoque citatus, et propter suam contumaciam excommunicatus, & postquam ad hoc deuenit fuerat, nos obtulimus paratos ad absoluendum eundem. Ipse tamen Do. Io. ad huiusmodi oblatio nem non aduertens dixit quod libēter recitaret coram nobis, & dictis confratribus meis, fidem suam, quam tenet, & affirmat. Siccq; licentia petita, & obtenta extraxit de sinu suo quandam schedulam indentatam, & contenta in eadem, publice ibidem perlegit, eandemque schedulam nobis realiter tradidit, & articulorum, super quibus extitit examinatus, quae est talis. Ego Io. Oldcastellus miles, Dominus de Cobham, cupio omnibus innotescere Christianis, testemque adhiberi Deum, nunquam me aliter induxisse animum, nec inducturum (ducente Domino) qua ut firma indubitataque fide, omnia illius sacramenta amplectar, quaecunque ab ipso ad usum suae ecclesiae sunt tradita. Praeterea ut in quatuor his generibus fidei meae apertius ex ponam sententiam. Principio credo uenerandum hocaltaris sacramentum, Christi existere corpus, sub panis specie, id ipsum inquam, quod a Maria natum matre, pro nobis crucifixum, mortuum ac sepultum sit,
units.tr: Excommunicated: Lord Cobham. On the Saturday next after the feast of St Matthew the apostle and evangelist, next to come, to set forth in person any reasonable cause, if he has one, why proceedings should not be taken against him to heavier measures, as a public heretic, schismatic, and enemy of the universal church; why he should not also be pronounced such; and why the aid of the secular arm should not be solemnly invoked against him; and further to answer, to do, and to receive concerning all and singular the aforesaid matters whatever justice shall suggest. On that term, namely the Saturday next after the aforesaid feast of St Matthew, the 25th day of the same September arriving, before us sitting on the tribunal in the chapter house of St Paul's, London, with our venerable brothers Richard, bishop of London, and Henry of Winchester, by the grace of God bishops, assisting us, there appeared in person Sir Roger Morley, knight, keeper of the Tower of London, and he brought with him the aforesaid Sir John Oldcastle, knight, and placed him before us (for shortly before he had been seized by the king's ministers and shut up in the Tower). To this Sir John Oldcastle, present in person, we set out the whole course of the matter, as it is contained in the acts of the preceding day, in good and modest terms and in a very gentle manner: namely, how the same Lord John had been detected and denounced concerning the articles recited above, in the convocation of the prelates and clergy of our province, as has been said. And how, having been cited and excommunicated for his contumacy, and after it had come to this, we offered ourselves ready to absolve him. The Lord John, however, not heeding this offer, said that he would gladly recite before us and my said brothers the faith which he holds and affirms. And so, leave having been asked and obtained, he drew from his bosom a certain indented schedule, and publicly read out there what was contained in it, and he handed that schedule to us in fact, together with the articles on which he had been examined; and it is as follows: "I, John Oldcastle, knight, Lord of Cobham, desire to make known to all Christians, and call God to witness, that I have never otherwise turned my mind, nor shall I turn it (the Lord leading me), but with firm and undoubted faith I embrace all his sacraments, whatever have been handed down by him for the use of his church. Moreover, that I may set out my opinion more openly in these four heads of my faith: first, I believe that the venerable sacrament of the altar is the body of Christ under the species of bread, that very body, I say, which was born of the Virgin Mary, was crucified for us, died and was buried."

units.la: Fides ac confessio catholica D. Cobham mi.
units.tr: The catholic faith and confession of my lord Cobham.

units.la: Sacramentum eucharistiae. demum post triduanam mortem redivivum, ac subductum ad dextram immortalis patris, nunc cum ipso triumphat sempiternae gloriae particeps. Tum de poenitentiae Sacramento ita habet fides mea, ut credam apprime necessariam quibuscumque, ad salutem anhelantibus, peccatricis vitae correctionem: talemque subeundam prioris vitae poenitudinem, ex vera confessione, indissimulata contritione, legitimaque satisfactione, qualem divinae nobis praescribunt literae, alioqui nullam futuram salutis spem.
units.tr: The Sacrament of the Eucharist. Finally, after dying and remaining dead for three days, he rose again, was taken up to the right hand of the immortal Father, and now triumphs with him, a sharer in everlasting glory. Concerning the Sacrament of Penance, my faith holds that the correction of a sinful life is absolutely necessary for all who long for salvation. Such repentance of the former life must be undertaken, by true confession, unfeigned contrition, and lawful satisfaction, of the kind which the divine Scriptures prescribe for us. Otherwise there is no hope of salvation.

units.tr: Thirdly, concerning images I think as follows: I do not regard them as mere representations of faith. After the faith of Christ was brought into the world, they crept into use with the Church's permission, so that they might serve the laity and the unlearned in place of a calendar, and so that, by their reminder, the martyrdoms of Christ and of other saints and their pious examples might more easily be brought before the eyes of memory. But if anyone misuses this representation otherwise,

units.la: Hodie repraesentatione secus abutatur, ut his ipsis sanctorum simulachris cultum eũ praestet, qui debetur ijs, quos repraesentant, imo huic potius cui debeant honorem debeant, hanc in eis collocantes fiduciam quae in Deum unice sit transferenda, siue ita erga mutas has imagines affecti, ut his aliqua parte sint affixi, aut huic quam illi addictiores, mea sententia nihil abscedunt ab ido lolatria, criminaliter peccates, in Deum, omnis honoris autorem. Postremo sic mihi persuadeo, nullum in terris inquilinum esse quin siue ad uitam, siue ad supplicium peregrinetur. Quisquis ita uitam insti-tuerit, ut in praecepta Dei quae aut nescit, aut doceri non uult, impingat, huic frustra salutem expectari, etiamsi orbis omnes angulos expatiatur. Contraque qui illius obseruat praecepta iusta, haud posse interire, quamuis nusquam ille in tota
units.tr: by paying to these very images of the saints the worship which is due to those whom they represent, or rather to Him to whom honour is due, placing in them that trust which is to be transferred to God alone, or if he is so attached to these dumb images as to be bound to them in some part, or more devoted to this one than to that, then in my opinion he is not far from idolatry, sinning criminally against God, the author of all honour. Lastly, I am persuaded that there is no dweller on earth who is not travelling either towards life or towards punishment. Whoever shapes his life so that he stumbles over the precepts of God, which he either does not know or does not wish to be taught, expects salvation in vain, even if he wanders through every corner of the world. On the contrary, he who observes God's just precepts cannot perish, even though he never wanders through the whole world

units.la: O urita perambulet, peregrinationis ergo, neque Romam neque Cantuariam, neque Compostellam, siue quocunque perambulare solet vulgus hominum.
units.tr: on pilgrimage, neither to Rome, nor to Canterbury, nor to Compostella, nor wherever the common crowd of men is accustomed to wander.

units.la: Qua schedula cum istis articulis contentis in eadem (ut praefertur) per dictum dominum Ioannem perlecta, nos cum confratribus nostris praedictis, aliisque pluribus Doctoribus, et peritis super his communi cauimus, ac demum de consilio, & assensu eorundem, praefato domino Ioanni Oldcastello, dixImus tibi idem. Ecce domine Ioannes in hac schedula plura bona continentur, & satis Catholica, sed uos habetis terminum istum ad respondendum super aliis, errores et haereses sapientibus, quibus per contenta in hac schedula, non est plene responsum, & propterea uos oportet ad eadem, & fidem uestram atque assertiones in eadem schedula expressas circa eadem plenius declarare. Videlicet an teneatis, credatis, & affirmetis quod in sacramento altaris, post con- secrationem rite factam remaneat panis materialis, uel non. Item an te- neatis, credatis & affirmetis quod in sacramento poenitentiæ, necessarium fuerit quod habens copiam sacerdotis confiteatur, de peccatis suis presbitero per ecclesiam ordinato. Quibus sic datis inter multa et varia per dictum Ioannem Oldcastellum dicta respondit expresse, se nolle prae dicta aliter declarare, nec aliter quam in dicta schedula continetur aliqua liter ad eadem respondere, unde nos ipsi domino Ioanni compatientes benigno & affabili modo diximus, tunc ibidem. Caveatis domine Ioannes, quia si ad haec vobis obiecta clare non respondeatis, in termino legitimo vobis iam dato per iudicem, poterimus vos pronunciare & declarare haereticum. Ipse tamen dominus Ioannes se tenuit ut prius, & non luit aliter respondere. Confequen- ter tamen nos cum dictis cofratribus nostris, & alijs de consilio nostro consuluimus, et de comunicato co- filio eorūdem, declarauimus eidem domino Ioanni Oldcaftello quid S. Romana ecclesia, in hac materia se- quens dicta beatorū Augustini, Hi- eron, & Ambrof, ac aliorū sanctorū determinauit, quas determinationes oportet quofcunq; Catholicos ob- seruare, ad quę idem dominus Ioan- nes respondit, quod bene uoluit cre- dere, & obseruare quicquid S. Ec- clesia determinauit, ac quicquid De us uoluit se credere, & obseruare. Sed quod dominus noster Papa, Cardinales, Archiepiscopi, et episco- pi, caeteriqe praelati ecclesiae habe- rent potestatem, talia determinandi noluit ad tunc aliqualiter affirmare. Vnde nos adhuc sibi compatien- tes, sub spe melioris deliberationis, promi-
units.tr: When this schedule, with the articles contained in it, had been read through by the said Sir John (as stated above), we, together with our aforesaid brethren and several other doctors and experts in these matters, took common counsel. Finally, with their counsel and assent, we said to the aforesaid Sir John Oldcastle: "Behold, Sir John, this schedule contains many good things and is quite Catholic. But you have this term to answer concerning the other errors and heresies, to which what is contained in this schedule has not fully responded. Therefore you ought to declare more fully your faith and the assertions expressed in this schedule concerning these matters. Namely, do you hold, believe and affirm that in the sacrament of the altar, after the consecration duly made, material bread remains, or not? Likewise, do you hold, believe and affirm that in the sacrament of penance it is necessary that one who has access to a priest confess his sins to a presbyter ordained by the Church?" To these questions, among many and various things said by the said John Oldcastle, he expressly replied that he was unwilling to declare the aforesaid otherwise, nor to answer them in any way other than as contained in the said schedule. Whereupon we, feeling compassion for Sir John himself, said to him kindly and courteously, then and there: "Take care, Sir John, for if you do not clearly answer these objections put to you within the legitimate term already given you by the judge, we can pronounce and declare you a heretic." Yet Sir John held to his position as before, and would not answer otherwise.
