Septa quaedam ac metas certas res haec habere uidetur, quas ne temere praeter filiamus, magnopere uidedum est.
units.tr: I said that it is lawful for a Christian to swear. But, led by the authority of the Gospel and of St James, and likewise by the clear testimonies of the doctors, I said that it is not lawful to swear by creatures, as people usually do. I also preached, fortified by the same and other witnesses, that one must by no means swear if the truth laid out before a lawful judge can be made clear otherwise. If not, I taught that the truth should be attested by a faithful oath, under the name of God alone, since he alone is eternal truth. Clerk: What do you say? Is it lawful for a subject, at his prelate's command, to bend the knees, touch the book of the Gospel, and kiss the book to this effect: "So help me God, and this holy Gospel of his, etc."? For whoever is a faithful subject will readily do whatever the prelate commands. William: This matter seems to have certain fences and fixed limits, which we must take great care not to cross rashly.

units.la: Quid si inhonestum aut illicitum quidpiam nobis, à ἀνυπάκοος ecclesia sticis, imperatum fuerit, protinus illis obsequendum putas? Archiep. De superiorum potentia nulla est hæsitatio, sed etiamsi iniusta præcipiant, erat obediendum tamen, nec ullum esset iurantibus subditis periculum. Guilielm. Hoc ὁ παραδοξος haud satis assequor, sed ad rem propositam. Pridem in ædibus patricii cuiusdam uiri pransus, eandē hanc, de iuramentis, controuersiam, inter theologum, & iurisperitum agitari audieram. Iurecōsultus id tuebatur, quod à iudice impulsus in re iusta manum adhibere non detrectaret; at si causam minus iustam intelligeret, denuo subtraheret, periculum ui taturus. Contra adductis rationibus disseruit theologus. Qui codici, inquit, manum admolitur, & Deum blasphemat, & proximo infert scandalū, Codex enim quid aliud quàm crea
units.tr: What if something dishonourable or unlawful were ordered of us by the disobedient ecclesiastics [ἀνυπάκοος]? Do you think we should obey them at once? Archbishop: There is no doubt about the power of superiors, but even if they command unjust things, subjects were bound to obey, and there would be no danger to those swearing. William: I do not quite grasp this paradox [ὁ παράδοξος], but to the matter at hand. Not long ago, dining in the house of a certain gentleman, I heard this same controversy about oaths debated between a theologian and a lawyer. The lawyer maintained that a man urged by a judge to put his hand to something just should not refuse, but if he understood the cause to be less just, he should withdraw again, to avoid danger by force. The theologian argued against him with reasons: "He who lays his hand on the book," he said, "blasphemes God and gives offence to his neighbour. For what is a book but a creature, or something made up of creatures? Wherefore, in this way, swearing seems to be nothing other than calling on corruptible creatures to witness the truth, which is eternal. By my reasoning this is utterly unlawful, and no less forbidden by the Lord in the law; indeed Chrysostom agrees with this, condemning both the one who swears so and the one who brings the book."

units.la: ILLEGIBLE HEADING MARK creatura est, uel ex creaturis conflatum quiddam? Quamobrem hoc pacto iurare nihil aliud uideri possit, quàm corruptibiles creaturas ad testandam ueritatem, quæ res æterna est, arcessere. Quod, mea ratione, prorsus illicitum est, nec minus à Domino in lege prohibitum, quin & huic astipulatur Chrysostomus utrumq; redarguens, & eum qui sic iurat, & qui librum adducit. Ad hæc dicta, assessores sacrifici in risum & conuitia, Archiepiscopus uero ad tormenta & minas conuertebatur, ni deserta opinione alium se uirum ostenderet. Guiliel·Hęc mea duntaxat opinio non est, sed & Christi seruatoris, Diui Iacobi, Chrysostomi, & sanctorum Patrum. Iussit tum Archiepiscopus in medium proferri Chrysostomi homeliam, quam is à Guilielmo surreptam Cătuarię, in schedula quadam scriptam, Ministro tradidit. Perlecta igitur homelia melia usq; ad clausulam eam, quod scelus sit etiam bene iurare: rogat Maluerenus Archiepiscopu, ab eo sciscitaretur, quo pacto hunc Chrysostomi locum intelligat. Quod & fecit Archiepiscopus. Ad quod ille attonitus primo, tandem Dei spiritu animatus respondit. Sunt qui in communibus vitae negotiis Deum ipsum plerunque (quo magis fide inueniant) in veritatis testem aduocent. Hoc tamen praeter religionem magnaque temeritate fit, cum sint ad id nullo iudice coacti, cumque Christus talibus dicat, Omnino non iurandum. Ad hos igitur Chrysostomi hic locus attinet. Hinc enim apud multitudinem nascitur peieranti et deierandi consuetudo, quo aut lucrentur, aut decipiant, aut poenas effugiant plerique. Archiepiscopus. Potest haec fortasse accommodari interpretatio. Tunc alius ad Guilelmum sacrificeus. Ultra ne moreris
units.tr: At these words the priest's assessors broke into laughter and abuse, while the Archbishop turned to torments and threats, unless I abandoned my opinion and showed myself another man. William: This is not merely my opinion, but that of Christ our Saviour, St James, Chrysostom, and the holy Fathers. Then the Archbishop ordered Chrysostom's homily to be brought forward, which he handed to the minister, having had it seized from William at Canterbury, written on a certain slip of paper. The homily was read through up to the clause where he says that it is a crime even to swear well. Maluerenus asked the Archbishop to inquire of him how he understood this passage of Chrysostom, and the Archbishop did so. At first astonished, he at last, moved by the Spirit of God, answered: "There are those who, in the common affairs of life, very often call God himself as witness of the truth, so that they may be the more believed. Yet this is done without religion and with great rashness, since they are compelled to it by no judge; and Christ says to such people, 'Do not swear at all.' It is to these that this passage of Chrysostom applies. For from this there arises among the multitude a habit of forswearing and of swearing falsely, by which most people either gain, deceive, or escape punishment." Archbishop: Perhaps this interpretation can be made to fit. Then another priest said to William: "Do not delay the Lord Archbishop any further..."

units.la: V
units.tr: V

units.la: Dominum Archiepiscopum, sed apposita libro manu, spondeas te illius & Ecclesiae ordinationibus assensurum. Guilielmus. Nonne prius id dixi, edoctum me a quodam theologiae magistro, in simili casu, idem esse codicem tangere, & per codicem iurare. Archiepiscopus. In Anglia haud ullus est magister, quin uel iussus iurabit, uel tecum poenas luet. Guilielmus. Chrysostomus nunquid idoniae autoritatis? Archiepiscopus. Est quidem. Guilielmus. Si pro blasphemo tunc eum habet qui librum iuranti offert, multo magis illum qui per eundem iurat. Archiepiscopus. Chrysostomum non approbamus, sicubi ab Ecclesiae sanxionibus diuersa doceat. Tum Sacrificus. Non ne eiusdem sunt autoritatis Deus & uerbum ipsius? Guilielmus. Quis inficiabitur? Sacrificus. Cur ergo subterfugis Euangelij iurationem tionem, cum idem sit Euangelium quod Deus: Guilhelmus. Augustinus negat Christianum esse, ut frater fratri simpliciter non credat. Paratus sum igitur, uestro periculo, in Dei uerbum iurare, cum mihi uiderim non aliter credi. Sacrificus. Adhibe tunc manum Euangelio Dei, & sume iusiurandi onus. Guilhelmus. Poterit Euangelium manibus tangi? Sacrificus. Facete iocaris. Guilielmus. Amabo, utrum horum Christiani officij potius esse uidetur, tangere ne, an legere Euangelium? Sacrificus. Legere. Guilielmus. Hieronymi testimonio, Euangelium non est perlecta litera, sed fide susceptum Dei uerbum. Non libri fragilia folia, sed corde credita ueritas. Euangelium, inquit, quod Dei uirtus est, in chartis membranicis non manet, sed in firmissma fidei radice. Non in atramentarijs literis, sed in occultis sacrarum literarum senten-tijs, idem & Paulus ad Corinthios astruit. No, inquit, in sermone est regnum Dei, sed in uirtute. Et Dauid, uox Domini in uirtute: uerbo Domini coeli firmati sunt & spiritu oris eius omnis uirtus eorum, tum angelorum, tum hominū. Sacrificus. Hisquoq; uelles nos tecum nugari. Nonne euangelia dicimus, quæ libris missalibus inscribūtur? Guilelmus. Dicitis quidem, sed per κατα-χρησιν. Apud philosophos plerunq; principalior pars, pro toto sumitur: ut anima hominis, quæ sensus fugit, pro integro homine. Visarboris quoque in radice est, quæ oculis nō patescit. Et ut, unde digressi sumus, ad tactum redeamus. Multi uiuentem adhuc Christum uiderunt, audierunt, & tetigerunt (ut & scriptu-ras nunc legunt interpretantur & scribunt) nec tamen pilo hinc melio res reddebātur. Sicut æterna deitas nunnunquam sine fide cognoscitur, sic nec Euangelium sine Christi spiritu percipitur. Sacrificus. Mystica sunt haec, & insipida quae narras. Si haec exigua, cum sitis populi praeceptores, non percipitis, timendum ne vobis coelorum regnū auferatur, ut olim sacerdotum principibus, & senioribus Iudaeorum.
units.tr: ...but, with your hand laid on the book, promise that you will assent to his and the Church's ordinances. William: Did I not say before that I was taught by a certain master of theology that in a similar case to touch the book is the same as swearing by the book? Archbishop: In England there is no master who does not either swear when ordered or pay the penalty with you. William: Is Chrysostom of suitable authority? Archbishop: He certainly is. William: If Chrysostom considers the one who offers the book to the one swearing a blasphemer, much more does he consider the one who swears by the same book so. Archbishop: We do not approve of Chrysostom wherever he teaches things different from the Church's sanctions. Then the priest: Are God and his Word not of the same authority? William: Who would deny it? Priest: Why then do you shrink from swearing by the Gospel, since the Gospel is the same as God? William: Augustine denies that a man is a Christian if he does not simply believe his brother. I am therefore ready, at your risk, to swear upon the Word of God, since I see that otherwise I shall not be believed. Priest: Then lay your hand on the Gospel of God and take up the burden of the oath. William: Can the Gospel be touched with the hands? Priest: You joke cleverly. William: Pray tell me, which of these seems more the duty of a Christian, to touch the Gospel or to read it? Priest: To read it. William: By the testimony of Jerome, the Gospel is not the letter read through, but the Word of God received by faith. It is not the fragile leaves of a book, but the truth believed in the heart. The Gospel, he says, which is the power of God, does not remain in parchment pages, but in the firmest root of faith. Not in inky letters, but in the hidden meanings of the sacred letters. Paul also asserts the same to the Corinthians: "The kingdom of God is not in word, but in power." And David: "The voice of the Lord is in power; by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power, both of angels and of men, by the breath of his mouth." Priest: You would have us trifle with you on these points too. Do we not speak of gospels, which are written in the missal books? William: You do indeed, but by catachresis. Among the philosophers the more principal part is often taken for the whole, as the soul of man, which escapes the senses, stands for the whole man; and the root of a tree, which is not open to the eyes, likewise. And to return to where we started, to touch: many saw, heard, and touched Christ while he still lived, and they read, interpreted, and wrote the Scriptures just as they do now, yet they were none the better for it, not a whit. Just as the eternal deity is sometimes not known without faith, so the Gospel is not perceived without the Spirit of Christ. Priest: What you say is mystical and unpalatable. If you, being teachers of the people, do not grasp these simple things, there is cause to fear that the kingdom of heaven will be taken from you, as once from the chief priests and elders of the Jews.

units.la: Tunc Maluerenus. Equiuocationes non nosti? Regnum coelorum diuersa significat. Sed quid tu coelorum hic regnum dicis? Guilielmus. Quemadmodum a doctoribus accepi uerbi diuini intelligentiam. Sacrificus. A quibus credis illum surripi? Guilielmus. A mundi prudentibus qui primas in synagogis cathedras quaerunt, & sese ita sapientes putant, ut nec Christum nec apostolos sibi imitandos censeant. Archiepiscopus. Praepositos spirituales, miser semper iudicas. Per Deum immortalem, iniuste rex facit, nisi te ac tui similes per- miserit condemnari. Quin & alius sacrificus ei obiicit. Quod præce- dente uenerís die, consilium dede- rit cuidam Archiprætulis familiari seruo, ne sua peccata homini, sed soli Deo in confessione detegeret. Perturbatus ex hoc Guilielmus, intellexit se ab astuto quodam Sycophanta circumuentum. Is, ante biduum, fraudulenter ad eum in carcerem accesserat, de confessione multa interrogans. Vt uideret ab illo se accusatum iri, deprecatur à Domino Deo hoc illi malum non imputari. Simulq; rogat sacrificum, ut uir coram adductus, summam rei coram omnibus, plena narratione, aperiat. Ait tum Archiepiscopus. Sufficiunt hi modo præsentes. Sed quid homini dixeras, Guilielmus. In carcere, me audiens, mundi corruptelam, Sacerdotum
units.tr: Then Maluerenus said: "Do you not know equivocations? The kingdom of heaven has various meanings. But what do you mean by the kingdom of heaven here?" William: "As I have received the understanding of the divine word from teachers." Sacrificer: "From whom do you believe it was snatched?" William: "From the prudent of this world, who seek the first chairs in the synagogues and think themselves so wise that they judge neither Christ nor the apostles worth imitating." Archbishop: "You always judge your spiritual superiors to be wicked. By the immortal God, the king acts unjustly if he does not allow you and your like to be condemned." Another sacrificer also objects to him that, on the day before you came, he gave advice to a certain servant of the archbishop's household not to disclose his sins to a man, but to God alone in confession. William, disturbed by this, understood that he had been got around by some crafty sycophant. This man had come to him in prison two days before, deceitfully, and questioned him at length about confession. So that he might see himself accused by him, William prays to the Lord God that this evil not be imputed to him. At the same time he asks the sacrificer that the man be brought before them, so that he may lay out the whole matter before everyone in a full narrative. Then the Archbishop said: "Those present now are enough. But what had you said to the man, William?"

units.la: [The first line is a fragment: the start of the sentence continues from the previous page.] dotum inscitiam, & interim male contractam ex aula contagionem lachrymabundis ut uidebatur oculis deflebat, desiderabatque ex Dei uerbo doceri, quae esset uoluntas eius bona. At ego perspecta hominis contritione, persuaseram, ut relictis erroribus pristinis deinceps sub Dei timore uitam transigat. Cumque adhuc instaret ille, an posset non adito sacerdote, sua deleri malefacta? Respondera[m] solius hoc Dei esse peccata remittere, unde ergo fit, inquit, quod penes sacerdotem sit absolutio. Ad quod dicebam idem esse absoluere quod peccata remittere, & sic utrunque a Deo expectandum. Mille post Christi incarnationem annis ignotus erat usitatus hic Ecclesiae absolvendi ritus, veruntamen soluendi & ligandi uis, piis & incredulis, per idem tempus, e coeconibus sacris latenter dispensabatur. Huic fimi- le quiddam olim audiuisse me me- mini ad crucem Cantuariæ à Mor- dono monacho Feuersamo, qui hic tum prædicauerat. Et hæc sunt quæ uestro illi dixeram. Archiepi- scopus. Hanc doctrinam Ecclesia non approbat. Guilielmus. Eccle- sia cuius ubique Christus est caput, hanc satis comprobat sententiam. Namqʒ intollerabilis hæc in eccle- siasticis temeritas uidetur, ad suas traditiones sub anathemate Chri- stianos sic stringere, quos sua mor- te seruator tam liberos reddidit, præsertim cum nec is nec apostoli has obseruari præceperint, sed mul- to uitari potius. Sacrificus. Eas deceptiones impauidus effundis, quas ab illis hauseris, qui zizanes- am & alia adulterina semina inter triticum proiecerant. At ego sua- serim, repudiatis his erroribus, te- met Domini Archiepiscopi committas fidei, sensurus fortassis eum & dominum propitium, & patrem benevolum. At alius sacrificus sico-phanta, ingenti furore illi exprobrat peruicaciam, Quod nuper Londini, ecclesiasticum quendam virum Al-kertonum, & doctorem alterum im-portunius impetierit, hunc hypocri-tam, illum adulatorem appellans. Erat autem Alkertonus hic Eccle-siastes Londinensis qui ante pau-cos dies in celeberrima Pauli cruce impudenter debacchatus erat in O-xoniensis cuiusdam cocionem, quę-tum, (ut uidebatur,) papistica fa-ctioni parum arridebat. Hæcque occasio erat, cur Alkertonus hic à Thorpo hypocrita appellatus sit. Respondit ergo sacrifico Guiliel-mus. Nullus est qui Oxoniensis il-lius concionem iuste accusare pos-sit, nec causa erat, cur Alkertonus Iuuenem hunc, ad crucem pauli ma-ledictis lacceraret. Omnia namque
units.tr: ...dotum ignorance, and the contagion caught from the court, and he bewailed with tearful eyes, as it seemed, the corruption of the world, the ignorance of the priests. He longed to be taught from God's word what his good will was. But I, having observed the man's contrition, had persuaded him that, leaving his former errors, he should from now on spend his life under the fear of God. When he still pressed the question whether his wrongdoings could be blotted out without going to a priest, I answered that the forgiving of sins belongs to God alone. "Why then," he said, "does the power of absolution rest with the priest?" To this I said that to absolve is the same as to remit sins, and so both must be expected from God. For a thousand years after the incarnation of Christ, this customary rite of absolving was unknown in the Church; yet the power of loosing and binding was, during the same period, secretly dispensed to the pious and the unbelieving alike from the sacred monasteries. I remember once hearing something similar at the cross at Canterbury from the monk Mordonus Feuersamus, who was preaching there at that time. And these are the things I had said to your man. Archbishop: "The Church does not approve this doctrine." Guilielmus: "The Church, whose head is Christ everywhere, sufficiently approves this opinion. For it is an intolerable rashness among churchmen to bind Christians under anathema to their own traditions, when the Saviour by his death has made them so free, especially since neither he nor the apostles ordered these things to be observed, but rather to be avoided. " Sacrificer: "You pour out without fear those deceptions which you have drunk from those who sowed tares and other adulterous seeds among the wheat. But I would advise you, having rejected these errors, to commit yourself to the faith of the lord Archbishop, perhaps finding him a gracious lord and a kindly father." Another sycophantic sacrificer, with great fury, reproaches him for his obstinacy, because recently in London he had attacked more insolently a certain churchman, Alkerton, and another teacher, calling the one a hypocrite and the other a flatterer. Now this Alkerton was a preacher of London who, a few days before, had impudently raged at the famous Paul's Cross against the sermon of a certain Oxford man, which (as it seemed) did little to favour the papist faction. This was the occasion why Alkerton was called a hypocrite by Thorpe. William therefore answered the sacrificer: "No one can justly accuse that Oxford sermon, nor was there any reason why Alkerton should assail this young man with curses at Paul's Cross. For all the things that the Oxford man preached were supported in a Christian and learned way, by the purest word of God, by the illustrious testimonies of teachers and by the clearest reasons."

units.la: Oxoniensis ... (marginal note, show-through, not transcribed) quæ Oxoniensis ille prædicauerat Christiane & docte, purissimo Dei uerbo, illustribus Doctorum testimoniis, & clarissimis rationibus astruebantur. Sacrificus. Adeo iniqua sunt quæ tum dicebat, ut amplius ea tutari non sit ausus. Guilielmus. Anglice & Latine circumfertur illa concio, multisque in precio adhuc habetur. Si causam iam is deseruit, miror. At hoc unum scio, quod cum Lambeti esset, nihil harum rerum denegabat, sed omnia, per biduum, coram Archiepiscopo, & doctoribus publice tuebatur. Alius Sacrificus, Quemnam ex illis nebulonibus hic narrat? (erant enim Oxoniæ plures) ah uisitandus est adhuc ille impurus, pro hac ipsa, quam ædidit, conciuncula. Nulli huiusmodi concionibus applaudunt, nisi tui consimiles moriones. Archiepiscopus, Maledicta hæc secta manibus nibus pedibusque laborat, Ecclesiae libertates conuellere. Guilielmus. Equidem haud ullos noue-rim, qui Christianae Ecclesiae commodo magis desudant, quàm hi quos pro haereticis tam crudeliter iudicatis. Fugiunt enim superbiam, luxum, ambitionem, auariciam, symoniam, idolatriam, & id genus uitia (quae Ecclesiam maximè infestant) animi paupertate simplices, Euangelicae praedicationis munus gratis administrant, ut Christi membra decet, corporis duntaxat uictu necessario contenti. Tunc Sacrificus ad Archiepiscopum, Domine, Inclinat iam dies, & nobis est equitandum, imponas ei finem, quem non quaerit. Nam eo obstinatior uidetur, quo tu tolerantior. Maluerenus. Guilielme, Submissis genibus, gratiam praecare, & Ecclesiae te filium pollicitare.
units.tr: Sacrificer: "So unjust are the things he then said that he has not dared to defend them any further." William: "That sermon is circulated in English and Latin, and is still held in high esteem by many. If he has now abandoned the cause, I am surprised. But this one thing I know: when he was at Lambeth, he denied none of these things, but defended them all publicly for two days before the Archbishop and the teachers." Another sacrificer: "Which of those scoundrels is this man talking about? (for there were many at Oxford) Ah, that filthy fellow must still be called to account for this very little sermon he has published. No one applauds such sermons except men like you, buffoons." Archbishop: "This cursed sect labours with hand and foot to overthrow the liberties of the Church." William: "Indeed, I know of none who labour more for the good of the Christian Church than those whom you so cruelly judge to be heretics. For they flee pride, luxury, ambition, avarice, simony, idolatry, and that kind of vice which most of all troubles the Church. Simple in poverty of spirit, they perform the office of evangelical preaching freely, content with the necessary food of the body alone, as befits members of Christ." Then the sacrificer said to the Archbishop: "Lord, the day is now declining and we must ride on. Impose an end on him, since he does not seek one. For he seems the more obstinate, the more tolerant you are." Maluerenus: "William, on bended knees, beg for grace and promise to be a son of the Church."

units.la: Guiliel. Sæpius ab Archiepiscopo expetiui, vel Christi nomine, omnem sepontergâ me malitiam, nec ultra impesiat in Christiani officij functione. Nihil in hac uita auidius cupio, quàm in hoc uocationis genere, domno meo fideliter inserui-re. Archio. Si mihi adhuc parueris, erit tuo ortasse commodo. Age modo, nerm ultra differas, hoc aut illud respondeas. Aut oblatam beneuolentiæ upplex amplectere, aut ingratus contemne. Guilielmus. Credendumne est Christum Deum esse & hominem, ueraq; esse, quæ se cit, & docuit? Archiep. Maximè credendum. Guiliel. Et quod doctrina Prophetica, & Apostolica à Spiritu autore profecta sit? Archi. Sanè quidem. Guiliel. Ea ergo ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem præ cæteris omnibus amplectenda est, necquic quam illi præferendum. Archiep. Assentior. Guiliel. Hanc enim so-
units.tr: William: I have often asked the Archbishop, even in Christ's name, to put aside all his malice toward me and no longer press me in the discharge of a Christian office. Nothing in this life do I desire more eagerly than to serve my lord faithfully in this kind of calling. Archbishop: If you obey me a little, it may perhaps be to your advantage. Come now, do not put it off any longer; answer this or that. Either humbly embrace the goodwill offered, or ungratefully spurn it. William: Must we believe that Christ is God and man, and that what he said and taught is true? Archbishop: Most certainly we must believe it. William: And that the prophetic and apostolic doctrine has come from the Spirit as its author? Archbishop: Certainly. William: Therefore this doctrine is to be embraced before all others for the building up of the Church, and nothing is to be preferred to it. Archbishop: I agree. William: For this sol-

units.la: lam-
units.tr: lone...

units.la: iam medelam aduersus [illegible, ~3 letters] uitia, & uniuersos dæmonum insu[?]tus ostendit, sine qua, nec uitæ tranquillitas, nec diuinæ uoluntatis [illegible, ~3 letters] acquiritur. Archiep. Non abuo. Guiliel. Quicquid secundum hanc doctrinam iusseris, diuino [illegible, ~3 letters] annixus auxilio, etiam cum uitæ periculo suscipiam. Archiepisc. Supplicias te ergo Ecclesiæ ordinationibus, quas tibi explanaturus sum. Guilielmus. Scis Christum esse Ecclesiæ caput, huius & Apostolorum suorum decretis, quicquid iusserint, obtemperaturum me profiteor. Tum Archiepiscopus mensa manu ingenti abie percutiens, magno affectu prorumpit. Per Dominum Iesum, nisi absque omni cauillo consenseris captum te in carceres dedam, tam strictè ut nullus sit æquè uinctus latro, at homicida. Maturè ergo tecum deliberà, quid agendum statues. Moc his dictis, in fenestram, tragicè hic Satrapas se recipit. At Maluerenus altero adiunctus sibi sacrifico, nunc blanditiis, nunc terroribus hominem aggreditur. Primum quàm graues, illi poenæ subeundæ sint exponit, post illas degradationem, execrationes, infamiam publicam, incendium, denique ad inferos damnationem exaggerat, nisi tempestiuius conquieuerit. Postremo epilogi uice adjciens. Hæc, inquit, ingentia & corporis & animæ periculla, facili subiectione, apud dignissimum Ecclesiæ patrem, qui tuæ animæ curam gerit deuitare potes. Tui igitur pro Christi æterna pietate miserearis. Simulcp tecum cogita, quàm erudite fuerint Lincolnienses, iam præsul, Herfordus, & Purueus. Brituellus quoque uir haud uulgariter peritus, Hi omnes uesanas, & sinistras opiniones reuocarunt, abiurarunt, & reliquerunt. Quin ergo uel horum, qui tanto te doctiodoctiores sunt, exemplo, in Ecclesiæ communionem recipere. Post hæc alius Archiepiscopi Sacrificus, Guilielmo persuasus, sese ab Herfordo audivisse refert, quòd maiorem populi nunc seriat gratiam, magisque in hæreticos iam incitatus sit, quam antea uerit tuendis eorum opinionibus blectatus. Addit-que Maluerenu Sia ccerfito sacerdote peccata exoneres, subeasque poenitentiam tibi à Domino Archiepiscopo præscriptam, non dubium, quin animum brui confirmatiorem persentias. Guilielmus. Si homines quatuor (quos mihi imitandos proponitis) honores, diuitias, & seculi luxum, contemplissent, Christi et Apostolorum simplicitate contenti, mihi alijsque fuissent in Christianæ pietatis exempla, sed quoniam veritate Dei sprei, hæc omnia, non sine multorum scandalo, sunt ample xi, ut nocentes Ecclesiæ pestes illos respuo, in animo firmiter statuens in hac uia Cain deinceps non abire, neque in receptione mercedis, qua deceptus est Balaam, sed neque in contradictione Chorae cum illis qui perierunt: ne & Dei in mudum uindictam provocem. Primu ob Christianę ueritatis assertionem plurimū per antichristos uexati sunt, nunc contra iuramentis obstricti, Christū ijdem persequūtur. Quocirca quan tumlibet doctrinam eorum praedicetis, haud quemquam ex nostris ea permouebit, imo multo magis nos confirmabit in doctrina fidei, cum sciamus sine Dei spiritu nihil esse humanæ eruditionis bracteas. Tum Archiepiscopus suis praecipit ne am plius ei consulant. Confoederati sunt, inquit, ne obedientiam Ecclesiae aut praesulibus praestent. Nam ex quo ad fenestram hic steterim, socius illius e carcere nuncium misit, se in uerba nostra omnino non iuraturum, quin & huic hoc idefuafit adolescentulo. Fecistis enim pro utili uestra, ut & hunc adductum Iuuenem in nassam uestram pellicetis (de illo enim loquitur qui nuncium adferebat) sed propositো quo excidistis. Nam et flens uestras reliquit imposituras, uos uestrique similes execrans, & Ecclesiae totu se subijciens. Re uera tot mortibus dignus es, quot simplices, dogmatibus exitiosis, seduxeris. Illuc igitur perduceris, ubi Herfordus, & Purueus pro simili cruciabantur malo. Nec despero quin aliu adhuc breui te inueniam. Experiar ibi, si potero, te tam tristem reddere, quam laetus eras in meo, ab Anglia, decessit. Per sanctum Thomam, tibi conuertetur in luctum? Guilielmus. De exilio tuo (ut ingenue fateor) non perinde exultabam, uerum de mea, per Londinensem, e carcere liberatione laetabar plurimum. Archiepiscopus. Ignorum tibi est cur Angliam exierim. Sed id ut scias uelim quod in hoc me reduxerit Deus, ut te cum tua secta deleam. Nec prius desi-stam (mihi crede) quo ad Angliam ita repurgem his factionibus, ut ne ueftigiolum quidem uestri, in hoc regno maneat. Guilihelmus, Di-cebat olim fatidicus Hieremias, ad pseudoprophetam Ananiam. Cum impleta fuerit prophetae praedictio, tunc re ipsa scietur, quod miserite-um Dominus. Frendens uero Ar-chiepiscopus, huc atque illuc se exa-gitat, dicens, Ferro mox ita te onu-stum dabo, ut uocem hanc breui mu-tare gaudeas. Haecatque alia in e-um uociferans Archiepiscopus, u-bi iam satis fanius, & scurrilibus di-cteriis hominem modestissimum pro libidine perstrinxisset, clam ad-uocato ad se sacrifico introduci iuf-sit custodem castri Saltuuodensis. Sub haec continuo irrumpunt laici complures, multa in eum ut olim Iudei in Christum minantes. Quidam instabant ut quamprimum combureretur: Alii ut mari, quod prope erat, submergeretur. In hoc panico rusticorum & sacerdotum tumultu, exortus quidam e medio sacrificulus procumbit in genua, flagitás ab Archiepiscopo, ut pro matutinis dicendis, liceat in Guilihelmo hoc operam ac diligentiam suam paululum experiri. Audeo, inquit, in me recipere, infra triduum hoc futurum, ut nihil suo praesuli sit negaturus. At pergit nihilominus bilis Archiepiscopi non dum satis decocta, ebullire, minitantis, se prospe\u00adturum ita ut dignum esset illo. Interea adueniens Castrarius Archiepiscopum adit, postquam tractata collo\u00adquia quaedam, iussu Archiepiscopi Guilielmus educit foras, qui et statim est denuo per Cantuarien\u00adsem reuocatus. Pergit adhuc sacrificus ab eo contendere, ut sese submitteret, quippe sic consultius fore quam si obstinatus decederet. Guilielmus archiepiscopo. Saepius hodie a me testatum est non solum velle me subiici divinis legibus, sed & cuique Ecclesiae membro, quod capiti Christo, doctrina & moribus non adversatur. Per hos enim admoneri & castigari, & instituì cuperem. Archiepiscopus. Praesagiebam quod nusquam sine his conditionibus se subderet impius. Deinceps obiurgationibus, scommatibus, probris, illusionibus, & minis impetitus, omnino stetit immobilis, ac tacuit. Et post pusillum interrogabat Archiepiscopus. Num vellet sanctae Ecclesiae ordinationes agnoscere. Guilielmus. Libenter, ea quam dixi, ratione. Alioqui non est consilium. Tunc Archiepiscopus Castrario in praeceptis dat, ut eum quam celer
units.tr: ...he shows the remedy against [illegible] vices and against all the assaults of demons, without which there is neither tranquillity of life nor attainment of the divine will. Archbishop: I do not refuse. William: Whatever you command according to this doctrine, relying on the help of God, I will undertake, even at the risk of my life. Archbishop: Then submit yourself to the ordinances of the Church, which I am about to explain to you. William: You know that Christ is the head of the Church, and I profess that I will obey whatever decrees of his and of his Apostles they have laid down. Then the Archbishop, striking the table with a huge hand, bursts out with great feeling: "By the Lord Jesus, unless you consent without any quibbling, I will have you thrown into prison, so tightly bound that no robber or murderer was ever more closely confined. So think carefully about what you decide to do." With these words he withdraws to the window, in tragic fashion, like a satrap. Meanwhile Malverne, joined by another priest, attacks the man, now with flattery, now with threats. First he sets out how grievous the punishments are that he must endure; then he magnifies degradation, curses, public infamy, burning, and finally damnation to hell, unless the man calms down in time. At last, adding what amounts to a summing-up: "These great dangers to body and soul you can avoid by easy submission before the most worthy father of the Church, who takes care of your soul. Have pity on yourself, for the eternal mercy of Christ. Consider too how learned the men of Lincoln were: the former bishop Herford, and Purvey. Brinton also, a man of no common learning. All of these recanted their mad and sinister opinions, abjured them and gave them up. Why not, then, at least by the example of men far more learned than you, receive yourself into the communion of the Church?" After this, another priest of the Archbishop's household, who had been won over by William, reports that he heard from Herford that the Archbishop now seeks the favour of the people more eagerly, and is more roused against heretics than he once was when he delighted in defending their opinions. He adds that Malverne says: "Confess your sins to a priest, and undergo the penance prescribed for you by the Lord Archbishop; no doubt you will then feel your mind more confirmed." William: If those four men whom you propose for me to imitate had despised honours, riches and worldly luxury, content with the simplicity of Christ and the Apostles, they would have been examples of Christian piety for me and for others. But since they have spurned the truth of God, all these things, not without scandal to many, have been ample [...]. I therefore reject those harmful plagues of the Church, firmly resolving in my mind not to go further in the way of Cain, nor in the reward for which Balaam was deceived, nor in the rebellion of Korah along with those who perished, lest I provoke the vengeance of God upon the world. First, on account of their assertion of Christian truth, they were much harassed by the antichrists; now, bound by oaths, the same men persecute Christ. Therefore, however much you preach their doctrine, it will move none of ours; rather it will confirm us far more in the doctrine of faith, since we know that without the Spirit of God, the gold leaf of human learning is nothing. Then the Archbishop orders his men to consult with him no further. "They have conspired," he says, "not to render obedience to the Church or to its prelates. For since I have been standing at this window, his companion has sent word from the prison that he will not swear to our terms at all, and indeed he has persuaded this young man too. You have done this for your own advantage, to lure the young man you have led into your net (for he is speaking of the one who brought the message), but your purpose has gone astray. For he has left your snares in tears, cursing you and those like you, and has submitted himself wholly to the Church. Truly you deserve as many deaths as the simple people whom you have led astray by your pernicious doctrines. So you will be taken to the place where Herford and Purvey were tormented for a similar evil. Nor do I despair that I shall soon find another such. There I will try, if I can, to make you as sad as you were glad at my departure from England. By St Thomas, will it be turned to mourning for you?" William: Concerning your exile (as I frankly confess) I did not rejoice in the same way, but over my own release from prison, through the Londoner, I rejoiced greatly. Archbishop: You do not know why I left England. But I want you to know that God has brought me back for this, to destroy you and your sect. Nor will I stop (believe me) until I have so purged England of these factions that not even a trace of you remains in this kingdom. William: The prophet Jeremiah once said to the false prophet Hananiah: when the prophet's prediction is fulfilled, then it will be known in fact that the Lord truly sent him. The Archbishop, gnashing his teeth, rages hither and thither: "Soon I will load you with iron so heavily that you will be glad to change this tune before long." Shouting these and other threats, and after he had sufficiently raged and assailed this most modest man with scurrilous taunts as he pleased, he secretly summoned the priest to him and ordered the warden of Saltwood Castle to be brought in. At this, many laymen rush in at once, threatening him much as the Jews once threatened Christ. Some urged that he be burned at once; others that he be drowned in the sea, which was nearby. In the midst of this panic-stricken uproar of peasants and priests, a certain little priest from the crowd falls on his knees and begs the Archbishop that, for the saying of matins, he may be allowed to try his own zeal and diligence a little on William. "I dare," he says, "to undertake that within three days this will be done, so that he will deny his prelate nothing." Yet the Archbishop's bile, not yet sufficiently boiled down, keeps seething, threatening that he would see to it that William was treated as he deserved. Meanwhile the warden of the castle arrives and approaches the Archbishop; after some discussion, by the Archbishop's order, William is led out, but he is at once called back again by the man from Canterbury. The priest still presses him to submit, since it would be wiser to do so than to leave obstinate. William to the Archbishop: It has often been declared by me today that I wish to be subject not only to the divine laws but also to every member of the Church, provided it is not opposed to Christ the head in doctrine and morals. For I desire to be admonished, rebuked and taught by them. Archbishop: I foresaw that the impious man would submit to no conditions. Then, assailed with rebukes, taunts, reproaches, mockery and threats, he stood entirely unmoved and held his peace. After a little while the Archbishop asked whether he was willing to acknowledge the ordinances of the holy Church. William: Willingly, in the sense I have stated; otherwise there is no agreement. Then the Archbishop gives orders to the warden that he should lead him away from there as quickly as possible.

units.la: Patientia Christiana. celerrime secum inde duceret. Perductus ergo ad carcerem foetoribus & immunditiis refertum, ac ignotum gratias egit Deo, non solum quod esset ab impietate eorum modo liberatus, sed etiam quod nec blanditiis, nec minis, contra Christi gloriam, eis in aliquo consensisset. In omnibus enim Archiepiscopi, & suorum sacerdotum persuasionibus Antichristianis aduersabatur in hoc tam longo certamine, & haec apud se in carcere orabat. Domine Deus, ad nominis tui gloriam, facnos in tua veritate unanimes, & quo celerius hoc fiat, ex animo deprecor, ut omnes qui haec, aut alia mea scripta uel legerint uel audierint, mecum, te eundem immortalem Deum invocent, & in fide nihil haec sitantes postulent, ut ineffabilis tua bonitas, mortalibus ris pie quoque concedat ne deinceps suae in tua domo strina salutis aduersentur. Sed in Christiana pace nobis uniti perfecta fide, spe, & charitate tibi felicius uiuant. Amen.
units.tr: Christian patience. Brought therefore to the prison, which was full of stench and filth, and to an unfamiliar place, he gave thanks to God, not only that he had been freed from their impiety, but also that neither by flattery nor by threats had he consented to them in anything against the glory of Christ. For throughout this long struggle he had opposed the Antichristian persuasions of the Archbishop and his priests in every respect, and in prison he prayed to himself thus: "Lord God, for the glory of your name, make us one in your truth. And that this may come about the sooner, I earnestly pray that all who have read or heard these or my other writings may call upon you, the same immortal God, with me, and that, asking in faith without wavering, they may obtain from your ineffable goodness that you graciously grant to mortals that they no longer oppose its salvation in your house. But may they live more happily for you, united with us in Christian peace, in perfect faith, hope and charity. Amen."

units.la: Post haec, testamentu animae suae ultimum aedidit, in cuius calce post admonitiones tum Christianas, tu pias, animam suam commendauit Domino, & corpus suum tortoribus cruciandu, ubicunq; aut quocunq; cruciatu Domino uideretur. Votisq; omnibus rogabat uniuersam credentium Ecclesiam, ut pro se misero, iamq; a mundo reiecto homine fideliter orent, quo gratiam, ac sapientiam e superius habeat, utq; Christi ueritate ad finem usq; perseuerans, sacrificium acceptum fiat Domino in odorem suauitatis, ad nominis sui gloriam, & Ecclesiae Christianae aedificationem. Amen.
units.tr: After this, he published the last testament of his soul, at the end of which, after Christian admonitions and pious words, he commended his soul to the Lord and gave his body to the torturers to be tormented, however and wherever it should please the Lord. And with all his prayers he asked the whole congregation of believers to pray faithfully for him, a wretched man now cast out by the world, that he might have grace and wisdom from above, and that, persevering to the end in the truth of Christ, he might be an acceptable sacrifice to the Lord for a sweet savour, to the glory of his name and the edification of the Christian Church. Amen.

units.la: Sunt qui testentur eum eodem anno Domini 1407 in Augusto exustum, sed locum non designant, ex quo, atque aliis quibusdam indicijs
units.tr: There are those who testify that he was burned in the same year of the Lord 1407, in August, but they do not name the place. From this, and from certain other indications,

units.la: cijs colligi poterit, quod in priuato carcere sit, uel fame, uel aliis, per tortores, supplicijs, Archiepiscopi consilio mulctatus, quod uerisimilius est.
units.tr: it can be gathered that he was kept in a private prison and worn down by hunger or by other torments inflicted by the torturers, on the counsel of the Archbishop, which is the more likely.

units.la: Anno 1447 Ioan. Maior libro sexto historiae nostrae plurimos extitisse tradit, qui pro haereticis iudicati sunt. Atque ex his qui constantiores inquit inuenti sunt, conflagrarunt. Verum quae causa nominaq; exustorum fuerant, certum adhuc non liquet.
units.tr: In the year 1447, John Major, in the sixth book of our history, reports that there were very many who were judged to be heretics. And, he says, of those who were found the more steadfast, they were burned. But what the cause and names of those who were burned were, is still not clear.

units.la: HISTORIA REGINALDI PECOCKI Episcopi Cicestrensis ob pietatem ac professionem Euangelij per pseudoepiscopos afflicti, ac post recantatas opiniones in carcere tandem extincti.
units.tr: THE HISTORY OF REGINALD PECOCK, Bishop of Chichester, who was persecuted by the pseudo-bishops for his piety and for his profession of the Gospel, and at last died in prison after recanting his opinions.

units.la: NEC MIRUM SI TANTOPERE in plebcios sacrificulos, horum grassata sit tyrannis, cum nec Episcopos ipsos, iam mitra, ac infulas tutos reddit. Vsque adeo nullum est conditionis, nec ordinis genus, in quo no aliqui fructus, ceu ex uinea botri, Deo suppullulant. Atque de sacerdotibus, de monachis, horumque fratribus, de laicis, de militibus, aulicisque, supra a nobis relatum. Restat adhuc unus Episcoporum ordo ἀκαρπώσος, tardaeque hactenus steriIitatis. Quanquam nec dubium, quin hic etiam suas habebat reliquias Dominus, quae non flexerunt genua ad Baal. Quemadmodum olim & Pharisaicus populus, suos Nicodemos, ac Gamalielos peperit, etsi perquam rarae hae aues extiterint, pauciores scilicet, metu periculi rerumque inopia, palam ausi sunt id profiteri, quod sentiebant. Inter caeteros unum producemus Pecokum Episcopum primum Ceftriae, deinde tituIo sancti assi, si quisquam tamen sanctus fuit istiusmodi. Hic postquam fcin-
units.tr: It is no wonder that the tyranny has raged so fiercely against the common priests, since it does not spare even the bishops themselves, safe as they are in their mitres and insignia. There is no rank or order of men in which some fruit does not sprout up for God, like grapes from a vine. We have already reported this of priests, monks and their brothers, of laymen, soldiers and courtiers. One order remains, that of the bishops, which has been unfruitful [ἀκαρπώσος] and barren until now. Yet there is no doubt that the Lord had his remnant here too, who did not bow the knee to Baal. Just as the Pharisaic people once bore their Nicodemuses and Gamaliels, though these birds were exceedingly rare, and fewer still, since they dared to profess openly what they felt, for fear of danger and for lack of means. Among the rest we shall bring forward Bishop Pecock, first of Chichester, then (in title) of St Asaph, if indeed any such man was holy.

units.la: [Text is partly garbled in the scan; some letters are uncertain.] scintillas aliquot sincerioris pietatis in animi sui uenas percepisset, tamen si nihil magnopere molitus est contra episcopos, in hac temporum perturbatione sibi quantum licuit consulens, non potuit tamen ita latere, quin tandem deprehenderetur.
units.tr: Although he had perceived some sparks of purer piety in the veins of his mind, and although he undertook nothing very much against the bishops, consulting his own safety as far as he could in this turmoil of the times, he could not remain so hidden that he was at last detected.

units.la: Tot isti notas, tot oculos, tot suspiciones habet, ut nihil tam minutum, esse queat, quod istos fallat. Nulla dignitatis tanta eminentia, ad quam non saeua audacia tyrannide isti irrumpunt, ut iam non uulgo tantum, sed & regibus incipiant esse formidabiles. Deprehensus itaque Pecokus obtorto collo labetum trahitur, praesidebat tum sacerdotum primas, Thomas Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis, Fit confluxus Doctorum, ac Episcoporum in Archiepiscopi Basileam. Aderat una in cofessu Dux Buckingamiae, Episcopo Roffensi, ac Lincolniensi comitatus. Impingitur Pecocko praeter alios articulos, praesentia panis in sacramento. Sic quod in maximum Ecclesiae solatium, ac iucundissimę concordię fœdus a Christo conparatum est, nescio quo pacto Satanæ invidia in materia gravissimæ inter Christianos dissensionis est uersum. Vt haud alia ferè res perniciosior, tot iam seculis, durauit Christia norũ salutì, quàm unde summũ humanæ uitæ, ac cõsolationis mutuę semina peti conueniebat. Quid enim illa corporis sanguinisq; dominici communicatio nobis denunciat, nisi primũ illius, in nos beneficij, tũ nostrę in illo coniunctionis symbolum. Quòd corpus illius semel fractũ, quasi omnibus, singulisq; nobis distributũ, ac donatum sit, ex pane intelligimus uiritim communicato. Similiter quod sanguis semel pro nobis effusus sit, nõ pro se solũ, sed veluti cuctis mortalibus ad salutè impensus, id patera declarat, per omnes sigillatim obambulans. Tum ne quis du= dubitet ociosam esse illā passionem, quin sola hęc in omnibus, quotquot credūt, credeturiue sint, mortalibus operetur absoluta pacē, ac æternam refectione animę, nimis iā longa inedia cōtabescentis, idcirco in huiusce rei figurā panis simul cum potu coniūctus, propositus est. Quibus in ex ternū homine acceptis, facile intelli gitur, quid in interna anima nostra efficiat corporis illius sacrificiū, fide nobis applicatū. Fide enim sacrificiū hoc applicandum est, si uelimus esse utile. Cibus enim ni recipiatur nullā parit alimoniam, itaque iussi sumus comedere. Ita ubi fides non accipit Christum, nulla est uitæ spes, nec requies animæ. Corpus, pane sumpto, uegetatur ad externam uitā, quanq; nec solus panis sine potu ita multū ualet. Nec aliter Christi corpus sanguisq; est ceu cibus quidā, sed mystī cus ac spiritualis, quo non corpora pascūtur, sed pars nostri spiritualis.
units.tr: Those men have so many marks, so many eyes and so many suspicions, that nothing is so small that it can escape them. There is no dignity so lofty that they do not burst into it with savage audacity and tyranny, so that they now begin to be feared not only by the common people but by kings as well. Pecock was therefore seized and dragged along by the neck. Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, then presided over the primate of the clergy, and a gathering of doctors and bishops came together at the archbishop's. The Duke of Buckingham was present at the meeting, accompanied by the bishops of Rochester and Lincoln. Besides other articles, Pecock was charged with the presence of the bread in the sacrament. Thus that which Christ provided for the greatest comfort of the Church and for the most pleasant covenant of concord has somehow, through the envy of Satan, been turned into a matter of the most grievous dissension among Christians. Scarcely any other thing, for so many centuries, has been more destructive to the welfare of Christians, when the seeds of the highest good and mutual consolation of human life ought to have been sought from it. For what does that communion of the Lord's body and blood declare to us, except first a symbol of his benefit toward us, and then of our union with him? That his body, once broken, was distributed and given, as it were to all and to each of us, we understand from the bread shared out to each person. Likewise, that his blood was once poured out for us, not for himself alone but as if offered for all mortals, the cup declares, passing round to each one in turn. Then, lest anyone doubt that this passion is idle, and that this alone works in all mortals, whoever believe or shall believe, perfect peace and eternal refreshment of the soul, which has already long wasted away from hunger, therefore bread joined with drink has been set forth as a figure of this thing. When these are received by the outward man, it is easily understood what the sacrifice of that body, applied to us by faith, effects in our inner soul. For this sacrifice must be applied by faith if we wish it to be profitable. Food, unless it is taken in, produces no nourishment; therefore we have been bidden to eat. So where faith does not receive Christ, there is no hope of life and no rest for the soul. The body, when bread is taken, is strengthened for outward life, though bread alone without drink does not avail so much. Nor is the body and blood of Christ otherwise a kind of food, but a mystical and spiritual one, by which bodies are not fed but the spiritual part of us.

units.la: Corporea enim corporeis conueniunt, Spiritualia spiritualibus. Dico autem cibum hûc spiritualem, quia quod cibus corporeus in corporea efficiat uegetatione, idem Christus efficit in anima spirituali, id est, pascit, reficit, uegetat, exhilarat, suffulcit & ad uitam sternam restaurat, pacem conciliat irrequietę conscien tię, patrem offensum reconciliat, peccati famem sedat, succum praestat coelestis gratię. Deniq; quicquid habet energiæ externus cibus in uisibili corpore, similem praestat uirtm Dei filius in inuisibili nostri parte, sed fide apprehensus. Vt non absurde cibus sit ille appellatus in scripturis mysticis, ubi sic prophetat Dominus. Nisi manducaueritis carnem Filij hominis, & biberitis eius sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. ubi non uerba, sed uerborum analogia respicienda est, sic ut Filius Dei sit cibus, fides uero nostra sit os & uenter. ter. Id quo pacto accipiendum est, iam olim in Iudaeis est ostensum qui in lege operibus ꝯ iustitiae salutem quaerentes, idcirco exciderunt, quia aliis cibis distenti, non manducaue-runt carnem in Filij hominis, id est non crediderunt in Christum hūc. Idem Turcis eueniet quantumcūꝯ in le-ge operatibus, quemadmodum nec nobis, in alia re ulla, constabit salutis firmitas, nisi in Christum solum cre-dentibus. Porro multa sunt ciborum genera, sed unicus est qui uitam pro-ducit immortalem. Habent Iudaei sua obsonia insipidae literae, quae ad hucarrodūt. Habent & Turcae suas insulsas betas, hinc inde collectas. Sed quae nihil quam distendunt ui scera nihil pariūt uitalis succi. Quin & nos paulo minus iudaizantes ha-bemus nostra fercula uariē ex mul-tis rituum, traditionum, superstitio-num, ac opusculorum leguminibus consarcinata. Hic multum fidit lon-gin= ginquis peregrinationibus, Ille domi deuotus est in statuas, Alius multum donat altari sacro, ac ædificadis templis, Alter sumit uestem sacram in qua tutus sibi uidetur à dæmonibus. Est qui multum sibi pollicetur ex frequentatis subinde missis. Iam quantum pręsidij plærîsq; statuitur, in emptitijs diplomatibus in criminum apud sacerdotem confessionem. Atq; ut hæ lactucæ nusquàm leguntur in conclusis hortis scripturarum: Ita sunt alia ad scripturas, proprius qui dem illa, accedetia, quæ tamen, cum nihil aliud sint, quàm unius cibi huius codimenta, sultè pro cibis ipsis arripiuntur à plerisque, cuiusmodi sunt ieiunia, orationes, uigiliæ, eleemosynæ, charitatis officia cæteraq; legis opuscula, quæ in loco ac pro conDimetis adhibita, reddùt quidè sapo resuû, At unicus est duntaxat cibus, qui manducantibus efficax sit ad uitam, Caro nimirum Christi Iesu, cuius mandu
units.tr: For bodily things belong to bodily things, and spiritual things to spiritual things. I call this food spiritual because what bodily food effects in the bodily growth, Christ himself effects in the spiritual soul: that is, he feeds, restores, strengthens, gladdens, sustains and restores to eternal life; he brings peace to the restless conscience, reconciles the offended Father, quells the hunger of sin, and supplies the juice of heavenly grace. In short, whatever energy outward food has in the visible body, the Son of God provides a similar power in the invisible part of us, but only when it is grasped by faith. Hence that food is not absurdly called in the mystical Scriptures, where the Lord prophesies thus: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you" [John 6:53]. Here we must regard not the words alone but the analogy of the words, so that the Son of God is the food, and our faith is the mouth and the stomach. How this is to be understood was shown long ago in the Jews, who, seeking salvation by works of the law and by works of righteousness, therefore fell away, because, puffed up with other foods, they did not eat the flesh of the Son of man, that is, they did not believe in this Christ. The same will happen to the Turks, however much they work at the law, just as firmness of salvation in any other thing will not stand for us, unless we believe in Christ alone. Moreover there are many kinds of food, but only one is that which produces immortal life. The Jews have their dainties, the insipid letters, which they chew even until now. The Turks too have their insipid beets, gathered here and there, which fill the belly but produce no vital juice at all. Indeed we also, though a little less Judaizing, have our own dishes variously stitched together from the pulses of many rites, traditions, superstitions and little works. One trusts much in distant pilgrimages, another devotes himself at home to statues, another gives much to the sacred altar and to building churches, another puts on sacred vestments, in which he thinks himself safe from demons. Some promise themselves much from frequently attended masses. As for how much protection is set up for most people in bought indulgences and in the confession of sins to a priest... And just as these lettuces are never gathered in the enclosed gardens of the Scriptures, so there are other things that come closer to the Scriptures, which indeed are nearer, but since they are nothing but the seasonings of this one food, they are eagerly seized by many in place of the food itself: such as fasts, prayers, vigils, almsgiving, the offices of charity, and the other little works of the law, which, when used in place of and as condiments, indeed give a certain flavour.

units.la: (Text ends mid-sentence; continues on the following page.) manducatio, si allegoriā interpretari uolumus, est fides nostra apprehendens Christū. Quę sola nos, sine omni adminiculo, & una iustificat, hæc ubi non ad fuerit peccatū est, stercus est, pānus mēstruatus est, quicquid agit hominum sanctimonia, stultitia est, quicquid molitur humana sapientia. Denique nulla re alia leuari potuit infelix animæ esuriēs, nisi cœlesti hoc pabulo, postquā è cœlo affulsit Christus, qui pro nobis delibatus est, morte sua pacificās omnia. Quisquis erant quæcunq; nobis ante porrigebant hominū traditiones. Adhibita sunt multa studia bonorū operū, quibus quisq; conatus est famē mitigare, sed nugæ erat, quicquid humanis uis, quicqd huius mūdi elementa ostendebat. Saucia erat ipsa anima, sibi medelam præstare nequibat, alio indigebat medicina. Profunda erat sitis, quæ redimi potuit, expleri non potuit. Sanguine rigari potuit, aliquis nullo humano liquore sedabilis,
units.tr: But there is only one food that is effective for those who eat it, unto life: the flesh of Christ Jesus, whose eating, if we want to interpret it allegorically, is our faith laying hold of Christ. This alone, without any aid, justifies us, and where it is absent, sin is dung, and the sanctity of men is folly, and whatever human wisdom devises is a menstrual rag. In short, the unhappy hunger of the soul could be relieved by no other thing than this heavenly fare, after Christ, who was tasted for us, shone forth from heaven, making all things at peace by his death. Whatever traditions of men offered us before, many efforts at good works were applied, by which each tried to lessen his hunger, but whatever human strength and whatever the elements of this world showed was trifling. The soul itself was wounded and could not provide itself a cure; it needed another medicine. The thirst was deep; it could be redeemed but could not be satisfied. It could be watered with blood, but it was something that no human liquid could quench.

units.la: Vnde non inappositè sese escam, ac sanguinem suum uere potum appel labat Dominus, non quòd ita habet res, iuxta sensum externū, sed ut sub hoc sacramenti inuolucro declaret, quid fides nostra in illum efficeret.
units.tr: Hence the Lord not unsuitably called his flesh food and his blood true drink. This is not because the thing is so according to outward sense, but to declare under this covering of the sacrament what our faith effects in him.

units.la: Tu fortasse in Christū credis, dicisque, pro te mortuum esse. Vis ergo quid mors illius in te efficiat cernere? Accedis ad cœnam hanc: principio, panis tibi ac uinum proponitur, quæ in corpus tuū abeunt. Quorsum id? Quorsum, nisi ut te nutriant, idcirco enim iuberis accipere, & comedere. Quid tu ubi comederis? Sanè si nihil aliud hic ageretur, haud ita multū inesset rei, nūc uero quum hæc non nuda tibi elementa, sed sub nomine ac memoria dominici corporis ac sanguinis proponūtur, sub esse in hoc, mysterii aliquid puta, quòd te admonere possit. Quid nā? Quid putes, nisi ut hinc quasi in si-gillo uideas, quid corpus ac sanguis Domini pro te effusus, agat, in ua anima. Nimirum, id ipsum, quod panis ille, & potus agat in externo corpore. Ideo enim panis & vinum accipiunt, corporis, ac sanguinis illius appellationem, ut ex altero, alterius vis ac operatio facile intelligatur: non ut idem sit panis, secundum sui substantiam, quod corpus Christi, sed ut virtutes ac effectus utriusque componentes, ex pane illo admoneamur, quid id sit, cuius memoriam in pane peragimus. Differunt ergo omnino panis Christusque in substantiae praedicamento: In qualitate, virtuteque quadamtenus convenient. Nam si in pane, vera corporis substantia offerretur ventri, iam non memoria ageretur mortis illius, sed mors ipsa Christi. Nunc omnis istorum est error duntaxat in praedicamento, dum qualitate pro substantia accipiunt. Dumque vim ipsam ac mysterium passionis ipsius mini Y
units.tr: Perhaps you believe in Christ and say that he died for you. Do you want to see, then, what his death effects in you? You come to this supper. At the outset, bread and wine are set before you, and these pass into your body. To what end? To what end, unless to nourish you? For this reason you are commanded to take and eat. What do you do when you have eaten? Surely, if nothing else were done here, there would be not much in the matter. But now, since these are set before you not as bare elements but under the name and memory of the Lord's body and blood, consider that some mystery lies hidden in this, which can remind you of something. What, then? What do you think, except that from this you may see, as in a seal, what the body and blood of the Lord, poured out for you, do in your soul? Surely the very thing that bread and drink do in the outward body. Bread and wine receive the name of that body and blood so that from the one the power and operation of the other may be easily understood. Not that the bread is, in its substance, the same as the body of Christ, but that by that bread we may be reminded of the virtues and effects of each, and of what it is whose memory we celebrate in the bread. Bread and Christ therefore differ wholly in the category of substance; in quality and virtue they agree to some extent. For if the true substance of the body were offered to the stomach in the bread, the act would no longer be a memory of his death, but his death itself. Now the whole error of these men lies only in the category, since they take quality for substance; and while they do not at all examine the power and mystery of his passion itself,

units.la: Y mè perscrutantur, sólùmodo in corpus ipsum affixi, sed quis uigor huius sit, mortis ac operatio, prętereun tes, (in quo tamè hic omnis uertitur cardo) in altero haud perinde multū fructus uel cōtemplantibus, uel contrectantibus excipitur. Afferamus huc ueteris scripturæ figuras, prĕsertim has, quę ad memoriam cōparatę sunt. Apud Aegyptios iussus est populus, in ipsa liberationis nocte, agnū mactare, qui nō dubiū, quin Christū uenturū præsignaret. At quo pacto præsignaret? Secundū substantiam aliquā? Nequaquam. Nemo enim agnū esse Christū dixerit. Verum secundum qualitates, ac proprierates quasdā, ideoq; anniculū, atq; immaculatū iussi sunt accipere. Quid autē agno simplicius? Quid immaculato purius. Denique quid Christo similius? contra in substantia, quid dissimilius? Idem dici potest de uacca reliquisq; Hebræorū uictimis, quibus
units.tr: but fix their attention only on the body itself, passing over what the force and operation of that death is (and yet on this the whole matter here turns), they receive in the other, not in the same measure, much fruit, whether by contemplating or by handling. Let us bring forward here the figures of the old Scripture, especially those which were designed to be a memory. Among the Egyptians the people were commanded, on the very night of their deliverance, to slay a lamb, which without doubt foreshadowed that Christ would come. But in what way did it foreshadow him? According to some substance? By no means. For no one would say that the lamb is Christ. Rather, according to certain qualities and properties; and so they were commanded to take a yearling, and an unblemished one. And what is simpler than a lamb? What is purer than the unblemished? Finally, what is more like Christ? On the other hand, in substance, what is more unlike? The same can be said of the heifer and the other Hebrew victims, by which Christ was announced, aptly indeed according to the marks, yet while their substance was far from agreeing.

units.la: Christus denunciabatur, secundum notas quidē apte, cum tamē substantia eorū longe repugnabat. Et cur in ijs tum sacramentis, tantopere quaerimus substantię conuenientia, cum ea haud multū ad rē attineat? Neque enim mysterium in materia ipsa latet, sed multo magis in occultioribus quibusdam rerū notis, quibus panis et corpus Christi, uinū & sanguis, sibi mutua analogia respondentinuicem. Quā analogiam dum secū consideret Christiana mēs, hinc magnā fidei cōfirmatione, simul et cōscientię consolatione cōsequi necesse est, præsertim ijs qui afflicto sunt spiritu & laborant onerati. Quid enim huiusmodi pectori dulcius aut plausibilius esse potest, cē ubi nō creditur solum, sed etiam uidet quasi ante oculos expressum, gratis condonari peccata omnia, longam inediam, ceu in communio expleri, famem in saturitatem verti, consilescere omnes mores
units.tr: And why, in those sacraments of the time, do we so eagerly seek agreement of substance, when that matters little? For the mystery lies not in the material itself, but much more in certain more hidden marks of things, by which the bread and the body of Christ, the wine and the blood, correspond to one another by a mutual analogy. When the Christian mind considers this analogy, it must of necessity draw from it great confirmation of faith and at the same time consolation of conscience, especially for those who are of a troubled spirit and labour burdened. For what can be sweeter or more pleasing to such a heart than to see set forth, as it were before the eyes, not only to believe, that all sins are freely forgiven, that long hunger is, as it were, satisfied in fullness, that famine is turned into satiety, that all the tumults of the mind grow calm,

units.la: Visus ac fidei nis cœnæ dominicæ dentis animi tumultus, cedere om‑nem damnationis formidinem, succedere firmissimā salutis spem, seque iam laetissima pace frui cū Deo suo, idque non ratione aliqua suorum meritorū, non ex suis laboribus aut exantlaris operibus, nō sitantum ieiunauerit, tot orationū modios impleuerit, non ex hac aut illa corporis sui laesione, non si hoc colore uestitus, uel in hac religione uersatus sit, sed gratis per solam in Christum fidem, qui factus est redemptio pro peccatis nostris, ut is solus merito sit panis uitę nostrę appellatus. Alioqui si alia essent praeter Christū ad salutem adminicula, iam nō is esset solus panis vitae. Atqui hic panis ut gratuitus est, qui de caelo descendit donatus nobis, ita unicus est, nec alia reli‑quit obsonia, quamuis alia obsonia requirūt panem. Tantū uides (Christianae lector) in hac morte coelestis potentiae, quae etsi sit inuisibilis, nec uideuideri possit carneis sensibus, utcunque tamen notari, uel saltem figurari potuit. Nullo autem pacto, tam re conditum mysterium, uel aptius exprimere, uel expressius figurare potuit Dominus, quàm in hoc tam sensibili sacramenti genere. Quid enim familiarius orbi quàm panis & potus quotidianus, quibus continua necessitate uita humana redintegratur, & quid ipsdem propius accedit ad tam inenarrabilis mysterii expressionem, certè si uires ac proprietates non substantiam contemplemur? Ex quo, non sine graui causa, panem & potum porrexit Dominus, quae pro suo corpore ac sanguine ne suscipieremus. Non ex ulla adeo in rebus ipsis necessitate, sed hac ratione cōsulens tarditati nostrae, quae haud aliter solet quàm sensibus oculisque duci, quo sic uel fidem nostram fortius confirmatam, uel consolationem in illo pleniorem certioremque redderet. Et unde in moribus Christianis tanta peruersitas, ut sibi ipsis tantam infelicitatem inuidentes, id nunc in exitij laqueum conuertunt, quod unicæ consolationis loco nobis à Domino est traditū. A Græcis olim eucharistia dicebatur huius communionis celebratio, in qua ipsi salutis beneficiū acciperent à Domino, Dominus uicissim ab ipsis gratiarū Vitulos acciperet. At quæ nūc ist æ sunt gratiæ, aut charites, ubi pro salute nostra à Domino accepta, nos fratrem perdimus, sanguinemq; illius effundimus, quem ipse sanguine redemit suo, idq; non ex alia occasione, nisi ex ea, quæ omnem clementiam erga homines nos docere debuit. Defendēda est doctrinę puritas, fateor. Sed quæ est hæc defensio, ubi primū homines occidimus, deinde an uera causa sit & certa, in synodis, in parlamentis, in Academijs, in diatribis disquirimus, & ad huc sub iudice lis est. Non meruit Dauid manus extruendo Dei templo admoliri, quod é multis prælijs, ac strage hominum cruentus uenerat, quamuis & eadem iustissima prælia, nec sine numine præscripta suscepserat tamen hoc negotium Salomoni perficiendum, qui totus pacificus succedebat, relinquebatur. Ita fingamus & hic causam esse veram certamque. Donemus quod nondum probari poterit, verba Christi inambiguum habere sensum. Attamen multum mea opinione interest, qua Christiani principes suam administratione, sacri isti Ecclesiæ dominicæ architecti, lenitate, suâ tractent. Videndum cæque ne quod in illis sit licitum, id nō perinde in hisprobetur Domino. Quot ante Pecokum istum, quot post eius morte, à cruentis episcopis absorbti sunt. An, uera causa, nō hic disquiro. Imo sit uerissima, attamen referat id, mea quidem sententia permultum, quibus manibus ad sacra Dei Ecclesiā erigendā accedatur. Vt interim hic, cū iniqua, quamcū falsa sit causa ipsa, nihil dicā. Sed redeo ad Pecokum, de quo tamē nec omnia sum cōmemoraturus. Longa est iniuria, longæ ambages. Sed summa sequar falsigia rerū. Intentatis ergo illi articulis, postquā dirū illud hæreseos nomē catholico episcopo impresserunt, mox ad iudicia propera-tum est. Hę sunt enim nūc Christianorū inter se dissertationes. Si quid usquam oboritur Ecclesiasticæ controuersiæ, uel de scripturæ sensu sor-tis ambiguo agitur, in tribunalia statim uertitur quod cōtrouertitur. Ingenia amiserūt libertatē suā. Scho-lę in prętorea immutātur, ubi nō spe-ctatur uter uincat: sed uter uiuat. Pro antagonista sedet lictor, pro stilo stringitur gladius, qui demū sæpe in-cidit non in deteriorē, sed inferiorē. At quæ hic in dicendis sententiis esse libertas potest, ubi alterius ante ora uersatur mors, in altero, etsi ratione uincatur, uincit tamen potentia. Immensum quantum à ueteris Ecclesiae uestigijs recessimus his temporibus Christiani. Quae unquam haeresEon feracior aetas quàm in qua uixit Hieronymus, ut ne hic commemorem quanto in grauioribus dogmatiis laborabat Ecclesia. Neqp tamen ad hac iudiciorum seueritatem exigebantur, si qui à reliquis dissentiebant, quippe nec opus erat. Doctorum libris, prodití, uexatiqp sunt errores, in quibus tacitus lector iudicium ferret, quid in utraqp parte consentaneum, quid secus foret. Quoties ad scripta, ad epistolas, ad apologias, quasi ad harenam aduersarios suos, aequo, ac aperto marte prouocat Hieronymus, nec sibi erepi ferés libertatem, nec aliis eripiens? Nolo, inquit, mihi ille, aut ille respondeat, qui me potentia obruere potest, docere nō potest. Nec minus hoc nomi ne tamen ualuit ille in explodendis opinionū periculis, imo multo fœli-cius, simul & ijs satisfaciens qui con-tendebant, & reliquos confirmans si qui fluctuabant. Quantulū iam Hel-uidius, Iouinianus, Pelagius, feredis suis opinionibus, proficere ualue-runt, emergentibus semel ac lectis Hieronymi, tanto cum nitore elima-tis uoluminibus: Quæ tam late graf-fata hæresis, non ilico, ceu adempta uoce, obticuit, semel in theatrum pro-deunte Augustino, uel fulminante in Ecclesijs Hieronymo, in libris nō minus fere formidabili, quàm qui-uis est in foro iudex? Sed nunc litera-rias has uelitationes amisimus, imo ut uerius dicam, amisimus in Eccle-sia proceres, Augustino, ac Hiero-nymo similes, qui stylo, ac eloquētia uelitari sciant, in quorum subijt ui-cem posteritas talis, quæ defendit plerunq̃, quę iudicare nequeat, me-raq̃ raꝗ potentia cum libris nō licet, rem aggrediatur. Et tamen ad horū illitteratam legem, doctis nunc uelint, non lint, loquendū est, aut Pecoki huius periculo tacere discant. Quo pacto enim hunc, num libris expugnāt maiorum exemplo, num eloquentia de ꝯiciunt, num stilo confodiunt, num argumentis pungunt, ac ἐπισομίζωσι, nū ingenio, ac iudicio obruūt, num pedem, pedi, ut inquit Hieronymus conferentes erroris latebras producunt, nū productas reuincunt, homi niꝗ ipsi quantumuis renitenti uicto riam extorquent. Deniqꝫ silentiū uel rubore potius illi imponūt, sic rationū retinaculis stringentes undiqꝫ, ut ne hiscere quidem cōtra, non solum nō audeat, sed nec possit etiā si uellet maxime? Atqꝫ huiusmodi praesidijs, in tali causa grassandū erat, si essent uiri docti. Si docti nō sint, cur praeficiuntur tractandis Ecclesiꝫ controuersijs, cur luscieti de coloribus iudiciū perspermittitur? Si falsum erat, quod su-stinuit Pecokus, nullum erat periculū, quin facile supploderetur ex thea-tro, si idoneis argumentis illi occur-risset doctus aliquis artifex, qui cau-sæ bonitatem eruditionis dexteritate, ac uigore scripturarū superiorem reddere potuisset, qualesq; maiorū temporibus, errores solebant conuel-lere. Nūc uero ita exi-stimari potest. Apud hos aut ueritati defuisse ido-neos doctosq; uindices, qui pares es-sent gerēdo negotio, aut imbecillē, nimisq; suspectā ṛjs ipsis uideri cau-sam, in qua non audebant, æqua di-micationis libertate periclitari, sed ad iudicia, ceu ad unicam arcē con-fugere, ubi non acumine, non libris, sed metu, ac autoritate facile est, qua-uis doctissimos disertissimosq; mi-nimo puluere opprimere. Pertra-ctus itaq; ante iudices, & præsides Pecokus, tametsi nequicquam labo-rat, multa tamē egregio digna theo-logo logo praestat, pro causa pariter ac uita tuenda omnibus se munit armis. Contra illi pro dignitate ac quaestu, pari sudore, certant, hocq; enixius, obiecto nunc isto sibi aduersario, cuius autoritas, quanto esset sublimior in Ecclesia, hoc graviorem suae tyrannidis ruinam tracturus uideba-tur apud populum. Id metuentes illi, quasi read triarios redacta, iam omni utendum apparatu, quantasq; possent maxime explicandas sibi uires existimabant. Accersuntur exquisitissimae argutiae, sophistae, philosophi, theologi, oratores. Nec desunt iurisconsulti ac decretistarum centuriones, quorum in his rebus usus est maximus, primum priuatis colloquijs tentata res, mox terribilis iudicij forma statuitur, praesentesq; uiro intentant omnia morte. His terricu-lamentis adijciuntur uerborum minae, exhortationes, expostulationes. Nec desunt frequenter illicibiles propromissionum blanditiae, ceu circeo veneficio illita pocula, denique nul lus lapis immotus relinquitur. Orant, mouet, fatigant, postulant, supplicant, minantur, promittunt, blandiuntur, concedunt insuper consultandi ac resipiscendi tempus, in quo mortis dilatio uitam redderet suauiorem. Iubet sibi mature consulat, abunde magnam superesse uitae spe, ac dignitatis etiam, si repudium his faceret opinionibus. Breuiter nunquam desistunt fascinatrices linguae, impellere, suadereque, orare usque adeo donec tandem uictus ab episcopis labascit episcopi animus. Paratur ilico palinodia ab episcopis obtrusa, quam populo caneret, quamquam ita tamen canens, ut nihilo secius, in carcerem iterum reductus sit, unde eximi non poterat, nisi suprema morte liberatus.
units.tr: By the sight and faith of the Lord's Supper, the tumult of the mind is calmed, all dread of damnation gives way, the firmest hope of salvation takes its place, and he now enjoys the most joyful peace with his God. This happens not by any reckoning of his own merits, not through his labours or the works he has performed, not because he has fasted or filled up so many measures of prayers, not through this or that mutilation of his body, not because he is clothed in this or that colour or lives in this or that religious order, but freely, through faith alone in Christ, who became our redemption for our sins, so that he alone is rightly called the bread of life. Otherwise, if there were other aids to salvation besides Christ, he would no longer be the only bread of life. Yet this bread, as it is free, descending from heaven and given to us, is also unique, and it leaves no other food, although other foods require bread. You see, Christian reader, that in this death the heavenly power, which is invisible and cannot be seen by carnal senses, has nonetheless been in some measure marked, or at least figured. Nor could the Lord have expressed or figured this mystery, so hidden in its reality, more fittingly or more clearly than in this most sensible kind of sacrament. For what is more familiar to the world than daily bread and drink, by which human life is renewed by constant necessity? And what comes closer to the expression of so ineffable a mystery, if indeed we consider their powers and properties rather than their substance? For this reason the Lord offered bread and drink, to be received in place of his body and blood, and not because of any necessity in the things themselves, but by this method, taking account of our slowness, which is usually led by nothing but the senses and the eyes, so that he might make our faith more strongly confirmed, or the consolation in it fuller and more certain. And whence comes such perversity in Christian morals, that, begrudging themselves so great a happiness, they now turn into a snare of destruction that which was given to us by the Lord in place of the one consolation? Formerly the celebration of this communion was called by the Greeks eucharistia [εὐχαριστία], in which they would receive the benefit of salvation from the Lord, and in turn the Lord would receive from them the calves of thanksgiving. But what thanks [χάριτες] are these now, when, having received salvation from the Lord, we destroy our brother and pour out the blood of him whom he redeemed with his own blood, and this for no other occasion than that which ought to have taught us all clemency towards men? I admit that the purity of doctrine must be defended. But what sort of defence is this, where we first kill men, and only afterwards inquire, in synods, in parliaments, in academies, in disputations, whether the cause is true and certain, while the case is still before the judge? David did not deserve to lay hands on the building of God's temple, since he had come back bloodied from many battles and the slaughter of men, although he had undertaken those same most just wars, not without the will of God prescribed; the task was left to Solomon, who succeeded him as a man wholly of peace. So let us suppose that here too the cause is true and certain. Let us grant what cannot yet be proved, that the words of Christ have an unambiguous sense. Yet in my opinion it matters greatly how Christian princes, those sacred architects of the Lord's Church, conduct themselves in their administration with gentleness. Care must also be taken that what is permitted in those men is not equally disapproved by the Lord in these. How many were swallowed up by bloodthirsty bishops before this Pecock, and how many after his death! Whether the cause is true I do not here inquire. Let it be most true; still, in my judgement it makes a very great difference with what hands one sets about raising up the sacred church of God. Meanwhile I will say nothing here of how unjust the cause itself is, however false it may be. But I return to Pecock, though I shall not recount all of his story. The wrong is long and the windings are long, so I shall follow the chief points of the matter. Therefore, after the articles were brought against him, and after they had branded the dreadful name of heresy upon a Catholic bishop, they hurried at once to judgement. For such now are the disputes of Christians among themselves.
