units.la: quicquid congregatio fidelium dicit, uel docet, uel quod remissio peccatorum dicit uerum &c. quod non est dicendum. Nam ideo poneba- tur in symbolo scilicet, Credo sanctam Ecclesiam catholicam, id est, unam generalem Ecclesiam esse sposam Christi, propter haereticos qui dicunt extra Ecclesiam non est remissio peccatorum, nec saluatio: cuius ecclesiae fides est fundamentum.
units.tr: whatever the congregation of the faithful says or teaches, or that the remission of sins says true," etc., which is not to be said. For it was therefore placed in the creed, namely, "I believe the holy Catholic Church," that is, that the one general Church is the spouse of Christ, against the heretics who say that outside the Church there is no remission of sins nor salvation. The faith of this Church is the foundation.

units.la: 9 Item est opinabilis fides, qua habemus ex communi lege Dei, dum huiusmodi sumus, de quibus ad Corinthios 13. Videmus nunc per speculum in aenigmate. Alia fides est scientialis, quę non cursorie habetur hic, sed in coelo, de qua loquitur ad hebraeos 11. Fides est substantia rerum sperandarum &c.
units.tr: 9 Likewise there is opinable faith, which we have by the common law of God while we are such as those of whom it is said (1 Cor. 13): "We now see through a glass, in a riddle." Another faith is scientific, which is not had here in passing, but in heaven, of which he speaks (Heb. 11): "Faith is the substance of things hoped for," etc.

units.la: 10 Item quod ad Gregorij dictum Fides non habet meritum, ubi humana ratio praebet experimentum. Di co quod sancti uiri aliquando deficiunt. unt. Ideo si scripta eorum possunt improbari, non sunt tenenda. In disciplinis Gregorij, sunt diversi defectus, quia implicant quod quaedam fides est quae habetur per experientiam, quae est contra eum, in eadem homelia. Quia uidisti me Thoma, & non credidisti, ubi dicit quod fides non habetur aperte, & secure cognoscitur. Igitur primum dictum suum, & ultimum non simul starent. Si quis dixerit, quod Gregorius in illis verbis, Fides non habet meritum, intellexit, quod ista cognitio genita per experientiam, nec est fides, nec est meritum. (quia eidem est praetentio eorūdem uerborum, quam uocant cognitionem, cui humana ratio praebet experientiam esse fidem) aliter se quereretur, quod loquebatur ipsa uerba indiscrete.
units.tr: 10 Likewise, as to Gregory's saying, "Faith has no merit where human reason affords experiment," I say that holy men sometimes fail. Therefore, if their writings can be disproved, they are not to be held. In Gregory's teaching there are various defects, since they imply that a certain faith is had through experience. This is against him in the same homily: "Because you have seen me, Thomas, and have not believed," where he says that faith is not had openly and is not known securely. Therefore his first statement and his last would not stand together. If someone should say that Gregory, in those words, "Faith has no merit," meant that this knowledge produced by experience is neither faith nor merit (because the same words are used for what they call knowledge, to which human reason affords experience, and this is faith), otherwise it would be complained that he spoke the words indiscreetly.

units.la: Item dicere quod cognitio geniτ ca super ueritate, per securam experientiam non habet meritū, est tertius defectus, quia non cognoscere id per securam experientiam, est uicio sum. Igitur cognoscere est meritorium, quia uirtuti semper uicium contrarium est, & contra.
units.tr: Likewise, to say that knowledge produced about truth through secure experience has no merit is a third defect, because not to know that through secure experience is a vice. Therefore to know is meritorious, since the contrary vice is always opposed to virtue, and conversely.

units.la: Item homo non debet habere meritum pro fide, nisi habeat euidentiam, ad sic credendum, quia aliter nō scit, quod sic deberet credere magis, quàm contrarium.
units.tr: Likewise, a man ought not to have merit for faith unless he has evidence for believing thus, since otherwise he does not know that he ought to believe thus rather than the contrary.

units.la: Equidem uideri possim nimis fortasse importune legendis istis, abutier otio tuo (pie lector) præsertim quū obsoleta hæc barbarici seculi monumenta tam parum ad rem præsente conducere uideantur, attamen antiquitatem ipsam annotandam existimaui, quo, superiores seculi, aliquæ saltem reliquiæ nobis superessent, quas (si opus sit) his in hos regeramus, qui calumniantur Doctrinam hanc nouam esse, quæcp omni antiquitate, careat. Verū isti, si aperiant oculos, facile perspicient, uel exijs nonnihil, uel ex alijs multo potius, quam longo temporis spacio, uiac tyrannide supplosa ueritas, non incoepit modo, sed erupit tandem. nō à nobis nata, sed à maioribus, ab episcopis, a Regibus etiam, ac primarijs doctissimisque uiris tradita, quod mihi difficile non erat demonstrare si superius à trecentis, aut quadringentis annis ante Vuicleuum historiae huius deductionem protrahere libuisset. Verum malui à Vuicleuo potius telam hanc exordiri, non quòd exempla superiora defuissent, sed ob uitandam infinitam rerum prolixitatem. Quanquam nec ea quidem pars posthac fortassis a nobis (aspirante Christi gratia) sua opportunitate negligetur.
units.tr: I may perhaps seem to be imposing too much on your leisure, kind reader, by publishing these things, especially since these obsolete monuments of a barbarous age seem to bear so little on the present matter. Yet I judged that the antiquity itself should be recorded, so that, if anything of the earlier centuries survived, at least some remnants would be left to us, which (if need be) we might throw back at those who complain that this new doctrine is new and lacks all antiquity. But if they open their eyes, they will easily perceive that the truth, not only begun but at length burst forth, after a long lapse of time and the suppression of tyranny in part, and in part far more fully, was not born among us but handed down by our forebears: by bishops, by kings even, and by leading and most learned men. This would not have been difficult for me to demonstrate, had I wished to draw the account of this history back three or four hundred years before Wycliffe. But I preferred to begin this web from Wycliffe, not because earlier examples were lacking, but to avoid an endless prolixity of matters. Yet, with Christ's grace breathing upon us, that part too will perhaps not be neglected by us in its proper time hereafter.

units.la: Interim habes hic (lector Christiane) priorem huius historiolae seriem, à Millesimo trecentesimo ad quingentesimum, qualicumque peni cillo nostro deliniatam, in qua si ob tumultuariam nimis festinationem, non satis uidebimur functi officio nostro: Aliud nihil respondeo, quā Socraticum illud ex Xenophonte, præstitisse me κατὰ δύναμιν. Neque enim in aliena patria exulanti suppe tebat ad manum parata librorum ac Registrorum copia, unde plenius ista desumerentur. Rursus nec am plius bimestri spacio ante nundinas Francfordianas mihi concedebatur ad hæc ex rudi ac informi syluula re colligenda, digerenda, rescribenda, ac componenda etiam pleraq;, præ-ter quotidianas insuper formularū typographicarum castigationes, ut nihil interim dicam de ualetudine, quæ tam inidonea omnibus gerendis munijs reddebatur, ut nulla spes esset, hanc qualemcumq; laboris no stri fœtura, uel ad dimidiatum par-tum prouehendi, nisi natura superi-or, Potentia Christi fractissimas uiri-culas
units.tr: Meanwhile, kind reader, you have here the earlier series of this little history, from the year 1300 to 1500, sketched with whatever poor pencil we have. If, owing to my hurried and somewhat disorderly haste, I seem not to have discharged my task adequately, I can answer only with that Socratic saying from Xenophon, that I have done what was in my power [κατὰ δύναμιν]. For, an exile in a foreign land, I had no ready supply of books and registers at hand from which these things might be drawn more fully. Nor was I granted more than two months before the Frankfurt fair to gather, digest, rewrite and even compose most of this from a rude and shapeless little wood of material, besides the daily corrections of the printer's forms. Not to mention my health, which was so unfit for carrying out all these duties that there was no hope of bringing this product of our labour, however it turned out, even to a half-finished birth, unless God's higher nature and the power of Christ had until now sustained our very weak little strengths, in his mercy, to whom alone every knee shall bow. Amen.

units.la: [Note: the words "culas" at the foot are the catchword.] culas hucusque nostras sustinuisset pro misericordia sua, cui soli cadat omne genu. Amen. Restat nunc altera huius narrationis complectio, videlicet a D. Martini Lutheri, uenerandae memoriae, Euangelistae, temporibus, ac deinceps. Sed hoc initium esse uolui alterius libri, quem nunc (συν τῳ χείσῳ) aggrediemur, tantoque aggrediemur alacrius (amice lector) si priorem hanc partem, comiter plausibiliterque tibi acceptu iri persensero. Rogemus ac amemus mutuum, in Christo Domino nostro, cui sit uni omnis gratia ac gloria. Amen.
units.tr: The rest of this narrative now remains, namely the times of Dr. Martin Luther, evangelist of venerable memory, and those that followed. But I wanted this to be only the beginning of another book, which we shall now take up (with God's help), and we shall take it up the more eagerly, dear reader, if I perceive that this first part will be received by you kindly and with favour. Let us love and pray for one another, in our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom alone be all grace and glory. Amen.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.

units.la: Hi sunt qui uenerunt ex magna afflictione, & dilauauerunt stolas suas, & dealbauerunt eas per sanguinem agni. Ideo sunt ante thronum Dei, & seruiunt ei die ac nocte in templo eius, & qui sedet in throno, habitabit super illos, &c.
units.tr: These are they who came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne shall dwell among them, etc.

units.la: AD OXONIENSES.
units.tr: To the Oxonians.

units.la: CIO SI QVID REActe in humanis rebus geratur, nulla esse hominis peculiarem, propriamq; laudem, at unius duntaxat Dei: A quo, ceu perenni fonte, universa haec, in nobis, recte agendi tum facultas, tum voluntas proficiscitur. Attamen quoniam uel organa ipsa plerunq;, ac instrumenta, per quae opes, in nos, suas transfundit Deus, amplecti ac magnificare consueuimus: Equidem inter caeteras Christianae Reip. scholas, nō in postremo humanae commendationis loco Academiā uestram (Oxonienses) collocandā duxerim. Vnde tot tantaq; bona, orbi Christiano, peperit caelestis prouidentia. Quanquam haec (ut dixi, iterumq; admoneo) nō loco, sed diuina benignitate metienda sunt. Neq; enim tanto pere refert, quid quo loco accipimus, sed quid hoc ipsum sit, quantaq; rei magnitudo spectandum est. Quis satis reputando aestimare poterit immensam, ac ineffabilem huius beneficii eij uim, quam nuper in propaganda euangelij lu ce, quaqua uersum omnes experti sumus. Quot erant in mundo conscientiæ, inopia diuinæ conso lationis contabescentes? Quot animæ peccatis saucia, dolore squallentes, falsis Episcoporum lar uis seductæ, desperatione deiectæ, metu gehennæ perterrefactæ, itemq; alijs alijsq; modis afflictæ? Breuiter carnificinam quandam bonorum Sa= tan exercuit in mundo. In tantis malis, hominu manus haud quicquam potuit. Prorsus diuino erat opus artificio. Sane nec desuit rebus despera tis diuina philantropia. Siquidem post diutinas humanæ inscitiæ miserias, cœpit tandem postli= minio Euangelici uigoris scintillula ἀναπνοή ζωῆς. Moxq; ex paruis initijs, uicina correpta materia, latius se sparsit incendium. Donec oc= cultis quibusdam uenis permeans, iamq; huma= na extinctione superior, flamma ἀσβέστος, uni= uersum demum Reipub. Christianæ corpus, salu tari ardore, corripuit. Ibi ilico concalescere con scientiæ, mentes hominum reuiuiscere, frontes exporrigi, longa inedia pene absumpta corpo= ris membra refici, desperatio in spem conuerti, luctus in lætitiam abire, tot iam annos inuetera= ta pontificum tyrannis labescere. Autoritas frangi, bullæ cum ampullis euanescere. Postremò mutata rerum facies, prorsusq; noua quædam in scenam huius mundi actio induci coepit. Amplissima profectò diuinæ pietatis in nos collocata munera, quæ non modo gratias nostras, sed & omnem cogitationis sensum exuperat. Quapropter quum tota huius beneficij laus ad Deum unicè spectat, nihil habet humana hic iactantia, quod ab illo non acceptum, sibi vendicet. Ettamen quoniam in huiusmodi acceptis beneficijs, quæ per se eximia ac immensa sunt, nõ solum rerum ipsarum pondus, sed & locum ipsum nonnunquam, ubi accipiuntur, notare solemus: Id si nunc quærimus ubi primum, obductus tam diu Euangelicæ doctrinæ vigor reuiuiscere, sesecq; proferre coepit, eam profectò esse Oxoniam vestram fateri necesse est. Nam vtcunq; nunc, ubiq; apud omnes ecclesias, recepta efflorescat Euangelij professio, certè prima huius initia haud aliunde quàm à vobis profluxerunt. Hic enim iacta sementis est, unde veluti ex traduce tot ista diuinæ cognitionis plantaria, per vniuersos fere mortales, nunc propagata cernimus. Hic enim salutiferum illud fermentum, à Deo acceptum, quo primum Boëmia, mox Germania, ac vicinæ nationes nationes fermentari coeperunt, donec tandem og culta diuinæ uirtutis efficatia, uniuersa insuper massa Christiani populi correpta est. Agnosci-tis itaq;, Oxonienses, fortunæ ac mnueris uestri fœlicitatem, superest ut pari constantia laudi-bus nunc uestris respondeatis. Diuinæ profecto fœlicitatis fuit, quòd olim religionis dedistis ini-tia, iterumq; mundo Christum ueluti parturi-ret Oxonia uestra. Vobis nunc acceptam, maio-rum uirtute, gloriam hanc exuperare, dignum est: certè non æquare, aut non conseruare uos, quam citra labores accepistis, non tam illis glo-riosum, quàm uobis probrosum fuerit. Quan-tulum enim refert, incœpisse præclarè, nisi ad fi-nem usq; perseuerantes, pulcherrimis incœptis parem Colophonem addideritis. Quod ut facia-tis hoc maiori uobis adnisu contendendum ar-bitror, quo iuxta Demosthenicum illud, scitis τὸ φυλάξαι πολλάκις τ' ἀγαθὰ, τῶ κτήσασθαι χαλεπώτερον ἐστιν. Fuit aliquando Oxo-nia uestra religionis parens, nunc uidendum uobis, ne degeneret in nouercam. Audio enim nuper à uobis Oxoniensibus subscriptum esse, obsoleto illi, ac iam dudum exploso articulo, de transubstantiatione. Quanquam autem mihi non non libet, tam ineptum illud, in uobis temere suspicari, attamen constantior uidetur rumor, quàm ut fide careat. Age & quos tandem causæ huius afflictæ ueritas sibi patronos, aut quod suf fugium inueniet, si uos, qui primi, in hoc certa- mine, πρόμαχοι stetistis, primi nunc in fugam uersi, ripsaspides uideamini? Etsi uero, huiusmo- di sit negotij huius natura, quæ ex æquo commu- nem omnium hominum causam quàm maximè at- tingat, tamen, nescio quo pacto, ad uos, peculiari quadam ratione, proprius quàm ad cæteras Ec- clesias, pertineat: Quippe qui primum in hac scena personæ prodijstis. Quod si igitur Io. Vui- cleuus electissimum Euangelij instaurandi organ- num, simulq; cum eo Oxoniensium complures, ea tempestate, quum omnia adhuc tenebris obnu- bilata, nec usquam per totam Europam auxilia- ru hyperaspistes ullus apparuit, soli tamen ipsi tam fortiter, causam hanc, aduersus hydram il- lam Romanam, sustinere sint ausi: quid uos nunc Oxonienses, post tot domestica exempla, in tanta Euangelij claritudine, denique eo tempore, quum multo maior, certè potior, omnium Ecclesiarum, pars, uelut iunctis fœderibus, eodem coeant, fa- cere conueniet? At fingite nunc Vuicleuum, cæ- terosque terosque (quos schola haec aliquando peperit) fortissimos Christianae militiae satellites, nunc revera uiuiscentes, post tot labores & aerumnas suas, uestram hanc, siue ignauiam, siue inscitiam contemplari, An non stupore quodam correpti grauiter meritoq; uos coarguant. Imo an eandem hanc esse academiam agnoscerent? quae adeo a pristina forma, nescio quam metamorphosin, incuria uestra pati uideatur. Certe qualis, qualis est, ipsi uobis marmoream reliquerunt; uobis ne lateritiam reddatis satagendum est. Si nouum aut inauditum uobis foret hoc dogma, quod tam indignereiciatis, aut nusquam per alias Ecclesias reciperetur, minus hoc in uobis, reprehendendum foret. Nunc tot ante annos in eadem re instituti estis, tot argumentis edocti, Quin insuper tot Martyrum effuso sanguine confirmati, & tamen doctrinae hoc genus, quasi nouum, e schola exploditis, & uetus illud uestrum accidens sine subiecto, publica subscriptione dignamini: Plane iuxta ueterē paræmiam, Coccyx enim (ut aiunt) non mutat suos modos. Verum quoniam temporis antiquitate, tantopere inniti uideamini, uetustatis, potius quam ueritatis discipuli: Age, ex bene subducta temporum ratione, uideamus,
units.tr: If anything is done rightly in human affairs, no part of the praise belongs to man himself but to God alone, from whom, as from a perpetual fountain, both the ability and the will to act rightly in us proceed. Yet we are accustomed to embrace and magnify the organs and instruments through which God pours his blessings into us. Indeed, among the other schools of the Christian commonwealth, I would count your University of Oxford (Oxonienses) among the foremost in human esteem. From this school heavenly providence has brought forth so many and such great benefits for the Christian world. Still, as I have said and repeat, these things must be measured not by place but by divine kindness. For it matters little where we receive something; what matters is what the thing itself is and how great its importance is. Who could sufficiently weigh the immense and inexpressible power of this benefit, which we have all experienced everywhere in the recent spreading of the light of the gospel? How many consciences were there in the world wasting away for lack of divine consolation? How many souls, wounded by sin, squalid with grief, led astray by the false bark of the bishops, cast down into despair, terrified by fear of hell, and afflicted in other ways besides? In brief, the servants of Satan carried on a kind of slaughter in the world. In such great evils human hands could do nothing. The work was entirely of divine craft. Certainly divine philanthropy did not fail in these desperate circumstances. For after long miseries of human ignorance, at last a little spark of evangelical vigour began, by a kind of recall, to breathe life. Soon, from small beginnings, the fire, having caught the nearby material, spread more widely. Until, penetrating by hidden veins and now rising above all human extinguishing, the unquenchable flame at last seized the whole body of the Christian commonwealth with its saving heat. There at once consciences grew warm, men's minds revived, foreheads were raised, limbs long nearly consumed by famine were restored, despair turned into hope, mourning passed into joy, and the tyranny of the popes, so long entrenched for so many years, began to totter. Authority was broken, bulls vanished along with their oil flasks. Finally the face of things was changed, and a quite new kind of drama began to be staged on the stage of this world. These are indeed most ample gifts of divine goodness bestowed upon us, which surpass not only our thanks but every power of thought. Therefore, since the whole praise of this benefit looks solely to God, human boasting here has nothing that it can claim for itself which was not received from him. Yet since in the reception of such benefits, which are in themselves extraordinary and immense, we are accustomed to note not only the weight of the things but sometimes also the place where they are received, if now we ask where the vigour of the evangelical doctrine, so long covered over, first began to revive and show itself, we must surely confess that it was your Oxford. For however the profession of the gospel now flourishes among all churches everywhere, certainly its first beginnings flowed from no other source than from you. Here the seed was sown, from which, as if from a shoot, we now see these plants of divine knowledge propagated among almost all mortals. Here was that saving leaven, received from God, by which first Bohemia, then Germany, and the neighbouring nations began to be leavened, until at last the cultivated efficacy of divine power seized the whole mass of the Christian people. Therefore, Oxonians, since you acknowledge the felicity of your lot and of your gift, it remains for you to answer your praises now with equal constancy. It was surely a matter of divine good fortune that once you gave the beginnings of religion, and that your Oxford, as it were, brought forth Christ again into the world. It is worthy that you should surpass now, by the virtue of your forebears, this glory which you have received; certainly it would be far more disgraceful for you not to equal or preserve what you received without labour than it would be glorious for them. For how little it matters to have begun splendidly, unless you persevere to the end and add a fitting conclusion to your most splendid beginnings. In order to do this, I think you must strive with greater effort, since, as that saying of Demosthenes has it, which you know: "to keep good things secure is often harder than to acquire them" [τὸ φυλάξαι πολλάκις τ' ἀγαθὰ, τῷ κτήσασθαι χαλεπώτερον ἐστιν]. Oxford was once the parent of religion; now you must see to it that she does not degenerate into a stepmother. For I hear that recently some of you Oxonians have subscribed to that obsolete and long-exploded article about transubstantiation. Although I do not care to suspect such a foolish thing of you rashly, the rumour seems too persistent to lack credit. Come now, what patrons will this afflicted cause of truth find, or what refuge will it discover, if you, who stood first as champions in this contest, are now seen to turn first to flight and to be deserters with the shield? And although this kind of business is such that it touches equally the common cause of all men, yet, I know not how, it pertains to you in a certain peculiar way, more closely than to the other churches, since you were the first to come forward on this stage. Indeed, if John Wycliffe, the most excellent instrument for restoring the gospel, together with several Oxonians at that time, when all things were still shrouded in darkness and no helper at all appeared anywhere through the whole of Europe, nevertheless dared to sustain this cause so bravely against that Roman hydra, what should you Oxonians now do, after so many domestic examples, in such a clear shining of the gospel, and above all at a time when a much greater and certainly a stronger part of all the churches, as if bound by joined covenants, is coming together in the same cause? But imagine now that Wycliffe and the others (whom this school once bore), most brave soldiers of Christian warfare, now truly come back to life after their labours and hardships, were to contemplate this your indolence or ignorance, whatever it is: would they not rebuke you gravely and justly, struck with a certain astonishment? Indeed, would they even recognise this as the same academy, which seems to have undergone some strange metamorphosis from its former form through your negligence? Certainly, whatever sort of university it is, they left it to you as marble; you must take care not to turn it back into brick. If this doctrine were new or unheard of to you, the doctrine which you so disdainfully reject, or if it were received nowhere else among the other churches, less blame would attach to you. But now you were instructed on this very matter so many years ago, taught by so many arguments, and moreover confirmed by the shed blood of so many martyrs, and yet you cast out this kind of teaching from your school as if it were new, and you deign to give public subscription to that old accident of yours without a subject. Plainly, according to the old proverb: "the cuckoo, as they say, does not change its tune." But since you seem to lean so much upon antiquity, you being disciples of age rather than of truth, come, let us see by a well-reckoned account of the times,

units.la: quam quàm peruetusta sit, (si mušis placet,) hæc uestra de transubstantiatione, reliquisque traditionibus opinio. Nam si Cornographis fidem adhibeamus, comperte liquet, decretum hoc uestrum de transubstantiatione anno 1215. aut non multo profecto superius incepisse.
units.tr: how very ancient (if the Muses permit) this opinion of yours about transubstantiation and the other traditions is. For if we give credence to the chroniclers, it is clearly established that this decree of yours on transubstantiation began in the year 1215, or not much before.

units.la: Tum enim in concilio Laterano, Eucharistia primum incœpit haberi pro articulo fidei. Nec obstat hic admodum, quòd missarum vestrarum celebritas, prius, per Gregorium secundum, introducta sit anno 713. Tum etenim Missa nec tot adulterata ceremonijs, & sine adoratione, & elevatione peragebatur. Ac ne antiquis testimonijs carere putetis <bl>ἀλλαχοῦ</bl> hanc assertionem nostram, possem hic Fredeuuardum constantissimum huius rei testem adducere an. 891. contra quem scripsit Paschasius uester.
units.tr: For then, in the Council of the Lateran, the Eucharist first began to be held as an article of faith. Nor is it much of an objection here that the celebration of your Masses was introduced earlier, through Gregory II, in the year 713. For at that time the Mass was not yet so corrupted with ceremonies, and was celebrated without adoration and elevation. And so that you may not think our assertion lacks ancient witnesses [ἀλλαχοῦ], I could here adduce Fredeuuardus, a most steadfast witness of this matter, in the year 891, against whom your Paschasius wrote.

units.la: Ut omittam hic interim Berengarium, qui, an. 1049. pontificem Romanum non ueritus est, uocare pulpificem. Idenim temporis superstitio hæc primas agere radices cœpit inter paucos. Nam adhuc publicum decretum de transjubstantiatione non obtrudebatur omnibus.
units.tr: To pass over Berengarius for the moment, who in 1049 did not fear to call the Roman pontiff a "pulpit-monger." For this superstition had only begun to take root among a few people at that time, since the public decree on transubstantiation was not yet being forced upon everyone.

units.la: Autsane si maximam eius antiquitatem res putetis,ultra concilium Versellense, eodem hoc anno celebratum, neutiquam eam referre poteritis:Quanquam, ex eo etiam tempore, Ecclesia nunquam caruit fidelibus ueritatis testibus.
units.tr: Indeed, if you think the doctrine is very ancient, you will by no means be able to trace it back beyond the Council of Verseil, celebrated in this same year. Yet even from that time the Church never lacked faithful witnesses to the truth.

units.la: Quippe non ita multo post,(restrente Caps grauo)Cantuariæ lis orta est non mediocris, An substantia panis maneret in sacramento.
units.tr: Not long afterwards, while Caps was presiding over it, a no small dispute arose at Canterbury over whether the substance of bread remained in the sacrament.

units.la: Nec sane graui autoritate carere dubet Henrici quarti uox,qui Henricum filium, his uerbis admonens,dixisse fertur.Isti te decipiunt, non in struūt,sub specie fidei,perfidiæ laqueos nestunt, dum præceptis diuinis, hominum traditiones præferrunt,anno 1107.
units.tr: Nor, indeed, does the voice of Henry IV lack considerable authority. He is said to have admonished his son Henry with these words: "Those men deceive you, they do not build up; under the appearance of faith they set snares of treachery, while they prefer the traditions of men to the divine precepts." This was in 1107.

units.la: Porro hæc tempora non ita multo post secuti sunt Valdenses e Lugduno cognomento pauperes,an.1155.Quorum dogmata,ut à pluribus tum temporis,recepta fuerant, ita apud nos illustre testimonium habere par est,contra fastum papæ,et abusus sacramentorum.
units.tr: Not long after these times came the Waldenses, named after Lyons, called "the poor," in 1155. Their doctrines, as at that time were received by many, ought to have an illustrious witness among us, against the pomp of the pope and the abuses of the sacraments.

units.la: Antuerpiæ etiam fuisse quosdam, autor est Masseus Matthæus, qui publicè docebant, Eucharistiam non esse Christi corpus, anno 1129.
units.tr: An author, Matthaeus Masseus, tells us that there were also certain people at Antwerp who openly taught that the Eucharist is not the body of Christ, in 1129.

units.la: Quid quod & Otto Frisingensis, Episcopus doctissimus, non obscure testatur, distinct. 11. sentent. Quosdam, suo seculo, extitisse, qui panem in sua substantia manere in Eucharistia senserint, anno 1146.
units.tr: And Otto of Freising, a most learned bishop, clearly testifies in distinction 11 of the Sentences that in his own age some people existed who held that the bread remains in its substance in the Eucharist, in 1146.

units.la: Prætereo interim, Petrum Abelardum pietate non minus, quam senectute venerandum, qui non credidit, in sacramento esse accidens sine subiecto, iuxta uestram hanc mathematicā, an. 1141.
units.tr: I pass over for the moment Peter Abelard, to be revered for his piety no less than for his age, who did not believe that in the sacrament there is an accident without a subject, according to your mathematical doctrine, in 1141.

units.la: Quin & magistros Parisienses huc adiungemus, quibus circa annum 1155. acceptum est uocabulum hoc, esse, pro significare, in uerbis Eucharistiæ. Si. Io. Tissyngtono credimus.
units.tr: Indeed we shall add also the Paris masters, among whom, around the year 1155, the word "esse" was taken to mean "to signify" in the words of the Eucharist. We believe John Tissington in this.

units.la: Accedamus ad annum 1200, quo fere tempore, circa concilium lateranum, centum & quadraginta in Narbonensi dioecesi, pro hæreticis incensi sunt, apud Massæum.
units.tr: Let us come to the year 1200, at about which time, around the Lateran Council, one hundred and forty people in the diocese of Narbonne were burned as heretics, according to Masseus.

units.la: Item Guilielmus Cornelius Antuerpiensis sacerdos post quadriennium a sepultura ad exhumationem repetebatur per Episcopum Cameracensem, anno 1245.
units.tr: Likewise, Guilielmus Cornelius, a priest of Antwerp, four years after his burial was dug up again by the Bishop of Cambrai, in 1245.

units.la: Quin & Begardum pro haeretico audiniamus Erphurdiae igni traditum esse, an. 1218. Sic & Oxoniae Diaconus quidam combustus est, anno 1222. iuxta Treuetum. Nec satis conijcere queo quae res istos ad incendium traheret, nisi de sacramento, uisi sunt sentire aliquid, aut docere quod non placebat omnibus.
units.tr: Indeed, let us hear that a Beghard was handed over to the fire at Erfurt as a heretic in 1218. Likewise a certain deacon was burned at Oxford in 1222, according to Trevet. Nor can I conjecture what would have drawn those men to the fire, unless they seemed to think or teach something about the sacrament that did not please everyone.

units.la: Accedamus nunc ad Vuicleui tempora propius. Quippe an. 1246. historicorum monumentis proditum est, Sueuiae praedicatores pontificem Romano restitisse. Nec erat opinor de nihilo, cur Manfredum Siciliae Regem, Alexander quartus excommunicaret, anno 1259.
units.tr: Let us now approach the times of Wycliffe more closely. In 1246, it is recorded in the monuments of the historians, the preachers of Swabia resisted the Roman pontiff. Nor, I suppose, was it without reason that Alexander IV excommunicated Manfred, King of Sicily, in 1259.

units.la: Vt interim Eckardum Dominicanum Heidelbergensem, ac Guilielmum Ockanum praeteremus, qui eadem de re, pro haereticis damnati sunt a papistarum filijs, an. 1330. Ex quo facile uidere licet, quo pacto in Ecclesia semper successionem aliquam bonorum conseruat Deus,
units.tr: To pass over for the moment Eckhard the Dominican of Heidelberg and William Occam, who were condemned as heretics for the same matter by the sons of the Papists in 1330. From this it is easy to see in what manner God always preserves some succession of good men in the Church,

units.la: quam propterea huc ascribere uolui, ut intelli‐gatis, etiam ante Vuicleui tempora, quàm multis antiquissimorũ testimonijs causa hæc innitatur, si quid ipsa tamen ad rem faciat antiquitas. Verum donemus, prorsus hoc nouum esse, attamen prudentes & graues decet uiros, ueritatem non tempore opinor, sed causa ipsa metiri. Alioqui audire illud oportet ex Cypriano. Quippe consuetudo sine ueritate, quid aliud quàm uetustas erroris est? Quamobrem agite tandem (Oxonienses fratres, patres) prudentiam appello uestram, ut cum Cicerone uos moneam, Hæc non numero, sed pondere metiamini. Si antiquitatem spectatis, Vuicleuum tot ante annos habuistis. Si doctrinam, nuper D. Petrum Martyrem, unicum huius ætatis Cratippum, ac theologicæ schole facile principem. Cuius admiranda eruditio, ac relicta monumenta, merito uos permouere possent: nisi cum termino lapide, omnino id dicere statuatis. Nulli cedam. Porro si exempla exigitis. Tot uidetis Ecclesias reformatas, unanimi consensu nobis hac in re suffragari. Aut si domestica uos magis capiant, è Cantabrigia præclarum sane exemplum petere licebit, unde nuper, (ut accepi) uiginti sex cordatissimi pari‐
units.tr: which I wished to cite here so that you may understand that, even before Wycliffe's time, this cause was supported by many most ancient witnesses, if antiquity itself helps the matter at all. But let us grant that this is entirely new. Nevertheless, prudent and serious men ought, I think, to measure truth not by time but by the cause itself. Otherwise we must hear that saying of Cyprian: "For custom without truth is nothing but the antiquity of error." Therefore, come now, Oxford brethren, fathers, I appeal to your prudence, and I advise you, with Cicero, that you measure these things not by number but by weight. If you look to antiquity, you had Wycliffe so many years ago. If to learning, you have lately had Master Peter Martyr, the unique Cratippus of this age and easily the prince of the theological school. His admirable erudition and the writings he left behind ought to move you deservedly, unless you have decided to say the opposite, come what may. I will yield to no one. Moreover, if you demand examples: you see so many reformed Churches agreeing unanimously with us in this matter. Or if domestic examples move you more, it will be right to seek a truly notable example from Cambridge, whence recently (as I have heard) twenty-six most sensible young men likewise emigrated from one college, so that they would not seem to be authors of so unjust a subscription.

units.la: ter adolescentuli, ex unis ædibus emigrarunt, nē tam iniquæ subscriptionis autores uiderentur. Quid ergo, Et uos soli quos cæteris omnibus duces esse par erat in hoc negotio, iam nec comites præbebitis (Oxonienses?) Primi omnium uulnus inflixistis antichristo, & nunc pro antichristo, contra Ecclesiam Dei bellum suscipitis? Quarquam dubium non est quin plerique uestrum ui magis ac impulsu alieno, quam uestro iudicio ducti, tantæ stultitiæ subscribitis. Et fieri posset, ut non publico academiæ consensu res sic acta sit, sed pauci, qui præsunt collegijs, admunctis sibi aliquot ex sententia confœderatis, priuata conspiratione rem inter se tractarint, ubi aliis forsan cordationibus interesse non licuit, alij inuidiæ metu, alij turbarum odio con quiescere maluerunt, nonnulli blanditijs etiam aleti, pedibus magis, quam animo in sententiam concesserunt, atq; ita priuato Syncretismo publica fortasse autoritas prætexitur, quo magis fucus fiat populo. Postremo ubi doctissima pars iam in exilium pulsa mittitur. Quid mirum si domi relicta pars deterior uincat meliorem?
units.tr: What then? Will you alone, Oxford men, whom it was fitting to be leaders above all others in this business, now not even provide companions? Did you first of all inflict the wound on Antichrist, and now do you take up war against the Church of God on behalf of Antichrist? Although there is no doubt that most of you are led to subscribe to such folly more by force and another's push than by your own judgment. And it could be that the matter was not so carried out by the common consent of the university, but that a few who preside over the colleges, with some men of like opinion joined to them, discussed the business among themselves in a private conspiracy, while others, perhaps wise men, were not permitted to take part, others preferred to keep quiet from fear of unpopularity, others from hatred of disturbances, and some, too, won over by flattery, yielded to the opinion with their feet rather than their minds; and so perhaps a public authority is pretended over a private agreement, so that the deception may be greater in the eyes of the people. Finally, when the most learned part has already been driven into exile and sent away, what wonder if the worse part left at home wins over the better?

units.la: Verum utcunque hæc habeant, Quæ hactenus nus gesta sunt tempori imputemus. Nunc aequitas, ac prudentia uestra uideat, quid uos aequum sit facere, quid Christus à uobis efflagitet, quid Ecclesia expectet, quid officium ac maiorum imitatio postulet. Ego quod in me situm erat ne rerum uestrarum tot egregia monumenta iacerent, effeci: Vobis ne laudibus nunc uestris, ac maiorum uirtutibus non satis respondeatis, adniten dum arbitror. Pluribus uobiscum perlubenter agerem (restabant enim multa) sed Typographo adeo properante ad nundinas, vix hæc, unius fere noctis lucubratiuncula, absoluere permitte batur. Gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi studijs uestris aspiret ad gloriam suam, cui sit omnis gloria. per omnes Ecclesias
units.tr: However these things stand, let us ascribe to the times whatever has been done so far. Now let your fairness and prudence consider what it is right for you to do, what Christ demands of you, what the Church expects, what duty and the imitation of your forebears require. As for me, so far as lay in my power, I have seen to it that the many outstanding monuments of your affairs should not lie neglected. I think you should take care not to fall short of your present praises and the virtues of your forebears. I would gladly have dealt with you at greater length, for much remained, but the printer, in such haste for the fair, allowed me scarcely to finish these few lines, the little work of nearly a single night. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ favour your efforts, so that they aim at his glory, to whom be all glory, throughout all the Churches.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.
